## Chapter 20: Mandrakes

The bird brought them up the pipe in less than a minute, and it was a quarter to eleven at night when they tumbled out onto the floor of Moaning Myrtle's bathroom in a heap.

Harry would remember very little of the next hour in the right order.

He remembered Myrtle hovering over the sinks with her hands over her mouth, both disappointed and delighted at once.

"Oh. Oh, you're *alive*."

He remembered Ginny sitting on the wet floor with her knees drawn up, and Lockhart lying on his side on the tiles with his eyes shut, very grey, and the bird perched on the cistern of the end cubicle, quite still, glowing a little in the dark.

He remembered going to the door, opening it and shouting.

He didn't remember what he shouted. Flitwick said afterwards that it had brought half the staff up from the second-floor corridor at a run.

Madam Pomfrey came first.

She went straight past Harry to Lockhart, knelt on the wet tiles and laid her hands flat on his back, and Harry read her. She was very calm, and beneath the calm, she was frightened, quite badly, in the plain, practical way of somebody who had just found out how bad something was.

"Don't move him," she ordered to nobody in particular. "Nobody move him. Filius, I want a stretcher and I want it flat. Rigid. Do you understand me? Not a sling. Rigid."

"Poppy, dear lady," Lockhart murmured without opening his eyes. "How lovely. I was hoping it would be you."

"Be quiet, Gilderoy."

"Yes, Poppy."

They carried him away very slowly on a stretcher that Flitwick had made from the door of the end cubicle, with Madam Pomfrey walking at its head and her hand on Lockhart's shoulder.

Then Professor McGonagall was standing in front of him.

She looked at Ginny, then at the sword and the Hat and the black wreck of the diary, and at the blood and ink on his robes. Her face didn't change at all.

Harry read her.

Relief surged through her so fast and so large that it filled her to the top. It was the biggest single feeling he had ever felt in Professor McGonagall, and she didn't let one ounce of it reach her face.

"Both of you," she said. "With me. Now."

* * *

The Headmaster's office was full of people.

Mrs Weasley was in a chair by the fire, crying, with Mr Weasley standing behind her and his hand on her shoulder. Percy Weasley stood by the window, very straight, with his badge on, looking at nothing. Fred and George sat side by side on the floor against the wall with their knees up, identical. Ron stood alone in the middle of the carpet.

And Dumbledore was there.

He was standing by the mantelpiece in the midnight-blue robes Harry had last seen in a gamekeeper's hut, with his hands folded in front of him. He looked up as the door opened, and the bird swept in over Harry's head and went to its perch beside him.

Mrs Weasley saw Ginny.

She made a single, short, enormous sound, and then she was out of the chair and across the room with Ginny in her arms. Mr Weasley was there too with his arms round both of them, and Ron was there, and the twins were up off the floor, and for a while it was all Weasleys, all of them talking at once.

"Gin, Gin, Gin," Fred kept saying.

"Let her breathe, Mum, let her *breathe*," George pleaded.

Percy had come away from the window and was standing at the edge of them with his hands at his sides, saying nothing at all, and he had taken off his glasses.

Harry stood by the door.

He read them, and it was very loud, eight people, all of it pointed at one small, wet girl in the middle. It was love and relief and fear that hadn't finished being fear yet, and a great deal of crying. It was so warm that it hurt to stand near.

He didn't go closer.

Then Ginny said something into her mother's shoulder that Harry didn't hear, and Mrs Weasley lifted her head and looked at him over Ginny's hair.

He read her.

She was looking at a boy in a green tie, filthy, with a sword under his arm, whom she had last seen across a platform at King's Cross and hadn't looked at twice. And all of that great, warm, loud thing, the whole of it that had been pointed at Ginny, turned in her the way a lamp turned, and came across the room at him.

Harry didn't move.

He didn't know what to do with it. Nobody had ever pointed a feeling that size at him. Nobody had ever pointed a feeling that size at him and meant it kindly.

Mrs Weasley let go of Ginny, came across the carpet and put her arms round him.

She smelled of wool and somebody else's kitchen. She held on to him very hard, sword and all, saying something into the top of his head that he couldn't hear, because he was reading it, and what he was reading was so loud and so warm and so entirely for him that for a moment there was nothing in the room at all but that.

He stood very still inside it.

He didn't put his arms round her, but he didn't move away either.

* * *

It was Dumbledore who asked him to tell it.

He did it gently, once Mrs Weasley had let go and gone back to Ginny and Professor McGonagall had sat down rather suddenly in a chair by the desk. He asked Harry to sit, and Harry sat and laid the sword and the Hat and the diary on the desk in front of him, and he told it.

He told them about the sink and the roof and the girl on the floor, and the boy who was a memory of himself at sixteen, and the snake, the bird and the sword.

He didn't tell them that he had found the diary in January.

He didn't tell them about six weeks of nights behind the green curtains, nor about the charms, nor about a freckled boy on the stairs. The whole time, he waited for somebody to ask how he had known what the diary was.

Nobody asked.

Ginny was sitting on her mother's knee by the fire with a blanket round her and her face very white. She had been there in the Chamber. She knew. She had heard Harry tell her on the wet floor that he'd had it for six weeks, and she kept quiet.

Harry read her and found that she was still frightened, and enormously ashamed, and that beneath both, very small and very fierce, was something else. She was keeping it for him. She had decided to, and she was doing it, and she wasn't going to stop.

Harry looked at the desk.

"Thank you, Harry," Dumbledore said when he had finished. "That was very clearly told."

He had the diary in his hand and was turning it over slowly, looking at the hole burned through the middle of it.

"Tom Riddle. I taught him, you know. Fifty years ago. Transfiguration. He was the cleverest student I ever had, and I did not like him, and I was ashamed of not liking him, which was a mistake," he said, putting the diary down. "I should have liked to know how he did this. I think I should not like it at all, when I find out."

He looked at Ginny.

"Miss Weasley will go to the hospital wing. Now, I think, and for some days. Nobody is to say a word to her about rules, or the walls, or anything else that has happened this year. Tom Riddle took in a great many people who were three times her age and ought to have known better."

He looked over his spectacles at Mr Weasley.

"He took in a Headmaster of this school, once, and very nearly everybody else."

* * *

Lucius Malfoy came at ten past twelve.

Harry heard him on the stairs, and he knew who it was before the door opened, because he had felt that triumph once before in a gamekeeper's hut. It wasn't triumph now.

It was fury.

The door flew open. Lucius Malfoy came in out of the dark with his black travelling cloak swinging and his silver-handled cane in his hand, and behind him, small and bent and running to keep up, came Dobby.

Dobby was wearing a filthy pillowcase, and his hands were bandaged.

Harry read him.

He was terrified. He was always terrified. Beneath the terror was the old, grinding grey misery Harry had first felt in Dudley's second bedroom, the same as it had always been. Tonight, though, there was something else in Dobby, small and wild, and when he saw the diary on the desk, it went up in him like a firework.

Dobby didn't speak. He looked at Harry, then at the diary and back at Harry. Then he pointed very fast at the diary and at Lucius Malfoy's back, and hit himself on the head with his fist.

Harry looked at him.

"Dumbledore," Lucius Malfoy said. "You have come back."

He said it to Dumbledore without looking at anybody else in the room, not the Weasleys nor McGonagall nor Harry. He looked at Dumbledore by the mantelpiece, and his voice was very smooth, and Harry felt the fury beneath it, cold and enormous and squeezed down very small.

"I have," Dumbledore replied.

"The Board of Governors suspended you."

"Yes," Dumbledore agreed without moving from the mantelpiece. "The Board wrote to me again at about nine o'clock this evening. Eleven of them did, as it happens, separately, and all within about twenty minutes of each other. They had heard that Arthur Weasley's daughter had been taken. And several of them seemed to remember the afternoon on which they signed the order a little differently from the way you remember it."

He smiled very slightly.

"One of them mentioned his grandchildren. I thought that rather touching."

Lucius didn't answer.

Harry read him. The fury had gone white, the colour of a fire burning very hot, and all of it was pointed at Dumbledore, and it wasn't going to go out.

"And the attacker?" Lucius asked. "Have you caught him?"

"We have," Dumbledore replied. "Harry did."

Lucius Malfoy looked at Harry for the first time.

"The same person as last time, Lucius. Using somebody else's hands. This time he was using a diary."

He picked it up and held it out across the desk so that the hole showed.

Harry watched Lucius Malfoy look at it.

His face didn't change. He was better at that than McGonagall. But Harry didn't need his face. He felt the fury sink all at once, very fast, into a small, cold, careful place, the way a man went very still when he heard a floorboard creak in a house where nobody should be awake. Beneath it, quite clearly and quite small, Harry felt fear.

"How fortunate," Lucius Malfoy said, "that the boy found it."

"Yes," Dumbledore replied. "Wasn't it."

* * *

Lucius didn't stay long. He looked at Mr Weasley only once, as though Mr Weasley were a mark on the carpet, and then he turned to go. Dobby, who had stood behind him the whole time with his bandaged hands knotted together, looked at Harry once more, then at the diary, then at the floor.

Harry looked at the diary.

He thought about Dobby in Dudley's second bedroom with the bedside lamp, and in the hospital wing at one in the morning saying *only to hurt, only enough*.

Then he bent down beneath the desk and took off his left shoe.

Nobody was looking at him. Everybody was looking at Lucius Malfoy. Harry took off his sock, which was grey and very dirty with a hole in the heel, and put his shoe back on without it. Then he picked the diary up off the desk, pushed the sock in between its burned pages and closed it.

"Professor," he asked. "Can I give it back to him?"

Dumbledore looked at him over his spectacles.

Harry read him, and Dumbledore was amused. It was a small, bright, quick amusement, the kind somebody had when they had just seen exactly what another person was doing and were pleased with them for doing it.

"I think," Dumbledore said, "that it is certainly his to have."

Harry went out after them.

He caught them at the top of the stairs. Lucius Malfoy turned round on the first step down, with Dobby behind him, and looked at Harry and the diary in Harry's hand, and his face was quite blank.

"Your diary, sir," Harry said, holding it out.

Lucius looked at it, and then at him.

"I have no idea what you mean. I've never seen it before in my life."

"Haven't you?"

Harry went on holding it out, and Lucius Malfoy didn't take it, and Harry read him. The fear had risen again, quite small, and on top of it, very large, was the fury, pointed at Harry now, a long way down at him from a long way up.

Lucius took the diary.

He took it the way one took something a dog had brought. Then his fingers found the sock, and he looked down and pulled it out from between the pages, and his lip curled. He held it up between finger and thumb, a dirty grey sock with a hole in the heel, and regarded it with an expression of the most perfect disgust.

Then he dropped it over his shoulder without looking where.

Dobby caught it.

* * *

Harry would remember Dobby's face for the rest of his life.

The terror went. It went out of Dobby all at once, every scrap of it, the way a candle went out in a draught, and the grey misery went with it, the way a great weight went when somebody had carried it up a great many stairs and finally put it down at the top. What rose in the place where it had been was so bright and so large and so entirely joyful that for a moment Harry couldn't feel anybody else on the stairs at all.

"Dobby," Lucius Malfoy snapped. "Come."

Dobby didn't come.

He was holding the sock up very close to his face, as though it were the most beautiful thing ever made. Then he looked at Lucius Malfoy with his great green eyes brimming and spoke in a high, cracked voice that shook all the way through.

"Master has handed Dobby a sock. With his own hand. In front of Harry Potter."

Lucius Malfoy went quite still.

He looked at the sock in Dobby's hands, then at the diary in his own. Then he looked at Harry, and Harry felt it coming, the whole of the fury all at once, so large and so fast that he had his wand out of his pocket before he'd thought about it.

Lucius didn't get as far as his.

There was a bang no louder than a door slammed hard in a house a long way off. Lucius Malfoy flew backwards up three steps and sat down very hard on the top one, his cane clattering away down past him into the dark.

Dobby was standing between them.

He was very small. He had one hand held up in front of him, bandaged palm out, and the sock clenched in the other, and he was shaking from his ears to his feet.

"You will not touch Harry Potter," Dobby declared.

Lucius looked at him.

Harry read him and found that the fury hadn't gone anywhere and wouldn't for a long time. Over it, though, quite clearly, was something else, and Harry thought it was the first time in his life that Lucius Malfoy had felt it in front of a house-elf.

He was afraid of Dobby.

He got up slowly without looking at the elf, went down the stairs past him without a word, picked up his cane at the bottom and was gone.

Dobby turned round.

"Harry Potter freed Dobby."

"Yes," Harry said.

"Harry Potter put a sock in a book."

"Yes."

Dobby looked at the sock in his hand. Then he looked up at Harry, and Harry felt it again, that enormous bright thing, all of it pointed straight at him, and this time it was so loud that he had to put his hand on the wall.

"Dobby will never forget," Dobby vowed. "Never. Not if Dobby lives to be a hundred and ninety. Dobby's mother lived to a hundred and ninety."

Then he vanished with a crack, and the sock with him.

Harry stood alone on the stairs with one bare foot inside his shoe and found that he was grinning.

* * *

Dumbledore was alone when Harry went back in.

The Weasleys had gone down to the hospital wing with Ginny, all seven of them in a crowd, with Mrs Weasley still holding Ginny's hand and Ron walking at the back. Ron had looked at Harry on the way out, and Harry had read gratitude in it, and dislike, and a sort of sore confusion, all tangled together.

Now there was only Dumbledore behind the desk and the bird on its perch. Dumbledore had the Sorting Hat in his hands and was turning it round slowly, the way he had turned the diary.

"Sit down, Harry."

Harry sat.

"The Hat tells me that you asked it for help."

"Yes, sir."

"It also tells me that it answered you rather rudely. I must apologise for it. It has very few chances to be rude to anybody, and I am afraid it enjoys them," Dumbledore said, setting the Hat down on the desk. "Did it surprise you? The sword?"

"Yes."

"It surprised me a little. The Hat has kept that sword for longer than anybody alive can remember, and it has given it out, in all that time, I think, perhaps four times. It does not keep a list of houses. I have never been able to discover what it does keep a list of."

He looked at Harry over his spectacles.

"Do you mind? That it was Gryffindor's?"

Harry thought about it.

"No. It was a good sword."

Dumbledore laughed.

Harry read him, and it was a real laugh, the large, warm thing he'd felt in him in front of the Mirror. Harry was glad of it, though he didn't know why.

He had meant to say thank you and go. Instead, he heard himself speak quite quietly.

"Why didn't anybody stop it?"

Dumbledore looked at him.

"The snake?"

"No," Harry said, looking at the desk. "Not the snake. The other thing. From December. When everybody decided it was me."

He found that he didn't know where to put his hands.

"Three-quarters of the school, sir. I counted. Hufflepuffs who wouldn't walk down the same corridor. A girl who thought *murderer* at me every time she passed me on the stairs. People in my own house giving me the best chair because they wanted me to be it."

He stopped.

"Professor McGonagall knew it wasn't me. You must have known. And nobody said anything. All year."

It was the longest thing he had said to an adult since Quirrell.

Dumbledore was quiet for a while.

"I did know, Harry," he said gently at last. "I knew from the very first night that it was not you. And I thought very hard about whether to say so."

He folded his hands on the desk.

"But what a school decides to believe is a very large and very stubborn animal. It does not listen to Headmasters. If I had stood up in the Great Hall in December and told four hundred frightened children that the boy they were afraid of was innocent, a very great many of them would have heard only that the Headmaster was protecting his favourite. And it would have been worse for you, not better."

He smiled a little sadly.

"Some things cannot be stopped. They can only be outlived. You have outlived this one. I am more sorry than I can say that you had to."

Harry read him.

There was relief, large and warm and very real, that the year was over and the thing in the pipes was dead.

There was pity, quite real, pointed at a boy in a green tie who had asked a question.

Beneath the pity, there was nothing.

Harry went on looking, the way he had gone down past the warmth in front of the Mirror and found the weighing.

There was nothing else there.

There was no guilt. There was no sense anywhere in him that there had been something he ought to have done. Relief and pity were the whole of it, and had been, Harry thought, all year.

He sat back in the chair.

He put it in the list beneath the other entries, in the same plain words. *He was sorry it hurt. He did not think he should have stopped it.*

"Thank you, sir," Harry said, getting up.

"Harry."

Harry stopped at the door.

"Professor Lockhart," Dumbledore said. "Madam Pomfrey has sent word. His back is broken, very low down, in a way that her skills cannot mend and that the phoenix could not mend either. He will go to St Mungo's in the morning. It will be a long time."

He paused.

"He asked Madam Pomfrey to tell you that he was in very good spirits, and that he was relying on you to get the height right."

Harry looked at him.

"Yes, sir," he said, and went out.

* * *

The Mandrakes were ready on the last Friday in May.

Professor Sprout brought the juice up to the hospital wing herself in four stoppered flasks in a wicker basket at a quarter past four in the afternoon. Harry was there. He had been there at a quarter past four every afternoon for three and a half weeks, in the chair by the window beside the end bed, with a book open on his knee that he didn't read.

Madam Pomfrey had stopped telling him to go away in the second week.

She gave the juice to Colin Creevey first, since he had been there longest, then to Justin Finch-Fletchley, then to Hermione Granger. Harry didn't watch them. He heard them. He heard each of them come up out of the stone one after another, quite suddenly, the way one heard a radio come on in another room. Colin was frightened, then thrilled. Justin was frightened, then embarrassed. Hermione came up thinking, so hard and so fast that Harry could feel her doing it from three beds away, and then she sat bolt upright.

"*Pipes*."

Then Madam Pomfrey came to the end bed.

Harry stood up.

She tipped Evelyn's head back and poured a little of the juice between her lips, very carefully, and stood back.

Nothing happened.

Harry reached for her. He did it before he could stop himself, and it was the same as it had always been. There was nothing. There was the silence, quite complete, the same as it had been for three and a half weeks, the same as it had been for a year and a half before that, and he couldn't tell, he still couldn't tell, he would never be able to tell…

Evelyn blinked.

She blinked twice. Then she closed her mouth and swallowed and turned her head a very little on the pillow and looked at the ceiling. Then she looked at her right hand, which lay open and empty on the blanket.

Then she looked at Harry.

"Where's my page?"

For a moment, Harry couldn't speak.

Then he put his hand into his pocket and took it out. It was soft and grey from being folded and unfolded, and it was torn very carefully along one side close to the binding, with a word in pencil in the margin in her small, neat hand.

He held it out.

Evelyn took it, unfolded it and looked at it.

"Good. I'll have to give it back to Madam Pince. She'll want to mend it. She'll be very upset," she said, folding it up again along the same lines. "What's the date?"

"Friday the twenty-eighth."

"Of May?"

"Yes."

Evelyn looked at the ceiling again.

"Then I've missed four weeks. And the History of Magic essay. And Professor Binns was going to do the Goblin Rebellion of 1612, which is the only interesting one."

She lay still for a moment.

"Did you find the pipes?"

"Yes."

"Was it a basilisk?"

"Yes."

"Is it dead?"

"Yes."

Evelyn turned her head and looked at him properly, the way she looked at a page she was going to have to read twice.

"You'd better tell me."

"Yes," Harry said. "I know."

* * *

He told her on the Saturday.

They went down to the lake in the morning, because the hospital wing was full of Colin Creevey talking about how he was going to tell his dad. They sat on the flat rock beneath the beech tree on the far side, where the Slytherin second-years didn't go, with their feet dangling over the water. It was a very fine day, the second fine day of the summer. The giant squid was asleep in the shallows a little way out with one long arm lying along the top of the water, and every so often the arm moved.

Harry told her everything.

He had meant to tell her some of it, but there was no way of telling her the parts without the rest coming too, all joined up like a string of handkerchiefs out of a sleeve.

He told her about the bathroom in January and the black book on the wet floor with the hunger in it, folded small. He told her about Tom, about the nights behind the green curtains with the ink rising out of the page, and *goodnight, Harry*, and *I'll be here*. About being understood.

He told her he had known whose it was. That he had seen it go into Ginny's cauldron in Flourish and Blotts and recognised it again on the bathroom floor, and said nothing to anybody.

He told her about the charms, the numbing jinx and the silent one for locks, and about the voice. He told her about the freckled boy on the stairs and what the voice had done to him, and how he had stood and watched it happen, and the small, bright, warm thing that had sat inside him whilst he watched.

He told her that he had decided to tell her at four o'clock in the morning on the first of May, and had sat at breakfast waiting, and she hadn't come.

He told her about Quirrell.

He had never told anybody. But it was joined on to the rest and came out with it, and once it had started, he didn't stop. He told her about the last room and the hands on his throat, and the self-hatred he had found too late at the bottom of everything. He told her how he had reached for Quirrell to read him and, instead of taking what was there, had given it back, louder, with his own fury on top of it.

He told her what Quirrell had done next with his wand, and why.

He told her that Dumbledore didn't know.

Then he stopped.

He had been talking for a long time. The squid had moved its arm four times, the shadow of the beech had crept a little way off the rock and his voice had gone hoarse, the way it did after a cold.

Evelyn hadn't said a word the whole time. She hadn't interrupted him or made a sound. She had sat on the rock beside him with her knees drawn up and her arms round them and her chin resting on her arms, looking at the water, and she had listened, and he hadn't been able to feel any of it.

He didn't try now.

He looked at the squid and waited. He thought she might get up and go. He thought she might call him a murderer, the way the girl on the stairs had thought it. He thought she might tell him it was all right, which would have been worse.

She did none of those things.

She sat quite still for a long time, looking at the water. Then she unfolded her arms, picked up a small, flat stone from the rock beside her and turned it over in her fingers twice, the way she turned a page.

"I've got a question."

"All right."

Evelyn looked at the stone.

"When it went. When somebody took it out of your trunk, at the end of February. Which did you mind losing more?" she asked, turning the stone over again. "Him? Or having something I didn't know about?"

Harry looked at her.

He opened his mouth to answer.

He found that he couldn't. He found that he didn't know. He sat on the rock with his mouth open and looked inside himself for the answer the way he looked inside other people, and it wasn't there, or it was there and he couldn't see it. Slowly, sitting on the rock in the sun, he understood that it was the worst question anybody had ever asked him.

"I don't know," he admitted.

"No," Evelyn said. "I didn't think you would."

She threw the stone.

It skipped three times across the flat water and sank quite near the squid's arm, and the arm moved.

"Next time," Evelyn said, "tell me first."

She said nothing more. She didn't say that it was all right, and she didn't say that it wasn't. She sat beside him on the rock in the sun with her chin on her knees, and after a while she took a book out of her bag, opened it at her place and began to read.

Harry sat beside her.

He didn't read her. He couldn't. He looked at the water and the far towers of the castle, and he found that he was very tired, and that something in the middle of him that had been held up hard since January, the way Lockhart had held the roof, had been let go.

He didn't know what to call it.

A long time afterwards, he would think it was the morning he stopped being on his own.

* * *

St Mungo's Hospital for Magical Maladies and Injuries was in London, behind the window of a closed-down department store, and Professor McGonagall took him there by Floo on the first Saturday in June.

The ward was on the third floor, long and white and full of flowers.

They were on every table and windowsill and along the floor at the foot of every bed, and very nearly all of them were for one person. Roses. Lilies. Great bunches of something blue and starry that sang very quietly as one walked past.

Lockhart was in the bed at the far end by the window, sitting up against six pillows in a forget-me-not blue dressing gown, signing photographs.

"Harry! My dear fellow! Minerva! Oh, how kind. Come in, come in, mind the lilies, they bite."

Harry came in.

He read him as he came down the ward, and it was all there, as it had been on the floor of the tunnel. The vanity was there, enormous and cheerful and quite unchanged, sitting on top of everything. The kindness was there, plain and warm as it had always been.

And beneath it was the pain.

It wasn't as large as it had been in the tunnel, but it was there all the time, low down and steady and grey. Harry thought it was going to be there for a long time, and that Lockhart knew it.

"Sit, sit," Lockhart urged, waving his quill at the end of the bed. "You'll have to forgive me if I don't get up. I've been told not to. They've got me in a sort of frame from the waist down, very fetching."

He held up a card.

"Eleven hundred and four get-well cards since Wednesday. I'm answering every one."

Harry looked at the card.

It had a sad-looking Kneazle holding daisies on the front. Inside, in violet ink, in Lockhart's large, looping hand, it read *With every good wish for a swift recovery! Gilderoy Lockhart.*

"You're signing your own get-well cards," Harry said.

"Somebody's got to. They sent them all the way from Bognor. I can hardly send them back blank."

Professor McGonagall made a small sound. Harry read her. She was trying very hard not to laugh, and she was very nearly managing it.

"How long?" Harry asked.

Lockhart put down the card.

"Two years, they say. Possibly a little more. There's a Healer called Pyke who's very good, terribly stern, I adore her. She says I'll walk again. She says I'll walk with a stick," he beamed. "I've always rather wanted a stick. You can do such a lot with a stick."

Harry read him.

The pain was there, steady and grey, with the vanity on top. Beneath both of them, he found, was something he had felt in Lockhart only once before, at the first turn of a tunnel beneath the lake.

He was frightened. He was frightened of two years in a bed.

He wasn't going to show it to anybody, ever.

"Professor," Harry began.

"Gilderoy, please, I've broken my back for you. We're practically family."

"They're saying you killed it."

Lockhart's eyebrows went up.

"In the *Prophet*. On Tuesday. That you went down and fought the basilisk and got hurt and I helped. Theo showed me. It had a picture of you."

"Ah. Yes. I did see that," Lockhart replied, studying him for a moment. "Did you mind?"

"No. But it isn't what happened."

"I know," Lockhart said with a smile. "I wrote to the *Prophet* on Wednesday, Harry, and told them exactly what happened, and that it was all you, and the roof, and a sword out of a hat, and that I spent the whole of the main event standing in a tunnel with my arm in the air. They printed the letter on page eleven. Under a recipe for rhubarb fool."

He picked up another card and signed it.

"They'll believe the first one. Not the letter. The picture. They always do. It doesn't matter what you tell them afterwards, it's what they saw first," he went on, blowing on the ink. "People see what you show them, Harry. Nearly everyone. Nearly always. I'm afraid that this time what they were shown was me."

He looked up.

"I'm very sorry. I really am. I'd have liked you to have it."

Harry read him.

It was true, all of it. He was sorry. He would have liked Harry to have it. And beneath that, very cheerfully and quite unashamed, the vanity was absolutely delighted.

Harry laughed.

It burst out of him all at once in the white ward full of singing flowers, and Lockhart looked at him and laughed too, then winced, then went on laughing anyway.

"That's better. You look like a boy who's been carrying a piano. Put it down. Eat a grape. Somebody sent forty pounds of them."

* * *

Harry went down into the Chamber on his own on the last Wednesday of term.

He told nobody. He went at ten at night beneath the Cloak, told the sink to open and went down.

Men from the Ministry had come in the first week of June to look at the basilisk, and they had cleared the rockfall and propped the roof with new timber that smelled of resin in the dark. Harry went past the place where Lockhart had stood and came to the round door with the two stone snakes on it.

The men from the Ministry hadn't got through it. There were scorch marks round its edge where they had tried.

It opened for him.

The Chamber was very quiet.

The basilisk lay where it had fallen between the pillars, and it had begun to go grey. Harry walked past it to the end, to the great carved face and the two enormous stone feet, and he stopped.

He hadn't come for the snake.

He had come because of something he had felt on the night of the fourth of May and hadn't had time to think about. He'd felt it with his back against the stone foot and the fang in his arm. He had felt it again, very faintly, every night since, lying in bed behind the green curtains, as though something a long way down beneath the castle had been left switched on.

He put his hand on the stone foot.

There was something behind it.

It wasn't a person. It had none of the diary's hunger in it, nor the snake's voice, nor the clean wind of the bird. It was very old and very still, and it was there, just there, behind the stone, a few feet from his hand.

And it was waiting.

He didn't know how he knew that. It was waiting the way a book waited on a shelf, the way a letter waited on a mat. It was waiting for somebody to read it.

Harry reached for it.

He reached for it the way he reached for people, all the way in, and he felt it notice him. It didn't wake, nor did it move. But it noticed, very slightly, the way a page seemed to turn towards the light. And then it did nothing at all.

He tried for an hour.

He tried in Parseltongue and with every charm Tom had taught him. He pressed his hands flat against the cold stone and pushed with all of himself, the way he had pushed into Quirrell without meaning to, and it didn't give. It didn't open.

At eleven, he gave up.

He stood back from the great stone feet and looked up at the carved face of the old man in the green dark, and at the place behind the stone where the thing was waiting, and he thought that he didn't know what it was, and that he was going to find out.

* * *

The Hogwarts Express left Hogsmeade station at eleven o'clock on Saturday the twelfth of June.

Harry had a compartment near the back with Theo and Millicent, and Evelyn by the window, reading. Hagrid had come back from Azkaban on the Monday, thinner and very quiet, and he had stood on the platform in the drizzle waving at the train with a handkerchief the size of a tablecloth until it went round the bend. Hermione Granger had looked into their compartment once from the corridor and looked at Evelyn, and Evelyn had looked back at her, and neither of them had said anything at all, and Hermione had moved on.

Slytherin had won the House Cup by a hundred and twenty points. Harry couldn't bring himself to mind.

He sat with his forehead against the cold glass and watched the hills go by.

He thought about eleven weeks at Privet Drive. He thought about Lockhart in his frame on the third floor of St Mungo's, signing his own cards. He thought about Dobby, wherever he was, with a grey sock.

He thought about a small black book with a hole through the middle of it, and the voice in it that had said his name the way a friend said it, and he found that he still didn't know which he had minded losing more.

He thought about the thing behind the stone feet.

It was there now. He could feel it very faintly even here on the train, a long way south of the castle. It was there the way a light was left on in a house one had just left, and it was waiting.

"Potter," Evelyn said without looking up from her book.

"What?"

"You're doing the face."

"What face?"

"The one you do when you're planning something you're not going to tell me about," she replied, turning a page. "You said you'd tell me first."

Harry looked at her.

"There's a door. Down there. Behind the statue. I can't open it."

Evelyn turned another page.

"Yet," she said.

Harry looked back out at the hills.

He was going down again in September.

## Chapter 21: The Knight Bus

Aunt Marge arrived on Monday the second of August in a taxi from Marjoribanks, with two suitcases, a bottle of brandy for Vernon and a bulldog called Ripper.

Harry heard her before he saw her.

He was upstairs with the window open, finishing an essay on the Shrinking Solution for Professor Snape, and he felt the taxi turn into Privet Drive from the corner. There was a driver in it who was tired and wanted his tea, and there was somebody else in it who was loud.

Very loud.

He put down his quill and listened to her coming up the path.

"Vernon! There you are. Look at you. Look at the size of you. Petunia's feeding you properly at last."

Harry read her through the floor.

She was pleased, and the pleasure was large and red and pointed at Vernon. That was the top of her. He went down to look at the rest, as he always did, as he had with every person he had ever met since before he could remember, and he found something he hadn't found very often.

There wasn't much else.

There was the pleasure. Next to it, out in the open, the same size and the same colour, sat something that liked to hurt things. The two of them sat side by side the way two people sat on a bus, and it was looking forward to the week.

Beneath both of those, there was nothing that minded.

Harry looked for it. With most people, there was always something at the bottom, smaller and older, that didn't quite agree with the rest. Uncle Vernon was frightened. Dudley, beneath the greed, was bored and a little lonely.

Aunt Marge wasn't anything.

She was cruel, and she enjoyed it, and that was all, all the way down.

"Where's the boy?" she demanded in the hall. "Is he still here? I thought you'd have got rid of him by now."

* * *

It was a long week.

She sat in Vernon's armchair, which Vernon surrendered without being asked, fed Ripper out of a saucer from Petunia's best tea service and talked.

She talked about dogs. She bred them on a farm outside Marjoribanks, twelve of them, and she talked about each of the twelve in turn and then started again at the beginning. She talked about joyriders, and what she would do to them if anybody had the sense to let her.

And she talked about Harry.

She did it at every meal, the way some people salted everything before they'd tasted it.

"Still here, then," she remarked at breakfast on the Tuesday without looking at him. "Still eating."

"Yes, Aunt Marge."

"Where is it you send him, Vernon? That school?"

"St Brutus's," Vernon replied. "Secure Centre for Incurably Criminal Boys."

"Do they use the cane?"

Harry read Vernon. Vernon didn't know whether they used the cane, because there was no such place, and he was afraid of the question in a small, hot way, and he looked at Harry.

"Oh, yes," Harry answered. "All the time."

Aunt Marge looked at him for the first time that morning.

"Good."

He read her. She was pleased again, the same large red pleasure, aimed at him now, the pleasure of a woman who had been told that a dog she didn't like had been kicked.

He ate his toast.

He was very good that week. He had decided to be before she came. Seven days was nothing. He had done eleven summers in this house before he knew what he was.

He didn't answer back. He did the washing up. He took Ripper round the block twice a day, and Ripper tried to bite his ankles all the way to Wisteria Walk and all the way back. He used the narrow place in his voice that made adults feel they had been answered, and he went to his room whenever it wasn't useful to be anywhere else.

He read her all the time, because she was the loudest thing in the house. Most of the cruelty he had known had been complicated. Vernon's had fear in it. Malfoy's had fear in it. Snape's had something in it that hurt the person carrying it. Aunt Marge's was like weather over flat country. It went over everything, and it wasn't sorry, and there was nothing behind it to talk to.

On the Wednesday, the television news showed a man's face.

Harry was in the doorway of the sitting room with a tray of tea, and he stopped.

It was a long, thin, hollow face framed by a great deal of dark, matted hair, with eyes that looked at the camera from very far back. The newsreader said the man's name was Black, that he had escaped from prison and that members of the public should on no account approach him.

"There's a nasty piece of work," Uncle Vernon grunted. "Look at the state of him. Look at his hair."

"Hanging's too good for them," Aunt Marge declared.

Harry looked at the man on the screen.

He tried to read him. He knew a television was only a box with glass on the front, but he tried all the same, and got what he would have got from a stamp, which was nothing. Then the newsreader was talking about a strike at a car plant in Oxford, and the face was gone.

He put the tray down.

"Something wrong with you?" Aunt Marge asked.

"No, Aunt Marge."

"Then pour."

He poured.

* * *

The last dinner was on the Sunday.

Petunia had done a roast because it was the last night. Vernon had opened the second bottle of wine before the potatoes came round. Ripper lay beneath the table near Harry's feet, breathing.

Harry counted.

He had been counting since Monday. Six days down, one supper to go. Then a taxi at ten in the morning, and he would write to Evelyn and tell her he had got through the whole week without doing anything at all.

Aunt Marge had had four glasses of wine.

Harry read her. She was very red now, inside and out, and the pleasure had gone loose and sloppy at the edges, as it did in people who had been drinking. The other thing, the thing that liked to hurt, hadn't gone loose. It was sitting up very straight. It had been sitting up all evening, waiting for him.

"Pass the potatoes, Vernon," she said. "No. Give them to the boy. Let him pass them. Let's see if he can do that much."

Harry passed the potatoes.

"Hah," Aunt Marge snorted. "You see, Petunia, I always said. It's all in the breeding. You can tell a lot from a dog by its parents. I've seen it a hundred times. A bitch from a bad line, you can feed it what you like, you can train it how you like, there'll be something wrong with the litter. Something always comes out."

"Marge," Petunia warned.

Harry read her. Aunt Petunia was frightened, very suddenly, and not of Marge. She was frightened of him.

He kept his face still.

"Nothing personal," Aunt Marge went on, taking a long drink. "But there it is. Vernon's told me all about it. The father a layabout. Never had a proper job. And the mother…"

Harry looked at his plate.

He had decided on Monday that whatever she said about his father, he wouldn't mind. He had never known his father. His father was a thin man with glasses and black hair who had been proud of him once, in a mirror, a long time ago, and nothing Aunt Marge said would get anywhere near that.

He hadn't decided anything about his mother.

"No better than she ought to have been, I shouldn't wonder. Running off with that sort. Getting herself into God knows what. And then wrapping the pair of them round a lamp post, drunk as lords, I expect, and leaving you lot to pick up the pieces. It's always the way with that kind," she sneered, pointing her fork at him. "It'll come out in this one. You mark my words. It's in the blood."

The table had gone quiet.

Dudley had stopped eating. Uncle Vernon had turned a dull red and was looking at the salt. Aunt Petunia was looking at Harry, more frightened than Harry had ever felt her, and the other thing in her, the thing he had no word for, had risen all the way to the top. It wasn't about Marge, and it wasn't about him.

Harry didn't move.

He thought about his mother in the mirror, with her face wet, smiling at him.

He thought about it for perhaps two seconds.

Then he decided.

It was nothing like what had happened with Quirrell, and afterwards he would think about that more than anything. With Quirrell, he had been on the floor with hands round his throat, and something had come out of him the way a shout did, and he hadn't known what he was doing until it was done.

This time he was sitting at a table with his knife and fork in his hands, quite calm, and he knew exactly what he was going to do before he did it.

He looked at Aunt Marge.

He reached into her, the way he reached into everybody, and found the place at the bottom where there should have been something that minded. There was nothing there. It was an empty room, and it had never had anything in it.

So he gave her something to put in it.

He didn't have to look far. He had a great deal of it. He had the freckled boy on the stairs, white in the face and running. He had six weeks of a black book behind his bed curtains. He had a man with a turban kneeling on a stone floor with his wand against the back of his own head. He had stood in the hospital wing looking at Evelyn's open eyes without knowing whether she was there, and he'd kept the diary anyway, and Ginny Weasley had nearly died of it.

He had all the shame anybody could want.

He took it and made it larger and put it into her.

It went in very easily. That was the second thing he would think about afterwards. There was nothing in the way. It went into the empty room and filled it and kept on filling it, and he pushed it in until he felt the room was full, and then a little more, and then he stopped.

It took about as long as passing the potatoes.

Aunt Marge put her fork down.

She looked at it lying on the tablecloth. Then she looked at Vernon, then at Petunia and Dudley, and then at Harry, and her big red face did something Harry had never seen it do.

It crumpled.

"Oh," Aunt Marge whimpered.

She began to cry.

* * *

She cried for an hour.

Harry knew it was an hour because the clock on the mantelpiece in the sitting room struck eight whilst she was still at the table and nine whilst she was on the sofa, and she didn't stop in between.

It wasn't ordinary crying. It came up out of her in great hopeless heaves, and she kept trying to say things and couldn't get to the end of them.

"I'm sorry," she sobbed to the tablecloth. "I'm so sorry. I'm so, I didn't, I never…"

"Marge," Vernon pleaded. "Marge, old girl. What's the matter?"

"I'm so sorry."

"What for? What are you sorry for?"

She didn't know. Harry read her, and she didn't know. She was enormously ashamed of everything at once and nothing in particular, as anybody would be if someone had poured a lifetime of it into them over a plate of roast beef, and there was nothing in her that had ever learned what to do with it. She'd had no practice. She was fifty-four years old and she had never once in her life been ashamed of anything, and now she was ashamed of everything, and she sat at her brother's table and wept into her napkin like a child who had been found out.

Uncle Vernon had no idea what had happened.

Harry read him. He was bewildered all the way through, embarrassed in front of his son and sorry for his sister in a clumsy way that Harry hadn't known he had in him. He patted her back and said "There, there, old girl," over and over, as though she were a horse.

Dudley went upstairs.

Aunt Petunia didn't go anywhere.

She stood by the kitchen door with a tea towel in her hands and looked at Harry.

She knew.

Harry read it in her very clearly. She didn't know what he had done, or how. But she knew he had done it, as surely as if she had watched him pour it out of a jug, and the thing in her he had never had a name for was right at the top now, mixed up with fear, and for a moment he thought it was nearly something he understood.

He didn't look at it. He got up from the table, took his plate to the sink, washed it, dried it and put it away in the cupboard. Then he went upstairs.

He sat on his bed.

Downstairs, through the floor, he could feel Aunt Marge still going. She had moved to the sofa, Vernon had got the brandy out, and Ripper was whining.

Harry sat with his hands on his knees and tried to feel bad about it.

He couldn't quite manage it.

He had expected to, the way one expected a bill after a meal. He had put all his shame into her, every bit of it, everything he had been carrying around since the summer before last, and now he went to look for it, and it was gone.

He didn't feel ashamed.

If anything, he felt rather light.

That was when he grew frightened.

He sat very still on his bed with the summer dark coming down over the gardens of Privet Drive and thought about how easy it had been, and how there had been nothing in the way.

He could do it again tomorrow, to anybody, and nobody would ever know.

It hadn't cost him anything at all.

At a quarter past nine, he got up and began to pack.

* * *

His trunk was in the cupboard under the stairs with his broom and his cauldron. The key was on the hook by the back door.

He didn't need the key.

He went down at half past nine with his school bag and Hedwig's empty cage. Behind the sitting-room door, Aunt Marge was saying "I'm sorry, I'm sorry" in a voice gone thin. Harry knelt by the cupboard, put his finger on the padlock and thought Tom's charm at it, the silent one, and it opened without a click.

He hadn't used it since February.

He noticed that, and he noticed that his hand didn't shake.

He pulled the trunk down the hall on its little wheels and opened the front door. The night came in, warm, smelling of cut grass and somebody's barbecue.

"Where do you think you're going?"

Uncle Vernon was in the sitting-room doorway with his sleeves rolled up and a damp patch on his shirt where Aunt Marge had cried on it.

Harry read him. He was still bewildered. Beneath that, rising slowly, was the old fear, the one that had gone away last summer when the letter from the Ministry came. Vernon didn't know why it was back. Some part of him had worked out that the boy was involved without being able to say how.

"Out," Harry said.

"You'll come back in here this minute."

"No. I don't think I will."

Vernon took a step towards him.

Harry looked at him. He didn't do anything. He only looked, and let Vernon see him look, the way he had looked at Aunt Marge across the table.

Vernon stopped.

The fear rose all the way, past the bewilderment and past the anger that was trying to get going and couldn't, and it settled at the top of him, where it had sat two summers ago when the letters came down the chimney.

"Goodnight, Uncle Vernon."

Harry pulled the trunk out onto the step and shut the door behind him.

* * *

He got as far as Magnolia Crescent.

It was three streets. The trunk was heavy and one of its wheels squeaked. He stopped beneath a street lamp that wasn't working and sat down on the trunk to think.

He had eleven Galleons in a sock at the bottom of the trunk. He had his wand and the Cloak. He had nowhere to go.

He couldn't go to Selwyn Hall at eleven o'clock at night and say he had made his aunt cry for an hour. Isadora would look at him and then say something, very courteously, that would be exactly true.

He didn't know where Theo lived. Millicent lived in Swindon with a dog that had eaten a chair. He didn't know how to get to London at night without Muggle money, and he thought he would have to use magic, and found that he didn't much care.

That was when he felt it.

There was something in the dark on the other side of the road. There was a gap between a garage and a fence, full of black, and something was in it.

Harry went very still and read it.

At first, he thought it was an animal, because it was low down and large, and now he could just make out its shape. It was a dog, a huge black dog with its head lowered, looking at him.

But it wasn't an animal's feeling.

Animals were far away even when they were close, like voices in another house. This was right there across the road, as close and as loud as a person.

It was a person's feeling.

It was enormous, very old and very tired and very thin, the way a feeling got when it had been kept going on nothing for a long time, and all of it was pointed at him. There was no hunger in it, nor anger. There was grief, he thought, and something wild and fierce on top of the grief, and beneath both of them something he would have called, in a person, a kind of wonder.

It was looking at him as though he were somebody it hadn't seen for a very long time.

Harry stood up.

He took out his wand and said "*Lumos*" aloud, without thinking about the Ministry at all, and held it up.

The light went across the road.

There was nothing in the gap between the garage and the fence but a dustbin, a bicycle with no front wheel and a great many weeds.

Then a tremendous noise came round the corner behind him, and he threw himself backwards off the kerb.

It was a bus.

It was three decks high and violently purple, and it had stopped dead six inches from where he had been standing with its headlamps blazing. The trunk had toppled over. Harry was sitting in the gutter with his wand still lit in his hand.

A door opened in the side of the bus, and a young man in a purple uniform leaned out of it.

"Evening. Knight Bus. For witches and wizards what's stuck. You stuck your wand out, so here we are. Stan Shunpike, conductor."

He stopped and looked down at Harry in the gutter.

"What you doin' down there?"

"I fell over," Harry said.

"What d'you fall over for?"

"You nearly hit me."

"Didn't, though," Stan replied cheerfully. "Ern's never hit nobody. Well. Not for ages."

He jumped down.

"Is that your trunk? Wotcher want? London?"

Harry read him.

Stan Shunpike was about eighteen, with big ears and a good many spots, and he was bored and interested at the same time, which Harry had always found the easiest kind of person in the world. He would tell anyone everything he knew if they only looked as though they wanted to hear it.

Harry looked across the road again.

The gap between the garage and the fence was empty. He couldn't feel anything in it any more. Whatever it had been, it had gone, and gone fast, and he hadn't felt it go.

"Yes," he said. "London. The Leaky Cauldron."

"Eleven Sickles to London. Two more for a drink of something 'ot," Stan said, heaving the trunk up the steps one-handed. "What's your name, then?"

Harry pushed his fringe down over his forehead.

"Tom."

He didn't know why he said it. It was the first name that came.

"Tom what?"

"Riddle," Harry said, and then wished very much that he hadn't.

Stan only wrote it down on a ticket with a stub of pencil.

"Right you are, Tom."

* * *

There were no seats on the Knight Bus. There were beds.

Six brass bedsteads stood on the bottom deck with candles in brackets beside them, and in one of them a small wizard in a nightcap lay asleep, murmuring "Not now, Mother, I'm pickling" every so often. The driver was an elderly wizard in thick glasses called Ernie, who drove with his nose very close to the windscreen.

"Take it away, Ern," Stan called.

There was a bang, and Harry found himself flat on his back on the bed.

The Knight Bus went through Little Whinging like something fired from a gun. It squeezed through gaps between parked cars that weren't wide enough for it, and the post box on the corner of Wisteria Walk jumped out of its way. The beds slid, and the wizard in the nightcap rolled gently from one side of his bed to the other without waking.

Harry clung to the bedstead.

He thought he had never been in anything so stupid in his life, and that he didn't want to get off.

"First time?" Stan asked from the end of the next bed, where he sat with his feet up, reading a newspaper. "You get used to it. Took me a fortnight."

Harry paid for the hot chocolate, and Stan poured it from a tall jug on a hump-backed bridge somewhere in Kent, and most of it went in the mug.

Harry looked at Stan's newspaper.

It was the *Daily Prophet*. The face on the front was the face from the television news, the long, thin face with the matted hair, and it was moving. It blinked. It turned its head very slightly, as though it had heard something to one side.

**BLACK STILL AT LARGE**, the headline read.

"Him," Stan said, turning the paper round so Harry could see it better. "You 'eard about him?"

"A bit. On the… I heard something."

Stan's face lit up.

Harry read him. He was frightened, genuinely, a long way down. But the top of him was something else entirely, bright and greedy and delighted, the way people were delighted by a very bad storm when they were indoors.

"Sirius Black," Stan said with relish. "Out of Azkaban. Nobody's ever done that. Thirteen people he killed. With one curse. Twelve Muggles and a wizard, in the middle of a street. And then he just stood there and laughed."

He lowered his voice.

"When the hit wizards come, he was standing in the road laughing. My mum knew a bloke who was there."

"Why?" Harry asked.

"Why what?"

"Why did he do it?"

Stan looked at him as though he had asked why it rained.

"He was You-Know-'Oo's man, wasn't he? Everybody knows that. And when You-Know-'Oo went, he was cornered, so he took a load of people with him," he explained, shaking the paper. "Twelve years inside. And now he's out, and nobody knows how."

Harry looked at the moving face.

It blinked at him from very far back.

He tried to read it and got nothing, as he always did from ink and paper. He thought about the black gap between the garage and the fence, and the thing in it that had looked at him as though it hadn't seen him for a long time.

He didn't think about the two things together.

He wouldn't think about them together for a long time.

"Where's 'e going to go, that's what I want to know," Stan said comfortably, turning to the sports pages. "Ern. ERN. Leaky Cauldron. Young Tom's for the Leaky."

* * *

The Knight Bus stopped outside the Leaky Cauldron at twenty past two in the morning. The record shop next door had a poster in its window for an album by somebody called Suede.

Stan got the trunk down onto the pavement.

"Ta-ra, Tom."

Then he stopped, because the door of the Leaky Cauldron had opened, and a small, portly man in a pinstriped cloak stood in it, with Tom the barman behind him holding a lamp.

Harry knew him.

He had last seen him through the window of Hagrid's hut on the first of May, turning a bowler hat round and round in his hands. He was holding the same bowler hat now.

"There you are," the man in the pinstriped cloak said. "Harry. There you are. Thank goodness."

Stan's mouth fell open. He looked at the man in the doorway, then at Harry. Harry watched his eyes go to his forehead, to the fringe, then back to the forehead.

"Tom," Stan said slowly. "Tom Riddle. You said."

"Sorry," Harry offered.

"Get on with you, Shunpike," the man in the doorway said quite kindly. "Thank you very much. That will be all."

Stan got on with him. The Knight Bus went off down Charing Cross Road with a bang, and the last Harry saw of it was Stan's face pressed against the glass of the back window.

* * *

The man was Cornelius Fudge, the Minister for Magic. He took Harry into a small private parlour off the bar, ordered tea and crumpets, sat down with a sigh and beamed.

He was very relieved.

That was the top of him, and it was large and warm and real. Apart from Hagrid on a rock and Mrs Weasley in Dumbledore's office, Cornelius Fudge was more relieved to see him than anybody had ever been.

"Well. Well, well. You've led us a merry dance, Harry. A merry dance."

"I'm sorry, sir."

"Not at all, not at all," Fudge insisted, waving a crumpet. "No harm done. You're here now, safe and sound, that's all that matters. Eat up."

Harry ate up.

He read Fudge whilst he ate. Beneath the relief was what Harry had felt in him through the window of Hagrid's hut, a man examining a situation very carefully to see whether any of it could be his fault. It hadn't found anything yet, and it was pleased.

"I'll be quite honest with you, Harry. We had a bit of a turn at the Ministry tonight. A bit of a turn. A Lumos charm at seven minutes past eleven, on a street corner in Little Whinging, and you nowhere to be found."

"I'm sorry," Harry repeated. "I know I'm not allowed."

"Oh, as to that," Fudge said, waving the crumpet again. "We are hardly going to expel a boy for lighting a lamp in the dark. Not at all. Not in the circumstances. Certainly not."

He leaned forward.

"What on earth were you doing out there at that time of night, Harry? With your trunk?"

Harry looked at him.

He had decided on the Knight Bus that the best thing to tell the Minister for Magic was something true, because something true could be checked, and then nobody would check anything else.

"My aunt came to stay. My uncle's sister. She doesn't like me. There was a row at dinner," he said with a shrug. "I left."

Fudge's face went soft and understanding.

"Ah. Families. Yes. Say no more," he said, patting Harry's arm. "Well, there's no need for you to go back there this summer. None at all. We'll put you up here, at the Ministry's expense, until term starts."

"Thank you."

He didn't mention that he didn't think his aunt and uncle were going to calm down.

"Only," Fudge went on, and his voice changed.

Harry read him.

Fudge was frightened.

It was much larger than the relief. It had sunk a long way down and spread out at the bottom, the way water spread beneath a floor, and it was very old for a fear about something that had only happened in July. It was the fear of a man who had stood in a street twelve years ago and seen what one curse could do.

And it was aimed, Harry noticed, very carefully at the door.

"Only I want you to promise me something, Harry. While you're here. I want you to stay in Diagon Alley. Not into Muggle London. Not Knockturn Alley, certainly. Just Diagon Alley, and back here by dark. Every night. Tom will keep an eye. Will you promise me that?"

"Why?" Harry asked.

Fudge laughed. It was a very jolly laugh, with nothing beneath it at all.

"Oh, well. You know. One likes to know where people are."

He reached for another crumpet.

He didn't mention a man called Black. And Harry, who had felt the Minister's fear go out towards the door every time a floorboard creaked in the bar, sat by the fire, ate his crumpet and promised.

* * *

It was the best three weeks of his life.

He knew it at the time, which he thought afterwards was unusual. Most people didn't know until later.

He woke every morning in a room on the second floor with a window over Diagon Alley, and nobody told him to get up. Tom brought him eggs and wouldn't take money for them. Then he went out through the back yard, tapped the bricks and spent the day doing exactly what he liked.

Mostly, what he liked was nothing in particular.

He looked in the window of Quality Quidditch Supplies, where a new broom called a Firebolt stood on a stand with a crowd round it and a sign announcing that its price was available on request. He bought his books, and the assistant in Flourish and Blotts had to put on thick gloves to get *The Monster Book of Monsters* out of its cage, and it bit him anyway.

He did his homework at a table outside Florean Fortescue's ice-cream parlour in the sun.

Florean Fortescue was round and pink and cheerful and knew a great deal about medieval witch burnings. He came out every afternoon with a free sundae and told Harry things for his History of Magic essay that weren't in any book. Harry read nothing in him but kindness and a quiet pleasure in being asked.

Nobody knew who he was unless he showed them. He kept his fringe down and his face ordinary and his voice quiet, and people looked at him and walked past.

He thought about Aunt Marge sometimes.

Mostly at night, with the noise of Charing Cross Road drifting over the roofs, he thought about the empty room at the bottom of her and how easily it had filled.

He didn't do it again.

He was careful. Twice in the first week, he felt the place in himself where it came from, the way one felt a step beneath one's foot before putting one's weight on it, and both times he stepped off. Once was when a wizard in the bar shouted at Tom about his bill. Once was when the assistant in Flourish and Blotts sneered at a small Hufflepuff girl who couldn't afford a second-hand book.

He didn't do anything either time.

Both times, he noticed that he wanted to.

* * *

Evelyn came on the Tuesday of the third week.

Her letter had arrived on the Saturday by way of Cato, the Selwyns' old grey owl, who liked Harry no better than he liked Evelyn and bit him on the way out of the window.

*Potter. Grandmother has business at Gringotts on Tuesday and I am coming with her. We will be at Fortescue's at half past two. Do not make me wait, there is a draught on that corner. You did not say in your last letter why you are at the Leaky Cauldron and not in Surrey. You said "it's a long story." I have time for long stories. E.S.*

He was at Fortescue's at two.

He saw them coming up Diagon Alley from Gringotts at twenty-five past, a long way off, since Isadora Hale was still the tallest and straightest thing in any street. She was in grey. She was always in grey. She wore the same small grey hat and the same long grey coat and carried the same silver-topped cane.

And she was walking with it.

Harry watched her come up the street.

Last summer, she had carried the cane the way some people carried an umbrella on a dry day. Now she put weight on it at every step, and the steps were shorter, and in each one there was a moment, very small, when she paused before going on.

Harry thought about it.

He looked at Evelyn beside her grandmother. Evelyn was carrying two parcels and a library book and walking at exactly her grandmother's pace, looking straight ahead, and she didn't glance at the cane once.

Then they reached the table, and Evelyn put the parcels down and looked at Harry, and Harry knew that she had seen him notice.

Neither of them mentioned it.

"Mr Potter," Isadora greeted him.

"Mrs Hale."

He held a chair for her. She put a hand on the table before she sat.

"Thank you. You are well?"

"Yes, thank you."

"You are brown. And you have grown. Evelyn tells me that you have been living in a public house for three weeks at the expense of the Ministry of Magic," she said, looking at him. "I hope it agrees with you."

"It does. Very much."

"Good. So few things do."

He tried her handle. He knew she would know, and he did it anyway, and there was nothing there, the same smooth, complete nothing as always. She looked at him with something in her face that might have been amusement.

"Evelyn. I am going to sit here for half an hour and eat an ice. Mr Fortescue will bring me one. You will both go away and walk somewhere, and come back at three, and Mr Potter will tell you his long story, and I shall not ask what it was."

* * *

They walked up to the top of Diagon Alley, where it turned and the shops grew smaller and older, and they stopped outside a shop that sold nothing but quills and looked at the quills in the window.

"Well?" Evelyn asked.

Harry told her.

On the way up the street, he had thought he would tell her the short version. Aunt Marge came, she was horrible, there was a row, he left. That was the version he'd told Fudge, and it was all true, and Fudge had believed it.

He found that he couldn't tell Evelyn the short version.

She always knew when he was leaving something out. She couldn't feel anything about anybody, and she knew anyway, by counting things. And he had said he would tell her first.

So he told her all of it. The week. Aunt Marge's nothing, all the way down. The dinner. His mother. The empty room, what he had put in it and where he had got it from. The hour. Aunt Petunia's face. How light he had felt afterwards.

Evelyn didn't interrupt.

She looked at the quills in the window. In the middle was a swan's feather, very long and white, on a little velvet stand, and she looked at it the whole time he was talking, as though she would be asked to describe it later.

When he had finished, she went on looking at it.

"How long did she cry?"

"An hour."

"An hour exactly?"

"About an hour. The clock struck eight and then nine."

"So between an hour and two hours," Evelyn reasoned. "If she started before eight."

She paused.

"Did you mean to?"

"Yes."

"You decided."

"Yes."

"Before or after she said the thing about your mother?"

Harry thought about it.

"After. About two seconds after."

Evelyn nodded slowly, as though that were an important figure, and it was the right one.

"Would you do it again?"

Harry didn't answer for a long time. A witch with a pram went past behind them. The pram held a small, furious baby, and Harry felt its fury, small and red and all-consuming, and then it was gone as the pram went round the corner.

"I don't know," he said.

Evelyn turned round from the window and looked at him.

He couldn't read her. He never could. He looked at her face, the same face as always, the one people forgot, and he had no idea at all what lay behind it. For the first time in two years, that frightened him a little, because he wanted very much to know what she thought of him.

"Thank you for telling me," she said.

That was all she said about it.

They walked back down the street. At the door of the apothecary, where three steps rose from the pavement, Isadora was waiting for them with her ice finished. She had come up the street to meet them, and Harry didn't know why.

When they reached her, she held out her arm to him.

He took it. He thought she wanted to be helped down the three steps, and she did. She leaned on him all the way down, and she was much lighter than he had expected, and much heavier than she had been a year ago when she had walked into Privet Drive and made Uncle Vernon sit.

At the bottom, she let go.

"Thank you, Mr Potter."

Evelyn was looking at the pavement.

* * *

The Weasleys came back from Egypt on the last night of the holidays.

They had won seven hundred Galleons in a *Daily Prophet* draw and spent a month in Egypt visiting their eldest son. Mr Weasley told Harry so three times. Ron told him once, very stiffly, then went red and went upstairs. Ron had a rat in his top pocket, old and thin and missing a toe.

Hermione Granger was there too, with a cat.

It was large and ginger and bandy-legged, with a squashed face. It hated the rat, and it looked at Harry with flat yellow eyes. Harry read it. It was faint, like all animals, and cleverer than a cat had any business being.

Hermione said hello to him, and he said hello back.

She looked as though she wanted to say something else, and didn't. Harry read that she was remembering a misty pitch at six in the morning, and a word, and him standing there. He didn't know what to do with that, so he did nothing.

He went to bed at ten.

His room on the second floor was next to the one Mr and Mrs Weasley had been given. The walls of the Leaky Cauldron were old and thin and full of gaps, and Harry didn't need gaps.

He wasn't trying to listen. He was lying on his bed thinking about the door behind the stone feet, which he could feel even here, faint and steady, a long way north.

Then Mrs Weasley was frightened.

It came through the wall all at once, the way it did when somebody had just been told something. It was very large and all aimed at one person, and it was a mother's fear, which was a particular kind, and which Harry had felt once before at King's Cross.

It wasn't aimed at Ron.

"…but he has a right to know," Mr Weasley was saying, low, though Harry could hear it. "Molly, he's thirteen. He's not a baby. He went down into that Chamber on his own…"

"Arthur, he's a child, and he's had the most dreadful year, and if you tell him there's a murderer looking for him he'll never sleep again…"

"He'll be safer if he knows. If he knows to keep his head down. Fudge wants him told nothing, Fudge wants everybody told nothing…"

"Fudge is right."

"Fudge is terrified," Mr Weasley said, his voice dropping further. "Molly. Listen to me. The guards at Azkaban said Black had been talking in his sleep. For weeks. The same thing. Over and over."

There was a pause.

"*He's at Hogwarts*."

Mrs Weasley had nothing to say to that.

"Black wants Harry Potter," Mr Weasley went on. "That's what Fudge thinks. He thinks Black's got it into his head that if he kills Harry, it'll bring You-Know-Who back. He was his right-hand man. He gave the Potters away. And Harry's the reason it all ended. Black's had twelve years in a cell to think about that."

Harry lay very still.

He read Mr Weasley through the wall. He was worried, deeply and steadily, and the worry was all for Harry. He wasn't lying, nor exaggerating. He believed every word.

So did Mrs Weasley. She was crying now, quietly.

"He's safe at Hogwarts. Dumbledore's there. He's safe there, Arthur. Isn't he?"

"There'll be Dementors at every gate. Fudge has insisted. Dumbledore's furious about it."

Another pause.

"Yes. He's safe there."

Harry read him.

He didn't believe it. He wanted to, very much, but he didn't.

Harry lay on his bed in the dark and looked at the ceiling.

He thought about the face on the newspaper. Twelve years. Thirteen people with one curse, and then laughing in the street. He thought about the word *gave*. He thought about his mother in the mirror, afraid for him.

A man had given his parents to Voldemort, and the man was out, and he was coming.

And he thought, very clearly and very calmly, the way he had at the dinner table in Privet Drive with the potatoes going round, about what he was going to do.

He wasn't going to tell anybody. Not Mr Weasley, who would want to help. Not Dumbledore, who would want to protect him. Not even Evelyn, yet.

He was going to go down to breakfast in the morning, say good morning to Mrs Weasley, eat his eggs, get on the train and be ordinary. He was going to do absolutely nothing that anybody could see.

He turned over and went to sleep.

He slept very well.
