## Chapter 28: The Hog's Head

"We're shut," the barman said.

He didn't look up. He was behind the bar at the far end of the one small room, wiping a glass with a cloth much dirtier than the glass. The room was dark, lit by two stubs of candle on tables nobody was sitting at, and it smelled strongly of goats.

"The door was open," Evelyn said.

"Door's always open. Doesn't mean I'm not shut," he replied, putting the glass down and picking up another. "What do two Hufflepuff second-years want in my pub at midnight? Besides a hiding."

Harry read him.

He had been reading him through the door, and it was the same now, only closer. The man was very old, tall and thin, with long grey hair and a long grey beard that both wanted cutting, and he was wearing something that might once have been a robe and was now mostly patches. And he was loud.

He wasn't loud the way Hagrid was, nor Aunt Marge. He was loud the way a cellar full of something was loud, from underneath, through the floor. Everything in him had been held down for so long that it had gone hard and packed together, like earth.

On top was irritation. That was ordinary, a man who wanted to go to bed.

Beneath the irritation was bitterness.

It was very old, older than anything Harry had ever felt in a person, older than Hagrid's grief or Filch's sourness or Snape's loathing. It had been there so long that it had a shape, and the shape was aimed quite precisely at one person. It wasn't aimed at anybody here. It was aimed at somebody a long way off, somebody the old man thought about every day without wanting to.

Beneath the bitterness, so deep that Harry nearly missed it, was something else. It was gruff and clumsy and didn't want to be there at all. It was aimed at the two of them. It was the feeling of a man who didn't like children and had never once in his life been able to stand by whilst somebody hurt one.

He wasn't going to tell anybody they were here.

Harry was nearly sure of that. He read it again carefully, all the way down, and he was sure.

There was one more thing, small and sour and very human, on top of the bitterness. The old man was used to being wrong about people, and used to being told he was wrong. He would have liked very much, just once, to be shown that he was right about something.

Harry let the faces go.

He did it all at once. He had been holding them for so long that letting them go was like putting down two suitcases at the top of a hill, and his knees nearly buckled. He put a hand on the back of a chair.

The barman looked up.

He looked at Harry, at the black hair and the glasses and the face and the scar. Then he looked at the robes, which were Slytherin green with a snake on them, and at Harry's height, which was a thirteen-year-old's, and at Evelyn beside him, plain and brown-haired, in the same green. His eyes were very blue, bright and sharp, and they didn't miss anything.

They went back to the scar.

The barman considered him for a long moment.

"Well," he said at last. "That's new."

He put the glass down.

"You're too short. And you're too young. And you're in the wrong house," he said, before looking at Evelyn. "And you're nobody I've ever seen. And you came out of nowhere at midnight wearing two other children's faces."

He folded the cloth.

"Sit down before you fall down. I'll get you something to eat. And then you can tell me as much as you like, and I'll decide how much of it I want to hear, which won't be much."

* * *

He gave them bread and a hard yellow cheese and two cups of milk that tasted very strongly of goat, and he sat down on the other side of the table with his arms folded and watched them eat.

He didn't ask them anything.

Harry ate three slices of bread and most of the cheese. He hadn't known he was so hungry. Evelyn ate one slice of bread slowly, in four pieces, and drank all of her milk without saying anything about the taste, and Harry knew from the way she set the cup down that it had been very bad indeed.

"There's a room upstairs," the old man said. "It's got a bed in it. It's not much of a bed. Nobody's slept in it for about ten years except a goat called Mabel, once, when she was poorly. You can have it."

"Thank you," Evelyn said.

"Don't thank me. I haven't decided anything," he replied, looking at Harry. "You're Potter."

"Yes."

"Not the one up at the school."

"No."

"I didn't think so. I've seen the one up at the school. He's taller, and he's got a face like a slapped arse every time anybody mentions the Ministry, and he's in Gryffindor, God help him," the old man said, looking at Harry's robes again. "Slytherin. Well. Well, well. Somebody somewhere got a nasty shock."

"Do you want to know where we came from?" Harry asked.

"No."

Harry looked at him.

"I've lived in this village a long time, boy. I've learned that people who come in at midnight and tell me where they came from are mostly lying, and the ones who aren't lying are mostly worse. You're here. You're hungry. You can't keep that face up much longer, I can see it on you," he said, nodding at Harry's hands, which were shaking slightly on the table. "That's all I need to know tonight."

He stood up.

"Aberforth. If you're wondering. Aberforth Dumbledore."

Harry went still.

He read him, and the bitterness rose right up to the top at the sound of his own surname, then settled again slowly, like silt in a glass of water, aimed at one person a long way off.

"Dumbledore," Harry repeated.

"Albus is my brother. Before you ask. I'll tell you once and then we needn't talk about him," Aberforth said, picking up the plate. "Bed's up the stairs and on the left. Mind the third step, it isn't there."

* * *

They stayed at the Hog's Head for two days before anything happened.

Harry slept. He slept for fourteen hours the first night in a narrow, lumpy bed in a room that smelled faintly of goat, whilst Evelyn slept on a pile of blankets on the floor, because she said she would rather sleep on the floor than in a bed Mabel had been poorly in. He woke at two in the afternoon not knowing where he was. Then he remembered, and he lay on his back for a long time looking at the ceiling, holding nothing.

He could feel the village.

It wasn't like the castle. The castle was a roar of three hundred children and a dozen teachers with Umbridge's quiet, sweet certainty beneath all of it. Hogsmeade was small and scattered. A woman in the house behind, worried about her sister. Two men in the street arguing about a cart. Somebody in the Three Broomsticks at the far end of the high street who was frightened all the time in a low, steady way, and who Harry thought from the weight of it might be Madam Rosmerta. A great many goats, very faintly, like voices in another field.

And beneath him, in the bar, Aberforth.

Aberforth was always there. He didn't seem to go out. He wiped glasses and served the few people who came in during the day, who were mostly hooded and mostly didn't speak. In the evening, he went out through the back to the goats, and Harry could feel him out there in the yard, and the bitterness in him went quiet when he was with the goats. Not gone. Quiet, as though it had been told to wait outside.

On the second evening, Harry went down and sat at the bar.

He didn't have a plan. He had found that he didn't need one with Aberforth. Aberforth said what he thought, and what he thought was usually exactly what he felt, which made him the easiest man to read that Harry had met since Hagrid.

"Where's the girl?" Aberforth asked.

"Asleep. Or reading. She found a book under the bed."

"That'll be the almanac. Nineteen sixty-two. It's under there to stop the leg wobbling," Aberforth replied, pouring him something from a jug. It was more goat's milk. "Tell her to put it back after."

"She will."

They sat. Aberforth wiped a glass.

"You can feel things," he said. "Can't you."

Harry looked at him.

"I watched you come in. You stopped in the door. You stood there like a dog that's heard something. And then you let those faces go, and you'd never have done that unless you'd made up your mind I wasn't going to sell you," Aberforth said, setting the glass down. "I've seen it once before. A long time ago. In a girl. She could feel things. Couldn't stop. Feeling everybody, all the time."

He picked up another glass.

"It didn't do her much good."

"What happened to her?"

"She died. She was fourteen," Aberforth said, wiping the glass. "Next question."

For a while, Harry didn't ask one.

He read the old man. The bitterness was there, but it had changed shape slightly. Beneath it was a grief even older than the bitterness, which had been there first and was what the bitterness had grown on, the way moss grew on a stone.

"You don't like your brother," Harry said.

Aberforth laughed, a short, hard sound like a stick breaking.

"Does it show?"

"A bit."

"I'll tell you something about my brother, boy," Aberforth said, setting the glass down and leaning on the bar to look at Harry with his bright blue eyes, which were Albus Dumbledore's eyes and nothing like them. "Since you're a Potter, and since it'll come in handy, whatever world you crawled out of. My brother loves people. He does. He's not lying about that. He loves people more than most, and he's cleverer than all of them, and he always knows what's for the best."

He tapped the bar with one finger.

"And he'll use you. He uses everyone he loves, and he loves you, so watch out."

Harry went quiet.

He was thinking about a mirror in a disused classroom, and an old man in a blue dressing gown telling him a kind lie, and the thing beneath the sorrow that had been turning him over like a stone in its hands. He was thinking about a hospital wing and a quiet satisfaction, the satisfaction of a man who had seen the last piece go exactly where he meant it to. He was thinking about a hut on a night in May, and calm.

He had three lines in his head beneath Dumbledore's name. He had kept them for two years and shown them to Evelyn once.

He added a fourth.

*His brother says: he uses everyone he loves.*

"I know," Harry said.

Aberforth looked at him.

"Do you," he said, and it wasn't a question. He looked at Harry for a long time, and the gruff, buried thing beneath the bitterness rose a little way and looked at Harry too. "Yes. I think you probably do."

He picked up the jug.

"I've sent word. To somebody. About you. Last night."

Harry went very still.

"Not to him," Aberforth said. "Don't look at me like that. I'd sooner feed you to Mabel. To somebody else. Somebody who's got a right to know there's a Potter in my upstairs room, and who won't go running to my brother with it, because he can't stand being told to sit still any more than I can."

He poured.

"He'll come or he won't. If he comes, it'll be by the back stairs, and it won't be in a hurry, because he's not allowed out. And if he comes, you'll want to be sitting down."

* * *

He came on the third night.

Harry was in the room upstairs. It was after eleven. Evelyn was sitting on her blankets on the floor with the 1962 almanac on her knee, reading the tide tables for Grimsby, because, she said, they were the only thing in it that wasn't out of date. Harry was at the window. It looked out over the yard at the back where the goats were, and a narrow lane, and beyond the lane the dark fields rising towards the forest.

He felt it before he saw it.

He felt it the way he had once before, on a street corner in Little Whinging, beside a dead lamp post opposite a gap between a garage and a fence.

It was a person's feeling.

It was coming up the lane from the fields, low down and fast, and it was enormous. It was loud the way only a very few people Harry had ever met were loud, Hagrid, Mrs Weasley, the whole of the Slytherin stand at a match. It was loud and all one thing, coming up the lane, and this time there was no grief in it and nothing wild. Harry had felt something like it only once before, in a room with a mirror in it, from a man with glasses and black hair who had stood behind him in the glass.

It was aimed at the window.

"Evelyn," Harry said.

She looked up.

Something came over the yard wall in one long leap and landed amongst the goats, who didn't seem to mind. It was a dog, a very large black dog, thin and shaggy, with eyes that shone in the light from the window. It looked up.

It looked straight at Harry.

Then it crossed the yard. Harry heard the back door, and heard it come up the stairs, and heard it miss the third step, which wasn't there, and swear.

Dogs didn't swear.

The door opened.

It was a man.

He was tall and thin, much too thin, with a great deal of black hair that had been washed recently and still needed cutting, and a face that had been handsome once and was still handsome beneath it all in a starved, hollow, used-up way. His eyes were grey and very bright. He was wearing robes much too good for the Hog's Head, and they were covered in dog hair.

He stopped in the doorway and looked at Harry by the window.

Harry knew the face. He had seen it on the television in Privet Drive, and on the front of Stan Shunpike's newspaper, and on a poster on the post office wall four nights ago, blinking at him from very far back. Now it was right here, six feet away, in the doorway of a room that smelled of goats, looking at him.

Sirius Black.

Harry didn't move.

He had a list in the inside pocket of his robes, folded twice. It said: *When he comes, I don't fight him. I read him instead.*

He read him.

And it was love.

It was all love. It came across the room at him like a wave rolling up a beach, and it didn't stop, and there was so much of it that for a moment Harry couldn't find anything else. Apart from Hagrid on a rock, it was the loudest thing he had ever felt, and nearly louder than that. It was so loud it was nearly painful, the way light was painful after the dark, and every bit of it was for him, and none of it was really for him. Most of it belonged to a boy in a tower two miles away who was taller and older and in Gryffindor. And it was for a man with glasses and black hair who had been dead for fifteen years. Harry was standing where both of them should have been, and it had nowhere else to go, so all of it came to him.

Beneath the love, when he could find it, was recklessness, a great deal of it, like a horse that had never been broken.

Beneath that was despair, grey and flat and very old, a cage of a feeling. The man had been living in it for a long time and hated it more than anything in the world.

And beneath the despair, rising through all of it right now, at this moment, looking at Harry, was delight.

"Merlin," Sirius Black breathed. "Look at you."

His voice was hoarse, like a voice that hadn't been used properly for a long time.

"Look at you. You're tiny. You're about twelve. You're a *Slytherin*."

He laughed, a bark of a laugh very like a dog's.

"Aberforth said. I didn't believe him. I said, Ab, you've finally gone, you've been at the goats too long. Look at you."

He took a step into the room. Harry didn't move.

The man stopped.

"Sorry. Sorry. You don't know me. Of course you don't know me. I'm…"

"I know who you are," Harry said.

His voice came out quiet, as it always did when he was angry. He hadn't known he was angry until he heard it.

Sirius Black looked at him.

The delight didn't fade. It stayed exactly where it was. But something rose quickly beside it, a sharp new attention, the attention of a man who had been hunted for a long time and had just heard a twig snap.

"Do you," he said.

"In my world," Harry said, "you're a murderer."

He said it quite carefully. On the window seat, before the dog came over the wall, he had thought about how to say it if he ever said it, and he had decided to say it plainly, because he wanted to see what happened when he did.

"In my world you were my parents' Secret Keeper. You were my father's best friend and you were my godfather, and you gave them to Voldemort inside a week. And then you killed a man called Peter Pettigrew in a street full of Muggles, and twelve Muggles with him, and you stood in the road and laughed. You've been in Azkaban for twelve years. You got out last summer. You came into the castle in February with a knife and stood over Ron Weasley's bed because you thought it was mine."

He stopped.

"I've been planning to kill you since December."

Evelyn had put down the almanac.

Sirius Black stood in the middle of the room.

For perhaps five seconds, he said nothing. Harry read him the whole time. The love didn't fade, nor the delight. But the despair rose slowly from the bottom all the way to the top and spread out over everything, grey and flat, and for a moment Harry thought the man was going to sit down on the floor.

He didn't sit down.

He laughed.

It was nothing like the bark of a moment ago. It was high and thin and dreadful, and it went on too long, and there was nothing funny in it. It was the laugh, Harry thought, of a man in a street full of bodies, and he stood by the window and listened to it and didn't move.

It stopped.

"Of course you have," Sirius Black said. "Of course you have. Why wouldn't you? Everybody else has."

He wiped his face with the back of his hand.

"Merlin. Merlin, I'm sorry. That wasn't for you. That was… you've no idea how funny that is. You can't have. Sit down. Please. Sit down, Harry, and let me tell you about a rat."

* * *

He told it all.

He told it sitting on the end of the narrow bed with his elbows on his knees and his hands hanging, the way Harry had sat in the Room of Requirement, and he didn't stop, and Harry didn't interrupt him once.

He told him about four boys at Hogwarts. James Potter, Sirius Black, Remus Lupin and Peter Pettigrew. He told him Remus was a werewolf, and that the other three had spent five years learning to become Animagi so that they could go with him at the full moon and keep him company, and that it had worked. James was a stag. Sirius was the dog. Peter was a rat.

"A rat," Sirius said. "Should've known. Should've known from the start. But he was so…"

He moved a hand.

"He was ours. He was always just ours. You don't look at your own like that."

He told him that when the Potters went into hiding, everybody had expected Sirius to be their Keeper, including Voldemort, and that Sirius had thought he was being clever.

"I said, use Peter. Nobody'll think of Peter. They'll come for me, and I'll hold out, and they'll never even look at him," he said with another very short laugh. "Brilliant. I was very pleased with myself. I thought I was a genius. I was twenty-one."

He told him that he had gone to check on Peter on the night of Hallowe'en and found his hideout empty with no sign of a struggle. That he had gone to Godric's Hollow, and seen the house.

He didn't tell him what he had seen. He stopped there and didn't go on for a while, and Harry read him and didn't need him to.

He told him about the street.

"I cornered him. Peter. Next day. I'd gone looking. I found him in a street full of Muggles and I had my wand out and I was going to kill him, I'm not going to pretend I wasn't. And he shouted. So everybody could hear. *Lily and James, Sirius, how could you.* And then, before I could do anything, he blew the street apart behind his back, and he cut off his own finger, and he turned into a rat, and he went down the sewer with the rest of them."

Sirius looked at his hands.

"That's the finger they found. That's all of him they found. His own finger. He cut it off himself. I've thought about that every day for fourteen years. I couldn't have done that. I'd never have thought of it."

"And you laughed," Harry said.

"I laughed," Sirius admitted without looking up. "Twelve dead Muggles and James and Lily gone and the little rat had done me, done me completely, in about four seconds, and I was going to Azkaban for it, and I knew it. Of course I laughed. What else was there to do?"

Harry read him.

It was true.

He read it the way he had read Hagrid in the Three Broomsticks, all the way down, every layer, and it was true, every word. There was no lie anywhere in it. There was the old despair, and beneath the despair the old fury, and beneath the fury, at the very bottom, so deep it had worn a channel in him, was grief. It was grief for James, the oldest, plainest, most worn-smooth grief Harry had ever felt. It was older than Aberforth's. It had been the floor of this man's life for fifteen years.

Harry sat on the window seat.

He thought about a list, folded twice, in the inside pocket of his robes. He thought about writing it in blue-black ink at a black stone desk with snow on his shoulders. He thought about the tenth line. *Quirrell did it himself.*

He thought about a big book with brass corners and a passage he had marked, and Evelyn sitting on her cushion with her face like a shut door, saying *I'm not going to be the person who looked it up.*

He thought about the eighteenth of December. Seven weeks and two days. And then the rest of February, and the beginning of March.

He had spent three months planning, very calmly and very neatly, to find the deepest thing in an innocent man and give it back to him until his heart stopped.

He said nothing.

His hands were shaking, and he didn't try to stop them.

"Which toe?"

It was Evelyn.

She was sitting on her blankets on the floor with the almanac closed on her knee, looking at Sirius, and her face was the same as always.

Sirius looked at her as though he had only just noticed she was there.

"What?"

"The rat," Evelyn said. "He cut off a finger. When he's a rat, which bit's missing? Which paw? Which toe?"

She didn't change her voice.

"If he's still a rat, somebody might have him. Somebody might have a rat with a toe missing. It would help to know which one."

Sirius stared at her.

Then something happened to his face, and the delight surged back up through the despair all at once, like a bubble through water.

"Who are you?"

"Evelyn Selwyn."

"Selwyn. One of Corvin's?"

"Yes."

"Merlin. I'm sorry for you."

He was grinning now. It was a real grin, a young one, and it made his starved face look about twenty.

"Front paw. Right front. The middle toe. Clean off at the first joint. I've seen him. I saw him in the paper, in my world, the summer before I got out. Some Ministry man won a prize and had his family photographed in Egypt, and there was the little rat, sitting on his youngest son's shoulder, bold as you like, with his toe missing."

Harry went very still.

"Egypt," he said.

"Egypt. The Weasleys. Arthur Weasley's lot. Big ginger family. Peter's been living as their pet for twelve years," Sirius said, looking at him. "Why? What is it?"

Harry thought about a bar in the Leaky Cauldron on the last night of August, and a red-haired boy saying very stiffly that they had won a prize, then going red and going upstairs. He thought about a rat in the boy's top pocket, old and thin and miserable and missing a toe.

He thought about a dormitory in Gryffindor Tower, and a man standing over the wrong bed with a knife.

Not the wrong bed.

The right bed. The bed with the rat on it.

"I've seen it," Harry said. "In my world. In August. Ron Weasley's got it. He had it in his pocket at the Leaky Cauldron."

He heard his own voice, very quiet.

"You didn't come into the tower for me. In my world. You came for the rat."

Sirius looked at him for a long moment.

"I'd imagine I did. Yes. I'd imagine that's exactly what I did," he said, rubbing his face with both hands. "Merlin. Me. In your world. Out there on my own with no idea who to trust, and a boy who hates me, and a rat in a tower."

He dropped his hands.

"Find it, Harry. When you get home. Find the rat. And for God's sake, save my other self some trouble."

* * *

He stayed until two in the morning.

Aberforth brought up a bottle of something that wasn't goat's milk and two glasses, and a third glass of goat's milk for Harry and a fourth for Evelyn, who looked at it and thanked him and put it on the floor. He didn't stay. He looked at Sirius on the end of the bed and Harry on the window seat.

"Don't be long. You're not supposed to be out. If my brother finds out I'll never hear the end of it."

He went back downstairs.

Sirius drank.

He talked about James. He couldn't stop talking about James. He talked about him the way some people talked about the weather or the news, because it was the thing that was there. James at eleven on the train. James at fifteen, failing to get anybody to go to Hogsmeade with him. James learning to be a stag.

"Took him three years. Three years of nothing, and then one night in our fifth year he got it, all at once, at about two in the morning, in the middle of the dormitory. And he was enormous. Antlers out to here. And he couldn't get out of the dormitory, because the door was a door, and he was a stag, and he couldn't turn back, because he'd forgotten how. So he stood there all night in the middle of the floor between the beds with his antlers wedged in the curtains of Frank Longbottom's four-poster, very dignified, absolutely silent, until about six, when he remembered."

Sirius was grinning.

"Frank slept through the whole thing. Never knew. Woke up and found his bed hangings full of holes and spent a week blaming the house-elves."

Harry laughed.

He didn't expect it. It burst out of him all at once, the way it had in a white ward at St Mungo's with a man signing his own get-well cards, and he couldn't stop it. He thought about a stag in a dormitory with its antlers in the curtains, very dignified, absolutely silent, until about six, and he laughed until he had to hold on to the window seat.

Sirius was watching him.

Harry read him, and the delight had risen all the way to the top of everything now, louder than the despair, louder than anything else in him. A man telling a good story didn't feel like that.

"That," Sirius said softly. "That's James. That's his laugh. You do it exactly like him."

Harry stopped laughing.

He didn't know what to say.

Sirius looked down into his glass.

"He's…"

He stopped.

"Harry. The other one. Mine. Up at the school," he went on without looking up. "You've seen him? Aberforth said you'd been up there a week."

"Yes. I've seen him."

"Is he all right?"

Harry didn't answer at once.

"I can't get to him," Sirius said. "I'm not allowed out. Dumbledore's orders. I'm stuck in a house I hate, with a house-elf who hates me, and a portrait of my mother screaming at me from behind the curtains in the hall, and he's up there with that woman, with Umbridge, and I can't… I get letters. Sometimes. When it's safe. He doesn't say much."

He turned the glass round.

"Is he happy? You'd know. You can tell, can't you? Ab said. Is he all right?"

Harry looked at him.

He thought about the tall boy in the corridor outside the library with his hands in his pockets and his face set, angry at everything, so angry that it had worn a groove in him. He thought about the red-haired boy and the bushy-haired girl walking either side of him, loving him, and the boy not noticing. He thought about a room full of people who trusted him like a staircase, and a stag walking through a wall.

He thought about the cold thing at the bottom of him, in the place where he lived, that wasn't his.

He read Sirius.

He read him very carefully. The love, enormous, aimed at the window and the tower and the boy in it. The recklessness. The despair, the grey, flat cage of it. And beneath all of it, right now, holding very still, waiting for the answer, was need. It was the simplest thing Harry had ever felt in him. It was the need of a man in a cage for one thing in the world to be all right.

It needed the answer to be yes.

"Yes," Harry said. "He's all right. He's got friends. Two of them. They're always with him. He's teaching a club. Defence. A dozen people. They'd follow him anywhere."

He paused.

"He's angry. About the Ministry. But he's all right."

Sirius closed his eyes.

Harry read the need go all at once, the way a held breath went. Something rose behind it so much like relief that Harry couldn't tell them apart.

"Good," Sirius murmured. "Good. That's good."

He opened his eyes, grinned again and finished his drink.

"Course he is. James's boy. He'd be all right in a cellar."

Harry looked into his glass.

He didn't know if it was true. He had read every part of the tall boy he could reach. He had read the anger and the love around him and the cold at the bottom, and he didn't know whether any of it added up to a boy who was all right. He had said yes because a man who was going back to a cage needed him to.

He thought he had done it very well. He thought it was the kindest lie he had ever told.

He wasn't sure the two things were different.

* * *

Sirius left at two.

He stood up and stretched, and his back cracked, and he looked round the small room with its goat smell and its lumpy bed and the almanac on the floor, and at Evelyn on her blankets, who hadn't said anything since the toe, and at Harry on the window seat.

"I'll come back. If Ab'll let me. If I can get out," he said, before hesitating. "You'll be here?"

"I don't know. We're trying to get home."

"Right. Course you are," Sirius said, looking at him. "If you get there before I come back. If I don't see you."

He stopped. Something moved in his face, quickly, and was gone.

"Find the rat."

"I will."

"And Harry," Sirius added from the door. "The other me. Out there in your world, on his own, with his knife."

He said it lightly.

"Go easy on him. He's had a rotten time. And he's an idiot. But he'd die for you, whatever he looks like. I know he would," he said with a grin. "I would."

He went out.

Harry heard him on the stairs. He heard him miss the third step again and swear again, more quietly. He heard the back door.

He went to the window.

The yard was dark. The goats were huddled asleep against the far wall. Then the back door opened below him, and a dog came out.

It was a huge black dog, thin and shaggy, and it crossed the yard without hurrying, between the sleeping goats, to the wall. It stopped at the bottom of the wall and turned its head and looked up at the window, at Harry, its eyes catching the light.

It looked at him for a long moment.

Then it went over the wall in one long leap and down the lane, low and fast, towards the dark fields and the forest. Harry stood at the window and watched it go, and went on watching the place where it had gone long after the lane was empty.

Behind him, Evelyn picked up the almanac again and opened it at the tide tables for Grimsby, and didn't read them.

## Chapter 29: The Other Watch

Evelyn showed Aberforth the watch on the Thursday after Sirius came, at the bar at eleven in the morning, because she had decided that a man who didn't want to know anything was the safest person in the world to show it to.

She set it on the bar between them, on a cloth.

"It stopped. When we came. It won't wind. I want to know who made it."

Aberforth didn't pick it up.

Harry was on the next stool. He had been reading Aberforth all morning out of habit, the bitterness and the grief beneath it and the gruff thing beneath that, and he was reading him when Evelyn put the watch down, so he felt it happen.

Aberforth went still.

From the outside, it wasn't a large stillness. He didn't move his hands, and his face didn't change much. He looked down at the small gold watch with its ivy-leaf lid on the dirty cloth, and he didn't touch it, and he didn't speak.

Inside, everything stopped.

The bitterness stopped, and so did the irritation. All of the packed old earth of him went quite still, the way a field went still when a hawk passed over, and then something rose through the stillness that Harry hadn't felt in him before. It was shock, very old shock, older than Harry, much older than Harry's parents, and it was so large and so sudden that Harry thought the old man might sit down. It hadn't risen in him like that, Harry thought, for fifty years. Perhaps more.

Aberforth reached out one finger and turned the watch over.

He looked at the back of the case, at the tiny mark beneath the ivy leaves, worn almost smooth, the little triangle with something inside it.

He turned it back.

"Where did you get this?"

His voice was perfectly ordinary. Harry read the shock still going on beneath it, enormous, with the ordinary voice sitting on top of it like a lid on a boiling pan.

"My grandmother gave it to me," Evelyn replied. "When I was eleven."

"Your grandmother."

"Isadora Hale."

Aberforth closed his eyes.

He kept them closed for about four seconds. Harry counted, because he knew Evelyn would be counting. When he opened them again, the shock had sunk a little way, and in its place was something Harry could only have called recognition. It was bitter, very bitter, and it wasn't aimed at anybody in the room.

"Who made it?" Evelyn asked.

"I'm not going to tell you that."

"You know."

"I know. I've seen work like it once in my life, and I've seen that mark more than I'd ever want to. I know whose hand made that, girl, and I'm not going to tell you."

"Why not?"

"Because it's not mine to tell," Aberforth said, pushing the watch back across the cloth towards her with one finger, the way one might push a coin back to somebody who had offered too much. "Ask whoever gave it to you."

"She's dead."

Aberforth looked at her.

"In February. In my world. In her sleep. In June, in yours. I found it in the *Prophet*," Evelyn said, her voice unchanged. "There isn't anybody to ask. That's why I'm asking you."

Harry read him.

The bitterness rose again slowly, and with it, just beneath it, the clumsy, gruff thing that didn't want to be there. It was looking at Evelyn, and it was very sorry.

"I'm sorry," Aberforth said.

"Thank you."

"I'm still not going to tell you."

"No. I didn't think you would," Evelyn replied, picking up the watch, closing it and holding it in her hand. "Then tell me what it is. You can tell me that. It isn't anybody's secret what a thing is."

Aberforth looked at her for a long time.

"A Seer made it," he said at last. "That's what it is. It's a Seer's piece. There's nothing else like it. Most people who see the future see it in fits and starts, in smoke, in tea leaves, in their sleep, and they can't do anything with it but shout. A few, a very few, see it plainly. And one or two of those, once in a hundred years, learn to put what they see into a thing. A ring. A glass. A watch."

He nodded at her hand.

"That's a watch that knows where the next hour is. Not the one after this. The one beside it."

"Beside it," Evelyn repeated.

"There's more than one way things could have gone. Every time. You know that, I expect, you're a clever girl. That watch knows the nearest. And if you wind it the wrong way, it takes you there," he said, looking at Harry. "As you've found out."

"How do we get back?" Harry asked.

Aberforth was quiet for a while. He picked up a glass and didn't wipe it.

"It'll have a twin. Here. A thing like that, made by a hand like that, would have been made more than once. Wherever the maker was, he made it again. Same hand, same watch, same girl to give it to."

He set the glass down.

"To go home, you'd need the twin from this side. Wound forwards. By somebody of the same blood as the girl it was made for. In a place where time is held still."

"What's a place where time is held still?" Evelyn asked.

"There aren't many," Aberforth replied without looking at them. "There's one I know of. In London. Under the Ministry. There's a part of it nobody talks about, where they keep things nobody understands, and in it there's a room full of clocks. I've never been in it. My brother has."

He made a small, sour noise.

"My brother's been everywhere."

"The Department of Mysteries," Evelyn said.

Aberforth looked at her sharply.

"My father sits on the Wizengamot. He mentions it. He doesn't say what's in it. He says it the way people say *the cellar*, when there's something in the cellar."

"Then your father's got more sense than I'd have credited a Selwyn with," Aberforth said, picking up his cloth. "Twin. Forwards. Her blood. A room full of clocks under London."

At last he began to wipe the glass.

"That's all I know. That's all I'm going to say. And you don't want to go anywhere near that building this summer, either of you. There's things moving there you've no idea about."

He turned away.

Harry read him all the way to the end of the bar. The shock had sunk, but it hadn't gone. It was sitting in him now beneath the bitterness, very large and very quiet, with something new beside it, and the new thing was fear. It wasn't fear for himself.

It was aimed at the watch.

* * *

"Same blood," Evelyn said upstairs, sitting on her blankets with her notebook. "Same blood as the girl it was made for. That's my grandmother. Or my mother. Or me."

She wrote it down.

"Or her."

"The other Evelyn."

"She's got the twin. She winds it every morning. Twenty turns. I've watched her," Evelyn said, closing the notebook. "She's of the blood. She's got the watch. That's two of the three. The third's a room under London that we can't get into."

"One thing at a time," Harry said.

"That's what my grandmother used to say," Evelyn murmured, looking at the closed notebook on her knee. "She used to say it in French, so Mother couldn't follow."

* * *

They went back into the castle on the Saturday through Honeydukes and the long passage, with Harry holding the two faces.

He was better at it now. He had slept for most of a week in the room over the bar, and eaten. The doors he held were still doors and the wind against them was still wind, but his shoulder against them was stronger. He could hold the two faces for a day. He thought he could probably hold them for two if he had to, and then he thought that he didn't want to find out.

They had a plan. It was Evelyn's plan, and it was very simple.

"I'm going to talk to her," she had said. "On my own. Somewhere nobody comes. And you're not going to be there."

"I should be there."

"You shouldn't. You'll read her. She'll know," Evelyn had said, looking at him. "She's me, Potter. She'll have had the lessons. Every morning from five. She'll be like me. You won't get anything from her, and your face will do the thing it does when you don't get anything, and she'll see it, and she'll want to know what you are."

She had folded her arms.

"And your face won't work on her either. If she's me. Nothing you put on her will take. She'll see you."

Harry hadn't thought of that.

He thought about it now, climbing up through the trapdoor beneath the one-eyed witch, with the corridor dark and empty and the castle quiet around him. Somewhere beneath the lake, in the dungeons, in a sixth-year dormitory, was a girl he couldn't read and couldn't fool and had never met.

There were two of them now.

He didn't know what he felt about that.

* * *

The Inquisitorial Squad caught him on the Monday outside the Charms corridor at twenty past four.

He was on his own. Evelyn was in the library, following the other Evelyn at a distance and waiting for an empty room. Harry had gone to check the Map in a disused bathroom on the third floor and come out at the wrong moment, and three of them were coming round the corner, two Slytherin fifth-years he didn't know and Draco Malfoy.

"You," Malfoy said.

Harry kept walking.

"You. Hufflepuff. Stop."

Harry stopped.

He read them. The two fifth-years were bored and slightly hopeful, the way people were hopeful when they thought they might be about to be allowed to hurt somebody. Malfoy was very pleased. He had a list in his hand, and he was looking at Harry's face, the round mousy face with the ears that stuck out, and matching it against something.

"Second-year. Hufflepuff. Ears. You're one of them, aren't you. The two that've been missing. Cuthbert," Malfoy said with a smile. "We've been looking for you for a fortnight. Professor Umbridge is going to be *delighted*."

Harry thought about running.

He thought about the Cloak in his bag, and the bathroom behind him, and the three of them, and he read Malfoy and found that Malfoy wanted him to run very badly, because it would be more fun.

He didn't run.

"Where's the other one?" one of the fifth-years demanded. "The girl."

"Don't know."

"He doesn't know," Malfoy sneered. "Of course he doesn't. Come on, Cuthbert. Headmistress's office. Let's see what you know when she's asked you nicely."

* * *

The headmistress's office wasn't Dumbledore's office.

Harry didn't know what Dumbledore's office had looked like in this world, but he had been in it at home on the night of the fourth of May, wet and filthy with a sword in his hand and Mrs Weasley's arms around him. He remembered the silver instruments and the portraits of old headmasters asleep in their frames and the phoenix on its perch.

None of it was there.

Or it was there and he couldn't see it. The office was round, as before, and the walls were the same walls, but they had been covered. Every inch he could see was covered in lace and pink and plates. Ornamental plates. There were dozens of them hung in rows, and on each one was a kitten. The kittens moved. They frolicked and played with balls of wool and pounced on each other and gazed out at the room with large, round eyes.

The portraits were hidden behind curtains. The phoenix's perch was empty.

Umbridge sat behind the desk.

She was writing with a short black quill. She didn't look up when Malfoy brought him in, and she let them stand there for about a minute, and Harry read her the whole time.

It was the same as at the staff table. Quiet, pleased, certain, and beneath the certainty, sweetly, the thing that enjoyed being the one who dealt with people. It was enjoying this. It was enjoying the minute.

She looked up.

"Well," she said in a soft, high, girlish voice that went very badly with the rest of her. "Well, well. Mr Malfoy. What have we here?"

"One of the missing second-years, Professor. Hufflepuff. Cuthbert, he says."

"Cuthbert."

Umbridge smiled at Harry. It was a wide, wet smile with nothing in it, and as she did it, Harry read that she was looking forward to the next ten minutes more than she had looked forward to anything all week.

"Do sit down, dear."

Harry sat down.

"There is no Cuthbert in the Hufflepuff second year. There is no Cuthbert in Hufflepuff. There is no Cuthbert at Hogwarts. I have looked," Umbridge said, putting down her quill. "And so I find myself wondering, dear, who exactly you might be, and what you are doing in my school."

Harry looked at her.

He thought about saying something very true and very clever, the way he had at the Leaky Cauldron with Fudge. Then he looked at the kittens, and the curtained portraits, and the empty perch, and the wide, wet smile, and he read the thing beneath the certainty, sweetly looking forward, and he thought that nothing true or clever would make the slightest difference to her.

So he did something else.

He had never done it to anybody who was looking straight at him. He had set coins on tables and faces on himself and Evelyn. He had never set something in front of somebody who didn't know it was coming whilst she watched him, and held it there.

He thought about a cat.

He thought about it very carefully. A very large tomcat, ginger, old and scarred and battle-torn, the sort of cat that sat on the wall behind the chip shop in Little Whinging and looked at people as though they owed it money. One ear half gone. A belly that swung. He held it in his head until he could see every whisker.

He set it on the desk.

He set it only for her. Not for Malfoy, nor the two fifth-years by the door. Only for the woman in pink, the way he would have set a coin on a table for one person. He put it on the desk at her elbow, sitting on her papers, enormous and ginger and very still, looking at her.

Umbridge's eyes went to it.

She stopped smiling.

Harry read her. There was no fear in it. It was more like outrage. It went straight up through the pleasure and the certainty all at once, outrage that something should be there, on her desk, on her papers, without having been given permission.

"*What*," Umbridge demanded in a much less girlish voice, "is *that*?"

Malfoy looked at the desk and then at Umbridge. He didn't see anything, because there was nothing to see.

"Professor?"

The cat stood up.

Harry made it stand up. He made it stretch very slowly all along its scarred ginger back, the way old cats did, and turn round once on her papers and walk to the edge of the desk and look up at the wall.

At the plates.

"Get down," Umbridge hissed. "Get *down*, you filthy creature."

The cat jumped.

It sprang off the desk in one heavy leap and landed on the lowest row of plates, and Harry made her hear the clatter and see the plate swing. The kitten on the plate screamed silently and ran off the edge of the china.

"*No*," Umbridge shrieked.

She was on her feet with her wand out.

The cat walked along the row of plates very slowly, with great dignity, and as it passed each one it put out a paw, quite casually, and knocked it. Each plate swung. Each kitten fled. Umbridge came round the end of her desk with her wand raised and her face going a dark, mottled pink, and she pointed her wand at the cat, and the cat looked at her over its shoulder, and Harry made it yawn.

"*Professor Umbridge?*" Malfoy ventured.

Umbridge didn't hear him. She fired a spell at the wall. It passed through the place where the cat was and struck a real plate, which cracked across the middle, and the kitten in it went white with fright and hid behind its own ball of wool.

The cat wasn't there any more.

It was on top of the curtained portraits, on the rail, washing itself.

"Get it," Umbridge screeched in a high, terrible voice. "Get it, get it, Draco, *get that animal out of my office*."

Malfoy looked at the curtain rail.

He looked at it very hard. Harry read him. Malfoy could see nothing on the curtain rail but curtain rail. He was confused, and beneath the confusion he was a little frightened, because a headmistress was shrieking at a curtain rail. Beneath that, a long way down and very quietly, a part of Malfoy that liked Umbridge no better than Harry did was beginning, very slightly, to enjoy itself.

"Professor," Malfoy said carefully. "There isn't…"

"*Get it!*"

Malfoy pointed his wand at the curtain rail and muttered something, and the curtain came down. Behind it, in a frame, an old wizard with a long white beard woke up.

"Good heavens, what's all this?"

Umbridge screamed at him too.

Harry stood up.

Nobody was looking at him. Nobody in the room was looking at anything but the curtain rail and the plates and the headmistress, purple in the face, firing spells at a wall. He walked to the door. The two fifth-years by it were staring at Umbridge with their mouths open, and he walked between them, opened the door, stepped out onto the moving staircase and closed it behind him, and as he went down, he let the cat go.

He held the face. He let the cat go.

He made it go very slowly. He made it walk to the window and sit on the sill and look at Umbridge for a long moment with great contempt, the way the cats on the wall behind the chip shop looked at everybody. Then he took it away, the way one took a coin off a table, and faintly through the door, as the staircase turned, he heard her shriek in a voice like a kettle about to boil.

"Where did it *go*?"

He went down the stairs.

He was smiling. He could feel it, and he couldn't stop.

He thought about Umbridge's face, mottled purple, firing curses at her own plates, and about a kitten going white with fright behind its ball of wool, and about a woman in a pink office who enjoyed dealing with people being dealt with, for once, by somebody she couldn't see.

He enjoyed it.

He enjoyed it very much all the way down the staircase and along the corridor and round the corner, and he didn't try to stop enjoying it. It wasn't until much later that he thought he had done to her more or less exactly what she enjoyed doing to everybody else.

* * *

Evelyn found her alone in an empty classroom on the fifth floor at ten past five on the Tuesday.

She had followed her there from the library at a distance, as a Hufflepuff second-year with freckles. She had watched her go in and close the door, and she had waited in the corridor outside for four minutes to see whether anybody else came.

Nobody came.

Nobody ever would, Evelyn thought. That was why she had chosen it.

She went in.

The other Evelyn was at a desk by the window with a book. It wasn't a schoolbook. It was a small, battered paperback with a green spine, and Evelyn recognised it from across the room before she could read the title, because she had the same copy in the false bottom of her trunk at home. Margery Allingham. *The Tiger in the Smoke.* Bought from Mr Ainsworth on Corve Street for sixty pence.

The other Evelyn looked up.

She looked at the door and at the person in it, and Evelyn waited, because this was the question, and she had been waiting since Saturday to find out the answer.

The other Evelyn looked straight at her.

She didn't look at freckles, or fair hair, or a pointed chin, or Hufflepuff robes. Evelyn watched her eyes, and they didn't stop on any of those things. They went to her face, her real face, her plain brown hair and her Slytherin badge, and they stayed there. The other Evelyn's own face didn't change at all, except that very slowly, over about three seconds, it went white.

"Close the door," the other Evelyn said.

Evelyn closed the door.

They looked at each other.

"I wondered," the other Evelyn said, "whether it was the light."

"It isn't the light."

"No."

The other Evelyn put the book face down on the desk very carefully, square to the edge.

"I saw you in the Great Hall on the twenty-ninth. At the Hufflepuff table. Everyone else saw a little fair girl. I saw you. I thought it was the light. Then I saw you in the corridor outside Charms, and the library, and on the stairs, and you were always you."

She folded her hands.

"I thought I was going mad. I decided I wasn't. I don't."

"No," Evelyn agreed. "We don't."

The other Evelyn regarded her for a long moment.

"What do you want?"

Evelyn had thought about how to say it for four days. In the end, she had decided to say it the way she would have wanted it said to her, which was in order, precisely and all at once.

So she did.

She told her about the watch. About the morning lessons and breakfast and twenty turns. About Potter, and a study beneath the Chamber, and a lamp that lit for him and not for her. About February, and the low chair, and *never wind it backwards*. About three turns and one tick. About the skeleton and the dust and the date in a pink frame. About Aberforth Dumbledore and a Seer's piece and a twin and a room full of clocks beneath London.

She didn't tell her about Isadora's last question, nor where Potter stood.

The other Evelyn listened to all of it without moving.

When it was finished, she sat for a while with her hands folded on the desk.

"You could be lying."

"I could be."

"You could be anybody. Polyjuice. A Metamorphmagus. Somebody who wants the watch," the other Evelyn said, her voice perfectly level. "I'd like to test you."

"Go on."

"What did Grandmother say, the first time she gave it to you?"

"*Wind it every morning.*"

"What else?"

"Nothing else. She didn't say anything else until December, this year. In my world."

The other Evelyn's hands tightened very slightly on each other.

"What did Mr Pelham say about Cicero?"

"That he was a bore," Evelyn replied without hesitating. "And Catullus was a scandal, and Tacitus was the only one worth reading. And then he made me read Cicero."

"How many yews in the walk?"

"A hundred and twelve each side. Great-great-grandfather counted them in eighteen sixty-one. I counted them in nineteen eighty-seven. I got a hundred and eleven on the left the first time and had to go back."

The other Evelyn closed her eyes.

"What's in the false bottom of the trunk?"

"Allingham. Sayers. Tey. Marsh. *The Nine Tailors*, first edition, nineteen thirty-four, the jacket mended with paper tape. *Bells are also a kind of clock.*"

Evelyn stopped.

"Did she give you that one?"

"Yes."

"When?"

"The Christmas I stayed at school. In my third year," the other Evelyn said, opening her eyes. "I stayed because the library was empty. And Lucan was trying. And because of Runes."

"That wasn't the reason."

"No. It wasn't."

They didn't ask each other what the reason was.

Evelyn thought she knew what hers had been now. It had been sitting in a common room at home at Christmas with Potter not twenty feet away, playing the Heir. She didn't know what the other Evelyn's had been. Perhaps the other Evelyn didn't know either. Perhaps there hadn't been one, and the other Evelyn had stayed at school over Christmas for a reason she couldn't put into words, and found when she got there that there was nobody in the castle who would have noticed if she had gone home.

"I believe you," the other Evelyn said.

"Thank you."

"I'm not going to help you."

Evelyn didn't reply.

"I've got no reason to," the other Evelyn went on quite reasonably. "You're a stranger. You've got my face and you've got my life, or a version of it, and you've got somebody. You've got a boy who reads people and a lamp that lights for him and a study under the Chamber and an adventure. And you want me to go to London with you, to a building under the Ministry that nobody's allowed into, and wind my watch forwards in a room full of clocks, so that you can go home."

She laid her hand flat on the paperback.

"And then I won't have it any more. Will I? The old man said. *Same blood, forwards, in a room where time is held.* He didn't say what happens to the watch."

"I don't know what happens to the watch."

"No. Neither do I," the other Evelyn said, looking at her. "It's the only thing she gave me. The only thing that was mine. The only thing anybody's ever given me that was just for me and nobody else. I wind it every morning. It's the only time all day anybody's thinking about me, even if it's only me."

She stood up, picked up *The Tiger in the Smoke* and put it in her bag.

"I'm sorry. I really am. I know what it is to be stuck somewhere. I'm not going to help you."

She went to the door and stopped in it.

"You should tell him," she said without turning round, "that his face doesn't work on me either. In case he hasn't worked it out. The little fair girl. I can see straight through it. If there's anybody else in this castle who's been taught what I've been taught, they'll see straight through it too."

She went out.

Evelyn sat down at the desk by the window where the other Evelyn had been sitting.

She sat there for a long time.

She didn't write anything down.

* * *

It was Pansy Parkinson who changed it.

Evelyn didn't see it coming. Potter would have. Potter would have felt it from the end of the corridor. But Potter was at the other end of the castle, hiding from the Inquisitorial Squad in a broom cupboard on the sixth floor because of something to do with a cat that he hadn't yet explained. Evelyn was on her own on the Thursday, following the other Evelyn down the stairs to the dungeons at a careful distance, and she only saw it when it was already happening.

There were four of them, Pansy and three other fifth-year girls. They were at the bottom of the stairs by the corner where the dungeon corridor turned, and the other Evelyn had to go past them to reach the common room.

Pansy put out her foot.

The other Evelyn stepped over it. She didn't stop or look at it.

"Oh, sorry," Pansy simpered. "I didn't see you. I never do."

The other girls laughed.

"What's your name again? I've been in the same house as you for five years and I've honestly never known. Selwyn, isn't it? Lucan Selwyn's sister? Isn't it funny, he was so *nice*, and so good-looking, and everyone knew who he was."

The other Evelyn kept walking.

"I heard your grandmother died," Pansy called to her back. "Two years ago. Didn't you go home for the funeral? Somebody said you went home for the funeral and nobody noticed you'd gone for a week."

The other Evelyn stopped.

She didn't turn round. She stood quite still in the dungeon corridor with her back to them and her bag on her shoulder and her hands at her sides.

Evelyn knew what she was doing. She was closing the door. Ten to seven, every morning since she was five. *Close the door, Evelyn. Again.* She was standing in the corridor with Pansy Parkinson laughing at her back, and she was closing the door.

Evelyn came down the last three stairs.

She didn't decide to. Afterwards, she couldn't remember deciding. She was simply at the bottom of the stairs, a small, fair, freckled Hufflepuff second-year as far as anybody but the girl at the end of the corridor could tell, standing in front of Pansy Parkinson and looking up at her.

"Parkinson."

Pansy looked down at her.

"Who are you?"

"Nobody. You've got ink on your left wrist."

Pansy's hand went behind her back.

It went very fast, too fast, and the other girls looked at it.

"I haven't."

"You have. On the inside. You tried to wash it off this morning, with soap, but it was the good ink, the kind from Scrivenshaft's that's charmed not to run, and soap won't touch it. You need lemon juice. There's a faint ring of it left," Evelyn said without changing her voice at all. "It's two letters. With a shape round them."

Pansy had gone very red.

"You don't know what you're talking about."

"*D. M.* And a heart. It's not a very good heart. One side's bigger than the other. You did it in Potions, I expect, because the lines are wobbly, the way they go when you're writing under a desk," Evelyn went on, looking at the other three girls. "You can see it from here if she holds her arm up."

The three fifth-year girls were looking at Pansy's hand behind her back. One of them had begun very slightly to grin.

"Lemon juice," Evelyn repeated. "Before Malfoy sees it. He comes down these stairs at twenty to six, every day, on his way back from the Squad. He'll be here in four minutes."

Pansy looked at her for one second longer.

Then she turned and went down the dungeon corridor very fast with her hand still behind her back, and the three other girls followed her, and the one who had been grinning was laughing out loud by the time they reached the stone wall.

Evelyn stood at the bottom of the stairs.

The other Evelyn had turned round.

She was looking at Evelyn, the real Evelyn, through the little fair freckled girl who wasn't there. She looked for a long time. Her face was quite still. It was Evelyn's face, two years older, and Evelyn couldn't read it either, and she found that she didn't need to.

Neither of them spoke.

Then the other Evelyn turned round again and went on down the corridor and through the wall.

* * *

She came to the Hog's Head that night.

Harry felt the door go downstairs at eleven. He didn't feel anything else. Nobody had come into the bar, which was empty except for Aberforth. Then he heard Aberforth say "We're shut," and somebody answer, and he couldn't hear what, and he couldn't feel who, and he knew.

He looked at Evelyn.

She had already put the almanac down.

There were footsteps on the stairs. They didn't miss the third step, nor swear. They paused and stepped over the gap and came on up, and the door of the room opened.

The other Evelyn stood in it.

She was in her school robes. She had come down through the passage, Harry thought, or out by the gates, past the Dementors that weren't there any more in this world. She had her bag on her shoulder. She looked round the room, at the lumpy bed and the blankets and the almanac, and at Harry by the window with his own face on, which she could see, and then she looked at Evelyn.

Harry didn't try to read her.

He didn't need to. There was nothing there. It was the same nothing as in Evelyn, the same smooth, complete wall, so exactly the same that for a moment, sitting on the window seat in the goat-smelling room above the bar, he couldn't tell which of the two silences was which.

He could tell. He always could. He didn't know how.

"I watched you," the other Evelyn said to Evelyn. "Both of you. For a week. Since the Great Hall. I watched you in the library, and the corridors, and at the Hufflepuff table pretending to eat."

"I know. I watched you too."

"I know you did."

The other Evelyn took a step into the room.

"He stands next to you. Always. Even when there's room somewhere else. On your left."

Evelyn didn't answer.

"I counted," the other Evelyn said. "I couldn't help it."

"No," Evelyn replied. "We can't."

The other Evelyn looked at Harry by the window and then back at Evelyn. Her face didn't change, nor did her voice. She asked the next thing very quietly and very precisely, the way she said everything, the way Evelyn said everything, as though it were a fact she was reporting about the weather.

"How long have you been friends?"

Evelyn looked at Harry.

She looked at him for only a moment. Then she looked back at the other girl in the doorway.

"Three years. Nearly."

The other Evelyn nodded slowly, as though that were the figure she had expected, and it was the right one.

"Nobody has ever looked for me," she said.

She said it the way Evelyn had said *two*.

Then she took her hand out of her cardigan pocket. A thin gold chain was wound round her fingers, and at the end of it, small and gold, with ivy leaves on the lid worn smooth in the middle, was a watch, ticking.

"I'll come," she said.
