## Chapter 36: Rita

The wands were weighed on the second Friday in November, in a small classroom off the second-floor corridor, with the desks pushed back against the walls and a long table at the front covered in a velvet cloth.

Harry was the last champion to arrive. He'd been in Potions. A third-year had come down to the dungeons with a message, and Snape had read it and looked at Harry with his lip curling.

"Go, then," he'd said, in the voice he used for things he found contemptible. "Go and be weighed."

The Slytherins had cheered. The Gryffindors hadn't.

He knocked and went in.

The other three were already there. Krum was in a corner, hunched and silent. Fleur Delacour was by the window, talking to Cedric in a low voice, and Cedric was listening with the expression of somebody trying very hard to understand French vowels. Ludo Bagman was bouncing on the balls of his feet by the long table.

And there was a woman.

Harry felt her before he looked at her. He felt her from the door, the way you feel a draught from a window somebody's left open.

Appetite.

It was the first thing in her and the last. Not like a Dementor's, flat and grey. This was bright. Gleeful. The appetite of somebody who's walked into a room full of food and is trying to decide which plate to start on. It had no bottom to it anywhere. Harry went down looking for the bottom of it, the way he always did, and there was only more of it, all the way down, delighted, hungry, sharp.

And it turned to him the moment he came through the door, the way a dog's head turns towards the kitchen.

"Harry!" the woman cried. "Harry Potter. At last."

She had elaborately curled blonde hair and a heavy jaw and spectacles studded with jewels. Her fingernails were two inches long and painted crimson. She had a crocodile-skin handbag over her arm, and she came across the room towards him with both hands out.

"Rita Skeeter," she gushed. "*Daily Prophet*. I wonder, Harry, if I could have a quick word. Just you and me. Before we start. Just a few teensy questions. You don't mind?"

"I mind," said Harry.

"Splendid," said Rita Skeeter, and took him by the arm.

* * *

She took him into a broom cupboard.

She did it so smoothly that he didn't realise until he was inside it, with the door shut and a bucket against his leg and Rita Skeeter perched on an upturned box with her handbag open on her knee. She took a quill out of the bag, very long and acid green. She set it on a piece of parchment, and it stood up on its own, quivering, its nib on the page.

"You won't mind if I use a Quick-Quotes Quill," she said. "It leaves me free to talk normally."

She smiled at him. She had three gold teeth.

"Testing. My name is Rita Skeeter, *Daily Prophet* reporter."

The quill shot across the parchment.

*Glamorous Rita Skeeter, whose fearless pen has never once flinched from the truth…*

"Lovely," said Rita. "So, Harry. What made you decide to enter the Triwizard Tournament?"

"I didn't," said Harry.

The quill wrote. Harry watched it. It wrote very fast, and it didn't write *I didn't*.

He read her. The appetite had found a plate. It was very pleased with the plate. It was looking at him across the broom cupboard the way Aunt Marge had looked at him over a plate of roast beef, only cleverer and hungrier, with no idea at all that it was being looked back at.

"Twelve years old," she purred, "you were. Twelve. And the whole school thought you were the Heir of Slytherin. Petrified children. A snake in the Great Hall. A ghost, Petrified. And then, of course, your little friend. The Selwyn girl."

She leaned forward.

"How did that feel, Harry? When they found her? Did you think it was your fault?"

The quill was writing very fast now.

Harry kept his mouth shut.

He thought about it a great deal afterwards. He could have done something. He thought about a woman in a pink office firing curses at a cat. He could have set something in front of Rita Skeeter's eyes in that cupboard that would have had her out of it and down the corridor screaming. It would have been very easy, and he'd have enjoyed it.

She'd have written about that too.

"No comment," said Harry.

"*No comment*," Rita repeated, delighted, and the quill wrote something much longer than that.

* * *

The article came out on the Sunday.

The Tournament hardly came into it. It was about Harry. Two pages, with a photograph of him at the weighing looking as though he'd just been told some very bad news. It called him *the controversial fourth champion*, and *the Slytherin some still call the Heir*. It said he'd been at the centre of a series of attacks on Muggle-born students two years ago, *which have never been satisfactorily explained*. It said he was a Parselmouth, *a talent shared by only one other wizard in living memory*. It said he'd vanished for four days in March under circumstances *the school has declined to discuss*.

It said he cried at night about his parents.

It said his only confidante was *Evelyn Selwyn, fifteen, a plain, bookish girl from one of Britain's oldest wizarding families, whose father sits on the Wizengamot and whose grandmother, the late Isadora Hale, was something of a mystery*.

Harry read it at breakfast, at the Slytherin table, with the whole school watching him read it.

He read it once. Then he folded it twice and set it down by his plate.

"Plain," said Evelyn.

She had her own copy. She was reading it with her egg. She didn't look up.

"I'm sorry," said Harry.

"Why? It's accurate." She turned the page. "*Bookish* is also accurate. *Confidante* is a word I don't like, but it isn't wrong. *Something of a mystery* is…"

She stopped. She looked at the line a moment longer than she needed to.

"It's very good writing," she said. "That's what's annoying. She writes very well. It's all true, nearly. She puts the true things next to each other in an order that makes them say something else."

"How did she know about the four days?"

"The school knows about the four days."

"How did she know I…"

Harry stopped.

"Cry," Evelyn supplied. "About your parents. At night."

"I don't."

"I know you don't. I've known you three years. You don't cry." She turned another page. "So she made that up. Everything else she found somewhere."

She put the paper down.

"I'd like to know where."

* * *

The school turned on him again.

He'd been waiting for it since Hallowe'en. He'd known it was coming since the Hufflepuff table stood up for Cedric with anger coming off it like heat off a road. The article on the Sunday was a match on dry grass.

Worse things had happened in his second year. That was what he kept noticing. In his second year he'd been twelve and frightened, and three-quarters of the school had believed he was trying to kill them. Now he was fourteen, and they only believed he was a cheat.

They wore badges.

The Hufflepuffs wore them first, then the Ravenclaws, then a good many Gryffindors. They were round and red and said *BACK DIGGORY: THE REAL CHAMPION*, and when you pressed them the letters changed to *POTTER CHEATED* in green.

Harry read the people wearing them.

Most of them didn't hate him. That was the thing. In his second year they'd been afraid of him, all the way down, and the fear had made them cruel. Now there was no fear. They were a little angry. A good deal jealous. Mostly they were enjoying themselves. It was a game, and he was what the game was about, and that was all.

He found he didn't mind it as much.

He found he was very good at walking down a corridor full of people who didn't like him. He'd learned it at twelve. He walked down the middle, not fast, not slow, his face still, and he read every one of them as he went and didn't let any of it in, and he didn't look at the badges.

Cedric wasn't wearing one.

Harry noticed. He passed Cedric outside the library on the Tuesday, with four Hufflepuffs round him all wearing the badges, and Cedric's robes were bare. Cedric looked at Harry and nodded, very slightly, and his friends didn't see.

Harry read him. Cedric was embarrassed. He'd asked them not to. They hadn't listened.

Harry nodded back.

* * *

The letter came on a Thursday, at the Owlery, at a quarter to five, and Evelyn didn't expect it.

She'd gone up to post a letter to her mother. She wrote to her mother on Thursdays now, since July. She'd never done that before. She didn't examine why. The letters were short and about the weather and the Tournament. Her mother's replies were long and loose and full of crossings-out, and sometimes, at the bottom, there was a line in a different, smaller hand that said *I'm so glad you're there, darling*, as though it had been written later, after something.

The Owlery was very cold. The coldest room in the castle, a round stone tower open to the wind on all sides, with straw on the floor and owls on perches all the way up into the dark. The sky outside the window-holes was grey and darkening. Evelyn chose a school owl, a small brown one, and tied her letter to its leg, and it went.

When she turned round there was somebody in the doorway.

It was the old man from Durmstrang. Varga. She knew him from the front steps and the staff table, and from a photograph in *Transfiguration Today* in nineteen ninety-one in which he'd been looking away from the camera with his hand half raised, as though the photographer had caught him in the act of refusing.

He was leaning on his stick and he was out of breath. The Owlery stairs were long, and he was very old.

"Miss Selwyn," he said.

He had a quiet, dry, very correct voice, with an accent she couldn't place more precisely than east of Vienna.

"Yes," said Evelyn.

"Forgive me."

He came one step into the Owlery and stopped. He came no closer.

"I have been asked to give you something. I was asked by somebody I owe a great deal to, and a great deal more than I would like."

He took a letter from the inside of his plain black coat.

"I agreed. I am sorry. I would rather not have."

He held it out.

Evelyn looked at it. A heavy envelope, cream-coloured, very thick, addressed in a hand she didn't know.

*Miss Evelyn Selwyn. By the kindness of Professor Varga.*

She took it.

When she looked up, the old man was already back in the doorway. He'd turned. He hadn't waited for her to answer. He was going down the Owlery stairs slowly, one at a time, with his stick, and he didn't look back.

"Professor," Evelyn called.

He stopped on the third stair.

"Who asked you?"

He didn't turn round. He stood on the stair with his back to her and his hand on the cold stone wall.

"You know who asked me, Miss Selwyn," he said. "I think you have known since July."

He went down another step.

"I am sorry. I am very sorry. He will tell you I am a coward. He is quite right."

He went on down.

Evelyn stood in the doorway of the Owlery and listened to his stick on the stairs, all the way down, until she couldn't hear it.

Then she sat on the bench by the window-hole, with the wind coming in, and opened the letter.

* * *

*My dear Evelyn,*

*You will forgive me for beginning with the weather. It is the only subject on which an old man in my situation can be sure of saying nothing he will regret, and I am told the English require it.*

*It is snowing here. It has been snowing since Thursday. I have a window, which is a narrow one, and through it I can see a great deal of snow and one mountain, which I have been looking at for forty-nine years and which has not, in that time, done anything I did not expect. I am told that in Scotland it rains. I hope it is raining on you now. I find I would like to think of you somewhere wet and ordinary, reading.*

*What are you reading? Your grandmother read detective novels in the bath and denied it. She said they were beneath her. She said this with a novel in her hand. I suspect you are the same, and I suspect you do not deny it, which is an improvement.*

*I should like to know about her last months. I have no right to ask. I have never let that stop me, and I am too old to begin now. Was she in pain? Did she read? Did she sit in the east window in the mornings and drink her coffee black and frighten your father? I know about the east window. I know a great many things about Selwyn Hall that I have never seen. She wrote to me once, in nineteen seventy-nine, a week after you were born, and in that letter she told me about the east window and the yews and that she had named you after nobody, so that you would have to make the name mean something yourself.*

*She did not write again. I did not expect her to.*

*Do you still wind the watch?*

*I ask because I made it, and a maker is always curious. I ask, also, because I should like to know whether it still works. I have a feeling that it does not. I have had the feeling since March. I am not often wrong about feelings of that kind, though I am frequently wrong about everything else.*

*If it does not, bring it to me.*

*I should like you to come at Christmas. Professor Varga can arrange it. He has arranged it before, for others, and he does it very well, and he will hate every moment. I would not ask, except that I have been looking at the mountain for forty-nine years and I find that I would very much like to look, for an afternoon, at something that might surprise me.*

*You may say no. Your grandmother will have told you that. She will have been right. She usually was, which is the only quality in a person I have never been able to forgive.*

*With every good wish, and some others,*

*Your grandfather.*

There was no name.

Evelyn read it three times, on the cold bench in the Owlery with the wind coming in.

Then she folded it along its creases, exactly, and put it back in its envelope, and put the envelope in the left pocket of her cardigan with the other one, and buttoned it.

She put her hand on the right pocket.

The watch was there. Not ticking.

*I have a feeling that it does not. I have had the feeling since March.*

She sat on the bench and didn't move for a long time. Above her, in the dark at the top of the tower, the owls shifted on their perches and settled, and she didn't count anything.

* * *

She noticed the beetle on the Saturday.

She noticed it because she noticed most things, and because it was on the wrong windowsill. It was on the sill of the library window above her table, behind the Goblin History shelves, at twenty past four. A largish beetle, shiny, greenish-black, sitting quite still in the corner of the frame.

It was November. There shouldn't have been beetles.

She looked at it for a moment and went back to her book.

On the Monday she saw it again.

It was on the windowsill of the empty classroom on the fourth floor where Potter practised shields with Nott. She only saw it because she'd come to find Potter to tell him something about the first task, and the door was ajar, and she looked in. Potter and Nott were talking about Rita Skeeter, and the beetle was on the sill.

She kept quiet.

On the Wednesday the *Prophet* ran a short piece on page six under the headline *CHAMPION'S CHUMS*, which quoted Millicent Bulstrode as saying that if anybody laid a finger on Potter she'd sit on them.

Millicent had said it. She'd said it on Monday, in the fourth-floor classroom, to Potter and Nott, whilst Evelyn stood outside the door.

Nobody else had been in the room.

Evelyn read the piece twice. Then she went to the library and asked Madam Pince for the Ministry's *Register of Animagi*. The library kept it in the reference section, in a green cloth binding, updated every January, and nobody had borrowed it since 1987.

It was a short book. There'd been seven registered Animagi in the whole of Britain in the twentieth century. She read every entry. A cat. A cat. A hawk. A tabby cat with markings round the eyes like spectacles, which made her pause for a moment before going on. A hare. A badger. A cat.

No beetle.

No Skeeter.

Evelyn closed the register and gave it back to Madam Pince.

Then she went to the potions stores, which weren't locked on Wednesdays between four and five because the third-years were doing inventory. She took a small glass jar with a screw-top lid, and she wrote in the stores book, in her own hand, *one jar, small, E. Selwyn, 5th yr, for a private study*, which was true.

* * *

She caught it on the Friday.

She'd sat at her table in the library every afternoon since Wednesday, with Potter or without him, talking loudly or not talking. On the Thursday she'd said, to nobody, in a clear voice that carried, that she thought Potter had a plan for the first task involving a broom and something else, and that she'd tell nobody what it was. It was true, in a way. She thought he probably did. She didn't know what.

On the Friday at twenty past four, the beetle was on the sill.

Evelyn had the jar in her lap beneath the table, with the lid off.

She went on reading for six minutes. Then she stood, as though to fetch a book from the shelf, reached past the window, brought the jar up over the sill in one movement, and clapped the lid on.

The beetle hit the glass and fell over.

She screwed the lid tight and looked at it. It was on its back on the bottom of the jar, legs going. When it righted itself she saw markings round its eyes, very faint, exactly the shape of the jewelled spectacles in the photograph at the top of Rita Skeeter's column.

"Good afternoon," said Evelyn.

* * *

She did it in the empty classroom on the fifth floor, the one where, in another world, she'd sat at a desk by the window and told her own face the truth.

She put the jar on a desk. She locked the door with a charm her grandmother had taught her when she was nine, for the door of the east wing, which she didn't think anybody at Hogwarts knew. She took out her wand.

She'd read how. It was in the third volume of *Transfiguration Today*'s collected articles, in a piece from nineteen sixty-eight about reversing an unwilling Animagus. She'd read it on Wednesday night in the library, twice.

She unscrewed the lid. She tipped the jar. She said the words.

It wasn't elegant. It took her three tries. On the third there was a sound like a cork leaving a bottle, and a great deal of blonde hair, and Rita Skeeter was sitting on the floor of the empty classroom with her legs out in front of her, her jewelled spectacles crooked and her crimson nails splayed on the boards, looking up.

She didn't look pleased.

"You," she spat. "You little…"

"Evelyn Selwyn," said Evelyn. "Fifth year. Plain and bookish. You've written about me."

Rita Skeeter got up off the floor, quite quickly for a woman in heels. She straightened her spectacles. Her face had gone a dark mottled colour beneath the powder.

"Do you know," she hissed, "what I can do to you? To your father? To that boy? Do you have the faintest idea, you stupid little girl, what I can *write*?"

"Yes," said Evelyn. "I've read it."

She sat down on the edge of the desk with the empty jar beside her. She didn't raise her voice. She'd never needed to.

"You are an unregistered Animagus," she said. "There are seven registered Animagi in Britain this century. You aren't one of them. I've checked the Ministry register, the library edition, updated in January. Under section four of the Registration of Animagi Act, nineteen fifty-two, failure to register is an offence. Under section nine, as amended in nineteen seventy-three, the use of an unregistered transformation to obtain information by stealth is a separate offence, and an aggravated one."

She paused.

"The sentence for the second, on conviction before the Wizengamot, is a term in Azkaban not exceeding five years. My father sits on the Wizengamot. He's sat on it for nineteen years. He has never once, in nineteen years, voted for leniency for anybody."

Rita Skeeter's mouth opened, and closed again.

"I'm not going to tell him," Evelyn went on. "I'm not going to tell anybody. Not the Ministry. Not the *Prophet*. Not Potter."

She looked at the jar.

"On one condition."

"Which is?"

"You will not write one word about Harry Potter for the rest of this school year," said Evelyn, "unless I've read it first and said you may."

The crimson nails curled slowly into fists.

"You can't be serious," said Rita Skeeter.

"I'm always serious. People find it tiresome."

Evelyn picked up the jar and screwed the lid back on, empty, and held it on her knee.

"You can write about the Tournament. You can write about the other champions. You can write about Krum's eyebrows and Delacour's grandmother and Diggory's hair, all you like. If you write about Potter, you'll send it to me first, by owl, and I'll send it back, and if I've crossed something out you'll leave it out. And if you print anything about him I haven't seen, I'll write a letter to my father, and another to the Department of Magical Law Enforcement, and a third to the *Quibbler*, which will print anything."

She paused.

"And I've already written all three. They're in an envelope. Somebody else has it. If anything happens to me, they'll be posted."

That wasn't true. Nobody else had anything.

She'd decided on Wednesday night that it was the one lie she'd allow herself, and that she wouldn't feel anything about it. She didn't.

Rita Skeeter stared at her.

Then she laughed. A short, sharp, unpleasant laugh, like a gate on a rusty hinge.

"Who taught you to do this?" she asked. "Your father?"

"Nobody taught me," said Evelyn. "I read."

* * *

She didn't tell Potter.

She thought about it, walking down from the fifth floor with the empty jar in her pocket. She thought about it in the library, and at supper, and in the common room in the chair by the draughty window, watching him across the room, reading the people round him the way he always did, with the look of somebody checking the weather.

He'd laugh. He'd be pleased, and then he'd want to know why she hadn't told him first. And then he'd look at her the way he looked at her when there was something she hadn't said.

And there was something she hadn't said.

There were two letters in her left pocket that she hadn't said.

She didn't tell him.

* * *

Hagrid took him to see the dragons on the Monday night, at a quarter to midnight, under the Cloak.

He'd sent a note at breakfast. *Come down to the hut tonight at half eleven. Bring that cloak. Don' ask why, jus' come. Hagrid.* Harry had gone, and Hagrid had been waiting outside the hut in his best hairy brown suit and a tie, his hair slicked down with something that smelled of axle grease. Harry had read him and found him so nervous and so pleased with himself that he wanted to laugh.

"Madame Maxime's comin'," Hagrid whispered. "Keep that cloak on. Stay close."

They went round the edge of the forest. Madame Maxime came with them, enormous, in a fur-trimmed cloak, her hand on Hagrid's arm. Hagrid talked to her in a low voice all the way, and Harry walked behind them under the Cloak and read them both and looked at the trees.

Then he heard the roaring.

It came from deep in the trees, a sound Harry had never heard before. A great tearing bellow that rose and rose and broke off in something like a scream, and the ground beneath his feet shook. There was firelight through the trunks. There was a great deal of shouting, men's voices.

And there were dragons.

He felt them before he saw them. He'd never felt a dragon, except a baby one in a kettle in a hut, a long time ago, all hunger and new fear. These weren't babies. He felt them come up through the trees like a furnace door opening.

There were four of them.

They were in an enclosure of thick wooden planks in a clearing, with thirty or forty wizards round them, wands out, and chains on the dragons' legs. The dragons were rearing up fifty feet tall, wings half spread and mouths open, fire roaring from their jaws in great jets up into the black sky.

Harry read them.

He couldn't have stopped if he'd tried. They were the loudest things he'd ever felt that weren't people.

They were furious.

That was the top of them, all four, and it was enormous. Nothing like Aunt Marge's cruelty or the Death Eaters' glee, or even the troll's rage on Hallowe'en in his first year. It was plain and huge and hot and it filled the whole clearing. Four dragons' fury at the chains and the wizards and the noise and the cold and the strangeness of a place they didn't know. It came off them the way heat comes off a fire you're standing too close to.

And beneath the fury, in all four of them, was something else.

He found it a moment later, the way he always found the thing underneath. It was just as large. It was larger.

It was for the eggs.

They were mothers. He knew it before Hagrid said so. Nesting mothers. Somebody had taken them from their nests and chained them in a clearing in a strange cold country, and they had their eggs with them, on the ground beneath them, and every scrap of the fury was for the eggs. None of it was anger at the wizards. It was terror for the eggs, so large that it had turned into fury, because fury was the only shape a dragon knew for it.

Harry stood in the dark under the Cloak at the edge of the trees and read four mothers screaming for their eggs, and he didn't move for a long time.

"Beau'iful, aren't they?" Hagrid said softly. "Hungarian Horntail, that one, the black one. Nasty piece o' work. Spikes on her tail, see. Common Welsh Green. Swedish Short-Snout. Chinese Fireball." He sighed happily. "They're fer the first task. Champions've got ter get past 'em."

"Get past zem," Madame Maxime echoed faintly.

"Somethin' like that," said Hagrid. "I don' know exactly. Charlie says it's somethin' ter do with the eggs."

Harry looked at the black one.

The Horntail was the biggest of the four. Black and scaly and lizard-like, with yellow eyes and bronze horns, and a tail covered all along its length in long bronze spikes. She was screaming. Harry read her. Her fury was the hottest of the four. Her fear for her eggs was the deepest.

He thought about getting past her.

He thought about it all the way back to the castle, under the Cloak, whilst Hagrid walked Madame Maxime back to her carriage and talked to her in a low voice about the stars.

* * *

He told Cedric on the Tuesday.

He found him in the corridor outside the library, without any Hufflepuffs, by luck.

"Diggory," he said quietly, from the wall.

Cedric stopped.

"Dragons," said Harry. "The first task. It's dragons. Four of them. One each. I saw them last night."

Cedric stared at him.

Harry read him.

He was surprised. That was the top, very large and very sudden. He hadn't expected it. He hadn't expected anything from Harry Potter except what his whole house said he was. A cheat, a sly Slytherin, the controversial fourth champion. He looked at Harry in the corridor, and the surprise was so large it had pushed everything else out of the way.

Then, slowly, beneath the surprise, something else came up.

Gratitude. Very simple and very plain and very warm, the gratitude of a decent boy for a decent act. Cedric didn't hide it this time. He didn't try.

"Are you serious?"

"Yes."

"Why are you telling me?"

Harry considered it.

He thought about saying *because it's fair*. That was true. Fleur and Krum would know already. Madame Maxime had seen, and Karkaroff, he was nearly sure, had been in the trees. Cedric was the only one who didn't know. It wasn't fair.

He thought about saying *because you didn't wear the badge*.

He thought about four dragons screaming in a clearing for their eggs.

"Because you'd have told me," he said.

Cedric searched his face a moment longer. Then he nodded, slowly, once.

"Yeah," he said. "Yeah. I would."

* * *

Evelyn sat on the bench by the window-hole in the Owlery at half past eleven at night with the wind coming in, a sheet of parchment on her knee, her pen in her hand, and no idea what to write.

She'd been sitting there since eleven.

She'd come up because nobody came up at night. She couldn't write it in the dormitory, where the other fifth-years might wake. She couldn't write it in the library, which was shut. She couldn't write it in the study, because Potter would be there.

The letter lay beside her on the bench. She didn't need to read it again. She'd read it eleven times. She knew it.

*Do you still wind the watch?*

She looked at the parchment.

It was blank, very clean and very white in the light from her wand. She'd written to her grandmother every Sunday from the age of eleven, and to her mother every Thursday since July, and to Potter every eleven days every summer. She knew how to write a letter. She'd never in her life not known what to put at the top of one.

She didn't know what to call him.

She sat for a long time with her pen poised over the page.

Then she wrote *Sir*, and looked at it, and crossed it out.

She wrote *Dear*, and stopped, and didn't cross it out, and didn't write anything after it.

The wind came in through the window-hole. Above her in the dark, an owl turned its head all the way round to look at her, and turned it back.

Evelyn looked at the one word on the page.

Then, beneath it, very small, in her own hand, keeping the tails of the *g*s and the *y*s short, she wrote one more line.

*It is raining.*

She looked at that for a long time.

Then, beneath it, she wrote another line.

<->

## Chapter 37: The Horntail

"Play to your strengths," said Moody.

He said it on the Monday before the task, in his office, with the door shut and the Foe-Glass on the wall behind him full of shadowy shapes that never quite came into focus. He'd kept Harry back after Defence. He'd looked at him with the ordinary eye and the blue one, both at once, for a long time. Then he'd said that.

"I don't know what my strengths are," Harry admitted.

"Course you do. Everybody does. Most people just don't like the answer."

Moody leaned forward on his stick.

"You're a flier, Potter. Everybody knows that. And you've got something else, haven't you? Something you don't talk about. I've watched you in my lessons. You look at people before they move. You look at a curse before it's cast."

The blue eye spun and stopped.

"Use it. Whatever it is. Don't try to be Diggory, or Krum. Be what you are."

Harry read him.

It was the same as always. It was always the same with Moody. The suspicion and the grimness on the top, and beneath them, aimed straight at Harry, that fierce enormous thing, so large and so steady that it was like standing next to a fire. It wanted Harry to win. It wanted it more than anybody in the castle wanted anything. More than the Slytherin table. More than Hagrid.

It was the strangest thing in the world, to be wanted to win so much by a man he'd met eleven weeks ago.

It must be because Moody had fought Voldemort, and lost friends to him, and had looked at the boy who survived him and decided something.

"Thanks, Professor," he said.

"Eyes open, Potter," Moody growled. "That's all it ever is. Now get out."

* * *

He had his plan by then. He'd had it since a clearing in the forest.

He told Evelyn on the Tuesday night, in the study, because he always told her first. She listened to all of it on her cushion, with her notebook open on her knee and her pencil not moving.

"Two of you," she said, when he'd finished.

"Two of me."

"For a dragon."

"It's an animal. It's angry and it's frightened. It looks at things. I can set things in front of things that look."

He was at the desk. The lamp was lit, cold and green.

"I'll Summon my broom. I'll get in the air. And whilst I'm getting in the air, there'll be another one of me on the ground, running the other way, and she'll go for him. By the time she works out he isn't there, I'll be over the eggs."

"How long does it take to Summon a broom from the castle to the enclosure?"

"I don't know. Twenty seconds?"

"Nott says it's nineteen. He timed you. He says the window of the dormitory has to be open." She wrote something. "How long can you hold something that large?"

"I don't know."

"You held a hippogriff for twenty minutes."

"The hippogriff wasn't trying to kill me. And nobody looking at it was angry."

He looked at the lamp.

"I've never held anything in front of something that wanted me dead. I've never held anything in front of something that big."

Evelyn looked at him.

"Then you'd better be quick," she said.

* * *

They practised every night that week in the fourth-floor classroom.

"Again," Millicent ordered from the door.

"I've done it eleven times."

"Twelve's a nicer number."

"Twelve isn't a nicer number," Evelyn said from her desk. "It's just a larger one."

"It's got more factors," Theo offered from the window. He had the Map open on the sill, so they'd know if Filch was coming. "Six of them. Eleven's only got two."

"There you are," said Millicent. "Theo says. Again, Potter."

Harry raised his wand at the cushion on the far side of the room.

"*Accio cushion*."

It came. It came across the room in a long flat line and hit him in the chest, and he caught it, and Millicent cheered.

"Four seconds," said Evelyn.

"It's a cushion. It's twenty feet away."

"The broom's in the dungeons. It's about three-quarters of a mile, by air, if it goes out through the window and round the east tower and over the trees." She wrote something. "If the window's open. If nobody's shut the window."

"I'll open it," said Theo. "On the morning. I'll stand by it."

"Somebody'll shut it after you've gone to the task."

"Then I'll stay."

Harry looked at him.

"You'll miss it," he said. "The task. You'll be in the dormitory with the window open and you won't see any of it."

Theo turned a page of the Map.

"I'll hear it," he said. "Everybody'll hear it."

He didn't look up.

"I'd rather be the person who kept the window open than the person who watched you get eaten because somebody shut it."

Millicent cleared her throat.

"Again," she said, a bit gruffly. "Potter. Again."

* * *

From half past one on Thursday the twenty-fourth of November, the champions waited in a tent on the edge of the enclosure, on the far side of the forest.

It was cold. Grey and cold and still, with a white sky and no wind, and the noise of the crowd came through the canvas of the tent like the sea through a wall. Harry could feel it. He'd turned it down to a roar and kept it there. He didn't bother looking for Evelyn in it, because he couldn't find her from inside a tent, and he'd known he wouldn't be able to.

He didn't like that.

He read the others instead.

Fleur Delacour was sitting on a low stool in the corner, very pale, with her hands clenched in her lap. She was terrified all the way through, and the terror was proud, and she was holding it down so hard that Harry could feel the effort from across the tent.

Krum stood by the entrance with his hands in his pockets and his shoulders hunched, staring at nothing. He was very quiet inside. The same as he'd been at the World Cup, high above the stadium, before he dived. He was alone, and didn't mind it, and he was concentrating on something nobody else could see.

Cedric was walking up and down. He was frightened and he was determined, both, quite plainly, and every time he passed Harry he looked at him and nodded, very slightly, the way he had in the corridor.

Ludo Bagman came in with a small purple silk bag.

"Now," he said.

He was very excited. Harry read him, and the excitement was large and bright and very slightly greedy. Beneath it was something else, worried and small and grubby, like a man who owes somebody money.

"Ladies first," Bagman said, and held out the bag to Fleur.

She put her hand in. She brought out a tiny dragon, perfectly made, a little green model, alive, that moved and stretched on her palm. It had a number on a ribbon round its neck. *Two*.

"The Welsh Green," said Bagman.

Krum drew the red one. The Chinese Fireball. Three.

Cedric drew the blue-grey one. The Swedish Short-Snout. One.

Harry knew what was left before he put his hand in the bag.

It was black. Perfectly made, the size of his thumb, with bronze horns and a long tail with tiny bronze spikes all down it. When he held it on his palm it spread its little wings and opened its mouth and hissed at him.

The ribbon round its neck said *Four*.

"The Hungarian Horntail," Bagman announced happily.

* * *

Cedric went first.

Harry heard it through the canvas. He heard the whistle, and the crowd roaring, and then a great many things he couldn't make out at all, roaring and screaming and gasping. Bagman's magnified voice rode over the top of it all. *Oh, close, very close, oh, he's taking risks, this one.* And the dragon screaming. Beneath all of it, the whole time, through the canvas and across the enclosure, Harry could feel Cedric. Frightened and determined, frightened and determined. Then, all at once, hurt. Then, a moment later, a great flood of something that was mostly relief.

The crowd cheered.

He'd got the egg.

Fleur went second. Harry felt her leave the tent, proud and terrified, and felt her across the enclosure the whole time. He felt the Welsh Green go to sleep, slowly, the dragon's fury sinking down and down and down like a fire being smothered. He felt Fleur refuse to let herself believe it until the very end.

Krum went third. Harry didn't feel much of Krum. He felt the Chinese Fireball. He felt it go from fury to something else, all at once, a great screaming confused blindness. He heard the crowd groan, and then roar. Krum had cursed it in the eyes. It had trampled half its own eggs.

Then the whistle went for Harry.

* * *

He walked out of the tent and through a gap in the enclosure fence.

He didn't look at the crowd. He knew where it was. All round him, up the sides of a great bowl of wooden stands, a thousand people, more. The whole school and the visitors and half the Ministry, all of them shouting. It came down at him from every side, louder than in the tent, louder than the Quidditch pitch, nearly as loud as the moor.

He turned it down. He didn't look for Evelyn. There wasn't time.

He looked at the dragon.

She was at the other end of the enclosure, crouched low over her eggs. Black and enormous, much bigger than she'd seemed in the clearing in the dark, because he was nearer, and she wasn't chained. Her wings were half open. Her yellow eyes were on him. Her tail was moving slowly from side to side, beating the ground, leaving yard-long gouges in the earth.

Harry read her.

He'd read her in the clearing. He'd thought he knew what she was. He hadn't known.

The fury came up off her at him, all of it, aimed, the whole of it, at the small thing that had just walked into her place. It was hotter than the fire inside her. It was larger than anything in the stands. It was so large and so hot and so close that for a second it pushed the crowd out of him entirely. There was nothing in the world but a dragon and her fury, aimed at him, and beneath the fury, beneath all of it, enormous, the thing that was always beneath it.

*Eggs. Eggs. Eggs. Mine. Mine.*

He didn't hear words. He felt it. It was the plainest thing he'd ever felt in anything, plainer than the spider's pain, and larger, and it went all the way down.

He raised his wand.

"*Accio Firebolt!*"

* * *

Nineteen seconds.

Theo had timed it. Harry had practised it every night for a week in the fourth-floor classroom, with Theo at the window and Millicent at the door, and Evelyn at a desk with a watch that didn't work and the long-case clock of Selwyn Hall in her head, counting.

He didn't have nineteen seconds.

The Horntail had seen his wand move. She was coming. She rose off her eggs onto all four legs, and her wings went up and out, and her head came round, and her mouth opened. Harry could see down it, red, all the way down, to where something very hot was rising.

So he gave her two of him.

He'd held it in his head for a week. He'd held it every night in the study until he could see it with his eyes shut, the same way he'd held the Galleon and the faces and the hippogriff. It was himself. Himself as Evelyn saw him, which was the only way anybody saw him truly, because she was the only one his faces had never touched. A boy of fourteen, not tall, in Slytherin robes with a number on the back, with black hair that wouldn't lie flat, and glasses, and a scar.

He set it on the ground beside him.

And then he made it run.

He made it run left, fast, across the enclosure, away from him, towards the stands, with its wand up. He set it in front of the dragon's eyes the way you set a lamp in a window, and held it there, and put everything he had behind it.

It was like holding a door shut against a hurricane.

He'd held doors before. He'd held two faces for six weeks in another world. He'd held three people not there and an empty room at the bottom of the Ministry of Magic with his nose bleeding into his mouth. He'd held a hippogriff in front of five pairs of eyes for twenty minutes.

None of them had been looking at him like this.

The dragon's attention was the heaviest thing he'd ever felt. It came against the door like the whole weight of the sea. It was so large and so hot and so furious that the door bent. He felt it bend, and he held it.

The dragon's head swung.

It swung left, after the running boy. Her mouth was still open and the fire came out of it and went left, a great roaring jet of orange and gold across the enclosure, at the boy running away from her. It went straight through him, and he kept running, because he wasn't there.

The crowd screamed.

Harry heard it. A thousand people seeing two Harry Potters. A thousand people seeing one of them burn and not burn. He heard it go up off the stands like a flock of birds off a field. He didn't look. He held the door.

He heard something behind him.

It was coming over the trees from the castle, very fast, a long thin shape against the white sky. His broom.

Seven seconds. Eight.

He held the door. The dragon was turning after the second Harry, all of her, her great black body coming round, her tail swinging. The second Harry was nearly at the fence on the far side, and she was nearly round, and when she was round she'd be facing the wrong way with the eggs behind her, and he'd have his chance.

The broom reached him. He swung his leg over it.

Nine seconds. Ten.

He kicked off from the ground.

Eleven.

The door broke.

He didn't let go of it. It broke. It went all at once, the way a dam goes, the way a held breath goes. It wasn't him letting go. There was simply nothing left behind it. The weight of the dragon's attention came through it and through him, and the second Harry by the far fence wasn't there any more. He flickered, and was gone.

And the Horntail knew.

She knew at once. She didn't stop to wonder, the way a person would have. She didn't look at the fence where the boy had been and think *where did he go*. She was a dragon. One moment there'd been a thing to burn, and then there wasn't, and there was another thing behind her, in the air, going up.

She came round.

She came round all at once, faster than anything that size should be able to move, and her tail came round with her, its whole length, all its bronze spikes, scything through the air at the height of a boy on a broom ten feet up.

It caught his shoulder.

He didn't see it. He felt it. It was like being hit by a cart. He was flung sideways, nearly off the broom, hanging on with one hand and his legs. There was a pain in his left shoulder so large and so sudden that it went white, and something hot was running down the inside of his sleeve.

He held on.

He held on with one hand, and the broom was climbing, because it was a Firebolt and it went where he looked, and he was looking up. He got his other hand back on the handle. He got his leg back over. He was a hundred feet up, and the Horntail was screaming below him, and the crowd was screaming round him, and his shoulder was a single white sheet of pain.

And the eggs were below him, uncovered.

She'd turned. She'd turned all the way round to get at the thing behind her, and now she was looking up at him, and she'd left them on the ground beneath where she'd been.

There was a golden one.

It lay amongst the grey ones, very bright. He'd known it would be there since the bag of tiny dragons. It was what they were all looking for.

He dived.

He did it the way he'd done it in his first year, for a Remembrall, and in his second, for a Snitch, with a broken arm. He did it the way the Firebolt did everything, as though he were falling, only faster. Straight down, past her head, past her snapping jaws, so close he felt the heat of her breath on the side of his face. He didn't think. He looked at the egg and he was there.

He put out his good hand.

He had it.

He was up again and away, out of reach, over the stands, a golden egg under his arm and his left shoulder pouring blood. The crowd was making a noise so enormous that he couldn't read anything in it at all.

* * *

Evelyn had sat beside Varga because there was an empty seat, and because she'd decided on the Wednesday night that she would.

He'd been at the end of the third row of the Slytherin stand, alone, in his plain black coat, leaning on his stick, when she came up. The Durmstrang students were all on the other side with Karkaroff, in a block of furs. Varga hadn't sat with them. Evelyn had looked at the empty seat beside him, and at him, and sat down in it.

He'd looked at her.

"Miss Selwyn," he'd said.

"Professor."

That was all. He'd sat silent through Diggory, through Delacour, through Krum, both hands on the silver end of his stick, watching the enclosure with an expression of polite attention, like a man at a play he's seen before.

When the whistle went for Potter, he'd leaned forward slightly.

Evelyn noted it.

She watched Potter walk out. She watched him look at the dragon. She knew the look. She'd seen it every day for three years, across tables and classrooms and the floor of a round stone room beneath the lake. It was the look he had when he was reading somebody, and she didn't need to see what he was reading to know that it was very large.

She watched him raise his wand. She heard him shout.

And then she saw nothing.

She saw Potter on the ground with his wand up, and the dragon rising off her eggs. She saw the dragon's head swing left, sharply, at nothing, and fire go across the enclosure in a great orange sheet at an empty stretch of grass by the far fence. She saw the crowd round her surge to its feet, every one of them, screaming, pointing at the empty grass.

She saw a broom come over the trees.

She didn't see a second boy. She didn't see anything at the far fence at all. She only saw the dragon turning and turning after nothing, and Potter getting on his broom, and the crowd screaming at a place where she could see there was nobody.

Beside her, Varga had gone rigid.

He'd come up off the bench. Not standing. Half risen, both hands on his stick, his knuckles white on the silver, and he was staring at the far fence, at the empty grass, and his face had gone the colour of paper.

He said something.

He said it under his breath, quickly, in a language she didn't know. Three or four words. She thought it was Hungarian. She couldn't have repeated it.

Then the dragon turned, and the tail came round, and Potter went sideways off his broom and didn't fall, and the crowd screamed in a different way. For some seconds Evelyn didn't look at Varga, because she was looking at Potter's left shoulder.

He held on. He went up. He went down. He came up again with the egg.

The stand went mad.

Evelyn sat down. She'd stood up at some point. She didn't remember doing it. She sat on the bench with her hands in her lap and found they weren't quite steady, and she put them in her pockets.

Varga had sat down too. He was staring straight ahead.

"Professor," said Evelyn.

He didn't answer at once.

"What did you say? Just now. When the dragon turned."

Varga looked at her.

He had very dark eyes behind the small round spectacles, and they were wet, though it wasn't cold enough for that. He studied her as though he were deciding something.

"I said," he replied in English, very quietly, "that it was a First Step."

"A first step of what?"

"That," said Varga, "I will not tell you. Not here."

He turned back to the enclosure.

"I have not seen one in forty years. I had thought I would not see one again."

He offered nothing more.

Evelyn sat beside him whilst the judges conferred, and the crowd shouted, and Potter was taken into the medical tent at the end of the enclosure with Madam Pomfrey's hand on his good arm. She watched the tent. She sat with her hands in her pockets and watched it for some time.

Then she looked at her watch.

It said what it had said since the second of March. She knew what time it actually was from the light and the stands and the order of things. Nearly half past three.

She'd agreed to meet Varga at half past three. About Christmas. At the gangway of the Durmstrang ship. He'd told her so in the Owlery on Tuesday, when she gave him her reply to take. One sentence, without looking at her, and then he'd gone down the stairs.

She looked at the medical tent.

She looked at Varga beside her, who had already stood and was leaning on his stick and wasn't looking at her at all.

"I'll walk down with you," she said. "Professor."

She didn't stay for the marks.

* * *

The medical tent smelled of something green and sharp, and Madam Pomfrey was furious.

"Dragons," she fumed, pouring something purple into his shoulder. "*Dragons*. Last year Dementors, the year before that a basilisk. They'll be bringing in Lethifolds next year, you mark my words, and I'll be the one sewing everybody back together." She held his arm still. "This will sting."

It stung.

Harry sat on the edge of the camp bed with his shirt off and his left shoulder open in three long ragged cuts where the spikes had gone in. He watched the purple stuff fizz in them and kept his teeth together. The pain was large and white and he held it the way he'd held the door, and it didn't break.

He read the tent.

Cedric was on the next bed, with a long burn down the side of his face covered in thick orange paste. He looked across at Harry.

Harry read him and it was relief. Plain, simple, warm. The relief of somebody who's watched a person he decided to trust go up against a dragon and come down alive, and there was nothing in it about the Tournament at all.

"That," said Cedric, "was mad."

"So was yours."

"Mine was a dog." Cedric touched his face carefully. "I Transfigured a rock into a Labrador. She went for the Labrador. For about a minute. Then she went for me."

He looked at Harry's shoulder.

"What was yours? Everybody was screaming. There were two of you. I saw it from the tent flap. There were *two* of you."

"I don't know," said Harry.

Cedric looked at him.

He didn't believe it. Harry read him not believe it, and decide, the way he'd decided in the corridor, not to say so.

"All right," said Cedric.

Fleur Delacour came in from the other end of the tent with a bandage round her hand and her silver hair singed at the ends. She stopped when she saw him. She looked at him with her chin up, and Harry read her. She was surprised. Surprised the way people are when something they've dismissed turns out to be something else. She didn't like being surprised. She was a little bit impressed, and she didn't like that either.

"*Zat*," she said, "was not a Summoning Charm."

"Some of it was."

She regarded him a moment longer. Then she said something in French that Harry didn't understand, and went out.

Krum was standing at the tent flap.

He hadn't come in. He stood in the opening with his hands in his pockets and his shoulders hunched, looking at Harry. He looked at Harry the way he'd looked at the Snitch at the World Cup, with the same still, solitary concentration.

Harry read him.

There was something in Krum that hadn't been there in the tent before the task. Very quiet and very plain. Respect. The respect of a flier for a flier. It had nothing to do with two Harrys. It was for the dive.

Krum nodded, once.

He went.

Harry looked past him, through the tent flap, out at the stands.

He could see the Slytherin stand from the bed, full and green and loud. Theo wasn't in it. Theo was beneath the lake by an open window. He could see Millicent with both fists in the air, roaring. He could see Draco Malfoy two rows down, not cheering, arms folded, looking at the medical tent.

He reached for the stand. He did it without thinking, the way he always did, the way he'd done it at the World Cup and on the Quidditch pitch and in the Great Hall at a hundred breakfasts.

He reached for the still place.

It wasn't there.

He went along the stand row by row, the way he went along the Map. He read Millicent, so loud and so glad that it was nearly a shout. He read Draco, frightened and furious and something else. He read the fifth-years and the sixth-years and Pucey and Warrington and a hundred Slytherins cheering his name.

He went along the whole of the stand twice.

There was no silence in it anywhere.

There was a seat at the end of the third row, beside an empty space where an old man in a black coat had been sitting. Harry could see it from the bed. It was empty.

He stared at it for a long time.

"Potter," Madam Pomfrey snapped. "Lie *down*."

He lay down.

* * *

They gave him forty points.

Krum got forty too, and Cedric thirty-eight, and Fleur thirty-seven. Karkaroff gave Harry four out of ten, and the Slytherin stand booed him so loudly that Karkaroff went red. Bagman gave him ten. Dumbledore gave him nine. Madame Maxime gave him eight, and afterwards she looked at him across the enclosure with something in her that Harry read as wariness.

Mr Crouch gave him nine.

Harry read him from the bed, across the whole enclosure, because he couldn't help it. Terror and shame and the locked thing, very hard, beneath the floor. The same as on the moor. The same as in the room off the Hall. It hadn't moved.

It was harder to reach now, he thought. Crouch looked greyer. He looked ill.

Harry didn't dwell on it.

* * *

The Slytherin common room was louder than on Hallowe'en.

He hadn't thought that was possible. He came through the stone wall at eight that evening with his arm in a sling and his shoulder bandaged and a golden egg under his good arm, and the noise came off the room at him like a wall coming down.

They had the chair out again. They had the Butterbeer out again. Somebody had got food from the kitchens, enormous platters of it, sausages and cakes and pies. Somebody else had charmed a banner over the fireplace that said *POTTER* in green letters three feet high, and every few seconds the letters changed into a small black dragon that breathed silver fire.

They roared.

He read them. He didn't have to try. They were adoring. That was the only word. It came off every one of them, a hundred Slytherins, first-years to seventh-years. It was the old wanting from his second year, and the triumph from Hallowe'en, and something new on top of both that was larger than either.

*Two of him.*

They'd seen it. They'd all seen it. A whole stand of them, a whole school of them, had seen Harry Potter split in two in front of a dragon. They didn't know how, and they didn't care how. They wanted it. They wanted it to be theirs. Beneath the adoration, very deep, Harry could feel them deciding that it was.

Warrington had him by the good arm. Pucey was shouting something in his ear. A crowd of second-years were standing on a table chanting his name.

He didn't enjoy it.

He noticed that, standing in the doorway with a golden egg under his arm and a hundred people roaring at him. He'd enjoyed it in his second year, when they gave him the chair. He'd enjoyed it in the Leaky Cauldron when he was eleven and a whole room turned to look at him. All his life he'd wanted to walk into a room and have it turn.

It had turned. It was turning as hard as any room had ever turned to anybody.

He didn't enjoy it at all.

He sat in the chair, because they wouldn't let him not sit in it. He drank a Butterbeer, because somebody put it in his hand. He let Millicent hit him on the good shoulder, gently, three times.

"You absolute idiot," she said, her eyes wet. "You absolute bloody idiot."

He let Theo sit on the arm of the chair, close, wordless, which was what Theo did when he'd been frightened.

He looked at the chair by the draughty window, at the far end of the room.

It was empty.

He looked at it every few minutes for two hours. He didn't mean to. Every few minutes he found that he was looking at it, and looked away, and then found that he was looking at it again.

At ten o'clock the stone wall opened, and Evelyn came in.

She came in quietly. Nobody noticed her. Nobody ever noticed her. She came through the wall in her grey cardigan with her hands in her pockets and her face exactly as it always was. She walked along the edge of the room, behind the crowd, through the noise, to the chair by the draughty window, and sat down in it, and took out a book.

Harry looked at her across the whole of the common room.

She didn't look at him. She opened the book. She turned a page.

He read her. He couldn't read her. He never could. He looked at her face, the one people forgot, bent over her book in the green light by the draughty window with the lake leaning on the glass behind her. There was nothing in it. There was nothing in her silence but silence, and he had no idea at all where she'd been.

He didn't ask. He didn't get up.

He didn't cross the room through a hundred people and say *where were you*.

He just watched her.

And then she turned another page, and without looking up, without moving her head at all, she said something. He couldn't hear it. He was too far away, and the room was too loud. But he saw her lips move, and he knew the shape of it, because he'd seen her say it at a library table and a breakfast table and on the floor of a round stone room beneath the lake, a hundred times, in three years.

*Potter.*

Then she said something else. Three words. He knew the shape of those too.

*You looked. Didn't you.*

He didn't answer.

She didn't look up. She turned another page.
