## Chapter 53: The Vision

The Defence Against the Dark Arts practical was on the Thursday of the second week of exams, in the Great Hall, at half past two, and Harry's examiner was the oldest person he'd ever seen.

She was tiny. So small and so bent that she came up to his shoulder, and so wrinkled that her face looked like a walnut somebody had left in a drawer for a century. She wore a hat with a feather in it that was older than the Wizengamot. Her name was Professor Marchbanks. She had a quill in one hand and an ear trumpet in the other, and she looked at him over both of them with very bright, very small, very black eyes.

"Potter," she said. "*The* Potter?"

"I suppose so."

"You suppose." She made a mark. "Go on, then. Show me a jinx."

He showed her a jinx. He showed her a counter-jinx, and a Shield Charm, and the Disarming Charm, which he did on a cushion she'd brought for the purpose. The cushion flew across the Hall and hit the far wall and fell down. He showed her a Stunning Spell. He showed her a Reductor Curse on a stack of bricks.

Harry read her the whole time.

There wasn't much. She was very old and very calm and very bored, the way a person is bored who's watched the same thirty spells done by four thousand fifteen-year-olds over sixty years. But beneath the boredom, steady and small, was a kind of hope. The hope of an old examiner who goes on examining because once, a long time ago, she saw something she's never forgotten, and she's been waiting ever since to see it again.

"Bonus point," she said at the end, without looking up. "If you can do a Patronus. Nobody can. Don't feel bad."

Harry raised his wand.

He thought about it for a moment. He thought about a stag in an alley in August, and a stag by a lake in his third year, and a stag walking across a hidden room in another world, past where he was standing, through a wall. He thought about what he'd use.

He thought about the whole of Hogwarts laughing on the marble staircase with fireworks going over its head.

"*Expecto Patronum.*"

It came out of him at full size.

He hadn't meant it to be that large. He'd meant a stag. What came out of his wand was a stag, silver and enormous, antlers up. It rose into the air of the Great Hall above the examiners' tables and went round once beneath the enchanted ceiling, which was blue and full of June clouds. The light came off it so brightly that every candidate in the Hall stopped what they were doing and looked up.

It went round the Hall twice. Its hooves made no sound. Wherever it went the light went with it, across the faces of the examiners and the candidates and the house tables pushed back against the walls, silver, the way moonlight goes across water.

Then it came down in front of Professor Marchbanks and stood there and looked at her, and went out.

Nobody in the Great Hall moved.

Professor Marchbanks had put down her ear trumpet. She was looking at the place where the stag had been. Harry read her, and the hope at the bottom of her had come all the way up, and it wasn't hope any more.

"Well," she said. "Well, well."

She made a mark on her parchment. A very large mark.

"I examined a boy in nineteen ninety-six who did that, you know," she said. Then she frowned. "No. Eighteen ninety-six. No. Nineteen hundred and… it was a long time ago. He did things with a wand I'd never seen before."

She looked at Harry over the top of the parchment with her small black eyes.

"I've waited a very long time to see another one. I didn't think I would."

She sniffed.

"You can go."

Harry went.

* * *

Umbridge caught him on the Monday night.

She'd been trying to catch him since March. He'd known it every day. He'd read it in her at every meal, the sweet domestic pleasure gone hard and aimed at him, and the hurt beneath it, set. She'd caught him in a corridor twice and given him detentions for nothing. She'd searched his trunk. She'd had Draco Malfoy follow him to every exam.

She caught him at eleven o'clock at night at the bottom of the West Tower stairs, coming back from the Owlery with a letter to Sirius that said only *exams nearly done*.

He didn't feel her coming. That was what he thought about afterwards. He'd felt the scar all evening, cold and steady, the preparation going on and on, nearly finished, and he'd been listening to it instead of the castle. He came round the bottom of the stairs, and she was there.

She had Draco with her, and Crabbe.

"Mr Potter," she said. "Out of bounds."

"I was posting a letter, Professor."

"At eleven o'clock at night. To whom?"

"My godfather."

He read her. The pleasure was enormous. The largest he'd ever felt it. The pleasure of a woman who's been waiting since March for one particular moment, and has it.

"Your godfather," said Umbridge, "is a convicted murderer and a fugitive from justice. Writing to him is a crime. Did you know that, Mr Potter?"

She smiled.

"Mr Malfoy, Mr Crabbe, you may go to bed. Thank you. I'll deal with Mr Potter myself."

Draco looked at her.

Harry read him look. There was surprise in it, and then a flicker of something that was nearly alarm, aimed at Umbridge, not at Harry. Then it sank.

"Yes, Professor," said Draco, and went.

* * *

She didn't take him to her office.

She took him up to the entrance hall, and he read her the whole way, and he knew before they got there what she wanted, because it was very simple and very loud.

She wanted Dumbledore.

She'd wanted Dumbledore since March. She'd sat in her pink office every night for three months and not been allowed into his. The Ministry hadn't found him, and she'd promised the Minister she would. And she'd decided tonight, at the bottom of the West Tower stairs, that Harry Potter knew where he was.

"Where is he?" she demanded in the entrance hall.

"I don't know, Professor."

"You're lying."

"Yes," said Harry.

She stopped.

He watched her not know what to do with that. He read it go into her and stick. She'd expected him to deny it. She'd had a great many things ready for when he did, and he hadn't, and none of them fitted.

He thought about it for perhaps two seconds.

He thought about a woman who enjoyed other people's pain the way other people enjoy a cup of tea. He thought about Neville on a staircase in October with his right hand cradled inside his left. He thought about twenty-seven people going through a small door at the back of a room whilst he held a wall across eight minds. He thought about *I must not tell lies* on the back of his own right hand, in his own small neat writing.

He thought about the Forbidden Forest, and who lived in it, and what they thought of witches from the Ministry who used the word *half-breed*.

He'd heard her use it. In a Defence lesson in February, about Professor Firenze, whom Dumbledore had brought in to teach Divination after Trelawney, and whom she'd wanted dismissed.

"He left something," Harry said slowly. "In the forest. Before he went."

Umbridge's eyes went bright.

"What?"

"I don't know what it is. He told me where it was. In case."

He looked at the floor.

"He said I should only use it if I had to."

He felt it go into her like a hook into a fish.

"Show me," said Umbridge.

"Now?"

"*Now*, Mr Potter."

"Shouldn't you bring…"

"No," said Umbridge. "Just the two of us, I think."

He read her say it. He read why. She didn't want the Inquisitorial Squad there. She didn't want Draco Malfoy, or Filch, or anybody. She wanted to walk into the Minister's office on her own and lay on his desk whatever Albus Dumbledore had hidden in the Forbidden Forest, and she wanted nobody else's name anywhere near it.

He'd known she'd say that.

He opened the front doors.

* * *

The forest at night was very dark and very loud.

Not with noise. With feeling. Harry had been in it before, in his first year, and on a night in his third year by the lake, and he knew it, but he'd never been in it like this, with the range he had now. He could feel everything. The small frightened things in the undergrowth and the large calm things in the trees. The spiders, far off to the left, thousands of them, a dry hungry clicking that he turned down as hard as he could. Something very old and very slow in a hollow to the right that might once have been a tree.

And he could feel them.

They were half a mile ahead, a little to the north, where the trees opened out. A great many of them, thirty or forty, and they were proud. A hard, old, settled pride, the pride of a people who've been here longer than the castle and don't intend to leave. Beneath it, very sharp, was anger. It had been there a long time. It was aimed at the castle, and at the Ministry, and at the people who made laws about where centaurs could live.

Harry walked towards them.

Umbridge walked behind him with her wand lit. She wasn't frightened yet. She was eager. He could feel it, bright and greedy, aimed at the dark ahead of them, where Dumbledore's secret was.

After a quarter of a mile she asked, "How much further?"

"Not far."

After another hundred yards she asked, "Are you quite sure you know the way?"

"Yes."

He didn't stop walking. And as he walked, he began to build.

He built a path.

That was easy. One mind, an ordinary one, in a dark wood, already looking for what he was going to show it. He built her a path through the trees, clear and narrow, going straight on. He built her his own back, a little way ahead, walking along it quite steadily. He built her the dark, and the trees on either side, and the sound of her own feet on dead leaves.

And then he stepped off the path.

He stepped off it to the left, into the trees, and stood still behind a beech. Umbridge went on walking along the path he'd built, following the back he'd built, straight ahead, towards the place where the trees opened out.

He went with her. He walked parallel, thirty feet to her left, in the dark, holding the path in her head. One door against one wind. It was nothing. He'd held it against eight people a few weeks ago with his nose bleeding. He could have held this one all night.

She walked into the clearing.

He let the path go.

* * *

He didn't see all of it. He stood behind a tree at the edge of the clearing, in the dark, with his wand in his hand and his face against the bark, and he read it.

He read her stop.

He read her look round and find that the boy she'd been following wasn't there, and that the path she'd been walking along wasn't there either, and that she was standing in an open space amongst very tall trees with her wand lit, alone. He read her fear begin. It began small. The fear of somebody who's got lost.

Then the centaurs came out of the trees.

They came out all round the clearing at once, thirty or forty of them, very tall in the dark, with bows. The light of Umbridge's wand went up their flanks and their chests and their faces. Harry read the pride in them, and the anger, and something that rose through both when they saw who it was.

Umbridge's fear went up like a flame.

"Stay back," she shrilled. "I am Senior Undersecretary to the Minister for Magic. I am the Headmistress of Hogwarts. I have the authority of the Ministry. I order you…"

"*Order* us?" said a deep voice.

"You are creatures of near-human intelligence," said Umbridge, faster and higher. "By law you are permitted to live in this forest only so long as… You will stand aside, or I will have you… you filthy… you *half-breeds*…"

Harry heard the word.

He felt it go into the centaurs. He felt the anger that had been in them a long time rise all at once, through the pride, and go hot, and then go very cold. And he felt Umbridge feel it go, and understand, for the first time in her life, that she'd said the wrong word to the wrong people, and that nobody was coming.

Her terror filled the clearing.

It was enormous. Larger than anything he'd felt in her. Larger than the self-satisfaction and the certainty and the sweet domestic pleasure all put together, and it had no bottom at all. The terror of somebody who's spent her whole life on the side of the rules, and found herself, in the dark, in a place where her rules don't go.

She screamed.

Harry stood behind the tree and read it.

He read it all the way down. The terror and the disbelief, and the very small, very old, very hard thing at the bottom of her that still couldn't believe this was happening to *her*. He read the centaurs close in. He read her wand fly out of her hand. He read her lifted off her feet, kicking and screaming, by somebody very large, and carried off into the trees. He read the terror go with her, going away through the forest, growing smaller, until he couldn't read it any more.

He didn't feel sorry.

He waited to. He stood behind the tree in the dark for some time, his face against the bark, and he waited, quite honestly, for it to come.

It didn't come.

He'd made a woman see a path that wasn't there. He'd walked her, on purpose, knowing exactly what he was doing and exactly who was waiting at the end of it, into a clearing full of people who hated her, and he'd stood behind a tree and listened to her scream. He looked inside himself for what ought to have been there, and he found the back of his right hand, and Neville's, and twenty-seven people going through a door.

He didn't find anything else.

* * *

A centaur found him on the way back.

A chestnut one, with a dark beard and a hard face. It came out of the trees in front of him on the path and stood there with its bow half drawn, and Harry stopped and read it.

Anger. Old pride. And beneath them, faint, a kind of grim, unwilling recognition.

"You led her here," said the centaur.

"Yes."

"You knew what she was."

"Yes."

The centaur looked down at him from a great height for a long moment.

"We do not harm foals," it said at last. "That is the only reason. Not because you brought her. Do not mistake us for your tools, human child. We are nobody's."

It lowered the bow.

"Go back to your castle."

Harry went back to his castle.

He went up through the entrance hall and down to the dungeons and in through the stone wall at twenty past one in the morning. The common room was empty. He went up to the dormitory and got into bed without waking anybody.

He lay on his back in the dark.

He thought he wouldn't sleep. He slept at once, and didn't dream. When he woke at seven, the scar was cold and steady and the preparation was still coming through, very quiet, very nearly finished.

At breakfast the Slytherin table was full of the news that Professor Umbridge hadn't come back to the castle in the night, that nobody knew where she was, and that Filch was crying.

Harry ate his toast.

Across the table Evelyn was eating her egg, with her fork in her left hand, her toast in four and her tea last, and she didn't look at him once. When she'd finished her tea she set the cup down in its saucer and turned it a quarter turn, and got up, and left.

He didn't need to read her. He knew she knew.

* * *

History of Magic was at two o'clock on Tuesday the eighteenth of June. The last exam.

Harry had worked it out in March. He'd looked at a calendar in the library and counted forward and found the date, and gone very still.

"What?" Evelyn had asked from the next table.

"Nothing," he'd said.

"You've just found something out."

And he'd told her.

The eighteenth of June. In another world it had been the eighteenth of June too. He'd stood in the Hog's Head at ten to six that evening and heard Millicent Bulstrode, who wasn't his friend in that world, run in out of breath and say the other Harry and five others had flown south from the forest.

It wasn't the same world. The calendars matched. That was all.

He sat at his desk in the Great Hall with the exam paper in front of him and the June sun coming in hot through the high windows, and wrote about the goblin rebellion of 1612, and the scar was cold and steady.

At twenty to three the cold changed.

* * *

He was in a corridor.

He knew it. He'd dreamed it every night for two months, and all last summer, and he'd been a snake in it at Christmas. Long and dark and windowless, with a black door at the end, and he went through the black door at last.

He was in a room full of shelves.

It was enormous. It rose higher than he could see and stretched further than he could see, rows and rows of tall shelves, and on the shelves were small glass spheres, thousands of them, each with a small yellowing label beneath. They glowed faintly in the dark, and he knew this room too. He'd been in this room. He'd stood in it whilst the shelves fell and the spheres broke on the floor all round him in their thousands, all speaking at once, and he'd watched a boot come down on one with his name on it.

At the end of row ninety-seven there was a man on the floor.

He was on his knees, and then he wasn't on his knees, he was on his side, and he was screaming. It was Sirius. Harry knew him. He knew the long black hair and the thin face and the voice. Sirius was screaming on the stone floor between the shelves, and somebody was standing over him with a wand, very tall and very white, and the somebody was pleased.

*Get it for me*, the somebody said. *Take it down for me, Black, or I will go on, and on, and on.*

Harry was in the somebody. He was looking down at Sirius out of red eyes, and he could feel the wand in his own long white hand, and he could feel the pleasure. He could feel, quite clearly, beneath the pleasure, the patience. Cold and enormous and quite unhurried.

He knew it.

That was the thing. That was what made him, even inside it, even with Sirius screaming, go quite still. He knew it. He'd read this. Not in this world. In another, two years ahead, in a boy in a Gryffindor scarf who'd sat in an exam and fallen asleep and seen his godfather on the floor of row ninety-seven. Who'd gone, and taken five friends with him, and walked into a room full of Death Eaters, and watched his godfather go back through a veil, laughing.

It was the same picture. Row ninety-seven. The shelves. The pleasure.

It was a trap.

It was the same trap.

* * *

And then, because he was inside, and because he was who he was, he did the other thing.

He didn't wake up. He didn't try to. He went down. He went past the picture of Sirius on the floor, which was at the front of the mind he was in, very bright, held there carefully the way you hold up a lantern. He went down behind it, into the rest of that mind, the way he'd gone down behind Snape's furnished rooms in November.

Sirius wasn't there.

That was the first thing he found. Behind the picture of Sirius there was nothing to do with Sirius at all. The picture was a lantern held up on a pole, and behind it, in the dark, the mind holding the pole was looking somewhere else entirely.

It was looking at the preparation.

It had been coming through the scar for two months. Somebody at a table, laying things out in a row, one after another, carefully, in the right order, counting them. Harry had felt it every night. He'd felt it nearly finished.

It was finished.

He could feel it now, from inside, very close, and it was enormous. The largest thing he'd ever felt in any mind. Not a feeling, exactly. A readiness. The readiness of somebody who's spent a very long time gathering the pieces of something back together, and has them all now, laid out on stone in a row, and is about to begin.

Harry felt the pieces.

He couldn't see them. He felt them the way he'd felt the diadem from thirty feet away under a Cloak. Each one was hungry. Each one was cold and patient and lonely and envious. Each one was Tom. There were several of them, in a row, on something hard and flat, all hungry at once, aimed at the mind that had made them, the way small children are aimed at their mother at the end of a day.

And behind them was an arch.

He felt it. He couldn't see it, but he felt it, the way you feel a cliff edge in the dark. It was old, older than the Ministry, older than anything, and it wasn't a feeling. It was an absence of feeling, a place where everything stopped. He'd felt it once before. He'd stood in a doorway in another world and looked down a corridor into a room with a stone arch in it and a ragged black veil, and watched the other Sirius go back through it laughing, and felt him go out like a blown-out flame.

The Veil.

It was going to happen at the Veil.

And it was going to happen tonight.

He felt that too. He felt it in the readiness, in its edges, the way you feel in somebody that they're about to stand up. Not next week. Not tomorrow. Tonight. The pieces were laid out on the stone steps at the foot of the arch, and the person who'd laid them out was holding up a lantern on a pole for Harry Potter to look at, a picture of Sirius on the floor of row ninety-seven, so that Harry Potter would come.

Because there was one piece missing.

He didn't know what it was. He felt it the way you feel a gap in a row of teeth with your tongue. A place at the end of the row that was empty, and the mind that had laid out the row was looking at the empty place, and waiting, patiently, for it to be filled.

And then it looked up, out of the dark, past the lantern, at him.

* * *

He was on the floor of the Great Hall.

He'd fallen off his chair. The exam invigilator, a thin wizard called Professor Tofty, was bending over him. Professor Marchbanks was coming across the Hall very fast for somebody her age, and the whole room was staring at him.

He was all right.

He said so. He said it several times. He said it to Professor Tofty, and to Professor Marchbanks, who peered at him with her small black eyes, and to the fifty other candidates, who'd all stopped writing. He said he'd been up late revising and had fallen asleep and had a nightmare, and he was sorry, and could he go to the hospital wing?

Professor Tofty let him go.

He didn't go to the hospital wing.

He went out of the Great Hall into the entrance hall and stood by the foot of the marble staircase in the hot June afternoon, with the front doors open and the lawns running down to the lake and the sound of people who'd finished their exams shouting on the grass. He read the castle, all of it, as far as it went.

He was looking for Evelyn.

He couldn't find her. He never could. He reached for her the way you put your hand out in the dark for a wall, and found the place where she wasn't, the silence, on the far side of the entrance hall, by the door to the dungeons.

She was standing in the doorway, looking at him.

"You fell off your chair," she said. "At twenty-two minutes to three. I could see you through the doors."

"It's tonight," said Harry.

Evelyn didn't ask what was tonight.

"At the Veil," said Harry. "In the Department of Mysteries. He's got them. All of them. Laid out on the steps. He's going to put himself back together. And he's showing me Sirius being tortured in row ninety-seven so that I'll come. Because that's what the other one did. That's what I did. In the other world."

"Is Sirius being tortured?"

"I don't know."

"Then find out," said Evelyn. "First."

* * *

There was only one fireplace in the castle the Ministry wasn't watching. It was in Umbridge's office, and Umbridge was somewhere in the Forbidden Forest.

Harry knew that because she'd told him.

She'd told him in November, over tea with milk, quite proudly. Hers was the only Floo connection in Hogwarts the Ministry had agreed not to monitor, because she was the Ministry, and she liked to be able to talk to the Minister in private.

He went up to the first floor. Evelyn came with him. Nobody was in the corridor. The Squad were at the lake with everybody else. The door to the pink office was locked. Evelyn took a hairpin out of her hair and put it into the lock with the tip of her wand beside it and opened the door in eleven seconds.

The kitten plates were still on the wall. They mewed at him as he came in.

He took a pinch of Floo powder from the pot on the mantelpiece and threw it into the grate. Green fire roared up, and he knelt on the hearthrug and put his head into the flames.

"*Number twelve, Grimmauld Place!*"

* * *

The kitchen was empty.

It spun round him slowly, the long scrubbed table and the fire and the dresser with the cracked plates, and there was nobody in it. Harry knelt with his head in the flames and his body in a pink office four hundred miles away, and couldn't breathe.

Then Kreacher came out of the boiler cupboard.

He came out slowly and looked at the fire, at Harry's head in it, and bowed very low.

"The young master," he said in his hoarse mutter. "The half-blood boy with the dead mother's eyes. In the fire. Oh, what would my poor mistress say."

"Where's Sirius?"

"Master is not here," said Kreacher.

He said it to the floor. Harry read him.

He read him through the fire, which he'd never done. It was faint, the way a voice is faint on a bad line, but it was there. The hatred. The grief at the bottom, like water in a well. And on top of both, bright and small and secret, the thing he'd felt in the kitchen on Christmas night with snow on the elf's shoulders.

Glee.

Glee, aimed at Harry, and at the answer Kreacher had just given.

"You're lying," said Harry.

Kreacher's head came up.

"Master has gone out," said Kreacher. "Master has gone to the Ministry of Magic, young master, oh yes, to rescue somebody, Master was very…"

"You're lying," Harry repeated, very quietly. "You're enjoying it. I can feel you enjoying it. You enjoyed it at Christmas, when you came in with snow on you, from wherever you'd been."

He held the elf's eyes through the fire.

"Get Sirius. Now. Or I'll tell him where you went on Christmas night. I'll tell him exactly how pleased you were."

He didn't know where Kreacher had been. He'd never known.

He read the glee go out of Kreacher all at once, like a match dropped in water, and something rise in its place that was very old and very frightened.

Kreacher bowed so low his nose touched the floor. Then he was gone.

Eleven seconds later Sirius came down the kitchen stairs three at a time.

* * *

He was alive. He was whole. He was in his shirtsleeves with his hair tied back and a rag in his hand, because he'd been upstairs with Buckbeak. He dropped to his knees on the hearth in front of the fire and looked at Harry's head in it, and Harry read him through the flames.

Alarm. Love. All of it, at full volume, faint along the line.

"Harry. What is it? What's happened?"

Harry told him.

He told him fast. Row ninety-seven. The picture. The trap. And the other thing, behind the picture, which was the only thing that mattered. The Veil, and the pieces laid out on the steps, and tonight.

Sirius went white.

"You're sure."

"Yes."

"How sure?"

"As sure as I've ever been about anything I've read."

Sirius looked at him through the fire for one second longer. Then he stood and turned and shouted up the stairs in a voice Harry had never heard him use, and the house woke round him.

* * *

They argued for twenty minutes.

Harry knelt on Umbridge's hearthrug with his head in the fire and his knees aching and Evelyn standing guard at the door, and the kitchen of Grimmauld Place filled up round him. Lupin came, from upstairs. Tonks burst out of the fireplace beside his own head in a flash of green, from the Ministry, where she'd been on a shift. Her hair was mouse-brown and she didn't change it. Moody came banging through the front door four minutes later. Kingsley's face appeared in the kitchen fire beside Harry's, from somewhere else, very calm.

"Dumbledore," said Lupin at once. "We need Dumbledore."

"Already sent," said Moody. "Fawkes, from my end. He's abroad. He'll come as fast as he can. Which isn't fast enough."

"Then we go," said Tonks. "Now. Us."

"We go," said Moody. "Not the boy."

"I have to come," Harry said from the fire.

"No."

"I'm the only one who can feel it," said Harry. "You don't know where it is. You don't know when it starts. You don't know what he's doing or which of you he's looking at. I do. I can feel it through the scar. I'll know the moment it begins. I'll know if he moves. I'll know if he's pretending."

He looked at Moody through the flames.

"You need somebody who can feel it. That's me. There isn't anybody else."

"You're fifteen," said Lupin.

"I was fourteen in a graveyard."

"That is precisely the point," said Lupin, very quietly. "Harry, it is exactly what he wants. You said so yourself. He's showing you Sirius on the floor so that you'll *come*."

"I know. And if I don't come, he'll know I didn't. And he'll do it anyway, without me, and you won't know when, or where he is in the room, or what he's going to do next."

Harry held Lupin's eyes through the fire.

"He wants me there. Fine. Then I'll be there knowing. That's the only difference I can make."

The kitchen fell silent.

Harry read them. He read them all, faint along the line, through the green flames. Lupin's fear, aimed at him, large and steady and very old, and beneath it, Lupin's agreement, which Lupin didn't want. Tonks's fear, bright and quick, and beneath it a fierce excitement she was ashamed of. Moody's suspicion, going round and round, and beneath it the cold practical thing that was already working out where Harry would stand. Kingsley, calm, deep, moving.

And Sirius.

Sirius hadn't spoken. He was standing by the table with the rag still in his hand, and Harry read him. What was in him was love, and fear, and fury, all three at full volume and aimed in the same direction, at the door.

"He's right," said Sirius.

"Sirius…"

"He's right, Remus. You know he's right. He's always right about this. He was right about Peter. He was right about the rat. He was right about Crouch, and the maze, and Arthur on the floor at Christmas."

Sirius threw the rag down on the table.

"And I'll tell you something else. If any of you tries to leave him behind, I'm going with him. Wherever he goes. However he gets there. You can lock me in this house for another year after, Alastor, I don't care, but tonight, if Harry goes, I go with him, and I go where he goes."

He looked at the fire.

"Got that?"

Nobody answered him for a moment.

"Merlin," said Moody at last, very sourly. "Fine. Fine. The boy comes. He stays behind me and he does what I tell him and the first time he doesn't I Stun him and put him in a cupboard."

The blue eye swivelled in the fire.

"We'll meet you in the Atrium. Seven o'clock. Not before. Not after. Can you get out of the castle?"

"Yes."

"How?"

Harry thought about it.

"There's a pub," he said.

* * *

He took his head out of the fire.

He knelt back on Umbridge's hearthrug in the pink office with his face hot and his knees stiff and the kitten plates mewing on the wall, and Evelyn at the door.

"Seven," he said. "In the Atrium. They're coming. Dumbledore's been sent for."

"Good," said Evelyn.

"I'm going."

"I know. So am I."

He looked at her. He didn't argue. He'd known, he found, since the entrance hall, that there was no point arguing, and that he didn't want to.

"And Bulstrode," said Evelyn. "And Granger and Weasley. And Longbottom."

"Why Neville?"

"Because the woman who did that to his mother is out of Azkaban," said Evelyn, "and she's one of his, and she'll be there. And because if we don't take him and he finds out afterwards, he'll never forgive any of us. Least of all you."

Harry thought about a lamp left on in an empty house.

"And Lovegood will come," said Evelyn. "Whether we ask her or not. She'll just be there. You know she will."

"And Theo?"

Evelyn hesitated.

"Ask him," she said. "But you know what he'll say."

* * *

Theo was by the lake.

He was sitting on the grass beneath a beech, alone, with his chessboard, playing both sides. Harry sat down beside him and for a while said nothing, and Theo moved a bishop.

Harry read him.

The calm sadness. The care. The curiosity. And beneath them, quite deep, quite settled, was something Harry had felt in Theo for a year now, since a churchyard, and had never once touched. A boy on the edge of a long drop in the dark.

"It's tonight," said Harry. "Something. At the Ministry. In the Department of Mysteries. I'm going. Some of the others are coming."

Theo moved a pawn.

"Who's going to be there?" he asked. "On the other side."

"I think all of them."

Theo went very still.

He sat with his hand over the board, holding a knight, not putting it down, and Harry read him, and the drop was very near the top.

"My father," said Theo.

"Yes."

"He'll be there."

"I think so."

Theo put the knight down. He put it down very carefully on the wrong square, a square where it could be taken at once, and looked at it, and didn't move it back.

"I can't," he said. "Harry. I'm sorry. I can't stand in a room and point a wand at him. I can't stand in a room and watch somebody else point one. I can't."

He was very white.

"I'm sorry."

"Don't be."

"I am, though."

"I know," said Harry. "Don't be anyway."

Theo looked at him then. Harry read him look. Beneath the drop, very small, was relief. Beneath the relief was shame at the relief. And beneath the shame was the care, from the chessboard, from four years ago, sharp and plain, aimed at Harry.

"I'll stay in the dormitory," said Theo. "If anybody asks, you're all in bed with a stomach bug. I'll keep the window open."

"I know you will," said Harry.

* * *

At six they went down through the one-eyed witch, seven of them.

Harry went first and Evelyn last. Between them was Millicent, who'd said only "Course." Ron and Hermione, who'd come up from the lake at a run when Harry's coin went warm in their pockets with a single word on its rim. Neville, who'd looked at Harry for three seconds when Harry told him, and then gone very red and said "Yes." And Luna, who'd been sitting on the third stair of the marble staircase when they came down it, as though she'd been waiting for them, and had stood up and dusted off her skirt and come.

Hermione had made the coins say words in May. She'd worked on it for seven months.

The word had been *NOW*.

They came up through the trapdoor in the cellar of Honeydukes, and through the shop, and out into the June evening of Hogsmeade. They went down the high street, past the post office with its row of owls along the roof, and down the side street to a sign with a goat's head on it.

Harry pushed the door open.

The barman looked up.

He was wiping a glass with a filthy cloth, and he looked at the seven of them standing in his doorway in their school robes. Harry read him. It was the same as ever, and he'd never seen Harry in his life.

"No," said Aberforth Dumbledore.

"We need your fireplace," said Harry.

"I know what you need. Alastor Moody's been in my fire for ten minutes telling me what you need."

Aberforth put the glass down.

"And I say no. You're children."

"Yes," said Harry.

"Children don't go to the Ministry of Magic at seven o'clock at night to fight Death Eaters."

"No."

"Then go home."

"No," said Harry.

They looked at each other across the dirty bar.

Harry read him. Irritation. The old bitterness, aimed far away. And beneath it, rising now, close to the top, the stubborn gruff protectiveness of children that was buried at the bottom of this man in every world there was.

He didn't push it. He didn't touch it. He didn't do anything to it at all.

He only said, "Your brother's coming. Moody sent for him."

Aberforth's face did something.

"Is he," he said.

"Yes."

"Course he is."

Aberforth looked at the seven of them for a long moment.

"Course he is. He always comes. He always comes *after*."

He came round the end of the bar. He went to the fireplace, which was black and cold, and took a pot down from the mantelpiece, and held it out without looking at any of them.

"Go on, then. Go on. I'm too old for this."

Harry took a pinch of the powder.

He thought about another night, in another world, in this same room, with this same man saying the same words at the same fireplace. He'd stood here with a borrowed face and a stopped watch and Evelyn beside him, and gone through, and come out in an Atrium full of fear.

He threw the powder into the grate.

"Ministry of Magic," he said.

* * *

The Atrium was empty.

It was seven minutes to seven. The long dark floor stretched away from the fireplaces towards the golden fountain, and there was nobody. The day staff had gone. The night staff hadn't come on. Golden symbols moved slowly across the peacock-blue ceiling. Water ran out of the golden wizard's wand and the centaur's arrow and the goblin's hat into the pool, and the sound of it was the only sound.

Harry read the Atrium.

It was empty. Empty all the way down. There was nobody on this floor, and nobody on the next, and nobody on the one after that.

And then, very far below, as far as he could reach, further than he'd ever reached in a building, there was something.

Pleasure. A dozen people, perhaps more, a long way down, deep in the rock, and they were pleased. The pleasure from a churchyard. The pleasure from the Hall of Prophecy in another world, hot and eager and waiting.

And in the middle of them, very cold, very large, very still, the readiness.

It hadn't begun.

"Seven," said Evelyn beside him, looking at her watch. "Exactly."

The fireplaces behind them roared green. One. Two. Three. Four. Five. Moody first, staff out, eye going round. Then Tonks, her hair still mouse-brown. Then Lupin, and Kingsley, and Sirius in a long black coat, his wand in his hand and his face very white and very calm.

Sirius looked at Harry across the Atrium.

He didn't speak. He didn't need to. Harry read him, and it was all there, at full volume, the love and the fear and the fury, all aimed at the floor beneath their feet.

"Right," said Moody. "Lifts."

* * *

The lift came up with a clatter of golden grilles.

They got in, twelve of them, too many, pressed together, wands out. The grilles slid shut. Moody pressed the lowest button on the panel, the one with no number beside it, only a small black square.

The lift began to descend.

It went down past the floors. Harry counted them. He counted them the way Evelyn would have, without meaning to, aloud in his head. Level Two. Level Three. Level Four. Level Five. The cool female voice announced each floor as they passed it, and nobody got on, and nobody got off.

He read downwards.

He read through the floor of the lift, and the floors beneath it, and the rock, as far as he could, and the pleasure was getting nearer. The dozen people, waiting, pleased. And in the middle of them, the readiness, very cold, very still.

It was looking up.

He felt it look up. He felt it turn towards the lift coming down through the rock towards it with twelve people inside, the way a head turns towards a door when somebody it's been waiting for is on the stairs.

It wasn't surprised.

It was pleased.

The lift went on down into the dark.

## Chapter 54: The Veil

The lift stopped at the bottom of the world, and the grilles slid back, and in front of them was the corridor.

Harry had walked along it every night for two months. He'd glided along it at Christmas, close to the floor, hungry. He'd walked along it in another world, with a borrowed face and two people made invisible beside him and blood running out of his nose. It was long and bare and windowless, with torches in brackets, and at the end of it was a plain black door.

"Nobody touch anything," said Moody. "Nobody open anything. Potter. Where?"

"Through the door. Then there's a round room."

"And then?"

"Then it gets complicated."

Moody's blue eye swivelled round to look at him.

"You've been here," he said. Not a question.

"Yes."

"When?"

"Not here," said Harry. "Somewhere like it."

Moody looked at him for one second longer. Then he grunted and went down the corridor with his staff out, and they followed him, twelve of them, close together, their wands lit. The black door opened when Moody reached it. It opened on its own, inwards, without a sound, the way doors open in dreams.

* * *

The round room was exactly the same.

It was circular and black, floor and ceiling and walls. All round the walls at regular intervals were identical black doors without handles, and between the doors were candles in brackets that burned with a cold blue flame. The flames were reflected in the shining black floor so that it looked as though there were dark water beneath their feet.

The door shut behind the last of them.

There was a rumbling, and the candles streaked sideways into long blue lines, and the walls spun. They spun very fast. Harry had known they would, and he shut his eyes, because it was worse with them open. When he opened them again the room was still, the candles were flames again, and every door looked exactly like every other.

"Twelve," said Evelyn. "Twelve doors."

"Brilliant," said Ron, a little high. "Which one's the way out?"

"None of them," said Evelyn. "That's rather the idea."

"Mark them," said Hermione. "If we open one and it's wrong, we mark it, so we don't…"

"They move," said Harry. "Marks won't help."

Hermione stared at him. "How do you *know* that?"

"Which one, Potter?" Moody asked.

Harry reached.

He reached through the black walls, through all twelve doors, and he did it fast, because he didn't know how long they had. He could feel the Department of Mysteries round him the way you feel a house in the dark. There were rooms. Some had nothing in them at all. One was full of something that wasn't feeling but was very like it, a slow, drifting, tangled awareness, a great many small things floating in a tank, thinking. One was very cold and very old and didn't feel like a room at all.

One was ticking.

He couldn't hear it. He felt it. A room full of something steady and regular and enormous, like a great many hearts beating at once. He knew it, because he'd stood in its doorway for fourteen seconds once whilst a girl with Evelyn's face wound a gold watch forwards and nothing happened.

And beyond it, further, below, through the ticking room and out the other side and down, was the readiness.

It was very close now. Cold and still and enormous, and waiting. Round it, scattered, were a dozen or more small hot points of pleasure, some near it, some nearer to Harry. Some were between him and it. Some were in a room he knew, a room as high as a cathedral and full of shelves.

"That one," said Harry, pointing. "Through the clocks. Then there's a hall full of shelves. They're waiting in it. Some of them. The rest are further on. Down. With him."

"How many in the hall?"

Harry counted.

"Nine," he said. "Maybe ten. They're pleased."

"Course they are," said Moody.

He looked round at the students, all seven of them, pressed together in the middle of the black floor with their wands out, and Harry read him look. Suspicion, going round. And beneath it, very fast, a cold, plain arithmetic.

"Right," said Moody. "Listen. All of you. When we go through, you stay together. You stay behind us. If I say run, you run, and you don't stop for anybody, and you don't come back for anybody, and that includes me."

His eye went round once more and stopped on Neville.

"Longbottom."

"Yes, sir."

"Your mum was the best duellist I ever trained," said Moody. "Don't go and prove it tonight."

* * *

The room of clocks was full of light.

It came off everything. Off the clocks, hundreds of them, large and small, on every surface, on shelves, on desks, hanging on the walls, ticking. Off a tall bell jar at the far end of the room, full of a bright sparkling wind, in which a tiny jewel-bright egg rose and hatched into a hummingbird and grew old and fell and became an egg again, over and over. Off the dust in the air.

Harry went through it fast.

He didn't look at the clocks. He didn't look at the place by the far wall where he'd once held a doorway as an empty room, in another world, whilst somebody wound a watch. He didn't look at Evelyn beside him, who wasn't looking at it either.

He could feel her not looking. That was strange. He couldn't feel Evelyn. He'd never once in five years felt anything from her. But he could feel the place where she was, the silence, walking beside him, and he could feel the silence keep its eyes very carefully away from that wall.

They went through the door at the far end.

* * *

The Hall of Prophecy rose into the dark.

It was as high as a church, and the shelves rose into the dark with it, row after row, hundreds of rows. On the shelves were the glass spheres, thousands and thousands of them, each glowing very faintly, each with its small yellowing label. The candles in the brackets between the rows were blue. The rows had numbers on their ends.

Harry had been here. He'd stood in this hall whilst it came down round him in a storm of glass and smoke and voices.

It was very quiet.

"Ninety-seven," he said. "That's where they want us. That's where the picture was."

"Then we don't go to ninety-seven," said Moody.

"They'll come to us."

"Let them."

"Harry," Neville whispered from behind. "Is she here? The… is Lestrange here?"

Harry reached. Far ahead and further down, beside the cold readiness, he found a heat he didn't like. A worship so large there was nothing left in it that was its own.

"Not in here," he said. "Further on."

Neville's jaw set. Harry read the small fierce thing in him go hard.

They went along the ends of the rows. Fifty-three. Fifty-four. Harry read the dark between the shelves, ahead and on either side, and the small hot points of pleasure were moving now. Moving inwards, between the shelves, from both sides, the way water comes in over sand when the tide turns. They were very pleased, and they were getting closer.

"Moody," said Harry.

"I know."

"They're…"

"*I know, Potter.*"

Seventy-one. Seventy-two.

And then, behind them, back the way they'd come, through the door from the room of clocks, Harry felt more of them. Six or seven, coming in fast from behind, from the round room, where they'd been waiting behind another of the doors. They were cutting them off.

Moody turned.

"Kingsley. Remus. With me. *Back.*" His eye went round to Sirius and Tonks. "You two, with the children. Get them down a row. Get them out of the middle. *Go.*"

The door from the room of clocks blew in.

* * *

It was very loud and very fast, and Harry didn't see most of it.

He saw Moody and Kingsley and Lupin turn back towards the door with their wands up and the light streaming out of them in a storm of red and white. He saw a masked figure come through the door and go straight backwards into a shelf. The shelf went over, and a hundred glass spheres smashed on the floor at once in a great ringing crash. From every broken sphere a thin pale figure of smoke rose, speaking, so that the end of the hall was suddenly full of ghostly people all talking at once in voices from a hundred years.

He saw Sirius grab Ron by the collar and Hermione by the arm and pull them into the end of row seventy-four.

He saw Tonks beside him, her hair suddenly a violent pink again, throw a curse over his shoulder at something he hadn't seen.

And then the pleasure that had been coming in between the shelves arrived.

They came out of the rows on both sides at once, from between the shelves, from the dark, in black robes and masks. Harry read them as they came. Nine. All of them pleased, the hot eager churchyard pleasure, and beneath it, in most of them, fear. Not of Harry. Of somebody further down.

"*Potter*," said a cold drawling voice. "How very kind of you to come."

* * *

Lucius Malfoy stood at the end of row seventy-four.

He'd taken off his mask. He held it in one hand and his wand in the other. His long white-blond hair was very smooth, and his pale pointed face was smiling.

Harry read him.

He'd read him in a churchyard, on his knees, terrified, calculating. He read him now, and it wasn't very different. The terror was still at the bottom, enormous, aimed further down. The calculation sat on top of it, working hard. And between the two, very bright, was greed. Not for gold. For one particular thing, and it was aimed past Harry, down row seventy-four and along it, towards the end of the hall.

Towards ninety-seven.

"You know what I want," said Lucius.

"Yes."

"Then you'll be sensible."

He smiled.

"Fetch it for me, Potter. There's a good boy. Row ninety-seven. It has your name on it. Only you can take it down from the shelf, you know. Only the people the prophecy is about. It's rather an elegant arrangement."

He lifted his wand an inch.

"And then I'll let your little friends go home."

Harry looked at him.

He thought about it very clearly, the way he'd thought about the answer to a chess problem in an alley in August, all the moves laid out.

Lucius Malfoy wanted the prophecy. He wanted it very badly. He wanted it because he'd been told to get it, by somebody further down, and because if he didn't, the somebody further down would be displeased with him. Lucius had been displeased with once before, in a churchyard, and hadn't enjoyed it. He wanted it so badly it was nearly all of him.

Harry already knew what it said.

He'd heard it in another world, from a smoke-shape rising off a broken orb beneath a running man's boot. He'd told it to Evelyn, and to Dumbledore. Nobody else in this world had ever heard it. Not all of it. Not the end.

"All right," said Harry.

* * *

Row ninety-seven was a long way down the hall.

He walked down to it with Lucius behind him and two masked Death Eaters behind Lucius, and Evelyn behind Harry, because she'd simply started walking when he did and nobody had stopped her.

One of the masked men was big and easy, and walked as though the floor belonged to him. As they passed the end of row eighty he turned his head towards Evelyn. Harry read him. Lazy pleasure and a cold interest, and beneath them, faint, a kind of fondness that was worse than either.

"There we are," the big man murmured behind his mask. "Evie."

Evelyn didn't turn her head.

"Hello, Uncle Thaddeus," she said. "You've put on weight."

The big man laughed.

Harry could hear the fighting at the far end of the hall, by the door, the crashes and bangs and Moody roaring. He could feel the others, Neville and Millicent and Luna, in row seventy-four with Tonks, being held back by three more. He could feel Ron and Hermione and Sirius somewhere in the dark to the right.

He found the orb.

It sat on a low shelf at about the height of his chest. Small and dusty, glowing very faintly. The label beneath it, in spidery writing, said *S.P.T. to A.P.W.B.D.*, and beneath that, *Dark Lord and (?) Harry Potter*.

He'd seen it before. He'd watched another boy drop it.

He put out his hand and took it down.

It was warm. Quite warm, like an egg, and heavier than it looked. He held it in his palm and turned round. Lucius Malfoy stood six feet away holding out his own hand, and his face was shining.

Harry read him.

The greed had come all the way up. It filled him. At that moment there was nothing else in Lucius Malfoy at all but the wanting of the small glass sphere in Harry's hand.

"Give it to me," said Lucius softly. "Now, Potter. You have no idea what it is. You have no idea what it means. You've lived your whole life not knowing why. Wouldn't you like to know why?"

"I know why," said Harry.

Lucius's smile didn't move. "Then you'll understand why I need it. Give it to me, and I will see to it that your friends walk out of here. You have my word."

Harry read the word. There was nothing behind it at all.

Harry looked at the orb.

He thought about a bored boy with a wand on a lawn by a lake, and a girl with red hair coming across the grass. He thought about a man at Godric's Hollow on a Hallowe'en night who'd been told, by somebody, about half a prophecy, and had come to a house to make sure of it. He thought about everything that had happened, all of it, his whole life, because of a few lines spoken in a harsh voice in a room above a pub.

*Nobody else gets to hear it.*

He opened his hand, and dropped it.

* * *

It hit the stone floor and broke.

And at the same moment, before the smoke had even begun to rise, Harry did the other thing. He reached into every mind in row ninety-seven. Lucius, and the two masked men, and Evelyn, on whom it wouldn't work and didn't need to. He put a noise into them. He put the end of the hall into them, the shelves coming down, a hundred orbs smashing, the ringing crash of glass and the roaring and the bangs. He made it very loud. So loud it was the only thing in their heads.

Out of the broken glass a figure rose. A woman made of smoke, with a shawl and enormous spectacles, and she began to speak in a harsh deep voice that wasn't her own.

Harry heard it. He alone.

He heard all of it again, standing in row ninety-seven with his hand still open, every word. The end of July, and the three times defied, and the mark and the power, and the one who must die at the hand of the other. And round him, Lucius Malfoy and two masked men stood with their mouths open and their wands half raised, hearing nothing at all but a crash of glass that wasn't happening.

The smoke-woman finished. She sank back into the broken glass.

She was gone.

Harry let the noise go.

The two masked Death Eaters looked round, bewildered, at the far end of the hall, where the noise had come from, and saw the shelves there still standing. Lucius didn't look round.

Lucius was looking at the broken glass on the floor at Harry's feet.

Harry read him.

He read the greed go out of him all at once, the way light goes out of a room when somebody draws the curtains. He read what rose in its place. No anger. Not even fear, at first. Something very quiet and very cold that went all the way through Lucius Malfoy from top to bottom. Harry had felt it before, in other people, on the night of a churchyard.

The feeling of a man doing a sum in his head and getting an answer he doesn't like, and checking it, and getting the same answer.

The somebody further down was going to be very displeased with him.

Lucius's face went white. Whiter than Harry had ever seen a face go, a dead papery white. The hand he'd held out for the orb stayed out, open, empty, as though he didn't know what to do with it.

"You stupid boy," he whispered. "You stupid, *stupid* boy. Do you know what you've done?"

"Yes," said Harry.

* * *

Then the end of the hall really did come down.

It was the Order. Moody and Kingsley and Lupin had driven back the six from the round room and come down the hall after them. Kingsley put a curse into the base of row ninety-six that brought the whole of it over sideways, a hundred feet of shelving, into row ninety-seven, and the glass came down on them like rain.

Harry didn't remember the next part clearly.

He remembered Evelyn's hand on his arm, pulling. He remembered running, bent double, beneath falling shelves, with glass breaking all round them and smoke rising from every broken orb and a hundred thin pale figures standing up out of the floor and speaking, all at once, in old voices, about weddings and wars and the deaths of kings. He remembered a masked man coming round the end of a row in front of them with his wand up, and Evelyn saying something very short. The man's curse stopped in the air a yard from Harry's face, red, spitting, perfectly still, like a firework in a photograph, long enough for Harry to get beneath it.

He remembered Hermione, at the end of a row to his right, turning, and a Death Eater with a long pale twisted face behind her raising his wand, and Harry knowing, from another world, exactly what was about to come out of it.

"*Hermione. Down.*"

She went down. She didn't ask why. A slash of purple flame went over her head where her chest had been and set a shelf on fire.

He remembered Neville in row seventy-four, standing very straight with his wand up and his face set, between a Death Eater and Luna, the Shield Charm in front of him, pale and silver and holding.

He remembered Millicent sitting on somebody. "Stay down," she said, quite calmly. "I mean it. I'm heavier than I look and I look heavy."

He remembered Ron, somewhere in the smoke, shouting "*Hermione!*" and Hermione shouting back "*I'm fine! Watch your left!*" and Ron shouting "*Which left?*"

And then the hall ended, and there was a door, and they were through it, all of them, students and Order and Death Eaters together, in a single roaring tangle of light and noise, tumbling down a flight of stone steps into the dark.

And the readiness was here.

* * *

It was a room like a pit.

Rectangular and very large and dimly lit, and sunk, so that its floor was twenty feet below the door they'd come through. Round all four sides, descending to that floor, were stone benches, wide and steep, like the tiers of an amphitheatre. Harry had come down them in another world with his face bleeding. He'd seen this room through a door.

In the centre of the floor was a raised stone dais, and on the dais was an arch.

It was very old. Cracked and crumbling, standing unsupported by any wall. From the top of it hung a tattered black curtain, or veil, which was moving very slightly, though the air in the room was quite still. Moving as though somebody had just walked through it.

Harry couldn't feel the arch. He'd never been able to. It was the place where everything stopped.

And on the steps of the dais, below the arch, in a row, were four objects.

A heavy gold locket on a chain, with a serpentine S set in green stones on its face. A thick, ugly gold ring with a black stone. A small golden cup with two fine handles and a badger engraved on its side. And a tarnished diadem with one dull stone at the front, which he'd last seen wrapped in Draco Malfoy's scarf.

Harry felt them.

He felt them all at once, the way you feel a room full of small children all crying at once. Hungry. Each one. Cold and patient and lonely and envious, each one Tom, and each one aimed upwards, past the dais, at the man standing at the top of the steps in front of the arch.

At the foot of the steps a great snake lay coiled, twelve feet long, as thick as a man's thigh, its head raised. Harry felt that too, and it wasn't only snake. There was the snake's own feeling, cold and simple and hungry in the ordinary way. And inside it, the way a stone sits inside a fruit, was another hunger. The same as the objects.

Six.

The man at the top of the steps turned round.

* * *

He was very tall and very thin and very white. His eyes were red, his face flat and noseless and smooth. He looked up at Harry, at the top of the stone tiers, twenty feet above him, through the light of a dozen wands and the smoke of a hundred broken prophecies drifting down through the door.

He smiled.

He opened his arms.

He opened them wide and slowly, as though Harry were a guest he'd been expecting for some time, who'd been held up on the road and had arrived at last. His high cold voice carried right round the pit without his raising it at all.

"Harry. There you are."

Nobody moved.

The Death Eaters who'd come through the door with them had stopped. They'd stopped on the tiers, all round, and Harry read them, and they were afraid. All of them. Every one. The pleasure had gone out of them at the door, as though somebody had wiped it off a board, and what was left was the fear that had always been beneath it, aimed down at the man on the dais.

The Order had stopped too.

Moody, on the third tier down, with his staff raised. Kingsley beside him. Lupin. Tonks, two tiers below Harry, her hair gone white. Sirius on the far side of the pit, halfway down, his wand pointing straight at the dais and his face like a blade.

And the students. Neville and Luna and Millicent near the top, close together. Ron and Hermione to the left. Evelyn beside Harry.

Harry read Voldemort.

He did it without deciding to, the way he always did, the way he breathed. And he found the cold. He'd found it in a churchyard, enormous, pleasure all the way down. He'd found it in a long room with high windows, satisfied, patient, at the bottom of a door in his own forehead.

He found it now, and it was like neither.

It was cracked.

He'd never noticed. He'd never been able to see it, because he'd never stood in a room with Voldemort and with the pieces of Voldemort at the same time. But he could see it now. The cold in the man on the dais wasn't whole. It was full of seams. Gaps. Places where things had been taken out of it long ago, and the edges had healed badly, like a plate that's been broken and glued and broken and glued. And every one of the objects on the steps below him fitted one of the gaps.

And one of the gaps had no object.

"Do you know," said Voldemort pleasantly, "how long I have looked for you, in my own head? For the last piece. I have been through every corner of myself. I have counted, and counted again."

His red eyes rested on Harry.

"And then one night in December I found a door I did not know was there, and on the other side of the door there was a boy sitting in my mind, listening. And behind the boy, a round room."

He smiled.

"And a book."

"*Harry*," Sirius shouted across the pit. "*Get back.*"

"Stay where you are, Black," said Voldemort, without looking at him. "You will want to watch this. It is history."

"*Nobody moves*," said Moody, very low, from the third tier. "Nobody. Not yet."

"He's going to…" Hermione began.

"I know what he's going to do, Granger. Wait for it. Potter. Tell me when."

"Now," said Harry. "It's starting now."

Voldemort turned round to the steps.

* * *

He began with the locket.

He held his long white hand out over it, palm down, and spoke. Harry didn't know the language. Not Latin, not Parseltongue, nothing he'd ever heard. It was very old and very short and had no music in it at all.

The locket cracked.

It cracked down the middle, across the green serpentine S, with a sound like ice on a pond, and something came out of it. Something dark. Neither smoke nor shadow. A kind of moving absence, a smear on the air the size of a man's hand. It rose off the cracked locket and into Voldemort's open palm, and was gone.

Harry felt it go.

He felt the hunger in the locket stop. He felt it leave the locket and go into the man, and arrive, and fit. He felt one of the seams in the cold close, like a cut closing, smooth.

The ring was next.

It cracked across its black stone with the same small sound, and the dark rose out of it into the long white hand, and another seam closed. Then the cup. The golden cup split from rim to foot and the dark rose out of it, and Harry felt it go in, and fit.

Then the diadem.

That was harder. Harry felt it fight. It had sat on a stone head in a city of hidden things for fifty years, alone, and it had grown used to being alone, and it didn't want to go. The dark hung above the cracked diadem, quivering, for two seconds, three. Voldemort spoke again, sharper, and it went.

Then the snake.

Voldemort turned to the great snake at the foot of the steps and spoke to it, and Harry understood him. He understood every word. It was Parseltongue, soft and coaxing, the way you speak to a dog. *Come, come to me, give it back, give back what I lent you.* The snake raised its head and opened its mouth very wide, wider than a snake's mouth should go. The dark rose out of it the way smoke rises from a chimney, and went into Voldemort. The snake shut its mouth and sank down on the stone and was a snake.

Harry felt the stone leave the fruit. He felt the snake become simple.

Five.

Five seams closed. The cold in the man on the dais was smoother now, much smoother, so smooth it was almost whole. Almost. There was one gap left. One seam, still open. He could feel it from twenty feet away.

He could feel it the way you feel a gap in a row of teeth.

Voldemort turned round.

He turned slowly, all the way, and looked up the stone tiers at Harry, and held out his hand.

"And now," he said. "The last."

* * *

Harry felt it answer.

It was inside him. Very far down. The cold point, the thing he'd found in a bare room in another world and called contamination, and found again in March and called it again, and felt swing towards a tarnished diadem in a city of hidden things like a needle swinging towards iron.

It swung now.

It didn't swing slightly. It turned, all of it, all at once, towards the long white hand held out on the dais below, and it pulled. It pulled the way a hooked fish pulls, with its whole body. It had been in him for fifteen years, since a night in Godric's Hollow when he was one year old and a green light had come at him and something had gone wrong, and it had grown in with him. It had grown round his roots. It had been in him so long and so deep that it didn't feel like a thing inside him. It felt like part of the floor.

And it was going.

He knew then. He knew all of it, at once, the way he'd known in a churchyard that he couldn't find a moment of decision in Voldemort to strike into. He knew why Tom's diary had been so easy to talk to. He knew why a stain had sat at the bottom of a boy in a Gryffindor scarf. He knew why the cold point had been in himself, and why he'd called it something else. He knew why Dumbledore had stood in front of a door with his whole weight against it.

Something tore.

It tore at the scar first. His forehead split. He felt it go, the old thin lightning-shaped line, open, like a seam ripping, and something hot ran down into his eyes. Then the tearing went inwards. It went down. It went down through him, through all of him, pulling, at the roots, at the floor of himself, and it hurt.

"Don't fight it, Harry," said Voldemort from the dais. His voice was quite gentle. "There is no need. It was never yours. I only lent it to you. I am asking for it back."

It hurt more than the Cruciatus Curse in a churchyard. It wasn't the same kind of hurt. That had been everywhere. This was in one place, and the place was the middle of him, and something was being pulled out of it that had grown there.

On the steps of the dais the great snake moved.

It had been sinking down on the stone, simple, a snake. Now it lifted its head. Something in the noise and the tearing had stirred it, or the smell of blood, and it uncoiled and began to slide up the stone tiers, fast, towards the nearest warm thing. The nearest warm thing was Luna Lovegood, on the second tier from the top, standing very calmly with her wand raised, regarding it with mild interest.

Harry opened his mouth.

He did it without thinking. He was on his knees on the stone tier with blood running into his eyes and something being torn out of the middle of him, and he saw the snake go for Luna, and he shouted at it. He shouted the way he'd shouted at a snake in a duelling club in his second year in front of the whole school, the way he'd spoken to a sink in a girls' bathroom, the way he'd spoken to the door of a chamber beneath the school.

*Leave her! Stop! Leave her, get back, get…*

He heard it.

He heard himself. He heard the hiss, the sibilant hiss that had come out of him all his life when he spoke to snakes, without his ever choosing it, the way breath comes out. He heard it come out of his mouth, *leave her, stop, leave*, and heard it go on, and heard it, halfway through the next word, in the middle of the word, change.

*…get ba… back. Get back. Get back!*

It was English.

He was shouting in English. He was shouting *get back* in plain English at a snake on a stone tier, in his own ordinary voice, and the snake didn't even turn its head, because it couldn't understand a word.

He heard it happen. He heard the hiss go out of his voice the way a sound goes out of a room when a door shuts on it.

And the thing inside him came free.

It came out of him. Up, out, through the split in his forehead. He felt it go the way you feel a tooth come out, a sudden lightness and a hole. It went across the pit in the air, a dark smear the size of a hand, and into Voldemort's open palm.

And was gone.

* * *

Kingsley's curse hit the snake in the side and threw it off the tiers. Luna stepped back from it, quite calmly.

Harry knelt on the stone with his hands on the step in front of him.

He didn't get up. He knelt there with the blood running down from his forehead into his eyes and off the end of his nose and onto the stone in small dark drops, and he looked at the stone.

He knew what he'd been.

He didn't say it to himself. He didn't need to. He'd known it at the moment the thing swung in him, and he knew it now, kneeling, and it was very simple. He'd been one of the objects. He'd been one of the things on the steps. A locket and a ring and a cup and a diadem and a snake. A piece of somebody else, carried about inside a boy for fifteen years, since he was one year old, and the boy had grown up round it.

The hiss had been Tom's.

All his life. Every word he'd ever said to a snake. The duelling club, and the sink, and the door of the chamber, and the door of the study. It had never been his.

He thought about a door behind a statue's feet that opened for a heart-reader. He thought about a round room with a lamp, and the book on the black desk, and a line in faded ink. *I will never go there again*, he thought, very clearly. He thought it the way you notice that a bridge behind you has gone into the river.

Then he lifted his head, because he had to.

* * *

Voldemort was standing on the dais in front of the arch.

He'd closed his hand. He stood very still, his eyes shut and his face lifted, as though listening to music a long way off, and the veil behind him moved in the still air.

Harry read him.

He found the cold.

There were no seams in it.

None. Not one. It was whole. Smooth from top to bottom, all of it, and it was smaller than it had been. Harry could feel that. Smaller than the cold in the churchyard, smaller than the cold in the long room with high windows, as though a great deal had been lost in the putting back. But it was one thing now, one cold, with no cracks in it anywhere, and Harry had never in his life read anything so complete.

It was like reading a stone.

Voldemort opened his eyes.

He looked down at his own hands, the long white fingers, and turned them over slowly, palm up and palm down, as though he'd never seen them before. And Harry read something rise through the smooth whole cold, small and very bright.

Wonder.

* * *

Then everything happened at once.

The Death Eaters on the tiers had been standing still with their fear aimed at the dais. Now the fear went and something else came, and it was the old pleasure, back, larger, roaring. They came down the tiers at the Order all at once, all of them, their wands blazing. And the Order went to meet them.

Harry got up.

He didn't know how. He got up on the stone tier with the blood in his eyes and the hole in the middle of him, and he wiped his face with his sleeve, and he looked for Sirius.

Sirius was on the dais.

He'd gone straight down the tiers when Voldemort closed his hand, and somebody had met him at the bottom, and they were duelling at the foot of the arch. It was a woman with long dark hair and a gaunt heavy-lidded face, and she was laughing. Sirius was laughing too. They were both laughing, darting and weaving, red light and white light going between them, on the steps of the dais, round the cracked objects, beneath the moving veil.

"You were always slow, Bella," Sirius shouted. "Twelve years and you're still slow."

"And you were always so *pretty*, cousin," she sang back, "and look where that got you…"

Harry had seen this.

He'd stood in a doorway down a corridor in another world and watched a man in a long coat, laughing, duel a laughing witch at the foot of this arch. He knew where she stood. Three steps up, on the left of the arch. He knew what she cast, and when, and where it went.

He knew which way Sirius would step.

She was going up the steps. One. Two. Three. On the left of the arch. Sirius was laughing at her, mocking her, coming after her up the steps with his wand out and his hair flying. In one second, less than a second, he was going to step to his right, towards the veil, to get round a cracked golden cup on the stone, and she was going to cast.

Harry didn't wait for her to cast.

He reached into Bellatrix Lestrange. He did it all at once, with nothing left over, the whole of himself, across twenty feet of pit, and he didn't bother to build anything slowly. He put Sirius one step to the left.

He put Sirius Black, in a long black coat, laughing, a yard to the left of where Sirius Black was standing. He made him so real she could have counted his teeth. He did it in her head, in her eyes, in the one second before she cast, and he held it.

She cast.

The red light shot out of her wand, very fast, straight at the laughing man a yard to the left of the real one. It went through him. It went through nothing. It went past the real Sirius's right shoulder by a foot and into the old stone of the arch. The arch rang like a bell, and a piece of it the size of a fist broke off and fell, and went through the veil, and didn't come out the other side.

Sirius didn't fall.

He was standing on the third step. He'd stopped laughing. He was looking at the hole in the arch beside his shoulder, and then at Bellatrix, and then, quite slowly, he turned his head and looked up the tiers at Harry.

"*Harry*," said Sirius. It wasn't a shout. It was hardly a word at all.

Harry let the illusion go.

His nose was bleeding again. It ran down over the blood that was already on his face.

He didn't care.

* * *

Voldemort lifted his wand.

He didn't look round. He didn't look at anything in particular. He stood at the top of the dais with his face still lifted and the wonder still bright in him, and he lifted his wand the way a man who's just been given a new hand lifts it to see whether the fingers work. He flicked it, once, out across the pit, over his shoulder, without looking.

A green light flew from it.

It crossed the pit, low and fast, in a long flat line, the way a stone skims across water. It went past Kingsley, and past a Death Eater, and past Moody, and over the edge of the dais, and it hit Tonks in the chest.

She was standing beside Sirius. She'd come down the tiers after him when he went for Bellatrix, and she'd been fighting a masked man at the foot of the steps, a yard from Sirius's left hand. She'd just Stunned him, and she was turning round, her hair gone bright pink and her face lit up, to say something to Sirius.

The green light hit her.

She fell.

She fell sideways, off the bottom step of the dais, onto the floor of the pit, quite softly. She didn't make a sound. Her wand rolled out of her hand a little way across the stone, and stopped.

She didn't get up.

Harry read her.

He reached for her across the pit, the way he'd reached for her on a broom over the M25 and in a drawing room amongst the photographs, and he found her. What he found was the bright quick nervousness and the enormous enjoyment and the plain friendly curiosity, and then he didn't find anything. It went out. It went out the way it had gone out of Cedric in a churchyard. All at once. And where Tonks had been, there was the place where a person had been.

Her hair was still pink.

It didn't change.

* * *

Voldemort lowered his wand.

For the first time he looked at the place where the green light had gone, over his shoulder. He looked at the woman lying at the foot of the dais with her pink hair spread out on the stone. Harry read him look. There was nothing in it about her at all. Only the wonder, and a small cool satisfaction. The satisfaction of a man who's tried a new key in a lock and found that it turns.

Then he came down off the dais.

He came down the steps between the cracked objects, past the snake, past Bellatrix, who'd gone down on one knee, past Sirius, who stood on the third step looking at Tonks and hadn't moved. He didn't look at any of them. He walked across the floor of the pit to the tiers on the far side, and up them, unhurried, the way a man walks up the steps of a building he owns.

The fighting stopped round him. It didn't stop because anybody stopped it. It stopped because nobody, Death Eater or Order, could bring themselves to raise a wand anywhere near him. He walked through it the way a ship moves through water, and it closed again behind him.

He went to the door at the top of the tiers.

Not the door they'd come in by. Another, on the far side, and Harry knew where it went. He could feel it. It led out of the Department of Mysteries and back along the corridor to the lifts, and the lifts went up.

Voldemort went through it.

He didn't look back at Harry. He didn't need to. He had what he'd come for.

He was going up to the Atrium.

* * *

Harry went after him.

He didn't think about it. He was on his feet and running before he knew he'd decided, up the stone tiers three at a time, with the blood in his eyes and the hole in the middle of him. Past Kingsley, who shouted something. Past a Death Eater on his knees. Towards the door at the top on the far side. Somebody was running beside him.

Evelyn.

He knew it was her because he couldn't feel her. He could feel the place where she was, the silence, running at his left shoulder, keeping pace, saying nothing at all.

"*Potter!*" Kingsley roared, somewhere below. "*Potter, no! Wait for us!*"

"*Don't*," came Moody's voice, harsher. "*Don't you dare, boy!*"

He went through the door. He went up a flight of stone stairs beyond it, round and up, towards the corridor and the lifts, and he could hear Voldemort's footsteps a long way above, unhurried.

And behind him, coming up the stone stairs after him, he could feel the Order.

He could feel Moody, and Kingsley, and Lupin, very clearly. They were terrified. Enormous, all of it, aimed up the stairs at him, at the boy running ahead of them after the most dangerous wizard in the world. Beneath the terror in Lupin, grief was already beginning. Beneath the terror in Moody was the counting, going on. One more. One more.

And behind them, further back, at the bottom of the pit, he could feel Sirius, who hadn't moved and wasn't afraid of anything at all. He could feel what was in Sirius instead.

He could feel Neville and Millicent and Luna and Ron and Hermione on the tiers behind him. He could feel the Death Eaters scattering. He could feel Bellatrix on one knee on the dais, and what was in her, a worship so enormous that nothing in it was left that was hers.

He could feel all of them.

He ran up the stone stairs with the blood on his face and the silence at his shoulder, and he could feel every one of them, the whole building, all at once, the way he always had.

He kept running.
