## Chapter 55: Sovereign

The lift doors opened on the Atrium, and Voldemort was standing by the fountain.

He hadn't hurried. Harry had run the whole way, up the stone stairs and along the corridor and into the second lift with Evelyn, and hammered the button, and stood with his hand pressed flat against the golden grille as it rose. Voldemort had walked, and he'd got there first anyway. He stood on the dark floor of the Atrium in front of the golden fountain, with the water running out of the wizard's wand and the centaur's arrow and the goblin's hat into the pool behind him, looking up at the peacock-blue ceiling with its golden symbols moving slowly across it.

He was looking at it the way you look at the ceiling of a house you've just bought.

Harry stopped in the open lift.

He read the Atrium. It wasn't empty any more. They were coming. He could feel them coming up through the building below him, in the other lifts, on the stairs. Death Eaters, fifteen or twenty of them, out of the Department of Mysteries, pleased again, the pleasure back in them now that the man they were afraid of was pleased too. And he could feel the Order behind them, and the students, scattered, coming up.

And there was something else.

He couldn't read it. He could feel its edges, the way you feel the edges of a fog. It was coming off the man by the fountain, outwards, slowly, in every direction, the way cold comes off a block of ice in a warm room. No feeling did that. Harry had no word for it.

"Don't go out there," said Evelyn beside him.

"I have to."

"I know you have to. I'm telling you not to. So that it's on record."

He went out.

* * *

The other lifts came up one after another, grilles clattering back, and the Atrium filled.

The Death Eaters came first. They came out of three lifts at once and fanned out across the dark floor, fifteen of them, sixteen, seventeen. Some still had masks on and some had lost them in the Hall of Prophecy. Bellatrix Lestrange came out of the second lift with her long hair wild and her face lit up, and went straight across the floor to the fountain and knelt on the stone at Voldemort's feet. A short, round, balding man with a silver hand came out after her and scuttled, not quite running, to stand at Voldemort's left shoulder, a little behind.

Wormtail.

Harry read him. Terror, very large. Self-pity beneath it, the old grey kind, like the inside of an old cushion. And a small mean triumph, aimed at nothing. At being on the winning side at last.

Then the Order. Moody, out of the next lift, with his staff up and blood streaming from a cut over the magical eye. Kingsley. Two Aurors Harry didn't know, a man and a woman, who must have come down after them. And Sirius.

Sirius came out of the last lift alone.

He'd left the pit. Harry didn't know how. He came out of the lift with his long black coat torn and his wand in his hand and his face quite empty. Harry read him, and there was nothing in him Harry had a name for, except what he'd felt on the third step of the dais, looking at a woman on the floor with pink hair.

Lupin wasn't with him.

Lupin had stayed. Harry knew that without asking. Lupin had stayed at the bottom of the pit beside her.

And the students. Ron and Hermione out of the same lift as Sirius, holding on to each other. Neville, with blood on his chin. Millicent. Luna, last, looking round the Atrium with mild interest, as though it were a new room in a museum.

They were all there.

Twenty Death Eaters, more or less. Five of the Order and the Aurors. Seven students. All spread out across the long dark floor of the Atrium of the Ministry of Magic, beneath the moving golden symbols, with their wands out.

And Voldemort by the fountain, amongst all of them, looking at the ceiling.

He lowered his eyes.

* * *

"Do you know," he said, "I have walked this Path since I was sixteen years old."

He said it quite quietly. He didn't need to say it loudly. The Atrium was very still, and his voice went out across it to the walls and came back, high and cold and pleasant.

"Fifty-three years. I found it in an orphanage, before I knew it had a name. I could make the other children do what I wanted. Not with a wand. Not with a spell. Simply by wanting it, and letting them see that I wanted it."

He turned his long white hand over and looked at it.

"And I walked it, all my life, further than anybody in this country has ever walked anything. And I could never reach the top. I stood at the foot of it for forty years and looked up and could not climb, and I did not know why."

His red eyes came round to Harry.

"And then a boy told me why," he said. "Without meaning to. In his sleep."

Harry kept his face still.

"So I should thank you, Harry," said Voldemort. "And I will. In a moment. First I should like to see what it is that I have been climbing towards for fifty-three years."

He smiled.

"I think we all should."

He lifted his wand.

* * *

Nothing happened.

That was what Harry thought for perhaps two seconds. Voldemort lifted his wand, a long pale wand that Harry had last seen in a churchyard, and held it out before him, level, pointing at nothing, at the middle of the Atrium. He didn't speak. There was no light.

Then Harry's arm moved.

He didn't move it. He knew that at once, the way you know at once that a stair you've put your foot on isn't there. His right arm, holding his wand, which had been down at his side, began to rise. Slowly. Quite smoothly. Not jerking, the way a puppet moves. Smoothly, the way an arm moves when its owner wants it to.

He didn't want it to move.

He told it to stop. He told it the way you tell your own arm anything, without words, from inside. And it went on. It went on lifting, at the same slow, smooth, even pace, and the wand in his hand began to turn.

It was turning towards the fountain.

He looked round.

Every wand in the Atrium was turning.

It was happening everywhere, all at once, all round him, on every side, slowly. The Death Eaters' wands. The Aurors' wands. Kingsley's. Moody's, and Moody's staff with it. Every wand in every hand in the great dark hall was lifting and turning, at the same slow, smooth, patient pace, the way the needles of a hundred compasses turn when somebody brings a magnet into the room.

They were all turning towards the man by the fountain.

Not to point at him. Harry saw that. They were turning the way flowers turn towards the sun. Turning to *face* him, every wand, every wand-hand, every arm, every body, all together. And as they turned, the people holding them began to go down.

They knelt.

It went across the Atrium like wind across a field of barley. The Death Eaters went first, and they went easily, gladly, as though they'd been waiting to. Then the others. The two Aurors went down on their knees on the stone with their faces white and their mouths open and their wands held out before them, offered, the way you hold out a coin. Kingsley went down slowly, so slowly that Harry could see every inch of it being taken from him. Moody fought. Harry could see him fight. His wooden leg locked and his face went purple and the blue eye spun in its socket, and he went down anyway, onto his good knee, with a sound like a tree cracking.

"*Fight it*," Moody roared from the floor. "*All of you! It's in your head, it's only in your head, fight the bloody thing…*"

"I can't," cried one of the Aurors, the man, in a high, astonished voice. "Alastor, I *can't*, there's nothing to fight…"

"*Then find something!*"

And none of it was a feeling.

That was what Harry couldn't hold on to. He'd read every feeling there was. Fear and terror and worship and devotion. He'd felt Death Eaters in a churchyard kneel out of fear. This wasn't fear. Nobody was kneeling because they were afraid.

They were kneeling because it was the rule.

As though something about the Atrium had changed. Not the light, or the air, or the floor. Something underneath. As though there were a law, older than gravity, that had always said things fall down, and it had been quietly rewritten whilst nobody was watching. Now it said *everything in this room turns to face him, and everything kneels.*

And everybody in the Atrium was obeying it, the way they obeyed gravity, unable to do anything else.

* * *

He read the students.

He couldn't stop himself. His arm was lifting and his knees were beginning to bend, and he couldn't stop either of them. But he could still read, and he read them, because they were his.

They were terrified.

The same terror in all of them, and nothing outside them had caused it. Terror of themselves. The terror of a person whose own body has stopped being theirs.

Neville was on his knees with his wand held out before him towards the fountain and tears running down his face, and he wasn't crying. His face wasn't doing anything. The tears were simply coming, because his body had decided to cry, and he couldn't stop that either.

Luna was kneeling quite calmly with her hands in her lap. She looked puzzled. Harry read her and found the still pond, and beneath it, for the first time, something that wasn't calm at all.

Millicent's knees were bending. Harry watched them bend. He'd watched Millicent Bulstrode sit on people and hit people and stand up to Pansy Parkinson and walk back down a room full of the Inquisitorial Squad to sit on Goyle. He watched her knees bend, slowly, against everything in her, and he read her fight it, and read her lose. What was in her as she went down on the stone wasn't fear. It was shame. Enormous, burning, helpless shame. The shame of the girl in the bathroom on Hallowe'en with a troll on its way.

And Ron.

Ron's wand hadn't turned to the fountain.

Harry watched it. Ron was standing beside Hermione, a yard from her, his arm lifting like everybody else's, and his wand was turning. But not towards the fountain. Sideways. Slowly. Quite smoothly. Towards Hermione.

Ron was looking at it.

He was looking at his own wand, in his own hand, turning towards Hermione's face. Harry read him, and what was in him was worse than anything Harry had felt that night. Worse than the Cruciatus on the floor of row ninety-seven. Worse than Millicent. It was a boy watching his own hand point a wand at the person he'd rather have died than hurt.

"*No*," said Ron. "*No, no, no*…"

Hermione was looking at the wand too. She wasn't moving. Her own wand was lifting, turning towards the fountain. She couldn't move out of the way.

"Ron," she said, very quietly. "It's all right. It isn't you. I know it isn't you."

The wand went on turning.

* * *

And Harry's own arm went on lifting.

It was up now, level with his shoulder. It had stopped turning towards the fountain. He felt it stop. He felt something reach across the Atrium from the man by the water and touch it, quite lightly, the way you touch a chess piece to adjust it on its square.

It began to turn the other way.

It began to turn towards him.

His own wand, in his own hand, at the end of his own arm, was bending back round, slowly, smoothly, towards his own face. The point came round past his shoulder. Past his ear. He watched it come. He couldn't close his eyes. He couldn't drop it. He couldn't open his fingers.

He read the man by the fountain.

He could. That was the strangest thing. In the middle of all of it, with his own wand coming round to point between his own eyes, he could still read. He read Voldemort, and found the smooth whole seamless cold, like reading a stone, and on top of it, very bright, very calm, the wonder.

And beneath the wonder, aimed at Harry, was something he recognised.

Curiosity. The curiosity of a collector in a junk shop. The curiosity from a churchyard. *That is not a spell. That is a Path.* It was aimed at Harry's wand, coming round to point at Harry's face, and it was waiting with interest to see what would happen.

Harry thought about a white room beneath the school. A man with two faces, turning his wand on the face in the back of his own head.

*He's doing it on purpose. He knows.*

He tried to build.

He tried to make himself not there. He tried to put a wall across the inside of the man's eyes, the way he'd put a wall across eight minds in a hidden room. He reached for it with everything he had.

There was nothing to reach with.

He couldn't find himself. He could read, but he couldn't *do*. Whatever it was that he did when he pushed, when he built, when he held a door against a wind, it wasn't his any more. It had been taken off him the way his arm had been taken off him. It was kneeling too.

The point of his wand was six inches from his face.

* * *

Evelyn was standing up.

She noticed it at eleven minutes past eight. She looked at her watch, which she did at moments when she needed to know exactly where she was. It was ticking, and it said eleven minutes past eight, and she was standing up.

She'd been standing up the whole time.

She noted that. She noted it as a fact, the way she'd have noted the date on a letter. She'd been standing out on the floor of the Atrium, a little behind Potter and to his left, with her wand in her hand, when Lord Voldemort lifted his own wand at the fountain. And everybody had begun to turn.

She hadn't.

She'd felt nothing. She looked for it. She looked carefully, the way she'd have looked through a drawer for a lost key. Nothing was pulling at her arm. Nothing was bending her knees. There was nothing in her at all that wasn't hers.

There never had been.

She'd been five years old, in a room in the east wing of Selwyn Hall with frost on the windows, when her grandmother first sat her down on a stool and told her to close the door in her head and keep it closed. She'd kept it closed every morning since. She'd kept it closed in the Hall of Prophecy, and in a lake, and in a classroom on the fourth floor with Potter shouting at her, and on a rock by the lake with Potter laughing. Never once in her life had she had a thought in her head that somebody else had put there.

Whatever Lord Voldemort had done to the Atrium, it had been done to minds.

And hers wasn't available.

She looked round.

Everybody was kneeling. Everybody. The Death Eaters, gladly. The Aurors, with their wands held out like coins. Shacklebolt, slowly. Moody, on one knee, purple, fighting. Longbottom, crying without crying. Lovegood, puzzled. Bulstrode, with her face like fire. Black, on both knees near the lifts, with his wand pointed at the fountain and his face entirely empty.

Weasley's wand was pointing at Granger.

And Potter's wand was pointing at Potter.

She looked at it. His arm was up, crooked back on itself at an angle no arm should make, and the point of his own wand was coming round towards his own face, slowly. His face was white, his eyes were open, and he wasn't doing anything. Potter, who always did something.

She counted the distance. Nine yards. Twenty-seven feet. About eleven of her steps.

She walked.

She walked across the Atrium of the Ministry of Magic through a room full of kneeling people. She walked past a Death Eater on his knees with his mask askew, who didn't look up. She walked past one of the Aurors, the woman, who did look up. The woman's eyes followed her as she went past, wide, the only thing in her body that could still move. Evelyn walked quite steadily, not quickly, not slowly, the way she walked into the Great Hall in the mornings, as though there were nothing in the room that had ever looked back.

Something did look back.

She felt it. Not in her head. On her skin. The man by the fountain had turned his eyes and was looking at her, and she could feel the look the way you can feel the sun on the back of your neck.

She didn't look at him.

She counted her steps. Seven. Eight. Nine.

Ten.

She noted, at the tenth step, that she was the only person in the Atrium standing upright because she'd decided to. She noted it the way she'd have noted a figure in a column. It was a strange thing to notice. She didn't know what to do with it, so she put it away to look at later.

Eleven.

She put both her hands on Potter's shoulders and pushed him over.

* * *

He went over sideways.

He didn't fall. Falling would have meant his body doing something by itself, and his body wasn't his. He was pushed. He went over like a statue, all in one piece, his arm still crooked and his wand still pointing at his face, and he hit the stone floor of the Atrium on his side with Evelyn's whole weight on top of him.

His wand went off.

Whatever it had been told to cast, it cast. It cast at the place where his face had been a second before, and his face wasn't there. It was on the floor with Evelyn's elbow in his ear. The jet of light, purple and very bright, went over both of them and hit the golden grille of a lift, and the grille melted.

And something let go of him.

Not all of it. Not much. But Evelyn was lying on top of him with her hands on his shoulders, and her mind, which had never once been anybody else's, was lying against his, an inch away, closed and silent and entirely her own. The thing that had been holding his arm couldn't hold it through her. It couldn't see through her. She was in the way.

His arm came down.

He could move it. He could move his fingers. He lay on the stone floor and opened his hand, and his wand rolled out of it, and he didn't pick it up.

"Thank you," he said into the floor.

"Don't," said Evelyn. "Stay down. He's looking at us."

* * *

The fireplace on the far side of the Atrium roared green.

Harry turned his head on the stone.

Dumbledore stepped out of it.

He stepped out of the green fire with soot on his shoulders and his long silver hair and beard wild, as though he'd come a long way very fast. He was holding his wand. He looked across the Atrium.

He didn't kneel.

Harry saw that at once. Dumbledore stood in front of the fireplace, very tall, and the rule that said *everything in this room turns to face him and kneels* went across him the way it had gone across everybody else. Harry watched it reach him and push, and Dumbledore didn't kneel.

He didn't stand up straight either. He stood the way a man stands in a gale, leaning into it. His wand hand was trembling. His face was very still.

He looked at the fountain.

Harry watched him look. He watched Dumbledore's eyes go from the man by the fountain to the kneeling people, to the turned wands, to Ron's pointing at Hermione, to Harry on the floor with Evelyn on top of him and blood all over his face from a split scar. He watched the eyes come back to Voldemort.

He watched Dumbledore understand.

Harry couldn't read him. He was closed, hard, the hardest Harry had ever felt him. But he didn't need to read him. He saw it in his face. He saw the old man by the fireplace look at the man by the fountain, standing whole and smooth and seamless in the middle of a room that obeyed him, and know exactly what had happened tonight, and what it meant, and where it had come from.

"Tom," said Dumbledore.

"Albus." Voldemort smiled. "You're late. You're always late. Do you know, I find it very restful? It's the only thing about you I can rely on."

"What have you done?"

"You know what I have done. You can see it."

"You have put yourself back together," said Dumbledore. His voice was quite steady. His hand wasn't. "All of it. Every piece you tore off and hid. You have given up the thing you wanted most for fifty years."

"I have exchanged it," said Voldemort, "for something better. You of all people should understand that, Albus. You made the same exchange yourself, I think, when you were young. Didn't you? A long time ago, on a hill, with a friend."

Dumbledore didn't answer.

"You see?" said Voldemort. "We are not so different, now. Two old men on two summits."

He spread his arms a little, his wand still level.

"Look at them. Look at all of them. Do you see anybody standing, Albus, apart from you?"

Dumbledore's eyes went, for one second, to Evelyn.

Then back.

"No," he said.

"No," Voldemort agreed. "And you are only standing because you are you. I can feel you holding. It is costing you a great deal. I wonder how long you can do it."

He tilted his head.

"Shall we find out?"

Dumbledore lifted his wand.

* * *

Harry had seen Dumbledore do magic before.

He'd seen him conjure armchairs and stun the Minister for Magic and vanish in a burst of phoenix fire. He'd heard Varga say *Transmutation* in a cabin on a ship, and Dumbledore say it himself, in his office, at two in the morning. *I have walked it since I was seventeen. It has cost me a great deal, and it will cost me more.*

He'd never seen this.

Dumbledore didn't cast anything. He didn't say anything. He lifted his wand and held it out before him, level, the way Voldemort was holding his, and he looked at the Atrium.

And the Atrium forgot what it was.

It started at the fountain.

The golden statues, the witch and the wizard and the centaur and the goblin and the house-elf, all gazing up in admiration, began to run. The gold went soft. It went soft from the top downwards, and ran, and dripped, and as it dripped it was no longer gold. It was water. It was rain. The golden wizard's raised wand became a column of falling rain, and the golden witch became rain, and the centaur and the goblin and the elf. The whole fountain came down into its own pool in a long, soft, shining downpour, as though it had been rain all along and had only been pretending to be statues.

Rain fell on Voldemort.

He didn't move. He couldn't. Harry knew that somehow, the way he knew things in dreams. Whatever Voldemort was doing, it held him to the place where he stood, the way a lamp is held to the place where it's plugged in. He stood in the middle of the falling rain with his wand level and his face lifted and the water running down it, and smiled.

The golden gates at the far end of the Atrium, the great gates that led to the lifts, became birds.

Harry watched it happen. One moment they were gates, high and gold and closed. The next they were birds, a thousand of them, small and gold and singing. They rose all at once into the peacock-blue ceiling with a roar of wings and broke against it like a wave, and came down again in a storm of gold feathers, and went round the Atrium, round and round, singing.

And the floor beneath the Death Eaters became water.

It went from stone to water between one second and the next. Seventeen kneeling people in black robes went down into it all at once, up to their chests, up to their necks, with a great splash, still kneeling, still holding their wands up before them. Bellatrix screamed.

"*My Lord! My Lord, let me, let me kill the old…*"

"Be still, Bella," said Voldemort, without turning his head, and she was.

Wormtail went under and came up spluttering, clinging to the edge.

And the floor beneath everybody else stayed floor.

Beneath Harry and Evelyn. Beneath the Aurors and Kingsley and Moody. Beneath Sirius, and Ron and Hermione, and Neville and Luna and Millicent. Beneath all of them, a ring of plain dark stone, and outside it and round it, the black water with the Death Eaters in it.

Dumbledore had chosen.

* * *

They met in the middle.

Harry couldn't see it. Nobody could have seen it. But he could feel it, even through the rule, even with the rule still on him and his knees still bent and his wand on the floor beside his hand. He could feel two things, enormous, coming out from two men standing at opposite ends of the Atrium of the Ministry of Magic and meeting in the middle of the room, over the black water and the singing birds and the rain.

One said *everything in this room obeys.*

The other said *nothing in this room is what it was.*

And neither gave.

It went on. It went on for a long time. Harry didn't know how long. The birds went round and round, singing. The rain fell. The Death Eaters stayed in the water, kneeling, up to their necks. The rule stayed in the Atrium, on all of them, pressing. Ron's wand stayed pointing at Hermione and didn't fire, because something else was in the room now that said a wand need not be a wand.

And where the two things met, over the black water, the air did something Harry had no word for. Neither light nor sound. The air was trying to be two things at once, and couldn't, and couldn't stop trying.

Harry watched Dumbledore.

He was lying on the floor on his side with Evelyn's arm across his chest and his face against the stone, and he watched the old man at the far end of the Atrium by the fireplace. He watched him hold his wand out, level, steady, against the man in the rain.

He watched his hair.

It had been silver. Silver all Harry's life, silver and long and very fine, the silver of old age that's still somewhere near the middle of it. As Harry watched, it went white.

It went white from the roots. It went white the way frost comes over a window, from the edges in, fast. In a minute it was white to the shoulders. In two it was white all the way down to the end of his beard, a plain flat white, the white of very old paper.

And his face went with it.

Harry watched the lines come. He watched them come in at the eyes and the mouth, and deepen, and spread, and new ones come in between them. He watched the cheeks fall in. He watched the skin of the hand holding the wand go thin and spotted and loose over the bones, like a glove that's been washed too often. He watched the tall straight back, leaning into the gale, begin, very slowly, to bend.

He watched Albus Dumbledore grow ten years older in front of him, in under three minutes, and not lower his wand.

* * *

The fireplaces on the left side of the Atrium roared green, one after another.

Five of them. Six. People came out of them fast, in robes, with wands, shouting. Aurors, a dozen of them, more, in the dark red robes of the Auror Office. They came out of the fireplaces at a run and stopped.

And in the middle of them, in a pinstriped cloak and a lime-green bowler hat, with his face pink and his mouth open and his hands up as though to say *what on earth is going on here*, was Cornelius Fudge.

He'd been told. Somebody had told him. A Ministry guard had seen something on the security charms in the Department of Mysteries, or a night watchman had heard the lifts, or a frightened clerk had run up to his office. He'd come down with every Auror he could find to see what all the fuss was about.

He stopped in front of the fireplace with his mouth open.

He looked at the black water where the floor had been, with seventeen people in black robes kneeling in it up to their necks. He looked at the rain where the fountain had been. He looked at the thousand golden birds going round and round the ceiling, singing. He looked at Albus Dumbledore, white-haired, bent, by the far fireplace, with his wand held out.

He looked at the man standing in the middle of the falling rain.

Harry read him.

He read the Minister for Magic look at Lord Voldemort, standing in the Atrium of his Ministry, tall and white and whole, with his red eyes and his flat noseless face and his wand held level and the rain running down him. He read the fear that had been in Fudge since a parlour in the Leaky Cauldron two summers ago. The fear that had gone hard in a hospital wing into *no*. The fear that had set all winter like concrete.

He read it break.

It broke all at once, the way ice breaks on a pond when somebody heavy steps on it. It broke from top to bottom, and beneath it there was nothing. No *no*, no refusal, no wall. Nothing but the plain terror of a man seeing with his own eyes a thing he'd spent a year telling a country didn't exist.

"*Minister!*" Kingsley was shouting from the floor, struggling up on one elbow. "*Minister, you see him? You see him?*"

"He's," said Fudge. His voice came out as a squeak. "He's… he's *here*. He's here. In the Ministry. He's *back*."

The witch beside him spoke very loudly. "*Minister. Look. There. That's Pettigrew.*"

Every head in the Atrium that could turn, turned.

Wormtail was clinging to the edge of the black water at Voldemort's feet, half out of it, his silver hand on the stone. He was soaked. His thin hair was plastered to his head. At the sound of his name he looked up at a dozen Aurors in dark red robes, and his small watery eyes went very wide.

"Peter Pettigrew," said Madam Bones. She was a stocky woman with a square face and short grey hair, and Harry had seen her before, in a courtroom, with a monocle. "Peter Pettigrew. *Alive.*"

Across the Atrium, on his knees near the lifts, Sirius Black lifted his head.

"Hello, Peter," he said. He didn't say it loudly. It carried anyway. "Hello. Fifteen years. You look well. A bit damp."

Wormtail made a small high sound, like a kettle.

* * *

Voldemort lowered his wand.

He did it quite slowly. And as he lowered it, the rule went out of the Atrium.

Harry felt it go. He felt it lift off him, the way a heavy coat comes off your shoulders. His knees were his. His arms were his. He could feel his own fingers on the stone, and the stone was cold, and he was lying on the floor of the Atrium with Evelyn's arm across his chest and his face wet with his own blood.

All round him people fell over.

They fell over because they'd been kneeling, held up by the rule, and the rule was gone. Kingsley put out his hands and caught himself. Moody went down flat on his back and lay there, roaring. Ron dropped his wand as though it had burned him and stood staring at his own hand, and Hermione took the hand in both of hers and held it.

"I'd never," said Ron. "Hermione. I'd never. I'd *never*…"

"I know," said Hermione. "I know. I know. Be quiet. I know."

At the far end of the Atrium, Dumbledore lowered his wand too.

The birds stopped singing. They went on flying, round and round the ceiling, but they were silent now, gold and silent, and one by one, as Harry watched, they began to come down. They came down onto the floor at the end of the Atrium where the gates had been, and as each one touched the floor it was a gate again, a piece of a gate. Gold bars stood up out of the floor at odd angles, as though somebody had put them back together in a hurry and not quite remembered how they went.

The rain went on falling where the fountain had been. It didn't stop. It didn't become statues again.

The black water stayed black water.

Voldemort looked across the Atrium at Dumbledore.

Harry read him. The smooth seamless cold. The wonder, still there, still bright, a little quieter now. And beneath it, very small, very new, something Harry hadn't felt in him in a churchyard or anywhere since.

Respect.

It was aimed at the old white-haired man by the fireplace. The respect of one person who's walked a long way up a mountain for another who's walked up the one beside it, and has just found out, standing on top, that the other one got there first.

"Another time, Albus," said Voldemort.

He held out his hand.

Bellatrix came up out of the black water and took it. She came up streaming, her hair in long wet ropes and her face blazing, and took his long white hand in both of hers as though it were something holy. Wormtail scrambled out of the water after her and grabbed at the edge of his robes.

And Voldemort looked round the Atrium, once.

He looked at the Aurors, and Fudge, and Dumbledore, and Sirius on his knees by the lifts. He looked at the Death Eaters in the black water. He looked at all of it, slowly, the way a man looks round a room he's leaving and will be coming back to.

Then he looked at Harry.

He looked down at him across the Atrium, at a boy lying on his side on the stone floor with blood on his face and a girl's arm across his chest. He didn't smile. He didn't frown. He looked at Harry for perhaps two seconds, his head a little on one side, and Harry read what was in him. Interest.

Plain interest. Cool and unhurried and quite patient. The interest of somebody who's put a thing down on a shelf to look at properly later, when there's more time.

There was no hurry in it at all.

He turned away.

There was a crack, very loud, and a whirl of black, and he was gone. Bellatrix with him, and Wormtail, still clinging to the hem of his robes.

* * *

After that the Atrium grew very quiet.

The Death Eaters in the black water were floundering. The Aurors were wading in after them with their wands out, shouting. Some of the Death Eaters were Disapparating and some were being dragged out by the collar. Fudge stood in front of the fireplace with his bowler hat in his hands, turning it round and round. *He was here*, he kept saying to nobody. *He was here, I saw him, he was here.*

Kingsley was helping Moody up.

Sirius hadn't moved. He was still on his knees by the lifts with his wand on the floor in front of him, looking at the place where Wormtail had been.

Evelyn took her arm off Harry's chest.

She sat up. She sat on the stone floor of the Atrium beside him with her knees drawn up and her back very straight, and she took the watch out of her cardigan pocket and looked at it.

"Eight twenty-six," she said. "Fifteen minutes."

"You stood up," said Harry.

"I didn't stand up. I was never down."

"He looked at you."

"I know. I felt it. On the back of my neck."

She put the watch away and buttoned the pocket.

"He didn't like it."

Harry had no answer.

He sat up too. He sat up slowly on the cold floor beside her, with his wand lying on the stone where it had rolled out of his hand, and he didn't pick it up. He looked across the Atrium.

Dumbledore was walking.

He was walking across the floor of the Atrium from the far fireplace, very slowly. He walked the way old people walk, his eyes on the floor two yards ahead, as though worried about the rug. He had his wand in one hand, and the other hand was held a little out from his side, for balance. His back was bent, and his long white hair hung down round his face.

He walked to the fountain.

To the place where the fountain had been. It was a round stone pool with a low rim, still, and in the middle of it, out of nothing, out of the air where the golden statues had stood, rain was falling. Falling softly and steadily, as though from a cloud nobody could see, into the pool. The pool was full of it, and it ran over the rim at one side and away across the stone in a thin dark stream towards the black water.

Dumbledore stood at the rim of the pool and looked at the rain.

Then he sat down on the rim.

He sat down carefully, the way a very old man sits down on a low wall, feeling for it behind him with one hand, lowering himself onto it an inch at a time. He sat with his hands on his knees and his wand across them and his white head bowed, and the rain fell beside him into the pool, and ran over the rim, and wet the hem of his robes.

He looked very old.

He looked older than Professor Marchbanks. He looked older than anybody Harry had ever seen.

He sat on the rim of what used to be the fountain, and didn't get up.

## Chapter 56: What Was Left

"I am old," said Dumbledore. "You will have noticed."

It was the Thursday, two days after, at eleven o'clock in the morning. The sun was coming in through the tall windows of the headmaster's office, which had let Dumbledore back in on the Wednesday without his having to say the password. The gargoyle had stepped aside before he reached it, as though it had been waiting. Fawkes was on his perch. The silver instruments whirred and puffed on their spindle-legged tables. The portraits were all awake and all pretending not to be.

Harry was sitting in the chair in front of the desk.

He'd noticed. He'd noticed on the rim of a fountain that was raining. He'd noticed in St Mungo's on the Tuesday night, where Dumbledore had sat for an hour beside Madam Pomfrey's bed whilst she put drops in Harry's split scar, and said nothing at all, and had to be helped out of the chair by a Healer when he went.

He was white. All of him. The hair and the beard and the eyebrows, a flat dry white like paper. The face beneath had fallen in, round the eyes and the mouth and under the cheekbones, and it was folded into lines that hadn't been there a week ago. The long hands lying on the desk were thin and spotted, the skin loose over the knuckles. He sat a little forward in his chair. He'd always sat upright.

"Yes," said Harry.

"I was a hundred and fourteen on Tuesday morning," said Dumbledore. "I find I am rather more than that now. Poppy says about ten years more. She is usually right about such things."

He looked at his own hands.

"It does not get better. I want you to know that. It is not a wound. It is simply time, and time does not come back."

Harry read him.

He could. Dumbledore was open. He'd been open since he came in and lowered himself into the chair behind the desk, very slowly, one hand on its arm. He didn't seem to be trying to close. Harry didn't know whether that was because he no longer could, or because he'd decided not to.

There was tiredness. A great deal of it, very old. There was grief, for a young woman with pink hair. There was the fear, the old fear from June, small and cold, aimed at Harry.

And there was no door.

Harry looked for it. He'd felt it in this room in March, in the middle of Dumbledore, held shut with his whole weight. He looked for it now, carefully, the way you put your tongue to the place where a tooth was.

It was gone. Not opened. Gone. As though whatever had been behind it had been let out, and there was nothing left to lean against.

"You knew," said Harry.

"Yes."

"Since when?"

* * *

Dumbledore told him.

He told him plainly, the way he'd told him about Horcruxes in March, as he'd have told anyone with a right to know. He didn't look away. He sat forward in his chair with his old hands on the desk and his eyes on Harry over the half-moon glasses, and he told it in order.

He told him that on the night of the thirty-first of October, 1981, Lord Voldemort had come to a house in Godric's Hollow and killed James Potter and Lily Potter and turned his wand on their son. The curse had come back on him, because of something the boy's mother had done, and torn him out of his body. And a curse of that kind, at that moment, rebounding from a man who'd already torn his soul so many times it was barely holding together, might do a great many things.

"I did not know what it had done," said Dumbledore. "Not for certain. Not then. I knew that you had a scar, and that the scar was not like other scars. I knew that you could speak to snakes, which Tom could do, and very few others in a thousand years. I knew that when you came to this school you could feel what other people felt, which Tom could not."

He paused.

"That confused me for a long time. It did not fit. If a piece of him was in you, I thought, you would be like him. And you were not."

"When did you know?"

"When you brought me the diary," said Dumbledore. "In your second year. With a fang through it. I knew then that he had made at least one Horcrux, and I knew what that meant. And I looked at you sitting in that chair, twelve years old, with the Sorting Hat on your knee and Godric's sword across it, and I thought, *the scar.* And I knew."

He looked down at his hands.

"I did not know for certain. I want to be honest with you. I suspected. I suspected so strongly that it was the same as knowing, and I let myself call it suspicion, because suspicion did not require me to do anything."

Harry waited.

"I suspected," said Dumbledore, "for four years. And I did not tell you."

"Why?"

"Because you were a child," said Dumbledore. "And then because you were not, and I had left it too late, and did not know how to begin. And beneath both of those, Harry, because I was afraid."

He looked up.

"I was afraid of what it would do to you to know. A boy who reads other people's hearts, and trusts nobody, and has only ever been able to rely on what is inside himself. I was afraid that if I told him that part of what was inside him was not his, but Tom's, he would never trust himself again."

He paused.

"I was afraid you would go looking for it. In yourself. Every day. For the rest of your life. Wondering which parts were yours."

Harry thought about a bare room in another world, and a cold point, far down, and *it's his, it's not mine*.

"So you let me find out on the floor of the Department of Mysteries," he said. "With him pulling it out."

"Yes."

"With everybody watching."

"Yes."

"With Tonks…"

He stopped.

Dumbledore let him stop. He sat with his old hands on the desk and didn't fill the silence. Harry read him not fill it, and what was in him was grief, enormous, aimed at a young woman on a stone floor with pink hair that didn't change.

"I am sorry," said Dumbledore. "I will say it once, as I said it once before in this room, and I will not say it again, because saying it again would only be asking you to forgive me, and I have no right to ask that. I am sorry. I should have told you in your second year. I should have told you in June. I should have told you in March, in this chair, when you sat there and told me everything, and I sat here and did not."

He was quite steady.

"I chose not to. It was the wrong choice. I have made a great many wrong choices in my life, Harry, and that is one of the worst, and I made it because I loved you and was frightened, which is no excuse at all. It is merely the reason."

Harry looked at him.

He was angry.

He found that out the way he found out most things about himself, by noticing it there, like a reading. He was very angry. It wasn't the anger of a year ago, the quiet list-keeping anger, getting quieter. It was simpler than that and much larger, and it was aimed straight at the old man behind the desk, and it was fair.

And he understood.

He found that out too. He sat there and understood exactly why. He understood a man who'd been frightened of what a thing would do to someone he loved, and had decided not to say it, and gone on not saying it until it was too late. He'd done it himself. He'd done it to Evelyn in his fourth year, for nine weeks, with *good* and *mm?* and Mabel the goat. He'd done it to Dumbledore.

And he was angry.

He sat in the chair and found that both of them were there at once, the anger and the understanding, side by side. Neither of them was going to make room for the other, and that was simply how it was going to be.

"I'm still angry," he said.

"Yes."

"I understand. And I'm still angry."

"Yes," said Dumbledore. "I would think less of you if you were not. And I would think less of myself, a great deal less, if I asked you to stop."

He took his glasses off and rubbed his eyes with his old thin fingers.

"Be angry, Harry. You have every right. I only ask that you be angry with me here, in this room, and not out there, alone, in your own head, where I cannot answer."

For a while Harry sat with that.

"There's more," he said at last. "About the other world. There are things I didn't tell you in June."

Dumbledore put his glasses back on.

"Then tell me," he said. "And I will listen. And I will not tell you anything back that I do not know is true."

So Harry told him the rest.

He told him about a girl at the end of a bench with two feet of empty space beside her and an identical watch. He told him about a barman who'd sheltered them and recognised the watch and wouldn't say whose hand had made it. Who'd said *my brother will use you, boy, he uses everyone he loves*. He told him what that barman's brother had looked like in that world, coming out of the green fire in the Atrium at the end, two years older than this one, and still silver.

Dumbledore listened. He said nothing about his brother. But when Harry told him what Aberforth had said, Harry read something go through him, very old and very quiet, aimed at a pub in a side street in Hogsmeade. It wasn't grief, and it wasn't guilt.

It was something more like being caught.

* * *

Myrtle's bathroom was as it had always been.

Cold and damp and gloomy, with the cracked mirror over the row of chipped sinks and the cubicles with their doors hanging off and a puddle on the floor that never dried. Harry went in at four o'clock on the Friday afternoon, when the corridor was empty, and shut the door behind him.

He went to the sinks.

He knew which one. He'd known since he was twelve. It had a tiny scratch on the side of one of its copper taps, so small that nobody would ever have noticed it, in the shape of a snake.

He stood in front of it.

He didn't want to do this. He'd known since the floor of the pit what would happen. He'd heard it happen. He'd heard his own voice change in the middle of a word, the hiss going out of it like a sound going out of a room when a door shuts. He knew. He didn't need to check.

He checked anyway.

He did it the way you check a pocket for a key you know you've lost. You put your hand in anyway. You feel round in the corners.

"Open," he said.

It was English.

He heard it. He heard his own ordinary voice say *open* to a sink, in English, in a girls' bathroom, the way anybody might, and the sink did nothing. The tap didn't glow. The sink didn't move. It stood there, chipped and white and ordinary, with its tiny scratch.

He tried again.

He tried to find the place in himself where the other thing had come from. He'd never had to look for it before. It had always simply been there, the way breath is there. When he looked at a snake, or thought of one, or pictured one very clearly, the words had come out of him by themselves, sibilant, without his choosing. He tried to picture one now. He pictured the snake on the tap. He pictured the great grey basilisk on the floor of the Chamber. He pictured Nagini on the steps of the dais.

"*Open*," he said.

English.

"*Open.*"

Nothing.

He stopped.

He stood in front of the sink with his hands at his sides and looked at the little scratch on the tap. He thought about what lay beneath. The pipe going down, and the tunnel, and a slab of stone that a man in a lilac dressing gown had once held up so that he could go on. A door with great stone serpents on it, and the Chamber beyond, and a statue with a long stone beard. A door behind the statue's feet that had opened for a heart-reader, and a small round room lined with shelves, and a lamp that lit for him and for nobody else.

A desk of black stone. A book, open on it, in faded ink.

He'd never see it again.

He'd sat in that room for three years. He'd read every book on those shelves he could understand, and some he couldn't. He'd learned there everything he knew about what he was. He'd learned to read thoughts there, and to build faces, and to put a wall across a mind. It had been the one place in the world that was his.

It had never been his.

The door had opened for a heart-reader. But the way to the door had opened for a Parselmouth, and the Parselmouth had been Tom.

He sat down on the floor.

He didn't decide to. He found he was sitting on the cold damp tiles with his back against the sinks and his knees drawn up, the puddle soaking slowly into the seat of his trousers.

He sat there for some time.

"*What* are you doing?"

He looked up. Moaning Myrtle was hovering over the end cubicle, pearly and transparent, with her thick glasses and her pigtails and her spots, looking down at him.

He read her. One thin grey note. Sadness. The same as always.

"Sitting," said Harry.

"On *my* floor."

"Yes."

Myrtle drifted down a little closer. She peered at him through her glasses.

"You've been crying," she said, with interest.

"No, I haven't."

"You look like you have."

"I haven't."

"I cried in here for three days once," said Myrtle. "Before I died. Olive Hornby said things about my glasses."

She looked at him a while longer.

"Nobody came, either."

Harry didn't answer.

Myrtle sniffed. She drifted back up over the cubicle and sat on the top of the door with her transparent feet dangling, looking down at him. After a while she began to hum tunelessly to herself.

She was still there when he got up and went out, an hour later.

He didn't know why that helped. It did, a little.

* * *

They buried Tonks on the Sunday, at a small grey church at the edge of Dartmoor, in a village called Sheepstor.

It was a bright, hot, cloudless day. There were skylarks over the moor. The church had a squat tower and a churchyard full of old slate headstones leaning at angles, and a yew tree, and a low granite wall with gorse growing over it. Yellow, the colour her hair had gone when she was happy.

There were a great many people.

The Order, all of them who could come. Moody in a dark coat, with a bandage over one eye and the magical one going round under his bowler hat. Kingsley. Mr and Mrs Weasley, and Bill, and the twins, quiet for once. Hestia Jones in her violet bonnet. People from the Auror Office Harry didn't know, standing together in a group, young and white-faced, the year she'd qualified with. Lockhart, on his silver-lion stick, in black, with his golden hair combed very flat, standing at the back by the wall and speaking to nobody, which was the strangest thing Harry had ever seen him do.

And her parents.

Her father was a big fair man with a moustache. He stood at the graveside with his hat in his hands and wept openly, without trying to stop, the way some men can. Harry read him and found there was nothing at all in him except her, and the place where she'd been.

Her mother looked like Bellatrix Lestrange.

Harry hadn't expected that. He stood on the grass at the edge of the crowd and looked at the tall dark woman beside the big fair man, and for a second he couldn't move, because it was the same face. The same heavy-lidded eyes. The same dark hair. The same bones. The face that had smiled at him out of the *Prophet* in January, that had laughed at the foot of an arch.

He read her.

It wasn't the same at all. There was no worship in her, no wildness, no laughter. There was grief, so large and so plain that it filled her the way water fills a glass to the brim. Over it, holding it, very hard and very straight, was the thing that keeps a person standing at the side of a grave when every part of them wants to lie down in it.

She didn't cry. She stood very straight with her hand on her husband's arm and looked at the coffin, and didn't cry at all.

Lupin stood at the foot of the grave.

Harry looked at him for a long time.

He didn't need to read him. He did, because he couldn't help it, and what he found was so large and so still that it was very nearly silence. But he didn't need to. Anybody could have seen it. Anybody standing in that churchyard on that bright day, with no gift at all, would have looked at the thin grey man in the patched robes at the foot of the grave and known.

Lupin's life had stopped.

It had stopped on the floor of a pit in the Department of Mysteries at about eight o'clock on a Tuesday evening, when he'd stayed behind whilst everybody else ran up the stairs. Harry didn't know what Tonks had been to him. He didn't know what he'd been to her. He knew only that Lupin was standing at the foot of her grave in the sunshine with his hands at his sides, quite still, and that everything in him that had ever moved had stopped, and wasn't going to start again.

And Sirius.

Sirius stood at the head of the grave, very straight.

He was wearing his black coat, mended. He stood with his shoulders back and his chin up and his face quite still, the way a man stands at attention. He didn't move once during the whole of the service. Not when the vicar spoke. Not when the coffin went down. Not when her mother stepped forward and dropped a single handful of earth on it. Not when her father made a sound that Harry would hear for a long time afterwards.

Harry read him.

There was grief, for his cousin's daughter, whom he'd met eleven months ago and liked enormously. There was the old fury, at the walls, at the world, at a man in the rain in the Atrium. And beneath both, at the bottom, was a question.

It was very simple. It was aimed at the coffin, and at the sky, and at Harry.

*Why me?*

* * *

Sirius found him by the gate afterwards.

Everybody else was walking down the lane to the village, slowly, in twos and threes. Harry had stopped by the low granite wall with the gorse on it. Sirius came and stood beside him and leaned on the wall and looked at the moor.

"It missed me," said Sirius.

Harry waited.

"Bella's curse," said Sirius. "At the arch. It missed me by a foot. I saw it go past. And I looked up, and you were on the tiers with your nose pouring blood, and I knew you'd done something."

He didn't look at Harry.

"I don't know what. I don't want to know what. But you did something, and it missed me."

"Yes."

"And then the other one didn't miss her."

"No."

Sirius was quiet for a long time.

"She was a yard from me," he said. "Less. She'd just Stunned somebody. She turned round to say something. I don't know what. I'll never know what."

He looked at the gorse.

"If I'd stepped left instead of right. If you hadn't… if Bella's curse had hit me, would he have…?"

He stopped.

Harry thought about it.

He thought about a green light going out across a pit, low and flat, like a stone across water, past Kingsley and past a Death Eater and past Moody. He thought about a man on a dais who hadn't looked where he was sending it. Who hadn't cared. Who'd flicked his wand over his shoulder the way you try a new key in a lock, to see if it turns.

It would have gone exactly where it went.

He was almost sure of that.

He didn't know.

"I don't know," he said.

Sirius turned his head and looked at him.

Harry read him look. The question was still there at the bottom, *why me*, and on top of it now, aimed at Harry, was something else, very large and very gentle. It was love, and it had no answer in it at all.

"No," said Sirius. "No. Neither do I."

He put his hand on the back of Harry's neck, briefly, the way you might steady a horse, and took it away again.

Then they walked down the lane together after the others.

* * *

The Astronomy Tower was the highest place in the castle, and at half past ten on the last Thursday night of term nobody was on it but Harry and Evelyn.

The sky was clear. It was the sort of June night that never gets quite dark, a deep luminous blue at the edges going to black overhead. The stars were out over the forest, and the lake was very still below.

They sat on the stone floor with their backs to the parapet.

For a long time Harry was silent.

He was reading her. Or he wasn't. He was doing the thing he always did with Evelyn, which was to reach for her and find the silence, and rest on it. He'd done it on a World Cup stand with a hundred thousand people roaring round him. He'd done it on a train, and in a lake, and in another world. He did it now, on top of the Astronomy Tower, and the silence was there, exactly where she was, beside him, closed, entirely hers.

He could feel the castle below them too.

All of it. Every floor. He could feel the Slytherin common room, beneath the lake, and Draco Malfoy in it, alone by the fire. Frightened for his father, who was in Azkaban, and full of a hatred aimed at Harry that was cold and new and very patient. He could feel Gryffindor Tower, and Ron and Hermione in it, sitting up late, close together, the shock in both of them sunk now into something quieter. He could feel the hospital wing, where Neville was having the cut on his chin seen to for the third time because he kept picking at it. He could feel a girl in Ravenclaw Tower, alone, reading, with her feet on a radiator, lonely in the old peaceable way.

He could feel all of it.

He'd known since the stairs. He'd known running up the stone stairs out of the pit with blood in his eyes and the silence at his shoulder and the Order's terror coming up behind him. He'd checked for it then without meaning to, the way you check your pocket for your wand. It had been there. It was here now.

It had always been his.

He didn't say so. He didn't say anything about it at all.

Neither did Evelyn.

She sat beside him on the stone with her knees drawn up and her arms round them, looking at the stars over the forest. She didn't ask how he was. She didn't ask what it had been like on the floor of the pit, with his scar split and his voice changing in the middle of a word. She didn't ask whether he could still do what he did. She didn't mention the sink, or the Chamber, or the study, or a round room with a lamp that lit for a heart-reader.

She knew all of it. He didn't know how. He hadn't told her.

She didn't say a word about any of it.

The stars wheeled, very slowly, over the forest.

"They'll send the OWL results at the end of July," said Evelyn.

Harry turned his head.

"History of Magic is marked by the Wizarding Examinations Authority in Leeds," Evelyn went on, "by a panel of three, and they don't see the candidates. They only see the papers."

She was looking at the stars.

"You fell asleep after forty minutes and slid off your chair at twenty-two minutes to three. You'd written a page and a half on the goblin rebellion of 1612. I expect you got the date of the Treaty of Ingleby wrong. Most people do."

"I got it right."

"Then they'll probably give you an Acceptable," said Evelyn. "For the page and a half. And then they'll look at the rest of it, which is blank, and think you were making a point."

Harry looked at her.

"About what?"

"About goblin rebellions," said Evelyn. "Binns will be thrilled. He'll think it's a new school of historical thought."

He laughed.

It burst out of him on top of the Astronomy Tower, quite suddenly, in the luminous June dark, and went out over the lake, and he couldn't stop it. He laughed with his head back against the stone of the parapet until his eyes were wet and the split in his scar ached, and he didn't care.

Evelyn waited until he'd finished.

"It was the twenty-second of March," she said. "The Treaty of Ingleby. Sixteen twelve. Not the twenty-third. The twenty-third was when it was ratified."

"I know."

"I'm only saying," said Evelyn. "So that it's on record."

* * *

The *Daily Prophet* printed Sirius's face on its front page on the Saturday after the battle.

It was the same photograph that had been on every lamp post and in every shop window in Britain three years ago, the wild-haired, hollow-faced man in the prison photograph shouting at the camera. But the word beneath it was different. The word beneath it, in letters two inches high, was INNOCENT.

Harry read the article at breakfast.

It said that a dozen Aurors and the Minister for Magic himself had seen Peter Pettigrew alive in the Atrium of the Ministry, at the side of He-Who-Must-Not-Be-Named. It said Peter Pettigrew had been declared dead in November 1981, after a street explosion that killed twelve Muggles, for which Sirius Black had been sent to Azkaban without trial. It said the Ministry had opened an inquiry. It said the Minister was *deeply troubled*.

It didn't say *sorry*.

Three weeks later, in July, the *Prophet* would print the same face on its front page again. A different photograph this time, a newer one, laughing, and beneath it the word HERO. Harry would cut it out and keep it in the back of his Potions book, beside the cutting from the July before that said *a certain boy*.

But that was later.

* * *

Dumbledore told him on the last morning of term.

He sent for him at nine, and Harry went up to the office. Dumbledore was sitting at his desk in the sunshine, old and white and folded, and he didn't get up.

"Sirius Black has been cleared of all charges," he said. "Formally. By the Wizengamot. Yesterday afternoon. Amelia Bones put it through in four hours, which I believe is a record. He is a free man. He may live where he likes."

He looked at Harry over his glasses.

"He would like to live in the house he hates, I am afraid, because it is the only one he owns. And he would like you to live there with him."

Harry held very still.

"I have said no to this for three years," said Dumbledore. "You will remember. I said no in your third year when he was a fugitive, and in your fourth year when he was a fugitive. I said it because your mother's blood protected you in your aunt's house and nowhere else, and I thought that protection was worth more than a godfather."

"I know."

"Tom has your blood now," said Dumbledore. "He took it in a churchyard. He can touch you. He did touch you, at the Ministry."

He put his old hands together.

"Your aunt's house still protects you from some things. From his followers. Less from him. A great deal less than it did. And it costs you."

He paused.

"I have watched it cost you for fifteen years. I find I no longer think the price is worth it."

Harry read him.

He read him say it, and he read what it cost. It was very simple. The cost of an old man who'd kept a boy in a particular house for fifteen years because he believed it was safest, and had told himself all that time that he was right, and was now saying aloud, in front of the boy, that he wasn't sure any more that he ever had been.

It was costing him a great deal. Harry could feel it.

"You may live with your godfather, Harry," said Dumbledore. "If you want to."

"Yes," said Harry.

"Yes, you want to?"

"Yes," said Harry. "Thank you."

Dumbledore nodded, once.

* * *

On the train Theo sat beside him the whole way, and neither of them spoke.

Theo's father was in Azkaban. He'd been taken out of the black water in the Atrium by two Aurors, very old, very slow, still on his knees. Harry had read Theo on the morning it was in the *Prophet* and found the calm sadness. Beneath it was a relief so large that Theo was ashamed of it. And beneath the shame, at the very bottom, was the boy at the edge of the drop, with a hand put out to him at last by nobody he'd have chosen.

Millicent had brought fudge. She put it on Harry's knee at Peterborough.

"Eat it," she said, and he ate it.

Evelyn read *The Singing Sands* at forty seconds a page and didn't look up until Kings Langley.

At King's Cross, when the train stopped, Harry stood in the corridor with his trunk and looked out of the window at the platform.

Sirius was there.

He was standing on Platform Nine and Three-Quarters in the middle of the crowd, in plain sight, in the open, at three o'clock on a Saturday afternoon, with families streaming past him and children shouting and owls hooting in their cages. People were looking at him. People were nudging each other and pointing. A witch in a purple hat walked straight into a pillar, staring.

He didn't seem to notice.

He was wearing a coat. Harry didn't know where he'd got it. A long coat, a Muggle coat, in a check of mustard yellow and brown and a sort of plum colour, with enormous lapels and brass buttons. It was the worst coat Harry had ever seen in his life.

He was waving.

He was waving with both arms, over the heads of the crowd, at the train, at the window where Harry stood, and he was grinning. Harry read him from forty yards away, through the glass and the crowd and the steam, and what came off him was so loud that it went over the whole platform like a wave coming up a beach.

Harry got off the train.

* * *

Evelyn's owl came at eight o'clock the next morning, to the kitchen of number twelve, Grimmauld Place.

It was her family's owl, a small grey one with a superior expression. It came in through the window Sirius had opened at seven because the kitchen smelled of burnt toast, landed on the table between the teapot and the marmalade, and held out its leg.

It was ten days early.

Harry noticed that before he noticed anything else. Ten days early. Evelyn was never early, and never late, and she'd stood on the platform yesterday afternoon with her bag over her shoulder and her hand in her right-hand pocket and said *every eleven days, as usual*.

He took the letter off the owl's leg.

It was a single sheet, folded twice, in her small exact upright hand. There was no greeting. There was no weather. There was nothing about a book. There was only one line, in the middle of the page, written very straight, with her initial beneath it.

*Lucan has taken the Mark, and Father has accepted a position.*
