## Chapter 66: Lament

The singing began at a quarter to two in the morning, and it didn't stop until it was light.

Harry heard it from the lawn. He was still on the lawn. He'd been kneeling on the wet grass beside Albus Dumbledore for nearly two hours, and people had come and gone round him. Somebody had put a cloak over his shoulders. Somebody else had tried to lift him by the arm and been told, very quietly, by Sirius, to leave him be. He hadn't moved. He hadn't read anything, because there was nothing in front of him to read.

Then the singing began.

It came from somewhere high in the castle. A phoenix. Harry knew it at once. He'd heard it in a chamber under the school at twelve, and it had gone through him like a clean wind, the bravest thing he'd ever felt. He'd heard it in a churchyard at fourteen, pouring out of a gold cage of light round two wands, and it had held him up.

This wasn't that.

It came down from the dark tower where the headmaster's office was, over the roofs and turrets, out across the lawn, and it was a lament. It was the most terrible sound Harry had ever heard. It had no words in it and needed none. It went out over the grounds and the lake and the forest, and into the castle, through every window, into every room.

And Harry read the castle.

He didn't decide to. He'd spent two hours not reading, kneeling on the grass, and the singing went into him and opened something, and he reached, the way you reach for a wall in the dark, and found the castle.

It was grieving.

All of it. Every room. He found it in the dormitories, in Gryffindor Tower and Ravenclaw Tower and the Hufflepuff basement and the Slytherin dungeon under the lake. He found it in the corridors, where people stood in their nightclothes at the windows, looking out at the lawn. He found it in the staff room, and in the kitchens, where a hundred house-elves stood quite still among the ovens. He found it in the hospital wing.

It was one thing. A thousand people, and it was one thing, the same in all of them.

He'd read the castle laughing once, on a marble staircase, with fireworks going off overhead, and he'd let it go through him without turning it down. He'd read a Hall full of disappointment. He'd read a stadium full of grief a year ago, coming over a sea wall.

He'd never read this.

He didn't turn it down.

He knelt on the wet lawn beside the old man in the starlight, with the phoenix singing over the roofs, and let the whole of Hogwarts go through him, every room of it, and didn't turn any of it down at all.

* * *

Sirius brought him the Cloak at dawn.

He'd found it on the lawn, halfway between the foot of the Astronomy Tower and the place where Harry knelt, lying in a heap in the wet grass where Harry had dropped it coming down. He brought it over and knelt beside Harry, very stiffly, because he'd been on his feet for four hours, and held it out.

"You dropped this," he said.

Harry looked at it.

He took it. He folded it very carefully into a small square, the way he always folded it, and held it in his lap.

"They're going to take him in," said Sirius. "Poppy and Minerva. Into the castle. They've been waiting. They didn't want to while you…" He stopped. "It's light, Harry."

Harry looked up.

It was. The sky over the lake had turned grey, then white, and there was a line of pink along the tops of the mountains on the far side. The lawn was wet and grey and strewn with something that glittered. Harry looked at it and saw what it was. Stones. Small clear stones, thousands of them, lying bright in the grass where the birds had fallen out of the sky.

"All right," he said.

He didn't get up. Sirius didn't make him. They knelt on the wet grass together whilst Madam Pomfrey and Professor McGonagall and Hagrid came down the lawn from the castle with a stretcher, and lifted Albus Dumbledore onto it very gently, and carried him away up the long grey lawn in the dawn.

Hagrid was crying. He was crying the way Ted Tonks had cried at a graveside in Devon, openly, without trying to stop, enormous, and Harry read him and found nothing in him but the old man on the stretcher and the place where he'd been.

The phoenix stopped singing.

It stopped all at once. The silence came down over the grounds like snow.

And then, very high up, Harry saw something leave the window of the headmaster's tower. A flash of scarlet and gold, very small against the white sky. It rose and went out over the lake and away to the west, and didn't come back.

* * *

Snape came back on the Thursday.

Harry heard about it before he saw it. Everyone did. He walked in through the front doors at eleven in the morning, alone, in his black robes, and went straight up to the headmaster's office, where Professor McGonagall was, and the door was shut behind him for an hour and a half.

Nobody knew what he said.

Harry knew a little. Not because he heard it. Because he read McGonagall leave the office afterwards and go down the spiral stair, and what was in her was fury and grief and exhaustion, and beneath them, very reluctant and very small, something that was neither quite belief nor quite disbelief. It was the feeling of a woman who's been told something she doesn't want to accept by someone she doesn't trust, and has found, to her horror, that she can't prove it isn't true.

He'd taken Draco Malfoy, he said. That was what had gone round the school by lunch, in pieces. He'd taken the boy off the tower and through the gates because the Dark Lord would have killed him for failing, and he'd taken him somewhere safe, and he'd come back.

That was all anyone knew.

Harry had been on the tower. He'd seen Snape raise his wand at Dumbledore with the Vow pulling round him like a rope, and he'd seen him lower it, and summon a wand up out of the grass, and hold it out without a word.

He told nobody.

* * *

He saw Snape on the Friday.

He was in the east courtyard at the foot of the Astronomy Tower at four in the afternoon. He didn't know why he'd gone there. He'd found himself there, sitting on the low wall by the greenhouse gate, where the Death Eaters had stood and thrown curses at thirty children. The flagstones had been scrubbed. There was nothing to see. There was a dark patch by the wall of the tower, near the small door, where the scrubbing hadn't quite worked.

Snape came out of the small door.

He came out of the tower into the courtyard without seeing Harry at first. He was walking with his head down, very fast, his black robes behind him, heading across the courtyard for the greenhouses, the way he walked down every corridor in the castle, as though the air were in his way.

He stopped in the middle of the courtyard.

He stopped very suddenly, the way a man stops when he's walked into something he didn't see. He was looking up. Harry followed his gaze. He was looking at the top of the Astronomy Tower, at the parapet, a hundred and fifty feet up against the blue June sky.

He stood quite still.

Harry read him.

He hadn't expected to be able to. Snape was closed. Snape was always closed. He'd been closed on top of the tower that night, apart from those few seconds when he came out of the stairway, and he'd been closed on Thursday walking in through the front doors, Harry was sure of it, smooth and complete, the wall he'd always been.

He wasn't closed now.

He was standing in the middle of an empty courtyard at four in the afternoon looking up at the top of a tower, and he thought he was alone, and he couldn't close. Harry could feel that he couldn't. He could feel him try. He could feel the wall come up and fail, and come up and fail, the way a man tries to shut a door against a wind too strong for him.

The grief came through it.

It came through the wall the way water comes through a cracked dam. This was no leak at the rim. It was everywhere. It came through every part of the wall at once, and it was so large that Harry, thirty yards away on the low wall by the greenhouse gate, sat very still and didn't breathe.

It was for Dumbledore.

It was raw. It was so raw it was almost pain. It was total. There was nothing in Severus Snape at that moment but grief for an old man who'd sat on a wet lawn and lain back and gone out, and it wasn't the grief of an enemy, or a servant, or a man bound to someone by a chain. Harry had read all of those. He'd read obedience in Snape, and resentment, and cold necessity.

This was none of them.

It was the grief of a man who's lost the only person in the world who knew everything about him and hadn't turned away.

Harry sat on the wall and read it.

He thought about a playground and a boy behind a bush. He thought about a lawn by a lake, and a word said that couldn't be taken back. He thought about the purest thing he'd ever felt in anyone, broken like a bone and carrying on, broken, for twenty years. He thought about who might have known that, all those years. Who might have been told it in a room at the top of a tower, and kept it, and never once used it.

He thought about a wand rising over a parapet out of the dark and being held out without a word.

He knew.

He knew it the way he knew which way a room would tip. All the way down. Severus Snape had been loyal. Not to the Dark Lord. Not to anything Harry had ever thought he might be loyal to. To the old man on the lawn. All along. All the way. Whatever he'd sworn, to whomever he'd sworn it, whatever he'd raised his wand to do on top of the tower, he'd been Albus Dumbledore's.

And Harry trusted him.

He found it there, sitting on the wall, the way you find you've already sat down. He hadn't decided it. It had been decided. He'd been frightened of Snape for three years and hated by him for six, and he'd climbed uninvited into the deepest place in his mind and been told he'd never be forgiven for it, and he sat on a low wall in a courtyard on a June afternoon and read the man's grief from thirty yards away and trusted him completely.

He didn't know what to do with that.

Snape looked down from the tower.

He saw Harry.

He saw him sitting on the low wall by the greenhouse gate, thirty yards off, watching. And Harry felt the wall come up all at once, the way a door slams, and this time it held. It held completely. Smooth and closed, with nothing coming through at all.

They looked at each other across the empty courtyard.

Snape's face didn't change. He looked at Harry for a long moment with nothing in his eyes, and Harry knew that he knew. He knew Harry had been reading him. He knew exactly what Harry had read. Harry had been inside him twice now, once in a playground and once in a courtyard, and both times he'd found the thing Severus Snape would rather have died than have anyone find.

Snape turned and went on across the courtyard, very fast, and out through the gate by the greenhouses, and didn't look back.

Harry sat on the wall for a long time.

* * *

Evelyn went to the hospital wing on the Wednesday morning at nine, a day and a half after.

She didn't go because she was hurt. She wasn't hurt. Madam Pomfrey had looked her over at two in the morning in the courtyard, by lamplight, after everything, and found nothing wrong with her at all, and said so sharply, and turned away.

She went because she'd sat her Ancient Runes NEWT at half past seven that morning.

She'd sat it. She noted that. The examiners had come up from the Ministry at seven, two days after the Headmaster had been killed, because the examinations had been arranged months ago and the Ministry didn't cancel things. Professor McGonagall had come down to the Great Hall at a quarter past seven, grey, as she'd been for two days, and told the seventh-years that anyone who didn't feel able to sit could defer to September, and nobody would think less of them.

Evelyn had sat it.

She'd sat at her desk in the Great Hall with eleven other people and translated three passages of Old Norse runes and one of Ogham. She'd written for three hours, quite steadily, in her small exact upright hand, and she'd noted at the end that she thought she'd done well, and that she felt nothing about it.

She hadn't felt anything new since a quarter to twelve on Monday night.

Not since she let the room go.

* * *

She'd let it go at a quarter to twelve.

She'd let it go when she felt Sovereign lift. It had been pressing at the edge of the room for nine minutes, like the sea against a sea wall, and then all at once it wasn't, and she knew the man on the lawn had stopped, and she let go.

Everything came back on. The lamps. The children's wands. Madam Pomfrey's wand. The thin gold thread from its tip.

It went into Justin Finch-Fletchley's chest, found nothing left to hold together, and went out.

And Evelyn felt it.

She felt nine minutes of it. She felt them all at once, standing at the edge of the courtyard, in one piece, arriving, as her grandfather had said she would. The terror of seven curses in the air over thirty children. The sea pressing at the wall. The children kneeling. And a thin gold thread stopped in the air above a boy's chest, and Madam Pomfrey's voice saying *it's stopped, I can't hold him, let it go*, and her own voice saying *I'm sorry*, and not feeling it.

She felt it now.

She felt it so completely that for some time she didn't know where she was.

She hadn't come apart. She'd noted that afterwards, with something close to surprise. In March, on the floor of the old Muggle Studies room, she had. In the courtyard she'd stood quite still at the edge of the flagstones with everything arriving at once, nine minutes of it, and a boy dead on the flagstones in front of her, and she hadn't moved or made a sound. When Professor Sprout came and put a hand on her arm, she'd said, quite clearly, "I'm all right, thank you, Professor," and walked back into the castle.

She hadn't slept on Monday night, or on Tuesday night either.

She'd sat on her bed in the seventh-year girls' dormitory under the lake with her knees drawn up and the watch in her hands, both nights, until half past six. Then she'd got up and dressed and gone to sit her Ancient Runes.

And then she'd come here.

* * *

The bed was at the end of the ward, by the window. It was empty. It had been freshly made up with clean white sheets, tight, the corners folded. There was nothing on it. There was nothing on the table beside it.

They'd taken him home to his parents. Madam Pomfrey said so. His parents were Muggles, and they'd come up in the night on the Knight Bus with Professor Sprout and taken him home to Surrey on Tuesday morning at six.

Evelyn stood at the foot of the empty bed.

She didn't sit. She stood with her hands in her cardigan pockets, where the watch was, and looked at the clean white sheets.

Madam Pomfrey came out of her office.

She looked very old. She looked as though she hadn't slept either. She stood in her office doorway with a bottle of something in her hand and looked at Evelyn standing at the foot of the bed, and Evelyn couldn't read her, because she couldn't read anybody, but she noted that Madam Pomfrey's hand wasn't quite steady on the bottle.

"Miss Selwyn," said Madam Pomfrey.

"I want to tell you what I did," said Evelyn.

Madam Pomfrey waited.

"I want to tell you exactly," said Evelyn. "So it's on record. So somebody knows."

She told her.

She told her standing at the foot of the bed with her hands in her pockets, in her flat precise voice, quite steadily, the way she'd give a date. She told her she walked a Path. That it was called Stillness, and her grandfather had taught her, though she didn't say who her grandfather was. That at its summit there was a thing called Dead Calm, and inside it all magic that wasn't hers was stilled. All of it. Curses and lamps and wands and Sovereign.

And charms.

"I knew," said Evelyn. "In March. I opened it once before, in an empty classroom, and there was a boy with a Self-Mending Charm on his jumper, and it stopped. I saw it stop. I knew then that it would stop anything. I knew it would stop healing." She was looking at the white sheets. "I didn't think about it. I put it away. I put it somewhere I wouldn't find it."

Madam Pomfrey stood very still.

"On Monday night I opened it," said Evelyn, "and I saw your charm stop. I saw the thread. I knew what it meant. I knew he'd die if I didn't let go." She paused. "And I didn't feel anything. Inside it I don't feel anything. I knew, and I didn't feel it, and so I didn't let go. I held it for four more minutes. Because if I'd let go, they'd all have knelt, and the ones at the gate would have got up, and he'd have come into the courtyard." She looked up at last at Madam Pomfrey. "I decided. I want you to know that. I decided. It wasn't an accident. I knew exactly what I was doing, and I did it, and he died at nineteen minutes to midnight. Inside it. Inside me."

The ward was very quiet.

Madam Pomfrey set the bottle on the table by the door. She came slowly down the ward past the empty beds and stopped beside Evelyn at the foot of Justin Finch-Fletchley's.

"Miss Selwyn," she said. Her voice was very low and not steady at all. "Evelyn. Listen to me. It was not your fault."

Evelyn looked at her.

"There were thirty children in that courtyard," said Madam Pomfrey. "Thirty. Kneeling. With curses in the air over their heads and seven Death Eaters at the gate. If you hadn't done what you did, I don't know how many of them would be in these beds now. Or not in them." She put her hand on Evelyn's arm. "That boy was dying when you came. He'd been hit before you got there. I was holding him, but I don't… I don't know how long I could have held him. Not long. It was a very bad curse." Her hand tightened. "It was not your fault."

"That isn't what I asked," said Evelyn.

Madam Pomfrey stopped.

"I didn't ask whose fault it was," said Evelyn. "I didn't ask you anything. I told you what I did. I wanted somebody to know. Exactly. That's all." She looked down at the hand on her arm. "I know whose fault it was. I was there."

She took her arm back, very gently.

"Thank you, Madam Pomfrey," she said. "I'm sorry I took up your time."

She left the hospital wing.

She went down the stairs and along the corridor, and she didn't go to the dungeons. She went to the library. She sat at the back table in the corner where Madam Pince couldn't see, took the notebook out of her bag, the fourteenth, small and black with a ribbon, and opened it at a clean page.

She wrote the date. *Wednesday 25 June 1997.*

She wrote the time. *9.41 a.m.*

Then she wrote his name. *Justin Finch-Fletchley.* And beneath it, in the same small exact hand, the time he'd died.

She wrote nothing else. She sat and looked at it for a long time, and she didn't cry, and she didn't come apart. She noted that she didn't.

She noted that since March she hadn't been able to find the door.

* * *

The headmaster's office was McGonagall's now.

Harry went up on the Saturday because she sent for him. The gargoyle let him through. He climbed the spiral stair, knocked, and went in, and the office was the same. The silver instruments whirring on their spindle-legged tables. The Sorting Hat on its shelf. The sword in its case. Fawkes's perch, empty.

And the portraits.

They were all awake. They were all looking at him. The old headmasters and headmistresses of Hogwarts in their frames round the walls had watched him come into this room a hundred times and pretended to be asleep. They didn't pretend now.

There was a new one.

It hung behind the desk in a frame of plain dark wood. It hadn't been there a week ago. It was a portrait of a very old man with long white hair and a long white beard and half-moon glasses, in robes of midnight blue, sitting in a high-backed chair.

He was asleep.

He really was asleep. Harry could tell. The others were watching him, wide awake, every one, and the old man in the new frame behind the desk was asleep in his chair with his chin on his chest and his hands folded in his lap, breathing slowly, in paint.

"He hasn't woken," said Professor McGonagall.

She was sitting behind the desk. She looked worn to the bone. She looked as though she hadn't slept since Monday, and Harry read her and knew she hadn't. There was grief, and exhaustion, and fury, and beneath it all, holding it all up, very hard and very straight, the thing that keeps a person standing at the side of a grave.

"The portrait," she said. "He hasn't woken since it appeared. On Tuesday afternoon. It just… appeared. They do, when a headmaster dies." She glanced at it over her shoulder. "Phineas says it can take a while. The first time. He says some of them sleep for weeks."

"Some of us," said a sharp-faced wizard with a pointed beard from a frame by the door, "never quite wake up at all, if you take my meaning. Dippet's been asleep since nineteen fifty-six."

"Thank you, Phineas."

Harry looked at the sleeping portrait.

He tried to read it. He did it without meaning to, the way he did everything. He reached for the old man asleep in the frame behind the desk, the way he'd reached for him in this room at two in the morning when he was fourteen.

There was nothing. Paint.

"Sit down, Potter," said McGonagall.

* * *

She told him about the funeral, which would be on Tuesday, by the lake. She told him about the school, which would close early, on Wednesday, the day after. She told him the governors were meeting and the Ministry was sending people, and that she didn't know whether Hogwarts would open again in September, and that she'd fight for it, and that she didn't know if she'd win.

She told him she was acting headmistress, and that she hadn't wanted to be.

"I was his deputy for thirty-nine years," she said. "Thirty-nine years, Potter. I thought…" She stopped. She took off her spectacles and pressed her fingers to her eyes. "I thought I'd be the one to go first. I was quite sure of it. He was always so very…"

She didn't finish.

Harry let her be.

He read her. He read the grief, and beneath it, very old, a thing he hadn't expected. It was the feeling of someone who's spent thirty-nine years arguing with someone every single day about everything, and has just realised there's no one left to argue with.

"He asked me to give you something," said McGonagall. "If anything happened. He gave it to me in April. He said I wasn't to give it to you before."

She opened a drawer of the desk.

"It isn't this," she said. "This is from the will. That comes later. Mr Prynne is coming up from London on Wednesday to read it. Dumbledore used the same solicitor as the Selwyns, did you know that? Small world." She took out a small box of plain wood. "This is just something he said you should have. Before the will. Because he thought you might need it sooner."

She held it out.

Harry opened it.

It was a sherbet lemon.

One sherbet lemon in a twist of paper, the kind Dumbledore had kept in a jar on his desk for as long as Harry had been coming to this office. The left jar, because the right one held Fawkes's cockroach clusters. It was a little old. The paper had gone soft.

There was a note beneath it. In the long thin slanting hand it said, *For the walk back down the stairs. A.D.*

Harry looked at it for a long time.

Then he put it in his pocket.

* * *

They buried him on the Tuesday, by the lake, on the far shore, under a beech tree.

It was a hot, bright, cloudless day, the first of July, and the lake was blue and still, and the whole school was there. They sat in rows of chairs on the grass by the water in their best robes, every house, every year, with the staff behind them and behind the staff a great many people Harry didn't know. Ministry people. Old people, very old, who'd been taught by Dumbledore eighty years ago. A tall man with a goatee from the *Prophet*. Madame Maxime, enormous, weeping into a handkerchief the size of a pillowcase.

And the Order.

Sirius sat at the end of the second row beside Harry, in a black coat Harry had never seen before, a new one, very plain, with no checks on it at all. He sat very straight. He didn't speak.

Lupin sat on Sirius's other side. He was thinner than at Tonks's funeral. He didn't look at the lake, or the coffin, or anything. He looked at the grass at his feet.

And on Harry's other side, in a cloak of the darkest grey, almost black, with no gold at the cuffs at all and his golden hair combed very flat, sat Gilderoy Lockhart. He had his silver-lion stick across his knees. He spoke to nobody. He sat with both hands on the stick looking at the white tomb by the water, his face quite still, and Harry read him and found the vanity still there, huge and warm, and the courage behind it, both very quiet and very far down, beneath something that was simply grief.

Evelyn was in the row behind, with Millicent and Theo.

Harry didn't turn round. He couldn't read her. He didn't need to turn round to know exactly where she was. He could feel the silence at the back of his neck, where it always was.

* * *

The merpeople came.

They came up out of the lake a long way out, in the middle of the blue water, and didn't come close. They stayed out in the deep water, dozens of them, a long line of grey-green heads and shoulders in the sun, and they sang. It was the song from the second task, in the strange screeching language that was beautiful under water and terrible above it. It was a lament. Harry couldn't understand a word.

He read them.

He'd read them once before, under the lake, three years ago. Cold. Curious. *Ours.*

He read them now, and it was grief.

The centaurs came out of the forest. They didn't come down to the lake. They stood at the edge of the trees, thirty or forty of them, very tall in the bright sun, with their bows, and they didn't sing. They raised their bows all together, then turned and went back into the trees.

Harry read them as they went. Pride, and old anger, and beneath both, very plain, respect.

Then a little man in black robes stood up beside the white tomb and talked for a long time about a great mind and a noble spirit. Harry didn't listen. He read the man and found he'd never met Dumbledore, and was nervous of the sound of his own voice, and was thinking about his lunch.

He read everyone.

He read the whole school on the chairs on the grass. Every row. Every house. The grief, which was one thing, the same in all of them, the thing he'd read from the lawn whilst the phoenix sang. And beneath it, different in each of them, the other things. Fear. Fear for themselves. Fear for September. Fear of what came next. A little anger. A little relief that it wasn't them. A first-year in the front row thinking about her cat. A seventh-year near the back thinking about a girl.

He read the staff. McGonagall, upright, holding. Sprout, crying. Flitwick, crying. Hagrid at the end of the staff row, enormous, his face in his hands. Slughorn in a velvet waistcoat, grieving and frightened and ashamed, the locked drawer in him rattling.

Snape wasn't there.

He read Sirius beside him. Grief. The fury at the walls, at the world. And still the question at the bottom, from another funeral. *Why me.*

He read all of it.

He sat very still on his chair on the grass by the lake in the bright sun and read the whole of Albus Dumbledore's funeral, every person in it, every feeling, all at once, and didn't turn any of it down, and didn't move, and didn't cry.

They laid him in the white tomb.

There was a moment, as the tomb closed, when bright white flames leapt up round it, very high, and in the flames Harry thought he saw something rise. A bird. A phoenix. Climbing, joyfully, into the blue.

Then the flames were gone, and there was only the white marble tomb under the beech tree by the lake, in the sun.

* * *

Mr Prynne read the will on the Wednesday in McGonagall's office at ten in the morning, after the school had gone.

He was a small dry man in a grey suit with a briefcase. He'd read Isadora Hale's will in the long drawing room at Selwyn Hall three years ago, Evelyn said, and he'd been very dull about it, and very exact. He was very dull and very exact now.

Dumbledore had left most things to the school. He'd left his books to the library, his instruments to McGonagall, and his Pensieve to the office, *for the use of whoever sits in it next*. He'd left a small sum to Aberforth Dumbledore, of the Hog's Head, Hogsmeade, with a line that said only *with my apologies, for everything, which I know will not be enough*. He'd left a pair of thick woollen socks to Hagrid, and Hagrid, standing by the door, had made a sound and gone out.

And to Harry he'd left two things.

The first was a box. A plain wooden box the size of a large book, full of notebooks. Old ones. Dozens of them. They were in Dumbledore's long thin slanting hand, from the very small, neat writing of a young man to the large, shaky writing of a very old one, and they were all about the same thing.

*Notes on the Paths*, said the label on the lid. *For H.J.P., who walks one. With the hope that they will be of more use to him than they were to me.*

The second was a letter.

It was in an envelope of thick cream paper sealed with purple wax, and on the front it said *Harry*, in the long slanting green ink that had once, a long time ago, said *Mr H. Potter, The Cupboard under the Stairs*.

Mr Prynne handed it to him.

"The testator's instructions," said Mr Prynne, "are that this letter is to be read by Mr Potter alone, and is not to be read aloud, or shown to any other person, unless Mr Potter so chooses."

Harry took it.

He didn't open it in the office. He put it inside his robes and went down the spiral stair, past the gargoyle, along the empty corridors of the empty castle. On the stairs he took the sherbet lemon out of his pocket, unwrapped it and put it in his mouth, and it was very old and very sweet and fizzed on his tongue.

He went down to the lake.

He went to the flat rock under the beech on the far side, where the squid slept in the shallows, and sat on it alone in the hot July sun, and opened the letter.

* * *

*Dear Harry,*

*If you are reading this, I am dead, and you have had a sherbet lemon, and I hope it was not too stale. They were never very good. I liked them because nobody else did.*

*I am going to be brief, because I have never been brief with you, and it is a little late to begin, but I should like to try once.*

*You will have the notebooks. They are everything I learned about the Paths in ninety-eight years. A great deal of it is wrong. Some of it is not. You will know which, I think, better than I did. You have always known things better than I did. I was very slow to see it.*

*I am sorry that I lied to you. I have lied to you a great many times, and I said I would stop, and I did not. You read it every time. I knew that you did. I did it anyway. I should like to tell you that each time it was for your own good, and some of the times it was, and some of the times it was for mine.*

*There is a thing I have not told you. You know there is. You read it in my face across a desk on a Friday night in May, and I read you read it, and we sat there, the two of us, saying nothing. I am not going to tell you now. I have thought about it a great deal, and I do not think it would help you to know, and I think it would hurt you very much. You will find it out one day. I am sorry for that too.*

*Look after Sirius. He is braver than he is wise, and he loves you more than he has ever loved anything, including himself, which is saying a great deal.*

*Look after Miss Selwyn. Or rather, let her look after you. I suspect she is better at it.*

*And Harry.*

*If I have treated you as a soldier, forgive me. I was afraid of what you would be. I am still afraid. That is not your fault.*

*Albus*

## Chapter 67: Seventeen

There was a leaving feast in the end, because Professor McGonagall said there would be.

She said it on the morning of the funeral, at breakfast, standing at the staff table in black with her face like grey stone. She said the school would close the next day, and she didn't know when it would open again. She said the seventh-years had sat their examinations in the middle of a war, two days after the Headmaster died, and they would have their leaving feast, however small, and their families were welcome, and she didn't want to hear one word of argument from the governors, the Ministry, or anybody else.

No one argued.

So on the Tuesday evening at seven, after the white tomb had closed under the beech on the far shore, the Great Hall was laid for a feast. Not the whole Hall. The house tables had been pushed back against the walls, and there was one long table down the middle beneath the enchanted ceiling, which showed a clear evening sky with the first stars coming out. The seventh-years sat along one side of it. Their families sat along the other.

There weren't very many families.

Harry counted. He couldn't help it. He'd learned it from her. There were sixty-one seventh-years and thirty-four chairs on the families' side of the table, and nineteen of those were filled. People hadn't come. People were frightened. People had read the *Prophet* and decided that Hogwarts on the night of Albus Dumbledore's funeral wasn't a place they wanted to be.

Evelyn sat at the end of the seventh-years' side, by the door.

The chair across from her was empty.

* * *

Harry wasn't supposed to be there. He was a sixth-year. He was supposed to be in the Slytherin common room, packing.

At four o'clock on the lake shore, after the funeral, Sirius had said, "There's a feast. For the seventh-years. Families invited."

"I know."

"Is anybody coming for her?"

Harry hadn't answered.

Sirius had looked at him a moment. Then he'd said "Right," quite short, and gone off up the lawn towards the castle with his new black coat flapping, and Harry had read him go. What was in him wasn't grief, for once. It was something with a great deal more energy in it than grief.

He found out at seven what it was.

* * *

The chair across from Evelyn was still empty at five past seven, when Professor McGonagall stood and said a few very short words about courage, and the future, and a man who'd have wanted them to eat.

At six minutes past seven Sirius Black came in through the great doors of the Hall in his new plain black coat, his hair tied back and his face shaved, and walked straight down the side of the long table, past the seventh-years and their families, all of whom turned to stare, to the end by the door. He pulled out the empty chair opposite Evelyn Selwyn, sat down in it, and put his elbows on the table.

"Sorry I'm late," he said. "Did I miss anything?"

Evelyn looked at him.

Harry, in the doorway, with the Cloak over his arm because Sirius had told him to bring it in case McGonagall objected, watched her look. He couldn't read her. He never could. But he watched her face, the face people forgot, and he saw it do something he'd seen it do perhaps twice in six years.

It didn't do much. It went very slightly pink.

"You're not my family," said Evelyn.

"No," Sirius agreed. "I'm much better. I'm a convicted murderer who turned out not to be. Your family's never managed anything half so interesting." He looked round. "Harry. Stop lurking. Come and sit down. Minerva won't mind. Minerva, you won't mind, will you?"

At the head of the table, Professor McGonagall regarded him over her spectacles.

"Sit down, Potter," she said. "Before he stands on something."

* * *

He stood on something anyway.

He did it at the end, after the food, when Professor McGonagall stood again with a list and began to read out the names of the seventh-years one by one. Each stood up and went to the head of the table and shook her hand and took a small rolled scroll tied with ribbon in their house colours. It wasn't their NEWT results. Those would come in August. It was a certificate saying they'd completed seven years at Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry, signed this year by an acting headmistress in very small careful writing.

The families clapped for their own. It wasn't loud. There were only nineteen of them. Each family clapped when its own name was read, and a few of the other seventh-years joined in, and then it was quiet again until the next name.

"Selwyn, Evelyn."

Evelyn stood up.

And Sirius Black stood up on his chair.

He did it in one movement, the way he did everything. He stood on the chair opposite her in his black coat in the middle of the Great Hall on the night of Albus Dumbledore's funeral, put two fingers in his mouth, and whistled so loudly the candles flickered. Then he began to clap. He clapped as though he were at a Quidditch match, hands above his head.

"*Selwyn!*" he roared. "*SELWYN! EVELYN SELWYN! SEVEN NEWTs! SEVEN! IN A WAR!*"

The whole Hall turned and stared at him.

"*She caught Rita Skeeter in a JAM JAR!*" bellowed Sirius. "*She signed for the JAR!*"

Harry, on the bench beside him, put his face in his hands.

He read the Hall. He couldn't help it. He read sixty-one seventh-years and nineteen families and the staff at the head of the table, all turning, all staring at a man standing on a chair, and for a second what was in them was astonishment. Then something else rose in some of them. Not all. Some. It travelled along the table from the head, where Professor Flitwick had begun, very quietly, to laugh.

It was the thing from the marble staircase, the day of the fireworks.

It wasn't as large. It couldn't have been, tonight. But it was there in the Great Hall on the night of the funeral, small and helpless and real, rising through the grief, and Harry let it go through him.

Evelyn stood quite still beside the table.

She didn't look at Sirius. She didn't look at anyone. Her face was very pink. She walked the length of the long table to its head at her ordinary pace, in her grey cardigan, with Sirius Black still whistling on a chair behind her, and shook Professor McGonagall's hand, and took her scroll.

Professor McGonagall held on to her hand a moment.

"Miss Selwyn," she said. Harry could only just hear it. "Seven. And I'm told the Ancient Runes was Wednesday."

"Yes, Professor."

"I took Ancient Runes in nineteen fifty-four," said Professor McGonagall. "I did it with a broken wrist. I've always thought that rather impressive." She let go. "Well done."

Evelyn walked back down the table.

She sat down opposite Sirius, who'd got off his chair, laid her scroll on the table in front of her, square to the edge, and folded her hands on top of it.

"That," she said to Sirius, very precisely, "was the most embarrassing thing that has ever happened to me."

"I know," said Sirius. "Wasn't it marvellous?"

Evelyn studied him for some time.

"Yes," she said.

* * *

Theo gave him the letter on the platform at Hogsmeade the next morning, folded inside a chess magazine.

He said nothing. He handed Harry the magazine as they boarded the train, the way he'd handed Harry chess magazines a hundred times, and went and sat in the corner of the compartment with his own, sleeve buttoned at the wrist, looking out of the window.

Harry decoded it between Peterborough and King's Cross with the magazine on his knee and a pencil in his hand, whilst Millicent ate fudge and Evelyn read *The Franchise Affair*, which she'd borrowed back from him because she said he hadn't appreciated chapter nine.

It was four positions.

*It will be soon. Weeks. Not months. Father says there are people in the Ministry who are already his. Thicknesse. Head of Magical Law Enforcement since Bones. He is under the Imperius. He has been since May. When it happens it will be from the inside and it will be fast.*

*There are positions waiting. Father knows the names. One of them is Selwyn. The father. Something to do with registers. Muggle-borns. The son has a post in the Minister's office.*

*I don't know when. I'll know when.*

*Don't come back in September.*

*T.*

Harry read it twice.

He looked across the compartment at Evelyn, reading with her feet up on the seat and her book on her knees, turning a page every forty seconds.

*The father. Something to do with registers.*

He folded the letter very small and put it in his shoe.

* * *

"I'm not coming back," he said.

He said it on the fourth of July at the kitchen table at Grimmauld Place, at nine in the evening, to Sirius and to Professor McGonagall, who'd come through the fire to talk about the school and was sitting very upright at the end of the table with a cup of tea she wasn't drinking.

Sirius put his cup down.

"Harry…"

"Theo says it'll be weeks," said Harry. "The Ministry. From the inside. Thicknesse is under the Imperius. When it goes, it'll go fast, and everything will go with it. The Ministry, and the *Prophet*, and the school." He looked at McGonagall. "If Hogwarts opens in September, Professor, it won't be yours. It'll be theirs."

McGonagall didn't contradict him.

Harry read her. He read the grief and the exhaustion and the fury. And beneath them, very hard and very cold, he read that she knew it was true. She'd known since the governors' meeting on Monday. She'd sat in a room with eleven governors and two men from the Ministry and known it, and said nothing, because she meant to fight it anyway.

"And you," said McGonagall at last. "Where will you be?"

"Somewhere else," said Harry. "Doing something else."

"Doing what?"

He didn't answer that. He didn't know yet. He knew one thing, from the top of a tower, with his best lie swallowed by a furnace without a trace. *Alone. He has to be alone.* He didn't know how. He didn't know where. He knew he wouldn't find out sitting in a classroom.

"I'm seventeen in four weeks," he said. "I'll be of age. I can go where I like."

"You can," said McGonagall. "You can, Potter." She set her cup down, very precisely, square to the saucer, and looked at it, and for a moment Harry thought she'd argue. He read her decide not to. "Albus said you would. He said it in April. He said, *Minerva, the boy will not come back for his seventh year, and you are not to try to make him, because you will not succeed and it will only hurt you both.*" She looked up. "He was usually right about you. It was one of the most annoying things about him."

Sirius was quiet for a long time.

Harry read him. Fear, large and plain and aimed at Harry. And beneath it, very quiet, something else. It was the thing from a room above a pub in another world, the thing that had once been aimed at a different boy. It was pride.

"Right," Sirius said at last. "Right. Then you'll do it from here. This house. With me. Wherever you go, whatever you do, you come back here. Every night if you can. Every week if you can't." He looked at Harry across the table. "That's the deal. Take it or leave it."

"I'll take it."

"Good," said Sirius. Then he turned in his chair and looked at the door to the kitchen stairs, where someone was standing very quietly in the shadow, in a grey cardigan with a bag over her shoulder. "And you."

Evelyn stood in the doorway.

She'd come through the front door five minutes earlier, at nine exactly, because Sirius had asked her to supper and she was never late. She'd stopped on the stairs when she heard what they were discussing, and hadn't come down.

"I'm not going home," said Evelyn.

Everyone looked at her.

"I decided in March," said Evelyn. "On the fifteenth. At fourteen minutes past eight in the morning. I'm not going back to Selwyn Hall. Not for the summer. Not for a day. Not ever." She was standing very straight. "I had a letter from my mother this morning. Father has accepted a position at the Ministry. A new one. To do with registers." She didn't look at Harry. "I haven't decided where I'm going yet. I thought I'd find a room. In London, perhaps. Or Ludlow. There's a woman in Ludlow with a bookshop who might…"

"No," said Sirius.

Evelyn looked at him.

"No," Sirius said again. "You're not finding a room. You're not going to Ludlow, or anywhere else, to sit in a room over a bookshop on your own whilst your father registers Muggle-borns. You're staying here."

"Mr Black…"

"*Sirius.* And you're staying here." He stood up. "There's a room on the second floor next to Buckbeak's. It was my brother's. No, sorry, that's Harry's. That one was my aunt's. It's got a very ugly wardrobe and a window that sticks and a portrait of a Black who died of dragon pox in eighteen ninety and is still extremely rude about it. You can have it. It's yours. For as long as you want it. Which had better be a long time." He looked at her. "That's the end of it."

Evelyn stood in the doorway.

Harry read nothing. He never had. He watched her face instead. He watched her stand very straight in the doorway of the kitchen at Grimmauld Place, in her grey cardigan with her bag over her shoulder, looking at Sirius Black, who stood at the kitchen table in his shirtsleeves, waiting.

"That's very kind of you," she said. Her voice was quite steady. "But you can't simply decide that I…"

"I can," said Sirius. "It's my house. I hate it. I can decide anything I like in it." He grinned. "It's the only good thing about owning it. Sit down, Evelyn. Have some supper. We've burned it specially."

Evelyn stayed in the doorway a moment longer.

Then she came down the last two stairs, put her bag down by the dresser, and sat at the kitchen table beside Harry, opposite Professor McGonagall, who was looking at all three of them over her spectacles with an expression Harry couldn't read, because she'd closed.

"Thank you," said Evelyn.

She said it to the table, very quietly. Harry nearly missed it.

Sirius heard. Harry read him hear it, and what rose in him was so large and so warm that it filled the kitchen to the ceiling.

"What did you burn?" asked Evelyn.

"Sausages," said Sirius.

"I'll have bread," said Evelyn.

* * *

He wrote to the Concordat on the tenth of July.

He told no one. He sat at the desk in his room at the top of the house, the room that had been Regulus Black's and that Sirius had painted a bad pale blue, and wrote it on a sheet of plain parchment in his own hand, very carefully.

He didn't know how to address it. He thought about it for a long time. In the end he wrote *To the Walkers of the Concordat, at the house with the green door in Malá Strana, Prague*, and beneath it, *Dona Inês Albuquerque*.

He wrote that Albus Dumbledore was dead. He wrote how. He wrote about Sovereign on the lawn, and a thousand children kneeling at the windows, and a wall of water fifty feet high, and an old man sitting down on the grass. He wrote that the man who'd done it had the Elder Wand now. He wrote that he was a Walker, that he stood on a Pinnacle, and that he'd opened it against children who couldn't walk. He wrote that this was exactly what the Concordat had been made to stop.

He wrote, at the end, that he walked the Path of Illusion, and that he'd be seventeen in three weeks, and that he was asking.

He signed it *Harry Potter*.

He sent it with Hedwig, because if anybody could find a green door in Prague, she could.

* * *

Hedwig came back on the fifteenth.

She came in through the window of his room at six in the morning, tired and ruffled, with a single folded sheet tied to her leg, and sat on the end of his bed and fixed him with her round amber eyes as though she'd flown a long way for nothing and wanted him to know it.

He untied it.

It was a small sheet of very old paper, thick and cream-coloured, with a watermark of a ship. The handwriting was very small, very shaky and very elegant, in brown ink, the hand of someone who'd learned to write long ago with a pen that had to be dipped.

There was one line on it.

*The Concordat does not go to war.*

Beneath it there was no signature. Only an initial. *I.*

And beneath that, very small, as though added afterwards in the same shaky elegant brown ink, two words in Portuguese that Harry didn't understand.

He looked at them for a long time.

Then he took the letter down to the kitchen, where the range was lit, opened its door, put the letter in, and watched it burn. It burned quite slowly, because the paper was thick. He watched the two Portuguese words brown at the edges and curl and go black, and he didn't try to find out what they meant.

He shut the range door.

He went back upstairs, told nobody, and didn't write to Prague again.

* * *

He turned seventeen on Thursday the thirty-first of July at Grimmauld Place, and it was the happiest evening of his life.

He didn't know it at the time. He thought afterwards, for a long while, that he ought to have known. That at some point in the evening, half past nine perhaps, with the noise going round him, he ought to have stood in the kitchen and thought, *this. Remember this.* He didn't. He thought nothing of the kind. He was too busy.

They came at six.

The Weasleys came first, all of them, through the front door in a great loud crowd. Mrs Weasley led the way carrying three enormous dishes stacked on top of each other under tea towels, with Mr Weasley behind her carrying a fourth, and Fred and George behind him carrying nothing at all and both talking at once. Ron and Hermione came together, and Ginny, and Bill, who said Fleur sent her love and would see them all tomorrow but couldn't come tonight because her mother had arrived from France and was rearranging the flowers.

Lupin came at a quarter past. He was thin and grey and very quiet, and he gave Harry a book and shook his hand and held on a moment longer than he needed to. Harry read him and found the stopped thing, still stopped, and on top of it, very small, for tonight, something that was trying.

Hagrid came at half past, through the front door, which he had to stoop very low for, and he brought a cake.

It wasn't the cake.

Hagrid's cake was in a box. It was a perfectly ordinary chocolate cake from a baker's in Hogsmeade with *HAPPY BIRTHDAY HARRY* on it in green icing. Hagrid set it on the dresser and stood back and looked at it and said, "Didn' make it meself. Thought I'd spare yeh," and Harry laughed, and Hagrid laughed, and it was the first time Harry had heard Hagrid laugh since a hut went up at the edge of the forest.

Millicent came at a quarter to seven by Floo, tumbled out of the kitchen fireplace into the coal scuttle, got up and said, "Potter. Seventeen. Here," and gave him a tin with a Highland cow on the lid. He didn't need to open it.

Neville came at seven, with his grandmother's permission and a plant in a pot. It was small and green and spiky, and it moved very slightly when you looked at it. Neville said it was a *Mimbulus mimbletonia* and Harry wasn't on any account to poke it. Harry didn't. Fred did, and was covered from head to foot in something dark green that smelt of manure, and Mrs Weasley shouted at him for four minutes without stopping.

Gilderoy Lockhart came at a quarter past seven by the front door, with his silver-lion stick, in a cloak of brilliant peacock blue with gold at the cuffs, because, he said, it was a birthday, and one didn't wear grey to a birthday, one simply didn't. He'd brought Harry a signed copy of every one of his books, in a crate, which Kreacher had to carry upstairs, weeping.

And Evelyn came down from the second floor, from the room next to Buckbeak's with the ugly wardrobe and the sticking window, where she'd been living for three and a half weeks, at seven o'clock exactly, and gave him a book.

It was a second-hand copy of *The Daughter of Time*, with a pencilled price inside the cover, one pound fifty, corrected to a pound.

"You've read it," said Harry.

"Twice," said Evelyn. "Theo gave it to me on my fifteenth birthday. This is a different copy. I wanted you to have one that wasn't mine." She looked at him. "It's about a man who can't get out of bed, who solves a five-hundred-year-old murder by looking at a portrait. I think you'll find it relevant."

"Why?"

"Because it's about somebody everybody thought was a monster," said Evelyn, "who turns out not to have been. And everybody had the evidence all along, and nobody looked." She paused. "Happy birthday, Potter."

* * *

Sirius had made a cake.

He'd made it himself that afternoon, alone, in the kitchen, with the door shut. He hadn't let anyone in. He'd sent Harry out for four hours to Diagon Alley to buy things they didn't need, and Harry had come back at five to find the kitchen full of smoke and Sirius standing in the middle of it in his shirtsleeves with flour in his hair and an expression of enormous satisfaction.

He brought it out at nine.

He carried it in from the scullery on a tray with the candles lit, all seventeen, and the whole kitchen sang, very loudly and very badly, the way people sing *Happy Birthday*, all at different speeds, with Lockhart a full beat behind everyone else and holding the last note for a long time.

He set it down on the table in front of Harry.

It was a terrible cake.

It was the worst cake Harry had ever seen. It was the worst cake anyone at the table had ever seen. It was badly lopsided, leaning to one side like a house on a hill. It was black at the edges. It had sunk in the middle, so that the seventeen candles stood in a sort of crater, leaning inwards, as though all trying to get a look at something at the bottom. It was iced in places with something meant to be white that wasn't quite, and on top, in green, in Sirius's handwriting, it said *HAPY BIRTHDY HARRY*, because he'd run out of room.

Everyone looked at it.

"Well," said Sirius. "I did it myself."

"We can tell," said Fred.

"It's very…" began Mrs Weasley, and stopped.

"It's *magnificent*," said Lockhart, with very deep feeling. "My dear fellow. It's like something out of a fairy tale. One of the dark ones."

"It's leaning," said Ron.

"It's leaning *towards* him," said Hermione. "That's rather nice, actually."

"Is it supposed to be that colour?" asked Ginny.

"Which colour?"

"Any of them."

"Blow the candles out, Harry," said Sirius, "before it collapses."

Harry blew the candles out.

He did it all at once, all seventeen, in one breath, and the kitchen cheered, and he read the kitchen whilst it cheered. He did it without deciding to. He did it the way he breathed.

* * *

He read all of them.

He read Mrs Weasley, warm and anxious and loving, all at once, aimed at everyone in the room, as it always was. Mr Weasley, tired, pleased. Bill, mild and happy, thinking about tomorrow. Fred and George, delighted, at the cake, at Sirius, at the dark green stuff still in Fred's hair. Ginny, quick and bright.

He read Ron and Hermione, sitting together at the end of the table the way they always sat, and what was in them both was nearly the same thing. It wasn't polite, or curious, or wary any more. It hadn't been for a long time. It wasn't as large as what he'd once read in them on the far side of a world, aimed at another boy. He didn't think it would ever be as large as that.

But it was aimed at him.

He read Hagrid, the loudest warm thing he'd ever felt, enormous, filling half the kitchen on his own. He read Lupin, the stopped thing, and on top of it tonight the trying, a little larger than at a quarter past six. He read Neville, pleased and shy. Millicent, plainly and simply happy, the way she'd been happy at the Yule Ball, eating cake. He read Lockhart, vain and warm and generous and brave, having the time of his life.

He read Kreacher in the doorway of the boiler cupboard, hating all of them, very loudly.

He reached for Evelyn.

She was sitting beside him eating a piece of the terrible cake very carefully with a fork, from the edge where it was least black. She hadn't said anything about it, and she wasn't going to.

He found the silence. Exactly where she was. Closed, entirely hers.

He rested on it.

And he read Sirius.

* * *

Sirius stood at the head of the table with the knife in his hand, cutting the cake.

He was cutting it very badly, because it wouldn't cut, because it was partly black and partly not cooked at all and partly something else, and every slice came away in pieces. He was handing the pieces down the table on plates, laughing, with flour still in his hair, and everyone was taking them and eating them and pulling faces and eating more.

Harry read him.

The joy was there. It was always there now, since a platform at King's Cross, since a mustard-and-plum coat. But it wasn't on top tonight. On top was something else. Something quieter and much larger.

The fury was gone.

Harry looked for it. He'd read it in Sirius every day for four years, at the walls, at the house, at the door, at the world, circling like a dog that wouldn't lie down. He looked for it, and it wasn't there. Not sunk. Not quiet. Gone. Sirius stood at the head of the table in his mother's kitchen, in the house he hated, with a terrible cake in front of him and twelve people round the table and his godson seventeen years old, and there was nothing in him anywhere that was angry with anything.

The question was gone too. *Why me.* Harry looked for it at the bottom, where it had sat since a churchyard in Devon. It wasn't there.

What was there was very simple.

He was happy.

Not the joy, which was loud and quick and went off like a firework. Something beneath the joy, holding it up. Something quite still and settled and complete, the way a lake is complete on a summer evening with no wind. He stood at the head of the table with the knife in his hand and flour in his hair, and he wanted nothing. He had everything he'd ever wanted. He had all of it, round this table, in this kitchen, tonight, and he knew it, and there was nothing in him anywhere that wasn't glad.

Harry had never felt that in anybody.

He'd felt joy, and pleasure, and delight, and love, more kinds of love than he could count. He'd never felt anyone be simply, completely, perfectly happy, with nothing at all underneath it and nothing missing.

He sat at the table with a piece of terrible cake in front of him and read it, and kept it to himself.

* * *

They left at midnight.

They went in twos and threes, the way they'd come, through the front door and the kitchen fire, and every one of them shook Harry's hand or hugged him or punched him on the arm, according to who they were, and said *see you tomorrow*. Because they'd all see each other tomorrow at the Burrow at eleven, for the wedding.

Millicent went last but one, through the fire, with half the Highland-cow tin of fudge, because Harry had made her take it. Lockhart went last of all, by the front door, sweeping his peacock-blue cloak. He stopped on the step and turned and said, "Seventeen, my dear fellow. Seventeen. I was seventeen once. I was *spectacular*." And went.

Evelyn went up to bed at ten past twelve.

She stopped halfway up the stairs and looked down over the banister at Harry in the hall and said "Happy birthday, Potter" again, as though she hadn't said it already, and then, "Read the book," and went on up. He heard her door close on the second floor, next to Buckbeak's.

The kitchen was a mess.

It was the biggest mess Harry had ever seen it in, and he'd seen it after a great many burned breakfasts. There were plates everywhere. There were glasses. There were the remains of Mrs Weasley's four dishes and Hagrid's chocolate cake and Sirius's terrible one, which nobody had finished and which still stood in the middle of the table, leaning, with a crater in it.

Sirius sat at the head of the table with his feet up on the bench and a glass in his hand.

Harry sat down beside him.

They did nothing about the mess. They sat in the kitchen at Grimmauld Place at half past twelve on the first of August, with the fire dying and the candles going out one by one, in an easy quiet.

"Seventeen," said Sirius at last.

"Yes."

"Of age. You can Apparate. You can do magic outside school. You can do anything you like. You're a grown man." He drank. "I'm never going to get used to it."

"You'll have to."

"I know. I'm going to complain about it a great deal, though." He looked at the terrible cake. "That was a terrible cake."

"Yes."

"Molly's going to tell everybody at the wedding."

"Yes."

"Good," said Sirius. "I hope she does. I hope she tells Fleur's mother. I hope it goes all the way round France." He set his glass down, stretched, and put his hands behind his head. "Wedding tomorrow."

"I know."

"Eleven o'clock. The Burrow. Molly's been planning it for a month. There's a marquee. There's a band. Bill says Fleur's mother has brought a cake from Paris that's taller than Hagrid." He grinned at the ceiling. "I'm going to dance, Harry. With everybody. With Molly, and Minerva, and Fleur's mother, and Evelyn if she'll let me, which she won't. I'm going to wear the coat."

"You can't wear the coat to a wedding."

"I'm going to wear the coat to a wedding," said Sirius. "I've been in prison for twelve years and a cave for one and this house for one. I'm going to a wedding in the sun, in a field, in the coat, and I'm going to dance until they throw me out." He shut his eyes. "I haven't been to a wedding since James and Lily's."

Harry read him.

He didn't mean to. He did it the way he breathed. He reached for his godfather, sitting at the head of the kitchen table at half past twelve in the morning with his eyes shut and his hands behind his head and his feet on the bench, and what he found was the same thing he'd found at nine o'clock with the knife in his hand.

Still. Settled. Complete. Nothing underneath it. Nothing missing.

Sirius Black was perfectly happy.
