## Chapter 68: The Burrow

The marquee went up in the field behind the Burrow at eight in the morning, and by eleven there were a hundred and twelve people in it, and every one of them was happy.

Harry counted. He hadn't meant to. He'd caught it from Evelyn years ago, the way you catch a cold, and now he did it without deciding to, standing at the entrance to the marquee in his dress robes with a programme in his hand. A hundred and twelve, not counting the band, and not counting Fleur's grandmother, who'd been asleep in a deckchair in the orchard since half past nine and was not, as far as Harry could tell, anything at all.

He read them.

He didn't turn it down. He'd turned it down at every meal he'd ever eaten in the Great Hall, every Quidditch match he'd ever played, every crowd he'd ever walked through, all his life, since before he knew he was doing it. He'd turned it down in the Atrium and on the tower and beside a white tomb a month ago. He stood at the entrance to the marquee in the bright August sun with a hundred and twelve people in front of him, and for once in his life he let it come all the way up.

It was like standing in a river.

It was warm. It was loud. It went round him and past him and over him, every kind of pleased there was, and no two of them alike. Mrs Weasley was pleased and anxious about the chairs. Mr Weasley was pleased and slightly tearful and trying to hide it behind his glasses. Fleur's father, a short round man with a pointed beard, was pleased in a way that kept bubbling over and needed someone to tell about it, and he kept telling it to Hagrid, who didn't speak French and was pleased anyway. The twins were pleased and plotting. Ginny was pleased and cross about her bridesmaid's dress. Somebody's great-uncle at the back was pleased to have been invited at all, because nobody had invited him to anything since nineteen sixty-eight.

None of it was afraid.

That was what he noticed, standing in it. There'd been fear in every crowd he'd walked through for two years. It had been under everything, in the Great Hall, in Diagon Alley, in the Atrium, in the shops, a low cold note like an organ pipe nobody had switched off. It wasn't here. All these people had come to a field in Devon in the sun and decided, for one day, not to be afraid of anything, and they'd managed it.

He stood in the entrance of the marquee and let it go over him, and didn't move until somebody walked into him from behind.

"You're blocking the door," said Evelyn.

"I'm reading."

"I know. You've got that face. You're blocking the door whilst you do it." She stepped round him. She was wearing a dark green dress Hermione had made her buy in Diagon Alley on Tuesday, and she had a programme of her own, and she was already reading it. "There are three mistakes in this."

"There aren't."

"There's an apostrophe in *Weasleys* that shouldn't be there. They've put Fleur's middle name as *Isobel* with an *o*, which it isn't, I asked her. And they've printed the name of the song for the first dance as *A Cauldron Full of Hot, Strong Love* with a comma after *Hot*, which is wrong, because it isn't a list."

"Did you tell anyone?"

"I told Fleur about the middle name. She laughed." Evelyn turned the programme over. "She laughs at a great deal. I've decided not to mind."

She went and sat at a table at the very edge of the marquee, by the canvas wall, where she could see everything and nobody would ask her to dance, took out a pencil, and began correcting the programme.

Harry watched her do it.

He couldn't read her. He never had been able to. In all that noise she was the one place with nothing in it, a square of quiet at the edge of the marquee, like a cool stone in a hot river. He didn't need to rest on it today. He found he wanted to anyway.

* * *

Bill and Fleur were married at a quarter past twelve under a canopy of white roses, by the same nervous little wizard in black who'd spoken at Dumbledore's funeral and who was thinking about his lunch again.

Harry sat in the third row between Sirius and Ron.

Sirius was wearing the coat.

He'd been told not to by Mrs Weasley, by Lupin, by Bill, and by Evelyn, who'd said at breakfast in the kitchen at Grimmauld Place, without looking up from her toast, that a mustard-and-plum check overcoat at a wedding in August was not a choice but a symptom. He'd listened to all of them with great attention and then put it on. He sat in the third row in it, sweating gently, his long hair tied back and his face washed and his eyes wet, and when Fleur came up the aisle on her father's arm in a dress that was very simple and very white and made every witch in the marquee sigh at once, Sirius was the first to start clapping. Mrs Weasley turned round in the front row and glared at him until he stopped.

Harry read him.

He'd read him at half past twelve the night before, at the head of the kitchen table with his feet on the bench, and thought it the best thing he'd ever felt in anyone. It was still there. Sirius, in the third row of a wedding in the sun, in the coat, with the bride going past and his godson beside him, was still perfectly happy. And on top of it today there was something new, which was simply joy, loud and silly and spilling over, at being in a field with a hundred people and allowed to clap.

Bill said his vows in a steady voice. Fleur said hers in a voice that wasn't steady at all, and laughed at herself halfway through, and Bill laughed too, and so did half the marquee. The nervous little wizard pronounced them bonded for life. A shower of silver stars fell out of the canopy and landed in everybody's hair and went on glittering.

Ron was crying.

He was doing it very quietly, jaw set, looking straight ahead at his brother, and Harry didn't look at him and didn't read him, because he didn't need to.

"Your mum's crying," said Harry.

"Shut up."

"So's your dad."

"Shut *up*," said Ron, and wiped his face on his sleeve.

* * *

The tables went round the edge of the marquee, the floor in the middle turned itself into a sheet of polished gold, the band began, and Sirius danced.

He danced with Mrs Weasley first.

It was dreadful. Harry hadn't known a person could dance that badly and stay upright. Sirius didn't know any of the steps and didn't care about any of them. He steered Mrs Weasley round the gold floor as though trying to handle a runaway cart with no reins, very fast, in a series of large enthusiastic swoops that bore no relation to the music. Mrs Weasley, who'd been prepared to be dignified, held on and shrieked and then began to laugh, and couldn't stop, and had to be deposited on a chair at the end with her hat over one eye.

"Black," she said, when she could speak, "you are a menace."

"I've been told."

"You have no sense of rhythm at *all*."

"I spent twelve years in prison, Molly. There wasn't a lot of dancing."

"That," said Mrs Weasley, straightening her hat, "is no excuse whatsoever." And then she patted his cheek, which Harry had never seen her do to anyone who wasn't one of her own, and Sirius went red for the first time in Harry's experience and went off to find someone else to fall over.

He danced with Professor McGonagall, who'd come for an hour and wasn't going to dance, and who was taken once round the floor at a stately walking pace and returned to her chair with her lips pressed together in a way Harry suspected was hiding a smile. He danced with Fleur's mother, who was beautiful and very gracious and kept stepping neatly out of the way of his feet as though she'd been warned. At some point in the afternoon he danced with Hagrid, which nobody who saw it would ever forget.

At half past five he came to Evelyn's table.

She'd finished correcting the programme. She'd moved on to the menu card, which she'd turned over and was writing on the back of in small square letters. She didn't look up.

"No," she said.

"I haven't asked."

"You were going to. No."

"I was going to ask whether you'd like some cake."

"No, you weren't."

"No," Sirius agreed, "I wasn't." He sat down opposite her in the coat, uninvited, elbows on the table. "Come and dance with me."

"No."

"Why not?"

"Because I've watched you dance for five hours, and you've stood on Molly Weasley's feet nine times and Professor McGonagall's twice and Madame Delacour's none, because she was too quick for you, and Hagrid's once, and he didn't notice." Evelyn turned the menu card round so he could see it. It was a list. "I've been keeping count. I don't want to be on it."

Sirius looked at the list for a long time.

Then he began to laugh.

He laughed so loudly the people at the next table turned round. He put his head down on his arms on the white tablecloth and laughed until his shoulders shook, and Harry, standing by the tent pole three yards away with a glass of pumpkin juice, read it come up out of him, and it was the happiest laugh he'd ever felt.

"One," said Sirius, when he could. "One dance. And you can count. And whatever the number is, I'll have it framed."

Evelyn looked at him.

Harry couldn't read her. He never could. But he'd known her six years, and he saw her look at the man across the table in the terrible coat, the man who'd given her a room on the second floor next to a hippogriff, and decide.

"One," said Evelyn. "And I'm counting."

She stood up.

They went out onto the gold floor together, and the band, who'd been watching Sirius all afternoon with the professional interest of people watching a fire spread, struck up something slow. Sirius took her hand, put his other hand very correctly on her shoulder blade, and set off, and she went with him.

He stood on her feet four times.

Harry knew, because she told him afterwards at the table, her face quite straight and a little pink. "Four," she said. "In three and a half minutes. That's better than his average. I think he was trying."

"Was he?"

"Yes," said Evelyn. She sat down. She picked up her pencil and looked at the menu card and didn't write anything. "He was trying very hard."

* * *

At half past six Hermione found Harry and Ron under the last trees of the orchard and sat down on the grass between them without being asked.

They'd gone down there to get away from the band. Ron had taken a plate of the Paris cake, which was taller than Hagrid, as promised, and tasted of almonds and was mostly air. Harry had taken nothing. They were sitting with their backs against the trunk of the last apple tree before the hedge, in the long gold light, watching the twins' dragons circle the marquee.

Hermione was quiet for a while.

She had her small beaded bag in her lap. She'd carried it all day, through the vows and the lunch and the dancing, and she hadn't put it down once. Harry had noticed. He'd noticed too what lay beneath her all day, under the pleasure and the dress and the dancing with Ron. It had been there since she arrived at nine, very quiet, very steady, held down hard.

"I did it this morning," said Hermione.

Ron put his plate down on the grass.

"Did what?"

"My parents." She was watching the dragons. "I've been planning it since Easter. I told you I was planning something. I didn't tell you what." She turned the bag over in her hands. "They're Monica and Wendell Wilkins now. They've always wanted to go to Australia. They've got tickets for Thursday. They don't have a daughter."

The orchard went quiet round them.

"It's quite a hard charm," said Hermione. "To do properly. I practised on the neighbours' cat in June. It forgot it had kittens for a week, and then it remembered, and it was very cross with me." She stopped. "My mother made me a cup of tea afterwards. This morning. After I'd done it. She was very polite. She asked if I'd like sugar."

"Hermione," said Ron.

"I'd always had it without. Since I was nine. She knew that." Hermione's voice didn't change at all. "She asked if I'd like sugar, and I said yes please, two, and she put two in, and I drank it."

Ron put his arm round her.

He did it badly, all elbows, the way he did everything, and she let him, and leaned against his shoulder, and still didn't cry.

Harry read her.

He'd known what was under her since nine o'clock. He hadn't known what it was for. He knew now. It was grief, very steady and already very old, though only eleven hours old. The grief of someone who's done the right thing and knows it was right and will never, for the rest of her life, be sure.

He didn't say anything about it. There was nothing to say that she'd want said.

"They'll be safe," he said instead.

"Yes."

"Nobody will look for them. They don't know anything. There's nothing to find."

"That's the idea," said Hermione. "Yes."

Moody came along the hedge towards them as the light faded.

He came stumping along the boundary with his stick, his magical eye going round, and he didn't stop, but he slowed as he passed the apple tree, and the blue eye swung down to the three of them on the grass and stayed there whilst the rest of him walked on.

"Thirty yards of hedge," he said to nobody, "and one gate onto a lane. Whoever chose this field for a wedding wants shooting." The eye swivelled again, to the lane. "I'll be at the gate. If anybody wants me. Which they won't, because they'll be dancing."

He stumped on up the field towards the top gate.

"He's been like that all day," said Ron, into Hermione's hair. "Mum asked him to dance. He said he'd rather be hexed."

"He means it," said Harry.

"I know he means it. That's what's funny."

Hermione laughed. It was small and wet and it surprised her, and Harry read it go through her, quick and thin, like a little warmth through cold water, and was glad of it.

* * *

Lockhart was signing napkins.

He'd been doing it since lunch. Nobody had asked him to. He'd come in a long cloak of sugared apricot with gold at the cuffs and hem, the one Madam Malkin had made for him in the spring, and he'd sat down at the table nearest the band and taken out a peacock-feather quill, and whenever anyone went past he signed whatever was nearest and handed it to them with a dazzling smile.

"My dear girl," he said to a small cousin of Fleur's, who couldn't have been more than eight and spoke no English, "for your collection," and gave her a napkin with *Gilderoy Lockhart, Order of Merlin Third Class* across it in looping purple. She took it gravely and curtsied. He was delighted.

Harry sat down beside him at a quarter to eight.

The light was going long and gold over the field. The band were playing something with a fiddle in it. Somewhere out in the dusk beyond the marquee the twins were letting off small fireworks that turned into dragons and chased each other round the orchard, with children running after them shrieking, and Fleur's grandmother had woken in her deckchair and was watching them with great disapproval.

"Harry, my dear fellow," said Lockhart. "Sit, sit. Have a napkin."

"I've got one."

"Have another. They're very good napkins. I've signed them." He pushed one across. "You've been watching everybody all day. I've been watching you watch them. You have a way of standing at the edges of things." He smiled. "It's very effective. Nobody notices you do it. You must teach me."

"You'd hate it," said Harry. "You'd have to be quiet."

Lockhart considered this.

"Yes," he said. "I suppose I would." He signed another napkin, slowly, with a great flourish on the L. "Sirius tells me you're not going back to school."

"No."

"Good. I never went back either, you know. For my seventh year. Well, I did go back. But I didn't *attend*. There was a Lethifold in Berwick that needed seeing to, and I thought, Gilderoy, you can sit your NEWTs any time, but a Lethifold…" He stopped. He looked across the marquee at the gold floor, where Sirius was attempting a waltz with Madame Maxime, and Harry read him, and found, beneath the vanity and the warmth, something he hadn't expected.

Lockhart was sad.

It was very quiet. It was aimed at nothing in particular. It was the sadness of a man at a wedding who'd never been married and never would be, and had known it a long time, and had decided it was a very good joke.

"Weddings," said Lockhart. "One goes to so many. One is always the most interesting guest and never the groom." He gave Harry a brilliant smile. "I don't mind, of course. Imagine the poor woman. She'd never get near a mirror."

Harry laughed.

At eight o'clock exactly, a lynx came down through the roof of the marquee.

* * *

It was silver. It came through the canvas as though the canvas weren't there and landed in the middle of the gold dance floor between Sirius and Madame Maxime, and the band stopped. Not all at once. The fiddle went on for a bar after the others, high and thin, and then stopped too.

The lynx opened its mouth.

It spoke in Kingsley Shacklebolt's voice, the deep slow voice like the bottom of a cello, but it wasn't slow now.

"Scrimgeour is dead. The Ministry is theirs. They're coming. Now."

Then it was gone.

For one second, nobody in the marquee moved.

Harry felt the second. He felt everyone in the marquee stop at once, mid-feeling, the way a room full of clocks would stop if someone laid a hand on all of them together. Every kind of pleased, held still in the air, not yet anything else.

Then it came.

Terror. All of it, at once, in all of them. It went through the marquee from the dance floor outwards like a ring spreading from a stone dropped in water, and it hit Harry where he sat at Lockhart's table, and for three seconds he couldn't see.

He'd felt crowds before. He'd felt the Great Hall at the Sorting, a hundred thousand people at the World Cup, the stands at the end of a maze. He'd never felt a hundred people go from joy to terror in one second. He'd been standing in it all day with nothing turned down, and it had been warm, and now it wasn't, and he couldn't turn it down fast enough. It was in his eyes and his mouth. It was every person in the marquee thinking of every other person they loved, all at the same moment, all aimed outwards and all the same.

A hand closed on his arm.

"Potter," said Evelyn's voice.

He rested on it.

The noise came down. Not all the way. Enough. He could see again. He was on his feet, and so was Lockhart, and so was everyone, and they were all moving, and some were Disapparating where they stood with sharp cracks like snapping sticks. The marquee was full of cracks. Fleur's grandmother was being carried out of her deckchair by two cousins. The twins stood in the doorway with their wands out and no fireworks at all.

"They've come up the lane," said Evelyn. "I heard them. By the gate."

Harry reached.

He found them at once. They weren't hard to find. They were at the edge of the wards, all round, on three sides of the field. About thirty. They were pleased, mostly, in the cold steady way he'd felt in a churchyard and on a lawn below a tower, and some were eager, and one or two were frightened of what they were about to do and doing it anyway. They were pressing on the wards from every side, and the wards were giving.

Somebody had already laid something over the field. He felt it as the cracks stopped. A dead flat weight settling over the marquee and the orchard and the yard like a lid going on a pan.

"They've jinxed it," said Lockhart. He had his wand out. He was quite calm, and smiling, and Harry read him and found him delighted. "Anti-Disapparition. Over the whole field. Clever. Very clever. Nobody else is getting out by Apparating, I'm afraid. Not from inside." He swept his cloak back over his shoulder. "We'll have to get them out to the edge, past the hedge. Or through the fire in the kitchen."

The wards went.

Harry felt them go, the way you feel a window break in another room, and then the Death Eaters were in the field.

* * *

He ran out of the marquee into the orchard.

It was dusk. The apple trees stood in rows with their shadows long across the grass, the twins' firework dragons still circling above them, small and bright and foolish, and the guests were running. They were running in every direction. Some towards the house, some towards the hedge at the bottom of the orchard, some just running, and the Death Eaters were coming over the top of the field from the lane in a long dark line, and the first curses were already flying.

Harry stopped under the first apple tree.

He didn't think about it. He'd thought about it for two years, in a classroom on the fourth floor, on a cliff in Cornwall, in a mine under the sea. He'd lain on a clifftop at night beside a man in a gold-embroidered cloak who'd told him, *not one perfect lie, my dear fellow. A hundred bad ones. Fast.*

He didn't make one perfect Harry.

He made fifty bad ones.

He threw them out across the orchard as fast as he could think them, and he didn't finish any of them. Some had no faces. Some had no feet. Some were only a running shape in dress robes between two trees, there and gone, and some were a voice shouting *this way* from where nobody stood, and some were the sound of somebody tripping over a wheelbarrow that wasn't there. He didn't hold any of them. He threw them and let them go and threw more, the way you fling handfuls of gravel, and the orchard filled with running people, and most of them weren't people at all.

The Death Eaters didn't know which ones to chase.

He felt them not know. He felt the cold steady pleasure in them turn into something quicker and more confused. A curse went into an apple tree where a Harry had been. Another went into the grass. Somebody shouted *there, he's there* at a shape with no face, and three of them went after it, down the orchard, away from the house, away from the real guests, who were running the other way.

"*Oh*, very good," said Lockhart beside him, wand raised. "Very, very good. A little more noise, I think, by the gate. Let me…"

He flicked his wand, and a sound burst from the far end of the orchard like a whole family of hippogriffs stampeding through a henhouse, and four Death Eaters turned and ran towards it, and Lockhart laughed out loud.

Harry kept throwing.

His nose had begun to bleed. He didn't stop. He felt the fifty go out across the orchard and come apart, and he threw fifty more, and the real people went through them, past them, under the apple trees and down to the gap in the hedge at the bottom of the field, where the jinx ended and you could Disapparate. He heard the cracks start again down there, one after another, and every crack was somebody out.

A small girl stood alone under the third tree from the hedge.

She was in a gold bridesmaid's dress. She stood very still with her hands at her sides, not crying, and Harry read her and found the same quiet he'd once found in a boy by some railings in Little Whinging, the quiet of an animal that has decided not to be noticed.

It was Gabrielle Delacour.

He went for her. He went through his own illusions, through the running shapes and the voices and the hippogriffs, and picked her up. She weighed nothing. She put her arms round his neck at once, very tight, the way she had in a side room off the Great Hall two summers ago, and said something into his collar in French. He didn't understand it and said "Yes" anyway, and turned towards the hedge.

From under the third apple tree he could see the whole of the yard.

* * *

The Burrow stood at the top of the yard with every window lit.

The kitchen door was open. The Weasleys were going in through it. He could see them. Mrs Weasley, pushing Ginny ahead of her. Mr Weasley with Fleur's father. Charlie with somebody's great-aunt over his shoulder. The twins, backing in with their wands up. They were going through the kitchen to the fire. The fire was a way out. The fire didn't care about the jinx on the field.

And in the kitchen doorway, holding it, was Sirius.

He was still in the coat. He had his back to the door and his wand up, and Death Eaters were coming across the yard at him from the chicken run and the shed, four of them, five, and he was holding them.

He was laughing.

Harry could feel it from across the garden. Even through the noise, through his own fifty illusions coming apart and the terror of every guest still in the orchard and Gabrielle's arms round his neck, he could feel his godfather laughing in the kitchen doorway of the Burrow with the light behind him. It wasn't the laugh of a man who didn't know he could die. It was the laugh of a man who'd spent twelve years in a cell and one in a cave and one in a house he hated, and was now at last in a doorway with his family behind him and a fight in front of him, and had found it was exactly where he wanted to be.

He was very good.

Harry had never seen him fight. Not properly. He saw it now, from under an apple tree in the half-dark. Sirius barely moved. He didn't need to. He stood in the doorway and his wand went from one to the next, quick and loose and almost lazy, and a Death Eater went over backwards into the water butt, and another went sideways into the chicken run, and a curse came at him and he wasn't where it went, and he laughed again, louder, and shouted something Harry couldn't hear.

Behind him, Mr Weasley went through the kitchen into the fire and was gone.

Then Mrs Weasley.

Harry turned towards the hedge with Gabrielle in his arms and ran.

He didn't see it. He'd think about that a great deal later. He didn't see it because he'd turned to run, and he was carrying someone, and you don't stop when you're carrying someone. He felt it instead.

He felt the laughter in the doorway stop.

It didn't fade. It didn't go quiet the way a person goes quiet when they're tired, or hurt, or frightened. It stopped. It was there, loud, the loudest thing in the yard, perfectly happy, and then there was nothing where it had been. Not silence. Not Evelyn's silence. The other thing. The thing he'd felt in a churchyard, and on a stretcher on a lawn, and on the floor of a chamber under the Ministry with pink hair spread on the stone.

The place where a person had been.

Harry didn't stop running.

He ran down the orchard with Gabrielle Delacour's arms round his neck and his nose bleeding into his collar, through the last of his own illusions, to the gap in the hedge. Fleur was there in her white dress with her mother, screaming her sister's name, and Harry put Gabrielle into her arms. Fleur took her and held her and Disapparated with a crack, and they were gone.

He turned round.

The kitchen doorway was empty. The light was still on behind it.

* * *

Moody was in the lane.

Harry felt him there as he turned. The searchlight, sweeping round and round, suspicious of everything, the hedges and the gate and the sky. Moody was at the field gate at the top of the lane, alone, with his stick and his wand, holding the gate the way Sirius had held the door. Harry could feel the searchlight sweep across the Death Eaters still pouring in from the lane, and the plain, stubborn, grudging decency beneath it, getting between them and the field.

Then the searchlight went out.

It went out the way a lamp goes out when somebody knocks it over. Harry didn't see how. He was two hundred yards away at the bottom of the orchard in the dark, and he felt it go, and after it there was nothing at the gate at all.

Something white came down out of the dark over the orchard.

Hedwig. She'd followed him from Grimmauld Place that morning, because she always followed him, and he'd let her, and she'd sat in the apple trees all day. Now she came down towards him through the dusk, white and quick and sure, and a green light crossed the sky above the orchard, and she wasn't there any more.

* * *

"*Potter.*"

Evelyn had his hand.

She'd come out of the dark from somewhere. There was blood on the sleeve of her green dress that wasn't hers, and her hair had come down, and her face was exactly as it always was. She had his hand in her left hand, very hard. In her right she had Ron's.

Ron had Hermione's.

Ron's face was grey. He was looking back up the orchard towards the house. Hermione was looking at Harry. She had her beaded bag over her shoulder, the small one she'd carried all day, and she was crying without making any noise at all.

"Your family's out," Evelyn told Ron. "All of them. I saw them go through the fire. All of them, Weasley. I counted." She didn't look away from Harry. "Hold on. All of you. Hold on and don't let go. I've got somewhere."

"Where?" said Hermione.

"Somewhere nobody knows. Not even him." She meant Harry. "Hold on."

Harry looked at her.

He didn't ask. He didn't read her, because he couldn't. He looked at Evelyn Selwyn at the foot of an orchard in Devon, in the dark, with somebody's blood on her sleeve and her hand round his like a vice, and he didn't think about the kitchen door, and he held on.

The orchard went out like a candle.

* * *

They landed in an alley in the dark.

It was a narrow back alley between two high brick walls, with bins along one side and a puddle in the middle that hadn't dried, though it was August. A long way off a car went by with its radio on. There was a smell of chip fat and wet brick. It was raining very lightly, the kind of rain you don't notice until it's in your hair.

Ron let go of everyone and was sick against the wall.

No one spoke. Hermione stood with her hands over her mouth. Evelyn let go of Harry's hand quite slowly, as though she had to remember how, and went to a door in the high brick wall on the left. It was a fire door, painted a dark red gone brown, with a padlock and chain, and she took a key from the pocket of her green dress. A Muggle key, on a ring with a plastic tag.

The padlock opened.

The chain came off. Evelyn put her shoulder to the door and it went in with a long low scrape, and behind it was a darkness that smelt of dust and old carpet and something very faintly sweet, like sugar spilt a long time ago.

"In," said Evelyn.

They went in.

She shut the door behind them, put the chain across on the inside, in the dark, by touch, and then lit her wand.

They were standing at the back of a cinema.

It was very large. Harry could see that much in the wandlight. It fell away from where they stood in long curving rows of seats, red plush gone grey with dust, hundreds of them, sloping down towards a great flat blankness at the far end that was a screen. Overhead the ceiling was gilded and painted, and most of the paint had flaked away, and what was left was the faces of women with stars in their hair, looking down out of the dark. There were boxes along the sides with gold rails and torn curtains. There was an orchestra pit full of folded chairs. There was a smell of dust, and mice, and the ghost of sugar.

"What is this?" said Ron. His voice was hoarse. "Where are we?"

"Leeds," said Evelyn. "It's called the Majestic. It's been shut since nineteen eighty-five."

"Whose is it?"

"Mine," said Evelyn. "In a manner of speaking." She looked down the long dark slope of seats towards the screen. "I'll explain in the morning. Sit down. All of you. Anywhere."

They sat.

They sat in the back row of the Majestic, in the dust, in their wedding clothes. Ron at one end with his head in his hands. Hermione beside him, holding his arm. Evelyn at the other end with her wand lit and laid across her knees and her face turned towards the blank screen. And Harry between Hermione and Evelyn, his nose still bleeding a little into the collar of his dress robes, his hands on his knees.

He read them.

He didn't decide to. He did it the way he breathed. He reached out in the dark and found Ron and Hermione beside him, and they were full. Ron was terrified for his family, even though Evelyn had counted them, and beneath the terror he was grieving, and the grief was aimed at the kitchen doorway of his own house and at a man in a mustard-and-plum coat who'd been the last thing standing between his mother and the yard. Hermione was grieving too. She was grieving for Sirius and for Moody and for the wedding, and beneath that, very far down and very quiet, for something else, something she'd done before she came out this morning, that Harry didn't understand and didn't try to.

They were both crying.

Evelyn was silent. She was always silent. She sat at the end of the row with her wand across her knees and was nothing at all.

At ten to ten Ron's pocket went warm.

He took out the coin. It was one of Hermione's from two years ago, the fake Galleons. The numbers round the rim had turned into letters, small and glowing in the dark. Ron held it out under Evelyn's wandlight, and they all read it.

*ALL AT MURIEL'S. ALL OUT. WHERE IS SIRIUS. G.*

Ron looked at it for a long time. Then he closed his hand round it.

Nobody answered it.

Harry sat in the back row of a dead cinema in Leeds with the rain on the roof and three people beside him, two crying and one silent, and he read every single thing in the building, the mice in the walls and the pigeons under the eaves and the grief beside him rising and falling like breathing.

He didn't cry.

## Chapter 69: The Majestic

Evelyn explained in the morning, as she'd said she would, at eight o'clock in the projection room, over a pot of tea made on a camping stove she'd bought in Leeds in the summer of 1995 and never used until today.

"I found it in July nineteen ninety-five," she said. "On the eighteenth. I came up on the train to look at a bookshop on Call Lane that had a first edition of *Busman's Honeymoon* in its catalogue, and it had been sold before I got there, and I walked back to the station the long way because I was annoyed, and I came past the front."

Ron was sitting on an upturned crate with a mug in both hands. He hadn't slept. None of them had, except Hermione, for an hour at about five, with her head on Ron's shoulder in the back row. Ron's eyes were red and his face was grey and he was looking at Evelyn as though she were a long way off.

"The front of what?"

"Of this. The Majestic. It has a very fine front. Nineteen twenty-two. There are elephants on it." She poured a second cup. "It was boarded up. There was a notice from the council in the window. The owners had gone into liquidation in nineteen eighty-five and it had stood empty for ten years, and nobody wanted it, because it's very large and very old and the roof leaks. I stood and looked at it for eleven minutes."

"Why?" asked Hermione.

Evelyn looked at her.

Harry couldn't read her. He never could. But he'd watched her answer questions for six years, and he watched her decide whether to answer this one, and decide she would, because it was morning and they were here and there was no longer any reason not to.

"Because I'd just been told my grandfather was alive," she said. "That summer. And who he was. And I thought that if my family were the kind of family that had that in it, then I ought to have somewhere to go that wasn't my family. Somewhere nobody knew about. Not my father. Not my brother. Not anyone." She put the teapot down. "It's called a contingency. My grandmother taught me the word when I was seven. She had several."

Ron stared at her.

"You bought a *cinema*," he said. "When you were *sixteen*. In case your family turned out to be evil."

"I didn't buy it. I rent it. From the council. Through a solicitor in Wakefield called Mr Ackroyd, who thinks I'm a Miss Gwendolyn Cuthbert of Ludlow who wants to turn it into an arts centre when she comes into her money." Evelyn drank some tea. "I sold a first edition of *Strong Poison* my grandmother left me. That pays the rates. Mr Ackroyd sends me a letter every quarter to an address in Ludlow, a bookshop, and the woman who runs it keeps them for me and doesn't ask. I've been paying it for two years and two weeks."

"And the wards," said Harry.

It was the first thing he'd said since the back row.

Evelyn looked at him over her cup.

"Elias Varga taught me," she said. "By letter. In the summer of nineteen ninety-six, after you'd met my grandfather. I asked him for the strongest ones a single person could set and keep. He sent me nine pages and a diagram, and a postscript saying he hoped I'd never need them." She put her cup down. "I came up in August that year, and again at Christmas, and set them. Muggle-repelling, on the doors and the front. Anti-Apparition, except in the alley, and only for my blood or anyone holding my hand. A watching charm on the roof. And one of my grandfather's, which I won't explain, because I don't entirely understand it."

The projection room was quiet.

"Nobody knows it's here," said Evelyn. "Except the four of us. And Mr Ackroyd, who thinks it's an arts centre. And the woman in the bookshop, who thinks I'm having an affair with a solicitor."

Ron put his mug down on the floor.

He looked round the projection room. It was a narrow room high at the back of the auditorium, with two enormous old projectors standing in it like iron animals asleep, reels of film in flat tin cans stacked against one wall, and a row of small square windows looking down into the dark. There was a camp bed in the corner, folded, still in its plastic. There was a box of tins. There was a shelf with eleven paperbacks on it, all with green spines.

"That," said Ron slowly, "is the most mental thing I've ever heard."

"Thank you."

"I didn't say it was good."

"No," said Evelyn. "But you meant it."

Ron opened his mouth and shut it again. Then he picked up his mug, looked into it, and said in a much smaller voice, "It's quite good, actually."

* * *

They lived in the Majestic for eleven weeks.

They lived in it the way you live in a ship, mostly in the parts that weren't meant for living in. They slept upstairs, on Evelyn's camp bed and three more Hermione bought on the second day from a shop on Briggate, paying in Muggle money from a roll of notes she kept in the beaded bag. The bag held everything. It held clothes and books and tins and a tent they hadn't needed, and a kettle, and the entire portrait of Phineas Nigellus Black, which Hermione had taken off the wall at Grimmauld Place in July without asking anyone because she thought it might be useful, and which spent most of August face down under a camp bed, complaining.

They cooked on the camping stove.

That was the first argument, and the longest. Ron couldn't cook. Harry could, after a fashion, the way he'd cooked for the Dursleys, which meant breakfast for four people who didn't like him, and he didn't want to. Hermione could follow a recipe exactly and produce something that tasted of nothing. Evelyn ate the same thing every morning, a slice of toast with Marmite cut into two triangles, and the same thing every evening, a tin of tomato soup, and said she didn't see the problem.

"The *problem*," said Ron on the fourth night, holding up a saucepan of something grey, "is that I'm *starving*. I've been starving for four days. My mum feeds people. That's what she *does*. She'd look at this and she'd cry."

He stopped.

The room went still. Ron set the saucepan down quite carefully on the camping stove and went down the projection-room stairs into the dark of the auditorium, and they heard him walk all the way down the slope to the front row and sit, and he didn't come back for an hour.

Harry read him from the projection room.

He didn't mean to. He read everyone now, all the time, from everywhere in the building. Ron was homesick. It was huge and simple and aimed at a kitchen in Devon with a nine-handed clock on the wall, and beneath it, very near the top, he was frightened all the time that one of the nine hands had moved somewhere he didn't want it to be. He couldn't go home. Home was watched. Muriel's was watched. His family were in hiding at an aunt's who hated all of them, and he was in a dead cinema in Leeds eating grey stew.

On the fifth night Harry went to Kirkgate Market at four in the afternoon and bought sausages and potatoes and onions and a pound of butter, and came back and cooked them on the camping stove in the projection room, the way he'd cooked bacon at Privet Drive when he was eight, and didn't burn any of it.

Ron ate four sausages without looking up.

Then he looked up at Harry across the stove, and Harry didn't read him, and Ron said with his mouth full, "Where'd you learn that?"

"My aunt's."

"Did she teach you?"

"No," said Harry. "I just watched."

* * *

The newsagent on the corner of the next street opened at six.

Harry went every morning. He bought a *Yorkshire Post* and, from the third week, a copy of the *Daily Prophet* that came folded inside it by arrangement with a hag who ran a stall in the market and had a cousin, and who didn't ask questions in return for Harry not asking about the cousin. The newsagent was a short bald man called Mr Akhtar who kept a cricket bat behind the counter, and he looked at Harry every morning over his glasses with mild interest.

"You at the college?" he said on the first Monday.

"Sorry?"

"The college. The university. You've got a student look about you."

Harry smiled at him. It was the smile he used on shop assistants and train guards and Madam Pince. He'd been using it since he was six.

"Something like that," he said.

"What are you studying?"

"People, mostly."

Mr Akhtar laughed and gave him his change.

He asked every morning after that. *You at the college? How's the studying?* And Harry smiled and said something like that, and took his papers, and walked back round the corner to the fire door with the chain on it, and read the *Prophet* up in the box whilst the others slept.

It was very bad.

He read it the way Evelyn had taught him years ago, for the shape of the sentences and for what was left out. The Minister had resigned for reasons of health. He hadn't died. Nobody in the *Prophet* had died. Pius Thicknesse was Minister for Magic and spoke of continuity and calm. There was to be a census of all witches and wizards, for their own protection. There was to be a Commission.

*The Muggle-born Registration Commission*, said the *Prophet* on the eleventh of August, on page two, *will be chaired by Mr Corvin Selwyn of Ludlow, a distinguished member of the Wizengamot for twenty-one years, who has long argued for a realistic approach to the question of magical heritage. Mr Selwyn's son, Mr Lucan Selwyn, has been appointed Senior Undersecretary to the Minister.*

There was a photograph.

Corvin Selwyn stood on the steps of the Ministry beside the new Minister, very still and very grey and very lean, hands folded in front of him, not smiling. He didn't need to. Beside him, half a step behind, his son was smiling with all his white teeth.

Harry looked at it for a long time.

Then he took it up to the top of the stairs, where Evelyn sat on the end of her camp bed winding her watch at seven o'clock, as she had every morning since she was eleven, and held it out without a word.

She finished winding the watch first. She put it back in her pocket. Then she took the paper, read the paragraph, looked at the photograph, and handed it back.

"*Realistic*," she said. "He'll have chosen that word himself."

That was all she said about it.

* * *

On the twenty-first of August the coin in Ron's pocket went warm at breakfast.

*SIRIUS BURIED THURS GODRIC'S HOLLOW BESIDE J & L. WATCHED. DON'T COME. BUCKBEAK WITH HAGRID. R.L.*

Ron read it aloud before he understood what it was. Then he stopped, the coin in his hand, and looked at Harry.

Harry was eating a triangle of Evelyn's toast. She'd started making four triangles in the second week without anyone asking. He finished it. He drank some tea.

"All right," he said.

He didn't go.

He didn't ask to go. He didn't argue about it. He'd known since the back row on the first night that there'd be a funeral and he couldn't go to it, because every Death Eater in Britain would be at the edges of it, watching, waiting for exactly one person to come. He'd known it and put it somewhere. He didn't take it out now.

On Thursday he trained for fourteen hours.

He read them all that day. He couldn't help it. Ron was grieving in the front row, quietly, with his radio in his lap, turned off. Hermione was grieving in the projection room over a book she wasn't reading, her hand flat on the page. Evelyn was in the foyer, sitting on the stairs to the circle with *The Nine Tailors* open on her knee, and she was silent. She'd been silent all day. She'd been silent for six years.

He read the grief of two people he'd known well for a year and one he'd known for six, and it rose and fell in the building like breathing, and none of it was his.

He didn't cry.

He went down to the front of the auditorium, to the screen, and worked.

* * *

Evelyn kept a notebook.

She'd kept notebooks since she was nine. This was the fifteenth. It was a cheap red one from the newsagent on the corner, because she'd left the fourteenth at Grimmauld Place, in the room on the second floor with the ugly wardrobe, next to a hippogriff who was now with Hagrid.

She didn't think about the fourteenth.

She wrote in the fifteenth every night at eleven, upstairs, by wandlight, after the others were asleep or pretending. She wrote the date. She wrote what had happened that day, in the order it had happened, the way her grandmother had taught her to write things, so they could be checked. And from the second week of August she began to write two numbers at the foot of every page.

The first was the number of hours Potter had spent in front of the screen.

The second was the number of hours he'd slept.

She didn't decide to do it. She noticed on the ninth of August at a quarter to midnight that she'd been listening to him down there for nine hours without stopping and hadn't heard him come up to bed, and she wrote *9* without thinking, and then looked at it. After that, she counted.

*Friday 15 August. Screen: 10. Sleep: 5.*

*Wednesday 20 August. Screen: 11. Sleep: 4.*

*Thursday 21 August. Screen: 14. Sleep: 2. (Funeral.)*

*Sunday 31 August. Screen: 11. Sleep: 4.*

*Monday 1 September. Screen: 12. Sleep: 4. (Term began. Snape is headmaster.)*

She showed the notebook to nobody. She didn't mention the numbers. She wrote them every night at eleven, underlined the second, closed the notebook, and put it under her pillow with the watch.

She didn't mind, particularly, that he trained.

He had to. She understood that perfectly well. They were four people in a cinema, and there was a regime in London with her father at a long desk in it, and Potter was the only one of the four who could do anything the regime couldn't do better. She'd watched him in the orchard at the Burrow throw fifty bad Potters across the grass with blood coming out of his nose, and she'd counted the cracks at the bottom of the hedge. Sixty-one. She didn't know how many of those people would have been dead without the fifty bad Potters. She thought most of them.

So she didn't mind that he trained.

She minded the second number.

It was a strange thing to notice. She'd never minded what Potter did with his sleep before. In six years she'd never known how much he slept, or thought about it. It wasn't her business. She wrote it down every night anyway, and underlined it, and lay awake for some time afterwards on her camp bed in the projection room, listening for him to come up the stairs.

Most nights he came up at about four.

She heard him every time. She didn't let him know. She lay with her face to the wall and her hand on the watch under her pillow and listened to him lie down on the camp bed by the projectors, and to his breathing slow, and she didn't go to sleep herself until it had.

That wasn't in the notebook.

* * *

The screen was forty-one feet across and twenty high, and it had been white once.

It was grey now, the grey of a sheet left out in the rain, with a long brown stain down the left-hand side where the roof had leaked one winter in the eighties, and a small rip near the bottom right corner. On the second morning Harry had walked up to it, put his hand flat on it, felt the cold canvas give under his palm, turned round, and looked up the long dark slope of the auditorium at eleven hundred empty seats.

He began with a candle.

One candle, in the middle of the screen, about the size of a real one. He made it the way he'd made his first coin in Slytherin's study four years ago, by pushing the idea of it out of his own head into the place where the eye meets the world. Except that there was nobody here to push it into. There was only the screen, and the dark, and the seats, and himself.

So he pushed it into himself.

He made a candle he could see, on a screen in an empty cinema, with nobody else watching, and he held it, and it burned. It was the first illusion he'd ever made for an audience of one, and the one was the person making it. It was very strange. It was like talking to yourself in a mirror and having the mirror answer.

He held it for an hour.

Then he made a second. Then a row. Then a room with the row of candles in it, and a table, and a window, and rain on the window. Then a street.

By the end of August he could fill the screen.

By the middle of September he didn't need the screen.

He'd stand in the orchestra pit with his back to the folded chairs and make the whole auditorium be somewhere else. Not for anybody else. For himself. He made it Diagon Alley on a Saturday morning, the cobbles wet and the shops open and two hundred people walking up and down buying things, each one a little different, each with a different face and a different walk and a different feeling coming off them, because a crowd that didn't feel anything was a painting, and a painting wouldn't fool anybody. He made it the Great Hall at the Sorting. He made it a beach in Cornwall at low tide. He made it Privet Drive at four in the afternoon on a Tuesday, with Aunt Petunia's net curtains, and stood in the middle of the road and looked at number four for a long time, and then let it go.

He didn't make Grimmauld Place.

He didn't make the Burrow.

He trained eleven hours a day, and his nose bled most days, and he learned to stop it with a charm Hermione found in the beaded bag, and learned to work through it when the charm didn't hold. He learned how long he could hold a hundred people. He learned how long he could hold a thousand. He learned that a thousand was easy if they didn't have to do anything and very hard if they did, and that the hardest thing in the world was one person walking across a room in a way that was quite ordinary and not quite the same as last time.

He learned Tonks had been right. The face was the least of it.

He didn't think about Tonks very much. He thought about her when he was making faces, and then he stopped.

* * *

Ron came down to watch in the third week of September.

He sat in the middle of the eleventh row with his feet on the seat in front and a bag of chips from the shop on the corner, and he watched Harry work for an hour without saying anything, which for Ron was a long time. Harry was making a railway station. It was King's Cross at eleven on a September morning, with the platforms and the trains and the pigeons, and he was trying to get the pigeons right, because the pigeons kept moving the same way, and real pigeons didn't.

"Can you do anything?" asked Ron.

"Not anything."

"Can you do Quidditch?"

Harry looked round at him.

Ron's face was quite serious. He had a chip halfway to his mouth. Harry read him, because he couldn't not, and found under the homesickness and the fear, which were always there now, a small hopeful thing, very young, the size of the boy Ron had been at eleven.

"Who's playing?" said Harry.

"The Cannons."

"Against?"

"Anyone. Puddlemere. Doesn't matter. The final. Of the League." Ron ate the chip. "They've never won it. Not since eighteen ninety-two. They come bottom nearly every year. I've supported them since I was four." He chewed. "Just once. I'd like to see them win it. Just once. Even if it's not real."

Harry turned back to the screen.

He let King's Cross go. He stood in the orchestra pit with his back to Ron and his hands at his sides and his eyes shut, and he built it.

He built a stadium. He'd only been in one once, in a box with Evelyn's father, and he built that one, the great oval of it with the stands rising into the sky in tiers of gold and the pitch below, green as a billiard table, and the hoops at either end. He filled the stands with a hundred thousand people in Chudley orange, a whole sea of it, waving and roaring. He put Puddlemere United in their navy and gold at one end. He put the Cannons at the other, in orange, with black cannonballs on their chests, and gave them faces, and gave them names Ron would know from the posters on his bedroom wall, which Harry had read off him that morning without meaning to.

Then he let them play.

He let them play for an hour and a half. He didn't let the Cannons win easily. He let Puddlemere go eighty points up in the first half and heard Ron groan behind him, and then he let the Cannons come back, slowly, goal by goal, the Keeper making saves no Keeper could make, the Chasers threading the Quaffle through gaps that weren't there, the crowd growing wilder and wilder, the whole stadium shaking. And at a hundred and seventy to a hundred and sixty, with Puddlemere's Seeker diving, he let the Cannons' Seeker see the Snitch first, a glint of gold by the left-hand hoops, and go for it flat out across the whole width of the pitch, and catch it six inches from the ground, and roll, and come up holding it high.

The stadium went mad.

Harry let it. He let a hundred thousand people in orange go mad all at once in a dead cinema in Leeds, and over the roar he'd made he heard behind him a real noise, a single real one, which was Ron Weasley standing on his seat in the eleventh row and shouting.

He let it go.

The stadium went out. The screen was grey again, with its stain and its small rip. The auditorium was dark and dusty and empty, and Ron was standing on his seat in the eleventh row with his fists in the air and chip papers all round his feet and tears running down his face.

He didn't get down for a while.

When he did, he sat down slowly and looked at the screen, and then at Harry standing down in the pit with blood on his upper lip.

"That," said Ron, "was the best thing I've ever seen in my life."

"Good."

"And the most worrying."

Harry wiped his lip.

"Why worrying?"

"Because I *believed* it," said Ron. "The whole time. I knew it wasn't real. I knew you were doing it. I could see you standing there. And I believed it anyway." He looked at the screen. "If you can do that to me when I know, what can you do to somebody who doesn't?"

Harry had no answer.

He read Ron, and found him delighted and frightened at once, in almost exactly equal parts, and couldn't tell which was on top.

* * *

The regime reached them through the papers and the radio and the coins.

The paper was the *Prophet*, every morning, folded inside the *Yorkshire Post*. The radio was Ron's, an old wooden wireless he'd taken from Muriel's in the spring and had in his pocket at the wedding because he'd forgotten to take it out. In the third week they discovered it could pick up a programme that came on at irregular times on irregular frequencies and had to be found with a password that changed. It was run by Lee Jordan, whom Ron recognised in four words, and the twins, and sometimes Kingsley, and once, gloriously, for six minutes, Lockhart, who said he was alive and well and in disguise and couldn't say where, but that it was somewhere with a very good view.

The coins were Hermione's, from the defence group two years ago.

There were eleven still out there that Hermione knew of. Neville had one. Luna had one. Ginny had one, at Hogwarts, which she wasn't supposed to have. Millicent had one at home. Theo had one.

Theo's came at odd hours. The numbers round the rim turned into letters, and the letters were never words. They were squares on a chessboard. *E4. QB3. KN5.* Harry would sit with the coin in his hand and Theo's code in his head, the one they'd made up over a Christmas holiday in a dormitory, and it would take him forty minutes to turn six squares into one line.

The lines were bad.

*CREATURE REGISTER NEXT.* *GOBLINS REFUSING.* *HOGWARTS: CARROWS TEACHING. CRUCIO IN CLASS.* *YOUR FACE ON THE WALL IN THE ATRIUM.*

And on the second of October, after an hour of squares, *GRANGER ON THE LIST.*

Hermione read it over Harry's shoulder.

She said nothing. She went quite white, then quite red, then sat down on the camp bed behind him, took out her wand, and looked at it for a while. Harry knew which list. It had been in the *Prophet* the day before, on page six, under a headline that said *COMMISSION THANKS COMPLIANT*. It was a list of Muggle-born witches and wizards who'd failed to present themselves to the Muggle-born Registration Commission for interview, and who were asked to do so at their earliest convenience, and who were in the meantime to be regarded as being in illegal possession of a wand.

There were forty-one names on it.

Hermione's was the eleventh.

"It's alphabetical," said Hermione after a while, quite steadily. "They've put Granger after Goldstein. Anthony Goldstein. He's a half-blood. They've got that wrong."

"They'll have done it on purpose," said Evelyn from her camp bed, without looking up from *The Nine Tailors*. "My father doesn't make mistakes like that. Somebody under him does, and he lets them, and then he can say it was somebody under him."

Hermione looked at her.

"He'll interview them himself," Evelyn went on. "He likes interviewing. He sits very still and lets them talk, and they always talk too much." She turned a page. "He did it to me at breakfast every morning for seventeen years."

After that, nobody spoke.

Harry read Hermione. She was frightened, as she'd been since the Burrow, and beneath the fear she was angry, and beneath the anger, at the very bottom, very quiet, she was thinking about a cup of tea with two sugars in it, in a kitchen in Hampstead, and two people who didn't know her.

He thought about it that night in front of the screen.

He thought about a man sitting very still at a long desk, letting frightened people talk.

He made Courtroom Ten on the screen, the way he'd seen it in a Pensieve, the tiers of benches rising into the dark and the chair with the chains in the middle, and stood and looked at it until three in the morning, and then let it go.

* * *

The doe came on the night of the fourteenth of October.

It was eleven o'clock. Harry was in the orchestra pit making rain. He'd been making rain for two hours, because rain was very difficult, every drop different and all of them falling, and he wasn't getting it right. Ron was asleep in the back row with the radio on his chest. Hermione was up in the box. Evelyn was sitting in the front row, as she sometimes did late at night now, without explanation, with a book she wasn't reading open on her knee.

The doe came through the wall.

It came through the left-hand wall of the auditorium by the side boxes with the gold rails, quite slowly, as though it had all the time in the world. It was silver. It was very bright in the dark. It walked down the side aisle between the seats and the wall, past the boxes, past the torn curtains, past the orchestra pit, and stopped in front of the screen, and turned its head, and looked at Harry.

Harry let the rain go.

He stood in the orchestra pit with his wand lowered and looked at it.

He knew what it was. A Patronus. He'd made enough of them himself to know what one looked like. But he'd never stood in front of someone else's and read it, and he didn't decide to now. He did it the way he did everything. He reached out to the silver thing standing before the screen.

A Patronus was made of feeling. He'd known that since he was thirteen, on the shore of the lake with a hundred and fifty Dementors coming over the water. You didn't make a Patronus out of a memory. You made it out of what the memory made you feel, made larger, and sent out. That was all it was. A feeling, sent.

He could read it.

He read it, standing below the screen of the Majestic with Evelyn Selwyn three yards away in the front row, her book shut on her knee.

It was love.

It was one love, and only one, and it was very old and very pure, and it had been kept for a very long time in a very small closed place where nothing else was allowed to touch it. It was so clear it was almost painful to read. It was aimed at a girl with red hair who'd been dead for sixteen years, and it hadn't changed in all that time. Not grown. Not faded. Not become anything else. It had been kept exactly as it was on the day it was made, like a flower pressed in a book.

Harry had read it once before.

He'd read it in a room in the dungeons two years ago, inside another man's head, in a memory of a playground and a boy in clothes too big for him watching a girl swing higher and higher, and let go, and fly. He'd read it, and been thrown out of the man's head and out of the room for it, and the man had never forgiven him.

He knew whose it was.

The doe opened its mouth.

It didn't speak in a voice he knew. It spoke in a voice with no colour in it at all, low and flat, a voice made not to be recognised. But the feeling beneath the voice didn't change. Harry would have known it anywhere.

"Do not go to the library on Saturday," said the doe. "Either of them. The Central or the Brotherton. There will be eight of them. They have been told a Muggle-born girl reads there on Saturdays. They do not know which girl. They will take any of them."

Then it stood and looked at him.

Harry didn't move.

He thought about Hermione in the projection room. Hermione had been to the Central Library on Calverley Street four Saturdays running, in a hat and a raincoat, to read old newspapers on microfilm, looking for any report of anything that might be a Death Eater in a Muggle town. She'd been planning to go this Saturday. She'd said so at supper.

He thought about a courtyard at the foot of a tower four months ago, and a man standing in it alone, thinking himself unseen, looking up at a parapet and unable to close.

He thought about a wand held out across a tower roof without a word.

"Thank you," Harry said to the doe.

He didn't know whether it could hear him. He didn't know whether the man at the other end was listening. He said it anyway, quite quietly, in the dark.

The doe looked at him a moment longer. Then it turned and walked into the screen.

It didn't go through it. It went into it, the way a figure goes into a painting, and stood there, silver on the grey, forty feet across, with the brown stain behind it and the small rip at its feet, and for a few seconds it was the only bright thing in the whole dark cinema.

Then it began to fade.

Behind Harry, in the front row, Evelyn made no sound at all.

He didn't turn round. He didn't need to read her to know what the nothing was. She'd seen a Patronus come through a wall from a man nobody trusted and tell Potter where not to go, and she'd seen Potter thank it, and she didn't trust anybody, and she hadn't said so.

He trusted it.

He stood in the orchestra pit and watched the doe go out on the screen like the last light going out of an evening, slowly, from the edges in, until there was only the grey, and the stain, and the rip, and he trusted it completely.
