## Chapter 70: The Commission

Theo's coin went warm on the first Sunday in November at twenty past three in the morning, and it took Harry fifty-five minutes to turn it into one line.

*THURS 13. CT TEN. 9AM. TWELVE. NOT COMING BACK.*

He sat on the edge of his camp bed in the projection room with the coin in one hand and a stub of pencil in the other and the squares written out on the back of a *Yorkshire Post*, and looked at the last three words for a long time.

Then he woke the others.

* * *

"Twelve people," said Hermione.

It was half past four. She was sitting up on her camp bed in one of Ron's jumpers with the sleeves pulled down over her hands, and she hadn't been asleep. Harry had known that. She hadn't been asleep at half past four for a month.

"Twelve Muggle-borns," said Harry. "Who didn't present themselves. They've been picked up. They're being heard on Thursday in Courtroom Ten at nine. By the Commission."

"And *not coming back* means…"

"It means Azkaban," said Evelyn. She was sitting on the end of her own bed with the watch in her hand. She'd wound it whilst Harry talked. It was ten to five. "Or worse. The Commission's hearings aren't trials. There's no defence. It's an interview. They ask you where you got your wand and who your grandparents were, and if you can't prove a wizard in the family, they find that you stole it." She put the watch away. "Theo means they've already decided. The hearing's there so it can be written down that there was one."

Ron was looking at Harry.

"You want to go," he said.

"Yes."

"Into the Ministry."

"Yes."

"The *Ministry*, Harry. Where your face is on the wall. Where they've got Dementors in the *lifts*." Ron's voice rose. "Where her *dad* is."

"Yes," said Evelyn. "I know where my father is."

The projection room went quiet.

Harry read them. Ron was terrified, and beneath the terror there was something hot and stubborn and Weasley that wanted to go anyway, because there were twelve people in a cell and that wasn't all right. Hermione was frightened in a quieter way, very steady, and beneath it, so close to the top it was nearly the same thing, she was thinking about her own name in the *Prophet*, eleventh of forty-one, and how easily she might be the thirteenth. And Evelyn was silent.

"I can get us in," said Harry. "I can get us in looking like anybody. I've been doing it on the screen for three months."

"On a *screen*."

"On a screen with nobody watching. I know." He looked at Ron. "That's why I need you. All of you. I can put a face on each of us, so anybody who looks sees somebody else. I can hold four for an hour. Maybe two." He looked at Evelyn. "But I can't see my own faces. Not properly. I can't tell when one's slipping. I'm inside them."

"I can," said Evelyn.

"You can't see them at all."

"No," she agreed. "I see you. All four of you. As you are. Which means that if anybody else is looking at you oddly, it's because the face has gone wrong, and I'll know before you do." She put her hands in her lap. "I'll be your mirror. It's the only thing I'm good for in there. I can't be anybody else. Your faces don't work on me, so I'll be the only person in the building who knows what you look like."

"Your face doesn't take either," said Harry. "On you. You know that. You've never been able to wear one."

"Then I'll go as myself."

"Your *father's* there."

"Yes," said Evelyn. "You said."

She looked at him. Harry couldn't read her. He never had been able to. He looked at her plain face in the wandlight at five in the morning in a dead cinema and couldn't see anything in it at all, and knew she'd decided before he woke her.

"I'll go as myself," she said again, "and you'll make *them* see somebody else. Not me. Them. Everyone who looks at me. You can do that. You did it at the Burrow fifty times. It's the same thing. You'll just have to hold it on everybody in the building instead of on me."

Harry didn't answer at once.

"That's harder," said Hermione slowly. "Isn't it? That's much harder. A face on a person is one thing. A face on every person who looks at a person…"

"Yes," said Harry.

"Can you do it?"

He thought about the Atrium. About two thousand people. About the screen, and a thousand people walking up and down Diagon Alley who didn't have to do anything, and how easy that was, and one person crossing a room in an ordinary way, and how hard.

"Yes," he said.

* * *

They went in on Thursday at a quarter past eight, through a tailor's shop in Great Scotland Yard.

The shop had been shut for twenty years. The window said so in gilt letters gone green. *Morrison & Daughter, Bespoke, Est. 1891.* Theo's next coin had told them about it. The old staff entrances had been changed in September, he said. Too many people knew them. Ministry staff now came in through the back of Morrison's, one at a time, by a fitting room with a long mirror, and you showed a brass token to the mirror and the mirror let you through.

They had no tokens.

Harry stood in the empty shop at a quarter past eight, with dust on the counter and a headless dummy in the window wearing a jacket from 1977, and looked at the mirror in the fitting room, and read it.

There was nothing in it. It was glass. But there was somebody watching it from the other side, a long way down, bored, at the end of a night shift, and the somebody was a person, and Harry could find a person anywhere.

He showed the person behind the mirror four brass tokens that weren't there.

The mirror let them through.

* * *

The Atrium had changed.

The fountain had gone. Harry had last seen it as rain, falling where a golden fountain had been, with Dumbledore sitting on its rim, very old. Somebody had cleared away the rim and put something else there.

It was a statue, black and very large, of a witch and a wizard seated side by side on two thrones, carved with great skill, their faces calm and beautiful, their hands on their knees. Harry looked at the thrones. They weren't thrones. They were people. Hundreds of carved naked people, men and women and children, piled on top of one another and twisted together, faces turned up and mouths open, and the witch and the wizard were sitting on them.

There were words cut into the base. *ORDER IS THE FIRST KINDNESS.*

Harry didn't look at it for long.

He was holding four faces. He'd built them on the screen over three days. Ron was a short, bald, middle-aged wizard with a moustache and a slight limp, called Reg in Harry's head, who worked in Magical Maintenance and hated his job. Hermione was a tall thin witch of about forty with grey hair in a bun and half-moon spectacles, very upright and very unhappy, a records clerk from the Commission. Harry himself was nobody. A young man in grey robes with a forgettable face, a junior clerk, the sort of person people look at and away from.

And Evelyn was Evelyn, walking beside him, and to every person in the Atrium who looked at her she was a pale young witch with straight fair hair and no chin, called Miss Hopwood, from the Commission's Records Office, carrying a file.

Harry held it.

It was the hardest thing he'd ever done. It was harder than the Horntail and harder than the graveyard, because it didn't stop. Two thousand people were crossing the Atrium at twenty past eight on a Thursday morning, and every one of them who turned their eyes towards a plain girl with brown hair had to see a fair one with no chin instead. They didn't know they were doing it, and they could turn at any moment, from anywhere, and he had to be there first. He couldn't hold it on the girl. He had to hold it on all of them.

He read the building to do it.

He'd never read a building before, not on purpose. He read it now because he had to, every person in it, so he'd know which of them were looking.

It was full of fear.

It was the first thing he felt and the last thing he'd remember. The Ministry of Magic was full of it, from the Atrium floor to the top of the lifts, like water in a tank. People were frightened walking in from the fireplaces. They were frightened queuing at the security desk. They were frightened in the lifts and the corridors above and the offices above those. It wasn't loud. Nobody in the Atrium was screaming. It was quiet and grey and everywhere, the fear of two thousand people who'd all decided at about the same time in August to keep their heads down and do their jobs and not look at the statue.

"Left," murmured Evelyn beside him. "The man by the post desk. He's looked at Weasley twice."

Harry found the man by the post desk.

The man was bored, and beneath the boredom, very small, he was puzzled, because Reg from Magical Maintenance had seemed for a moment to be taller than Reg was. Harry put Reg back to his proper height in the man's head, and made him a little shorter for good measure, and the man stopped being puzzled and went back to sorting memos.

"Thank you," said Harry, without moving his lips.

"Keep walking," said Evelyn.

* * *

There were two Dementors at the foot of the stairs to the courtrooms on the tenth level, and the cold rose up the stairs to meet them.

Harry felt the appetite before he felt the cold. He'd felt it in an alley in Little Whinging two years ago and on a lake shore before that, and it hadn't changed. Two great cold pulls at the bottom of the stairs, aimed at everything warm that came down them.

He couldn't put a face on them. They had no faces to put one on. There was nothing in them to fool. Nothing that looked, nothing that believed. There was only the wanting.

They went past them anyway.

Hermione's hand was shaking. Harry could feel it through the face he was holding on her, the thin grey upright clerk, and he held the face very firmly and didn't let it shake. Ron walked with his eyes on the floor. Evelyn walked as she always walked, quite straight, the file under her arm, and looked at the two tall black hooded shapes as they passed, and Harry saw her look, and saw that she was counting something.

The door of Courtroom Ten stood open.

* * *

He'd been in it before.

He'd been in it in a Pensieve, standing beside a young Dumbledore, watching a boy with straw-coloured hair scream that he was innocent. He'd been in it on a hot August morning two years ago, at fifteen, and walked out free. It hadn't changed. The same dark stone walls, the same dim torches, the same tiers of benches rising on every side into the dark. The same chair in the middle of the floor, with the chains on its arms.

The benches were nearly empty.

There were perhaps a dozen people in the lowest tier. Clerks with quills and long rolls of parchment. Two Ministry wizards in plum robes, very bored. And on the high platform at the front, behind a long desk, three people.

On the left sat a squat woman in pink, with a black velvet bow in her hair and a cat brooch at her neck. She was smiling. She had a cup of tea in front of her and a plate with two biscuits on it, and she held her quill as though it were something delicate.

Harry read her, and found exactly what he'd found in an office with kitten plates on the wall two years ago. A sweet, sincere, cosy enjoyment. She was enjoying this morning. She was going to enjoy all of it.

On the right sat a young wizard Harry didn't know, writing.

In the middle, very still, sat Corvin Selwyn.

Harry hadn't seen him since the World Cup. He'd seen his photograph in the *Prophet* in August, standing on the Ministry steps. He looked exactly as he had in it. Lean and grey and very upright, his long pale hands folded on the desk before him, quite motionless, his face composed and polite and attentive. He had no tea. He had no biscuits. He had a single sheet of parchment, and he wasn't looking at it.

He was looking at the woman in the chair.

She was about thirty. She had short dark hair and a Muggle cardigan buttoned up wrong, and the chains on the arms of the chair had closed round her wrists, and she was holding herself very still, the way you do when you think that if you move you'll cry.

Behind her, along the wall at the back of the floor, on a long bench, sat eleven more.

They were all ages. There was a boy who couldn't have been more than seventeen. There was an old man in a dressing gown who looked as though he'd been taken from his bed. There was a girl of about twenty with a baby's blanket over her shoulder and no baby. They sat in a row on the long bench, with a Dementor standing at either end of it, and they didn't look at one another.

Harry read them.

He did it all at once, because there was no way not to, and it was the worst thing he'd felt since a stone chamber under this same building, with a snake coiled on the steps. It was terror. Not loud terror. It was past loud. It was the quiet, flat, finished terror of twelve people who'd been in the cells under this floor for days with Dementors at the door, and who'd stopped expecting anything except what was going to happen.

"Mrs Pell," said Corvin Selwyn.

His voice was low and reasonable and quite pleasant, a voice like water running over a stone. Harry had heard it once before, at the World Cup, saying *the boy is a credit to his house*, and he'd thought then that it was the stillest voice he'd ever heard.

"Mrs Pell, you were asked a question."

"I'm sorry. I don't… I don't understand…"

"It's a very simple question, Mrs Pell. You have told us your wand is rowan, ten inches, with a core of dragon heartstring. You have told us it was sold to you at the age of eleven by Mr Ollivander. Mr Ollivander is, unfortunately, not available to confirm this." He paused, quite gently. "So I'm asking you. Which witch or wizard did you take it from?"

"I didn't take it from anybody. It *chose* me. In the shop. I was eleven. My mother was…"

"Your mother," said Corvin Selwyn, "was a dinner lady. At a primary school in Swindon. I have it here." He didn't look down at the parchment. "Your father drove a bus. Neither of them was a witch or a wizard. Neither of their parents was a witch or a wizard. You have no magical relations that we have been able to find. And yet you have a wand." He let a little silence pass. "You can see the difficulty, Mrs Pell."

Harry read him.

He reached for him across the floor of Courtroom Ten, carefully, beneath all the faces he was holding, and found what he'd found in a box at the World Cup three years ago.

Attention.

That was all. That was almost all of it. Corvin Selwyn was paying very close attention to the woman in the chair, the way a man watches a board in a game where he already knows how it ends and wants to see how long the other side takes to notice. There was no hatred in it. There was no pleasure either, not like the pink woman. It was a careful, cold, patient interest. And beneath it, a long way down, a very small satisfaction aimed at nothing in this room. The satisfaction of a man who's backed the winning side, and been right, and is enjoying having been right.

He didn't think about the woman in the chair at all, except as the woman in the chair.

"Now," said the pink woman sweetly, picking up a biscuit. "Shall we move on, Mr Chairman? There are eleven more this morning, and I do so hate to keep the poor Dementors waiting."

* * *

Evelyn had counted the steps from the door of Courtroom Ten to the foot of the high desk on the way in. Thirty-one. She walked them now, with the file under her arm.

She hadn't been told to. That wasn't quite true. She'd told herself to, at five in the morning in the projection room, when Potter said *I can hold four for an hour, maybe two*, and she'd looked at his face and seen he didn't know whether it was one or two. She'd decided then that somebody would need to make the hearing slower. And the only person in the room who could make Corvin Selwyn slower was somebody who knew exactly how he liked things done.

She was the only person in the world who knew that.

Twenty steps. Twenty-one.

She could see her own hands holding the file. She could see her own grey sleeve. She knew nobody else in the room could. Every person who looked at her saw a fair-haired girl with no chin called Miss Hopwood, because Potter was standing at the back of the courtroom in a face that wasn't his, holding a face that wasn't hers on a dozen minds at once, and three more besides, and she didn't know how long he could hold it, and neither did he.

She didn't look round at him.

Twenty-six. Twenty-seven.

Her father looked up.

He looked at her the way he looked at anyone who approached his desk without being sent for. Politely. Attentively. Hands folded, quite still. His grey eyes went over her face and stopped there, and stayed there a second, and nothing happened in them at all.

He didn't know her.

Evelyn noted it.

She'd wondered, walking down the stairs past the Dementors, whether she'd feel anything when he looked at her and didn't know her. She'd thought she might. It seemed the sort of thing a person ought to feel something about. She noted now, standing at the foot of the high desk in Courtroom Ten with the file under her arm and her father's eyes going over a face that wasn't hers, that she didn't feel anything.

That wasn't true either. She noted that it wasn't true, and put it away, and didn't look at it.

"Yes?" said her father.

"Miss Hopwood, sir. Records."

"Yes, Miss Hopwood."

"I beg your pardon, Mr Chairman." Her voice was quite steady. It was her own voice. Potter couldn't change voices. She'd said so in the projection room, and he'd said he'd make them hear somebody else's, and she'd said that was too many things at once and she'd simply speak quietly, and he'd said all right. She spoke quietly. "There's a procedural difficulty."

The pink woman put down her biscuit.

"A *difficulty*, dear?"

Evelyn didn't look at her. She looked at her father.

"Under the Commission's terms of reference, sir. Paragraph eleven, sub-paragraph two. As laid before the Wizengamot on the fourth of September." She opened the file. There was nothing in it but a copy of the *Yorkshire Post*. Nobody could see that. She didn't need them to. She'd read the terms of reference in the *Prophet* in September, three times, in the projection room at eleven at night, because she read everything, and she'd kept them in her head the way she kept everything. "A person under interview is entitled to have the full particulars of the finding sought read to them before any question is put. In writing. And a copy given." She looked up. "Mrs Pell hasn't had the particulars read. Neither have the others. I've checked the record. There's no entry."

There was a short silence in Courtroom Ten.

The young wizard on the right had stopped writing. The two bored men in plum had stopped being bored. The pink woman's smile had stayed exactly where it was, which Evelyn noted was a sign that it wasn't really a smile.

Her father looked at her.

She'd been looked at by him every morning across the breakfast table at Selwyn Hall for seventeen years. She knew every look he had. She knew the look for Lucan, which was approval. She knew the look for her mother, which was patience. She knew the look for herself, the one he gave a piece on the far side of the board that hadn't moved for a long time and might never move, and so wasn't worth thinking about.

This wasn't any of those.

He was giving her the look he gave a junior official who'd found a mistake he hadn't found himself. She'd seen it once through a study door, aimed at a Ministry lawyer. It was cool and careful and interested and very slightly amused, and it had respect in it.

"Paragraph eleven," said her father.

"Sub-paragraph two, sir."

He didn't look at his parchment. He looked at her for three seconds more. She counted them.

"Quite right," said Corvin Selwyn. "Thank you, Miss Hopwood. That was an oversight." He turned his head very slightly towards the young wizard on the right. "We'll have the particulars read. All twelve. In full. And copies made." He turned back. "Will you see to the copies, Miss Hopwood?"

"Yes, sir."

"Thank you."

She closed the file.

She'd corrected him once before, at nine years old, at breakfast, about the date of the Goblin Rebellion of 1612. He'd gone on eating his toast and hadn't answered, and the next morning he'd sent Lucan to tell her that a lady didn't contradict her father at table. She hadn't corrected him again for nine years.

He'd conceded. Politely. To a stranger.

He'd never once in her life conceded anything to her.

She turned and walked back across the floor of Courtroom Ten, thirty-one steps, past the chair with Mrs Pell in it, past the bench with the eleven others, past the Dementors, towards the clerks' table by the door, where the confiscated wands were kept in a long wooden box with a brass catch.

She noted that her hands were perfectly steady.

She noted, a little further on, that she'd very much like to sit down.

* * *

It took eleven minutes to read the particulars.

The young wizard on the right read them in a flat voice for Mrs Pell, then began again for the boy who was seventeen. Hermione, at the clerks' table in the face of the tall grey records clerk, made copies with a Duplicating Charm, her hand shaking. Ron, in the face of Reg from Magical Maintenance, stood by the door with a mop he'd found in a cupboard on the tenth floor, mopping the same yard of stone floor over and over.

Evelyn stood beside the long wooden box with the brass catch.

Harry stood at the back of the courtroom and held everything.

He held Reg. He held the grey clerk. He held his own nobody. He held Miss Hopwood with no chin on every mind in the room, every time anyone looked. Eleven minutes. He could feel the faces beginning to thin at the edges, like ice on a puddle when the sun gets to it. His nose had begun to bleed inside the face, where nobody could see, and he could taste it.

He read the room.

He'd been reading it since he came in. Now he read it the way he'd learned on the screen, as a place, with every person in it a point of light. The pink woman, enjoying herself. The young wizard, bored and frightened under the boredom. The two plum-robed men. The clerks. Corvin Selwyn, attentive, waiting. The twelve on the bench and in the chair, flat and grey and finished.

And the two Dementors at either end of the bench. Two pits in the room, where the light went in and didn't come out.

He looked at Evelyn.

She was standing by the wand box with her hand on the brass catch. She looked back at him across the courtroom. She was the only person in the room who could see his real face. She saw it now, and he saw her see it, and she gave him one small nod.

"Now," said Harry.

He let the faces go.

All of them, at once. He felt them go out of every mind in the room like lamps in a house when the power fails, and for one second every person in Courtroom Ten looked up and saw a short bald wizard become Ron Weasley, and a thin grey clerk become Hermione Granger, whose name was eleventh on a list, and a forgettable young man in grey become Harry Potter, whose face was on the wall in the Atrium.

And a fair girl with no chin become a plain girl with brown hair, standing by the wand box, looking at the high desk.

Harry wasn't looking at the high desk. He didn't see what Corvin Selwyn's face did. He'd ask Evelyn weeks later, and she'd say *nothing*, and he wouldn't be able to tell whether that was true.

"*Expecto Patronum*," said three voices together.

The stag burst from Harry's wand at a gallop. An otter came out of Hermione's, and a small fierce terrier out of Ron's, and they went across the floor of Courtroom Ten at the Dementors like three lights thrown at once, and the cold broke.

Everything happened together after that.

The pink woman was screaming. Not in fear. In outrage, high and furious, *seize them, seize them*, on her feet behind the desk with her teacup knocked over. The two men in plum had their wands half out, and Ron hit one of them hard in the stomach with the mop before Harry had time to Stun the other. The young wizard on the right dived under the desk. The Dementors were going up, backwards, up the tiers of benches into the dark at the top of the room, away from the three silver animals, and the cold went with them.

Evelyn had the wand box open. She was taking wands out of it one after another, quite fast, and throwing them across the floor towards the bench, where they rolled and clattered on the stone.

Hermione was at the chair. "*Relashio*," she said, and the chains came off Mrs Pell's wrists with a clang.

Corvin Selwyn hadn't moved.

Harry saw that in the middle of everything, the way you see a single still thing in a running crowd. Evelyn's father sat behind the high desk with his hands folded on it, exactly as he'd sat all morning. He had his wand out. It lay on the desk in front of him, under his hands. He hadn't lifted it. He was watching. He was watching the plain girl with brown hair by the wand box throwing wands across the floor of his courtroom, and Harry reached for him, quickly, under everything, and found nothing in him but attention. Close, cold, careful attention.

"*Go*," Harry shouted at the bench. "Pick up a wand. Any wand. *Go*."

Nobody on the bench moved.

* * *

They couldn't.

Harry read all twelve in the same instant, and understood. They'd been in the cells under this floor for days. They'd had Dementors at the door every night. Everything warm in them had been drawn up and out, the way the sun draws water up out of the ground, and what was left was flat and grey and couldn't stand. The doors were open. The wands were on the floor at their feet. The Dementors had gone up into the dark. And twelve people sat on a long bench and in a chair with their hands in their laps and looked at the wands on the floor and didn't pick them up, because there was nothing left in them that could believe it would make any difference.

There were footsteps on the stairs outside. Many of them. Coming down.

"*Harry*," said Hermione.

He had perhaps a minute. Perhaps less.

He reached into them.

He didn't ask. There was no time to ask, and if there had been they couldn't have answered, and he didn't think about asking. He reached into the girl with the baby's blanket over her shoulder, and the old man in the dressing gown, and the boy who was seventeen, and Mrs Pell still in the chair with the chains hanging off it, and all the others, one after another, so fast it was nearly all at once, and in every one of them, a very long way down beneath the grey, he found something.

He'd done this once before, in a mine under the sea, to two children.

It was very small. A coin at the bottom of a deep pocket. In the boy it was a fight in a school playground in Rotherham, and getting up after being knocked down. In the girl with the blanket it was a baby, and a door, and someone on the other side of the door she'd have gone through a wall for. In the old man it was a hill in Wales in nineteen forty-four and a field gun and his friend Davey. In Mrs Pell it was her own mother, a dinner lady in Swindon, standing up at a parents' evening and telling a headmaster exactly what she thought of him.

In every one of them there was some small piece of courage the Dementors hadn't been able to reach, because it was too far down, or too small, or too old.

Harry took hold of it in all twelve of them at once and made it larger.

He made it very much larger.

He pushed it up through the grey and the flatness and the finished terror like fire going up through a dry wood, and it rose and filled them, and every one of the twelve people on the bench and in the chair stood up at the same moment, as though somebody had pulled a string.

The boy from Rotherham picked up a wand first. Then the old man. Then all of them.

"Out," said Harry. "Up the stairs. Behind me. Don't stop."

They didn't stop.

He'd never seen people move like that. They went out of Courtroom Ten in a body, past the Stunned men in plum, past the desk where the pink woman was still screaming and Corvin Selwyn was still sitting, and up the stone stairs. The people coming down met them halfway, four Ministry wizards with a Dementor behind them, and the twelve went into them like a wave hitting a sea wall, and over them, with wands they hadn't held for a week going off in every direction. A Dementor came down the stairs, and the old man in the dressing gown turned and shouted something at it in Welsh, and a thin silver shape that might have been a dog came out of his wand, and the Dementor stopped.

Harry ran behind them.

He was holding nothing now. No faces. He didn't need faces. He threw an empty corridor into the minds of everyone they passed on the ninth level, and a lift that had already gone into the minds of everyone waiting for one. In the Atrium, as they spilled out of the lifts in a pack, he threw two thousand people's eyes at the far end of the hall, at a fireplace that had apparently begun spouting green fire to the ceiling, and they all turned to look at it. The twelve and the four went the other way, past the black statue with the people underneath it, through the staff door, into the fitting room of Morrison & Daughter, Bespoke, and out.

* * *

Great Scotland Yard was grey and cold and full of traffic, and it was twenty to ten in the morning.

Bill Weasley was standing on the pavement outside the tailor's with an armful of old boots.

"Twelve?" he said.

"Twelve," said Hermione.

"Right." Bill was already handing them out. "Portkeys. Each one goes to a different house. Don't swap. Hold it with both hands, it goes in ten seconds. Go on." He looked at the twelve, standing on the pavement in Whitehall with their wands in their hands and their faces lit up, the old man in the dressing gown still breathing hard, the boy from Rotherham laughing, Mrs Pell holding the hand of the girl with the baby's blanket. He looked at them for a long moment. "Merlin," he said. "You lot look ready to go back in."

The boots went one after another with small pops. Then Bill was gone with them.

The four of them stood outside a closed tailor's shop in Great Scotland Yard with buses going past.

Hermione turned to Harry.

"Thank you," she said.

"For what?"

"For that. All of it. For getting us in. And for…" She stopped. She'd seen it. Harry knew she had. She'd been standing at the chair with the chains in her hand when twelve people who couldn't stand up stood up all at once, as though somebody had pulled a string. "Harry. What did you do to them?"

He told her.

He didn't lie. He didn't need to. He told her in plain words, standing on the pavement, what he'd found at the bottom of each of them and what he'd done with it. A playground in Rotherham. A baby. A field gun. A parents' evening in Swindon. Made larger. Without asking.

Hermione listened to all of it.

When he'd finished she said nothing. She looked at him for a long time. Then she looked at the traffic. Then she went quite quiet, in a way Harry could read very clearly. The quiet wasn't anger, and it wasn't fear either. It was a careful, deliberate stillness that Hermione laid over something when she didn't yet know what she thought about it and didn't want to find out in front of anyone.

"It was worth it," said Ron.

He said it loudly, as though somebody had argued. Nobody had.

"Twelve people," said Ron. "They'd have gone to Azkaban. Or worse. You heard Selwyn. You heard her. You got them out. All of them. It was worth it. Whatever it was."

"Yes," said Hermione quietly. "I know."

Evelyn said nothing at all.

She was standing a little apart from them by the window of Morrison & Daughter with the headless dummy in it, her hands in the pockets of her grey cardigan. She wasn't looking at Harry. She was looking at the reflection in the shop window, at the four of them standing in a row on the pavement as they really were.

Harry couldn't read her.

He'd learned over six years that when Evelyn Selwyn said nothing, it was the loudest thing she ever said.

He didn't ask her what it meant.

* * *

He went down to the screen that night at eleven and didn't make anything on it.

He sat in the front row of the Majestic, where Evelyn sometimes sat, with his feet on the rail of the orchestra pit and the grey canvas in front of him, and thought about Courtroom Ten.

He thought about twelve people on a bench, flat and grey and finished.

He thought about reaching into them one after another, finding the coin at the bottom of each, and taking hold of it.

He thought about the moment they stood up. All twelve at once, as though somebody had pulled a string. And the somebody had been him.

He sat in the dark for a long time.

He'd expected to feel sick. He'd felt sick after Quirrell, for years. He'd felt sick after a boy in the bathroom going quiet in the red water. He'd felt nothing much after the children in the mine, and had noticed that, and put it away. He sat in the front row of a dead cinema and looked for the sickness now, carefully, the way you feel for a coin in a pocket, and it wasn't there.

What was there was something else.

He found it and looked at it, quite calmly, for some time.

It had been the best moment of his day. Not the faces, not the Atrium, not getting out. The moment twelve people stood up because he'd decided they would. He'd felt it go through them, all of them, his own hand on twelve strings at once, and it had worked perfectly, and it had been the cleanest, simplest, most certain thing he'd ever done.

He'd liked it.

## Chapter 71: The Hour of His Death

Gellert Grindelwald had known for some time which hour it would be.

He'd known since the spring. Not the date. Dates were something other people needed. He'd known the hour the way you know the shape of a room you've lived in for half a century, by walking into its corners in the dark. It was a morning. It was winter. There was new snow on the slot of the window, a finger's depth, blue in the first light. There was a sound on the stairs.

He'd seen it a great many times.

He'd seen it, in fact, more often than anything else in his life, because for some months now, whenever he closed his eyes, it was very often this hour that came. He'd be lying on the narrow bed in the cell at the top of the tower, with the lamp on the floor and the one chair empty, and he'd close his eyes to rest them, and open them, and it would be that morning, with the snow on the sill and the sound on the stairs. Then he'd close them again and open them, and it would be an afternoon in the rue Mouffetard in 1938, with a woman in a green dress laughing at him across a table covered in the small brass parts of a watch. Then it would be the hill above Godric's Hollow. Then the morning again.

It was the cost. He'd paid it for sixty years, and he'd stopped minding. A man who's seen every hour there is, in every way it could go, doesn't keep his grip on which one he's standing in. He'd let go of it slowly, the way a man lets go of a rope he's too tired to hold, and now he lived, as he'd told the boy the summer before last, in eleven different afternoons and some mornings, and wasn't always sure which.

He was sure today.

He opened his eyes a little after eight, and the snow was on the sill, a finger's depth, blue. And it stayed there. He closed his eyes and opened them, and it was still there. It didn't become Paris, or the hill, or Prague. It stayed.

So.

He lay on his back on the narrow bed and looked at the ceiling of his cell, which he'd looked at for fifty-two years and knew better than any face, and thought, with great clarity and a certain irritation, that it was a pity it was today, because he'd been halfway through a letter.

* * *

The letter was on the floor beside the lamp.

He couldn't see it from the bed. He didn't need to. He'd written it the night before by lamplight, in his small careful hand, which had become a great deal less careful in the past year and which he resented. It was to the girl. It was about a book.

She'd sent him a book in November. It had come with Elias, as everything came with Elias, in a parcel tied with string, with a note in her small square hand that said only *You will dislike the ending. E.* It was a detective novel. It was about a man in hospital with a broken leg, lying on his back looking at a ceiling, who had nothing to do and so decided to solve a murder four hundred years old that everyone else had already solved, wrongly.

He'd read it four times.

He'd disliked the ending very much, and had written to tell her so, at length, and had got as far as the third page, explaining why the author was quite wrong about the nature of historical guilt, which he was in a position to know about, when he'd grown tired, and put the pen down, and slept, and woken to snow.

He thought about the letter now.

He thought she wouldn't get it. That was quite certain. In most of the hours he'd seen, nobody ever read it. In one or two, a man with a wand read it, standing in this cell, and that was much worse, and was why he'd been thinking about this hour every night since the spring.

He thought about the girl.

She'd sat in the chair, the one chair, by the slot window, for three winters and four springs. She'd sat very upright and told him the news as though reading out the minutes of a meeting, and corrected his dates, and refused to be impressed by him, and shown him nothing in her face at all, and he'd loved her for it more than he'd loved anyone since a woman in a green dress in Paris.

In most of the hours he'd seen, the man with the wand learned she existed.

Not all. Most.

He'd counted them, as well as a man can count things that aren't yet, and aren't quite. There were a great many ways this morning could go, and he'd walked into the corners of all of them, and in nine out of every ten the man came up the stairs and went into his head and found her there. Her face in the chair. Her voice. Her name. And then the man would know what she was, and whose, and the man would go to England, and that was the end of all the ways that mattered.

In the tenth way, he didn't.

He'd found the tenth way in April. It was very narrow. It ran between the other nine like a path along a cliff. It needed a number of things to happen in exactly the right order, and some of them were things only he could do, and one of them was a thing he didn't want to do at all.

He'd been practising it in the dark every night since.

Somebody was coming up the stairs.

* * *

It was Elias.

He knew it was Elias long before Elias reached the top. He'd heard Elias climb those stairs a great many times in fifty years, and Elias always climbed them the same way, the silver-tipped stick going down on every third step, and a rest on the hundred and ninetieth, where a narrow window with a ledge looked out over the valley. Elias was old. He was nearly ninety. He climbed slowly.

He wasn't climbing slowly now.

He was running. Grindelwald lay on the narrow bed and listened to him run, which he'd never heard him do, up three hundred and eighty-one steps in the dark a little after eight in the morning, the stick going down on every step instead of every third, his breath coming in great tearing gasps, and he didn't stop at the hundred and ninetieth.

He was coming to warn him.

Grindelwald knew that. He'd seen it. Elias had come through the gate below and seen something on the mountain road, or felt something in the wards he'd set and kept for half a century, and had known at once what it was. He hadn't gone back down the mountain to the inn in the valley, where he'd have been safe. He'd come up.

He'd always been a coward. He'd said so himself, many times. He'd said it to the girl, in a letter, the first time he carried one.

Two hundred and forty. Two hundred and sixty.

Grindelwald found he was sitting up.

He didn't remember deciding to. He was sitting on the edge of the narrow bed with his bare feet on the cold stone floor and his hands on his knees, listening to an old man run up a tower, and he thought very clearly, *go back down, Elias. You fool. Go back down.*

He didn't say it. Elias couldn't have heard him.

Three hundred and ten.

There was a second sound on the stairs, further down. It wasn't running. It was walking, quite unhurried, quite light, the way a man walks up a staircase in a house he's just bought, looking at the pictures.

Three hundred and fifty.

Elias reached the landing below the cell, the small square landing where the stair turned for the last time, and stopped, and Grindelwald heard him turn round. He heard the stick come down on the stone. He heard Elias's voice, very hoarse and very out of breath, say three words in Hungarian, which Grindelwald had taught him in 1943 in a cellar in Budapest, and which meant, more or less, *not this way.*

A flash of green light came under the door.

It lit the bottom inch of the cell. It lit the lamp on the floor and the letter beside it and the legs of the one chair and Grindelwald's own bare feet on the stone, quite brightly, for less than a second. Then it was gone.

Something fell on the landing. The stick fell after it, rolled, went down two steps, and stopped.

Grindelwald sat on the edge of the bed with his hands on his knees.

He was sorry.

He noticed it with some interest, as something he hadn't entirely expected. He'd seen this a great many times, and he'd been sorry every time, distantly, the way one is sorry about something in a book. He found he was sorry now in a way that wasn't distant at all. Elias Varga had been twenty-two when he came to him, a thin serious boy from Debrecen who wanted to make the world better and believed every word he said. He'd spent fifty years ashamed of having believed it, and carrying letters up these stairs anyway, and keeping a child's shoe in his pocket keyed to a girl's blood, and being afraid. He'd run up three hundred and eighty-one steps at nearly ninety to say *not this way* to a man who'd already decided which way.

*You fool*, thought Grindelwald. *You good, brave fool.*

That was as far as it went. He wasn't a sentimental man. He'd killed a great many people himself in his time, for reasons he'd believed in and some he hadn't, and he didn't have the right to be more than sorry about one more.

He was sorry, and he let himself be, for the space of four of the footsteps still coming up.

Then he put it away, because there was work to do.

* * *

The door of the cell opened.

It didn't need unlocking. It hadn't been locked since 1994, when he'd told Elias he was too old to go anywhere and the key was a waste of iron. It swung inwards slowly, and the light from the landing came in, the grey light of a winter dawn through the window on the stair, and a tall man stepped over something on the landing that Grindelwald didn't look at, and came into the cell, and stood just inside the door.

Grindelwald looked at him.

He'd seen this face a great many times. It was still a shock. Not because it was terrible, though it was. Because it was so young.

The man in the doorway was seventy years old. Grindelwald knew that. He'd been born on the last day of 1926, in a London workhouse, to a woman who'd died before nightfall. He was seventy, and his face was white and smooth and quite without lines, and his eyes were red, and he had no nose to speak of, only two slits. He stood in the doorway of the cell with the straight easy back of a man of thirty and looked about him with interest, at the stone walls and the slot window and the one chair and the lamp on the floor and the old man sitting on the side of the narrow bed with his bare feet on the stone.

He was whole.

Grindelwald could see that. He didn't need to look for it. He'd walked a Path for seventy years, and he knew what a Walker looked like when he'd reached the top of one, and this man had. There was a stillness to him. A completeness. He stood in the doorway the way a mountain stands in a landscape, as though the rest of the room had been arranged round him.

He was holding a wand.

It was long and pale and very old, with a pattern along it like knots in wood, like beads on a string.

Grindelwald looked at the wand for some time, and the wand, he'd have sworn, looked back.

"Good morning," said Lord Voldemort.

His voice was high and cold and quite courteous. It was the voice of a man who'd been well brought up by somebody who didn't love him.

"Good morning," said Grindelwald. "You'll forgive me if I don't get up. There's only the one chair, and I'm told I'm a hundred and fourteen."

"You don't look it."

"I look a hundred and forty. You're being polite. It doesn't suit you." He nodded at the chair by the slot window. "Sit, if you like. It's the best seat in the house. I'm told the view is very fine. I've been looking at it for half a century and I'm no longer a reliable judge."

Voldemort didn't sit.

He stood just inside the door and looked down at the old man on the bed, and Grindelwald looked up at him, and for a moment neither of them spoke.

Two monsters, thought Grindelwald. Of different vintages. One young and whole and very pleased with itself. One old and tired and sitting on a bed in its nightshirt with cold feet.

He found it extremely funny.

"You know who I am," said Voldemort.

"I know who you are. I've known who you are since you were sixteen. I saw you once, you know, in a corridor, in an hour that never happened, standing in front of a door with a knife, carving two words on it." He smiled. "You spelled them correctly. I remember being surprised."

Something moved in the white face. It was very small. It was gone at once.

"You know why I've come."

"I know why you think you've come." Grindelwald leaned back a little on his hands, on the thin blanket. "You've come about the wand."

* * *

Voldemort turned the wand over in his long white fingers.

He did it slowly and with great care, the way a man handles something he's paid a great deal for and is beginning to suspect he's been sold. Grindelwald watched him. He'd seen this too, in a good many of the hours. It was always the same. The fingers turning the wand, and the small line, so faint it was barely there, between the places where the eyebrows ought to have been.

"It is the most powerful wand ever made," said Voldemort.

"Yes."

"It was made by Death. Or so the children's story says."

"The children's story says a great many things. Most of them are true. That's what makes it so tiresome." Grindelwald shifted on the bed. His feet were very cold. "It was made by a man. A clever, unpleasant man called Antioch, who wanted to win every duel he ever fought and was prepared to pay for it. Death is what he paid. The story leaves out the arithmetic."

"I took it from Dumbledore."

"I know. I saw you."

"You saw…"

"From here. In June. On a lawn." Grindelwald looked at the slot window, at the snow. "I saw the water go up, and the birds. I saw him lie down. I saw you take it out of his hand. I've seen it eleven times since. It doesn't get better." He looked back. "You took it out of a dead man's hand, Tom. You bent down on the grass and took it out of his fingers, very gently, the way you'd take a toy from a sleeping child. I thought that was rather beautifully done. I've been meaning to tell somebody."

The red eyes didn't change.

"It does not answer me," said Voldemort.

"No?"

"It answers. It does everything I ask. It is stronger than any wand I have held. But it answers…" He stopped. He didn't like the word he'd been about to use. Grindelwald could see him not like it. "Late."

"Ah."

"A fraction. A hair. Nobody else would notice. I notice." Voldemort lifted the wand a little and sighted along it, the way a man sights along a gun barrel. "Why?"

Grindelwald began to laugh.

He hadn't meant to. He'd seen this hour so many times he'd thought there was nothing left in it that could surprise him, and he'd been quite right, there wasn't, but it was funny every time, and it was funnier now that he was actually in it, sitting on a bed in his nightshirt with cold feet, with the most frightening man in the world standing in his doorway asking why his toy didn't work properly.

He laughed until he had to put his hand flat on the blanket to keep himself upright.

He laughed until it hurt, and then a little longer, because at a hundred and fourteen one doesn't get many chances.

Voldemort waited.

He didn't move. He didn't raise the wand. He stood quite still in the doorway with the grey dawn behind him and waited, with great patience, for an old man to stop laughing, and Grindelwald, wiping his eyes with the back of a hand like a bundle of sticks, thought the patience was the most frightening thing about him. Tom had never been patient at sixteen. He'd been patient since the summer before last. Since the arch.

"Forgive me," said Grindelwald. "Forgive me. It's only that Albus asked me exactly the same thing. In nineteen forty-five. In a field outside Wrocław. He'd just taken it from me, and he stood over me with it, and it answered him a hair late, and he looked at it with exactly that face." He shook his head. "You'd have hated each other less if you'd ever compared notes."

"And what did you tell him?"

"Nothing. I was bleeding at the time." He put his hands back on his knees. "Wands are like cats, Tom. They decide who they live with. You can feed them and stroke them and give them the best cushion in the house, and one day they get up and go and sit on somebody else. That wand has a master. It's had one since a spring night on a tower. It isn't you. It wasn't Albus by the end either, I think, though I couldn't see who it was, and I've looked."

"Who?"

"I don't know."

It was true. He let Tom see that it was true. He'd looked many times, and it was a dark place in all the hours, a door he couldn't open.

"If I did know," said Grindelwald, "I wouldn't tell you. And I'd enjoy not telling you a great deal. So it's a pity, really. For both of us."

"Then I will look for myself," said Voldemort.

He raised the wand.

* * *

This was the narrow path.

Grindelwald had walked it four hundred times in the dark since April, and he walked it now, for the last time, with his eyes open.

The first thing was that the man must point the wand at him.

He did. The long pale wand came up and its tip came to rest a foot from Grindelwald's forehead, and Grindelwald looked at the knotted pattern along the wood, at the place halfway down where there was a small dark nick like a burn, which he'd put there himself in 1932 on a bridge in Prague.

The second thing was that he mustn't be afraid.

He wasn't. He'd been afraid of a great many things in his life. Of being nothing, as a boy. Of being stopped, as a young man. Of being alone for fifty-two years in a tower, of losing his grip on the hours, of dying before the girl came again. He wasn't afraid of the man in front of him. He'd seen him too often.

The third thing was the wand.

A Pinnacle is opened through a wand one has used for years. Every Walker knows that. Every Walker who's ever been taken prisoner knows what it means, and Gellert Grindelwald had known it for half a century, sitting in a tower without one, unable to open his own summit. He'd held the Elder Wand for forty-five years. He'd stolen it from a wandmaker's workshop in 1899 and carried it across Europe and done terrible things with it and some fine ones, and it had known his hand better than any wand had ever known any hand in the history of the world. It had been taken from him. It hadn't forgotten him.

It was a foot from his face.

"*Legilimens*," said Lord Voldemort.

And Grindelwald reached out, not with his hand, along the foot of air between them, and laid hold of the wand from the other end, the way you take an old friend's arm in a crowd, and opened Every Hour for the last time in his life.

* * *

He'd always described it, to the very few people he'd described it to, as standing in a room with a thousand doors, all open at once.

It was nothing like that. But it was the nearest he'd ever come, and the girl had nodded when he said it and written it down, so he supposed it would do.

He stood in the room.

He felt the man come into his head, cold and fast and sure, the way a knife goes into a loaf. He felt him begin to look. He felt him reach at once, without hesitation, for the thing he'd come for, which was the wand and the master of the wand, and then, because he was thorough, for anything else he could find.

And Grindelwald, standing in the room with a thousand doors, chose.

He showed him the hours.

Not the true ones. Not the chair by the slot window with a girl in a grey cardigan sitting in it very upright, saying *the Battle of Vinnitsa was in nineteen forty-two, not forty-three, Grandfather, I've checked.* Not a parcel tied with string and a note in a small square hand. Not a gold watch held in his palm whilst its fine second hand quivered and began, very slowly, to move.

He showed him the others.

There were a great many others. He'd been collecting them since April. He'd walked into every corner of every hour of his life he could reach and found the ones where there was nobody in the chair. They were all real, in their way. They were hours that might have been, in a world very slightly to the left of this one, where a woman in a green dress had left him in 1944 and taken nothing with her, no child, no daughter, nobody at all, and he'd sat in this tower for fifty-two years with nothing but the snow.

He showed Tom a thousand of them.

He showed him Elias coming up the stairs with a newspaper and reading it aloud and going down again. A thousand times. He showed him the chair, empty, with the light from the slot window falling across its seat in winter and in summer and in winter again. He showed him the lamp on the floor and the narrow bed and a man growing old on it, writing letters to nobody and burning them. He showed him every afternoon of fifty-two years in which no one came.

It was the loneliest thing he'd ever made.

It was very easy. He found he had a great deal of material.

And he felt Tom look at it, in the room with a thousand doors, and believe it. Almost.

Almost.

He felt the cold mind turn, quite slowly, the way a hound turns when it's lost a scent and isn't sure it has. He felt it begin to lift its head. Tom was a Legilimens of the first rank and a liar of the first rank, and he knew, because he'd told so many, that a lie with nothing true in it is a house with no foundation, and it stands only until somebody leans on it.

He was going to lean.

So Grindelwald gave him something true.

He'd known since April that he'd have to. It was the thing he didn't want to do. He'd hoped every night in the dark, walking the narrow path, that he'd find another way, and there hadn't been one. A lie as large as this needed something under it heavy enough to hold it down. Something the man would want so badly he'd stop looking at anything else.

Grindelwald opened one more door and let Tom see through it.

It was a hill. A graveyard on a hill, in a village in the west of England, a long time ago, on a summer evening. A young man of eighteen with yellow hair knelt before a very old headstone, tracing with one finger a mark cut into the stone. A line, inside a circle, inside a triangle. And beside him on the grass lay a book open at a page about three brothers, with a drawing in the margin in the young man's own hand. A wand. A cloak.

And a stone.

A small, black, uneven stone, the kind you might find on any beach. Set, in the drawing, in a ring.

In the room with a thousand doors, Grindelwald felt the cold mind stop.

He felt it stop looking at the hours. He felt it stop looking at the chair. He felt the whole of it turn all at once away from everything else in his head and fasten on the drawing, and then, with a slowness that was almost like a living thing, like a man waking, turn away from the drawing and look down.

At his own right hand.

At the long white finger, the middle one, and the ring on it. A cracked gold ring, very old, with a black stone in it, uneven, the kind you might find on any beach.

He'd worn it since April of last year. He'd cracked it at the foot of an arch and drawn a piece of himself out of it and put it back on his finger, because it was his grandfather's ring and his grandfather's grandfather's, and because he liked it. He'd looked at it a thousand times. He'd never once known what it was.

Grindelwald let go.

* * *

He was sitting on the edge of the narrow bed.

His feet were on the cold stone. His hands were on his knees. The wand was a foot from his face, and the man holding it stood in the doorway of the cell, quite still, the grey dawn behind him, looking down at his own right hand.

He didn't move for a long time.

Grindelwald watched him. He didn't try to read him. He'd never been able to read people the way the boy could. He'd only ever been able to see where they'd go. He watched Tom look at the ring, and saw with great clearness all the hours that went out from this one, and in none of them, not one, did the man in the doorway think about an empty chair again.

The lie would hold.

It would hold because it wasn't quite a lie. It would hold because it sat on top of the truest thing Grindelwald had ever told anyone, and the man would never look underneath it, because he'd be looking at his hand.

He was very tired.

The cost was coming. He could feel it. It came every time after Every Hour, and every time it was worse, and he knew precisely how much worse it would be this time, because he'd seen it. In a moment he wouldn't be able to tell this hour from any other. The snow on the sill would become Paris, and the hill, and Prague, and the field outside Wrocław, and then all of them at once, and he wouldn't know where he was.

He didn't mind.

He'd arranged it. He'd walked the narrow path to the end, and it had been very narrow, and he'd done it with his eyes open.

"Two," said Voldemort, very softly.

He was still looking at the ring.

"Two of three," said Grindelwald. "Yes. You'll want the third now. I never found it. That's true too. You can check, if you like. I looked for it for forty years." He smiled. "I imagine you'll be quicker."

Voldemort looked up.

He looked at the old man on the bed for a long moment, wand still raised, and Grindelwald saw quite clearly in the red eyes that there was nothing more he wanted from the room. Nothing. He'd come for one thing and been given another, much larger, and he was finished here.

"Thank you," said Lord Voldemort.

It was quite sincere.

"Don't mention it," said Gellert Grindelwald.

The snow on the sill had begun to change.

He saw it go. He saw it become a window in the rue Mouffetard with rain on it, and a woman in a green dress at a table covered in the small brass parts of a watch, laughing at him because he'd dropped the escapement wheel on the floor for the third time. He saw her bend down for it. He saw her put it in his palm.

*So you'll never be in only one,* he'd said. *World. Hour. One of anything. If you ever need another, wind it backwards.*

*And how will I get back?*

*I'll make sure,* he'd said. *I'll always make sure.*

He saw a gold watch, very small, with ivy leaves on the lid, in a girl's hand. A plain girl in a grey cardigan, sitting very upright in the one chair, holding it out to him on her open palm. He saw the fine hand quiver and begin to move.

He saw her look up at him over it.

*Grandfather,* she was saying, *you've got the date wrong again. It was the seventeenth.*

He opened his mouth to tell her he hadn't got it wrong, he'd never once got a date wrong in his life, he'd simply been testing her.

There was a green light.

* * *

Evelyn wound the watch at eleven minutes past seven on Wednesday the seventeenth of December, which was eleven minutes late.

She hadn't meant to be late. She'd been late on four mornings in the whole of her life, all of them in the hospital wing. She'd been awake until twenty past four, lying on her camp bed with her face to the wall and her hand under the pillow, listening for Potter to come up the projection-room stairs, and he hadn't, and she hadn't gone to sleep until he did. And then she'd slept through the time she always woke, ten to seven, and woken at nine minutes past with the grey light already in the small square windows over the auditorium, and the others asleep, and Potter on the camp bed by the projectors with his boots still on.

She took the watch out from under the pillow.

She sat up on the camp bed in her cardigan with her feet on the cold floor, held it in her left hand, took the crown between the finger and thumb of her right, and began to wind.

Forwards. Always forwards. Twelve turns. She'd done it every morning since she was eleven. She'd done it in the Slytherin dormitory and the hospital wing and Selwyn Hall and on the second floor of Grimmauld Place and in a carved wooden inn in a valley in Austria, and she'd done it every morning here, in a dead cinema in Leeds, at seven o'clock, before anybody else was up.

One turn. Two.

She counted, as she always did. She didn't need to. She did it anyway.

Five. Six.

Seven.

The watch stopped.

It stopped under her fingers. She felt it stop. She'd felt it going for a very long time, ever since a cell in a tower in Austria three years ago, when an old man had touched the glass and the fine hand had quivered. It had gone ever since, quietly, under her fingers and in her pocket and under her pillow, the small steady tick she'd stopped hearing years ago because it was always there.

It wasn't there.

She looked at the face.

The hour hand was at seven. The minute hand was at eleven minutes past. The second hand, the ordinary one, stood quite still a little before the twelve. And the other hand, the very fine one most people never noticed, which didn't seem to move and which she'd seen move exactly once in her life, on the palm of an old man's hand, stood quite still where it had always stood.

She wound the crown again.

It turned. Nothing caught. It turned and turned under her fingers, loosely, the way it had for four months in her third year, before she knew who'd made it.

She stopped winding.

She sat on the edge of the camp bed with the watch in her hand at twelve minutes past seven and did nothing at all.

She knew.

She didn't know how. She didn't know anything about it. She didn't know the hour or the way or who. She didn't know there was a letter on a stone floor beside a lamp, three pages long, about the nature of historical guilt, or an old man in a black coat on a landing below it with his stick two steps further down. She didn't know any of it, and she wouldn't know any of it for some days, and some of it she'd never know.

She knew the watch had been reset by its maker, and that it had stopped.

That was all. It was enough.

She thought about the chair by the slot window.

She thought about the Battle of Vinnitsa, and the date he'd got wrong, which she was almost entirely sure he'd got wrong on purpose.

She thought about the book she'd sent him in November. *You will dislike the ending.*

She thought she'd never find out whether he had.

She didn't cry. She noted, quite distantly, that she didn't, and that it was strange, and that she'd cried for twenty-two minutes on the floor of a classroom in March after holding something still for four, and that this was very much larger, and she wasn't crying at all. She sat on the side of the camp bed holding the watch, and her hands were perfectly steady, and she was nothing.

Across the projection room, Potter was awake.

She didn't know how long he'd been awake. He was lying on the camp bed by the projectors with his boots on and his eyes open, looking at her. He had dark marks under his eyes like bruises. He'd slept for two hours and fifty minutes. She hadn't written it down yet.

He couldn't read her. He never had been able to.

He didn't try.

She saw him not try. She'd watched him for six years. She knew what his face did when he reached for somebody and found nothing, the small frown, the slight narrowing, as though listening for a sound in another room. It didn't do it. He lay on the camp bed and looked at her, and didn't reach, and waited.

"My grandfather is dead," said Evelyn.

Four words.

Potter got up. He crossed the projection room in his socks and boots, past the two old projectors standing like iron animals asleep, and sat on the camp bed beside her. Not close. A few inches. Enough that she could feel he was there.

He didn't speak.

He didn't ask how she knew. He didn't say he was sorry. He didn't put his arm round her, or take her hand, or do any of the things Hermione would have done, or Sirius, or Ron. He sat beside her on the edge of the camp bed with his hands on his knees, the way she was sitting, and looked at the same patch of floor she was looking at, and was there.

They sat like that until the light in the small square windows had gone from grey to white.

At some point she put the watch down.

She set it on the table between the two camp beds, the folding table where they ate, beside a jar of Marmite and a cold mug of tea and a copy of the *Yorkshire Post* folded open at the crossword, which Potter did every morning and never finished. She put it down very carefully, face up, with the ivy-leaf lid open.

Seven. Eleven minutes past. The fine hand where it had always been.

It didn't tick.
