## Chapter 72: Malfoy Manor

The wood was called Tollard's Hanger on the Ordnance Survey map Hermione had bought at a petrol station outside Salisbury, and it ran along the top of a chalk ridge two miles north of Malfoy Manor. At ten past four on the afternoon of Saturday the tenth of January, in a thin grey drizzle, Harry's hold on Ron's face slipped.

He felt it go.

He'd been holding faces for nine days. Not on the screen. On people. They'd been out of the Majestic on four raids since Christmas, one after another, because Theo's coin had started coming every other night and every message was worse. A house in Wigan with a family in the cellar. A warehouse at Tilbury. A Snatchers' camp in the Forest of Dean. And this, the fifth, two lines at two in the morning on the seventh, which had taken Harry an hour and a quarter.

*LOVEGOOD AND OLLIVANDER IN THE MANOR CELLAR. HE IS AWAY. BACK SUNDAY.*

He'd held four faces on four raids in nine days and slept, according to a red notebook he wasn't supposed to know about, eleven hours in all. He'd held Ron as a ginger-bearded hiker with a walking pole all the way up the side of the ridge from the lane, and Hermione as an older woman in a waxed jacket, and himself as a thin young man with a long nose, and he'd made every bird and every rabbit and every Snatcher in the wood see four Muggles out for a walk in the rain.

And at ten past four under a beech tree, with the drizzle coming down through the bare branches and the Manor's chimneys just visible through the trees below, the face on Ron went out.

Not all of it. One side. For one second the ginger beard was on the left of Ron's face and not the right, and the right was Ron, freckled and long-nosed and pale.

It was enough.

"Oi," said a voice behind them. "Oi. You four. Stand still."

* * *

There were six of them.

They came out of the trees on three sides, wands up, in a loose ring, and they weren't Muggles out for a walk. They were filthy and cheerful, in a mixture of old robes and Muggle coats, and they were pleased, and Harry read the pleasure in all six at once and knew exactly what it was. The pleasure of men who were paid by the head.

"Well, well," said the one in front. He was thin and pale, with a red neckerchief and a lot of oily hair. "Walking, are we? In the rain? On the Malfoys' land?"

"Footpath," said Harry. "It's a public footpath."

"Is it." The thin man smiled. "Funny. 'Cause I could've sworn your mate's face just moved."

Harry put it back.

He put Ron's beard back on and held it there, hard, and made all six of them see it, and he felt three of them believe it at once, two not care, and the thin one with the neckerchief not believe it at all. The thin one was suspicious. It was a small, sharp, greedy suspicion aimed at Ron, and it didn't go away when the beard came back. It grew sharper.

"Names," said the thin one.

"Dudley," said Harry. "Dudley Dursley. This is my uncle Vernon, my aunt Marge…"

He had perhaps a second. Perhaps less.

He did what Lockhart had taught him on a clifftop. Not one perfect lie. A hundred bad ones, fast. He threw a shout into the trees on the left, a dog barking on the right, a running figure disappearing between the beeches behind, and three of the Snatchers turned, and the thin one didn't.

He had nothing left for the thin one.

He knew it at once. He reached for the next illusion and it wasn't there. It was like reaching for a step in the dark and finding the stair had ended. He'd held too many for too long, and his nose was bleeding, and his hands were shaking, and the thin man with the neckerchief was raising his wand, and the beard on Ron's face went out again, both sides, and stayed out.

"*Weasley*," said the thin man, delighted. "That's a *Weasley*. I'd know that hair in the dark."

Hermione's wand moved.

Not at the Snatchers. At Harry.

He felt it hit him in the face, a hot hard sting like a hornet's, and his whole face swelled at once, burning, his eyes closing to slits, his lips going thick, and half a second later, with the part of him still thinking, he understood what she'd done and why. His own face was coming through the illusion. She'd seen it coming before he had. And she'd turned it into a face nobody would know.

Then there were wands in their backs and someone had his arms, and the ring of Snatchers closed.

* * *

"Name," the thin one said again.

Harry was on his knees on the wet leaf mould with his hands tied behind him and his face burning. He couldn't see well. He could see the thin man's boots.

"Dudley," he said through his thick lips.

"Dudley what?"

"Dursley."

"Never heard of him." The boots turned. "Her?"

"Penelope Clearwater," said Hermione at once. "Half-blood. I can prove it."

"Course you can, love. Him? The Weasley?"

"Stan Shunpike," said Ron.

Somebody laughed. "Stan Shunpike's one of ours, you thick git."

"Barny Weasley, then. Cousin. Half-blood."

The boots turned again and stopped in front of Evelyn.

Harry could just see her. She was standing between two Snatchers with her hands tied in front of her, and her face was exactly as it always was. He hadn't been able to put a face on her, because nobody ever could, and none of the six had looked at her twice. They looked at her now.

"And you?"

"Hopwood," said Evelyn. "Mary Hopwood. I work in Records."

"Do you." The thin man looked at her for about two seconds, the way people always looked at Evelyn Selwyn, and then his eyes slid off her face as though there were nothing on it to hold them, and went back to Harry. "Never mind her. Nobody's ever going to pay for her. It's him I want." He bent down. "What's wrong with your face, Dudley?"

"Stung," said Harry.

"Stung." The thin man looked closer. He took hold of Harry's hair and pushed it back off his forehead, and looked, and Harry felt his greed sharpen to a point. The swelling had gone right up into his hairline. There was a scar under it somewhere, stretched and blurred and lost in the puffy skin. The thin man couldn't quite see it. He couldn't quite not.

"Greyback'd know," said one of the others.

"Greyback's in Bristol." The thin man let go of Harry's hair. "Doesn't matter. Doesn't matter." His voice had gone very soft. "We'll take them down the hill. Let the family have a look. If it's him, that's a lot of gold, lads. That's more gold than any of us has ever seen." He straightened. "And if it's not him, well. The lady of the house has got a sister who likes company."

They took them down the hill.

* * *

Malfoy Manor stood at the end of a long straight drive between high yew hedges, lit in every window, and Harry read it as they came up the drive in the rain and found it full of fear.

Not the Ministry's fear. That had been grey and quiet and everywhere, like water in a tank. This was smaller and sharper and much nearer the top. There were only a few people in the house, and every one of them was frightened, each in a different way.

The iron gates opened by themselves.

The front door was opened by a house-elf Harry didn't know, small and old and shaking, and the Snatchers pushed them through it into a great hall, and across the hall, and through a pair of tall doors into a drawing room.

It was very large. It had a crystal chandelier the size of a cart, and portraits of pale people with pale hair on the dark purple walls, and a fire burning in a marble fireplace, and a carpet so deep Harry's feet sank into it. There were three people in it.

"What is this?" said a cold voice. "What are you…"

It was Narcissa Malfoy.

She was standing by the fire, tall and fair and very thin. Harry had seen her four times in his life, at King's Cross and at the World Cup, and she'd always been beautiful in a way that looked arranged. She was still beautiful. It had stopped being arranged. She looked at the four of them on the carpet, and at the Snatchers, and Harry read her and found her afraid.

Not of them. Of everything.

It was a fear that had been in her a long time. The fear of a woman who's made tea at four o'clock every day on the good china for a man who says *no thank you, Narcissa*, and has stood in her own corridor afterwards, not moving. It was aimed, Harry found, almost entirely at one person, and it wasn't herself and it wasn't her husband.

Lucius Malfoy sat in a chair by the window.

He'd been in Azkaban until August. Harry had read it in the *Prophet*. *Released on review.* He looked as though he'd been in Azkaban a great deal longer than that. His long fair hair was dull and uncombed. His face was grey, and his hands lay on the arms of the chair like things somebody had put down there and forgotten. He had no wand. Harry saw that at once. He had no wand, and there was nothing in him to read but a kind of dull grey shame, so old and so constant it had stopped being a feeling and become a temperature.

And the third person was Draco.

He was standing behind his father's chair. He'd grown taller since June. He was thinner. The scars on his face, the three white lines from temple to jaw and the one across the bridge of his nose, had gone silvery and flat, and they caught the firelight when he turned his head.

He turned his head.

He looked at the four of them on the carpet, and at Harry, and Harry, on his knees with his face swollen and his eyes nearly shut, read him.

Draco knew.

He knew at once. It was the first thing Harry felt in him, before the fear, before anything. Recognition. Total, instant, absolutely certain. Draco Malfoy had sat in the same common room as Harry Potter for six years and been read by him every day of them, and he knew him the way you know the back of someone's head across a crowded room, by the way they hold their shoulders, and a swollen face wasn't going to make any difference.

He knew it was Harry. He knew it was Weasley. He knew it was Granger. And he knew it was Evelyn Selwyn standing at the end of the line with her hands tied, looking at him with no expression at all.

"Draco," said Narcissa. "Come here. Look at him."

Draco came.

He came round his father's chair and across the deep carpet, slowly, and stopped a yard from Harry and looked down.

"Well?" said the thin Snatcher. "Is it? Is it him? It's Potter, isn't it? Say it's Potter."

Draco looked at Harry for a long time.

Harry read him. He read everything. He read the recognition at the top, total and certain. He read the fear beneath it, enormous, which Harry had known in Draco for six years and could have drawn with his eyes shut. He read something beneath the fear, and something beneath that, a long way down, and he couldn't tell what they were.

He didn't know why he couldn't. He'd always been able to tell with Draco. It was the one thing between them that had never changed.

He couldn't tell now.

There was the recognition. There was the fear. And beneath them was a kind of tangle, three or four things knotted round one another very tight, and none of them would come loose. There was something that might have been hatred and might have been the memory of a bathroom full of red water. There was something that might have been his mother. There was something that might have been the Dark Lord's face, very close, saying *I am disappointed, Draco.* There was something very like what Harry had once felt in him, crying in front of a mirror, before he saw who was behind him. And there was something else, very small, that Harry had felt in him once in the Room of Hidden Things, when Draco asked *what did it feel like, when I was going?* and Harry said *like Cedric*, and Draco had looked at him and not known what to do.

They were all there. They were all knotted together. Harry couldn't tell which was on top.

"I can't," said Draco. "I can't tell."

"*What?*"

"I can't tell. His face is all… I can't see. It could be." He looked away from Harry, at his mother. "I'm not sure."

"Draco," said Narcissa.

"I'm not *sure*, Mother. I'm not going to say it's him if I'm not sure. If I say it's him and we call…" He didn't finish. Everyone in the room knew whom they'd call. "And it's not him. If it's not him."

He didn't look at Harry again.

Harry knelt on the carpet with his swollen face and read Draco Malfoy walk back across his mother's drawing room to stand behind his father's chair, and couldn't tell, then or ever, why he'd done it.

* * *

Bellatrix came in four minutes later.

Harry felt her before the door opened. He'd felt her once before, in a stone chamber under the Ministry, duelling Sirius beside an arch, both of them laughing. He'd put a second Sirius one step to the left in her head that night, and her red light had gone into the arch instead. She came down the stairs into the hall like something let off a chain, the loudest thing in the house by a very long way, and what she was was glad.

Not pleased. Not cold, like her master. Glad, and hot, and hungry, the way a child is glad on Christmas morning.

"Visitors," she said in the doorway. "Cissy, you didn't tell me we had *visitors*."

She was tall and dark, and her heavy-lidded eyes went over the four of them on the carpet, and over the Snatchers, and over her sister and her sister's husband and her nephew, and stopped on Hermione's beaded bag, which one of the Snatchers was holding.

"What's that?"

"Hers," said the thin man. "Haven't looked in it yet. We were waiting on…"

Bellatrix had the bag out of his hand before he'd finished. She looked into it. She put her arm in up to the shoulder, and her face changed, and she drew it out again holding a silver-backed hairbrush and a tin of beans and a copy of *Hogwarts: A History*.

"Undetectable," she said. "Extension Charm. Clever girl." She turned round very slowly and looked at Hermione. "Clever, clever girl. Who are you, clever girl?"

"Penelope Clearwater."

Bellatrix laughed.

"No," she said, "you're not," and pointed her wand at the Snatchers. "Take the others down. The cellar. Not her. I want to talk to this one."

"Hold on," said the thin man. "Hold on. What about our gold? If it's Potter…"

"If it's Potter, he'll keep. In the cellar. And if it's Potter," said Bellatrix, very sweetly, "and you've brought my Lord's enemy into my sister's house and then stood about arguing with me about *gold*, I'll feed you to Fenrir in very small pieces, and he'll thank me." She smiled. "Take them down."

* * *

The cellar was dark and cold and smelt of damp stone and old wine, and there were two people in it already.

"Harry," said a dreamy voice out of the dark. "Is that you? Your face looks very odd. Have you been stung by something? There are Plimpies in the moat here, you know. Or there were. They might have died."

"Luna," said Harry.

"Hello." She was sitting against the far wall with her knees up and her arms round them, in a jumper with radishes on it. She'd been there since the week before Christmas. There was a bruise on her cheekbone, going yellow. She sounded exactly as she always had. "This is Mr Ollivander. He's not very well. He's been here since August. Mr Ollivander, it's Harry Potter. He's been stung."

An old man lay on a pile of sacks under the stairs. He didn't look up. Harry read him and found him very weak and very frightened and, beneath the fear, very faintly, interested, the way he'd been interested in Harry at eleven across a counter in Diagon Alley, a long time ago.

The door at the top of the stairs closed. A key turned.

Ron sat down against the wall. Evelyn didn't. She stood at the bottom of the stairs in the dark with her tied hands in front of her, quite still, and Harry couldn't read her.

Above them, through the floor, Bellatrix began.

* * *

He felt it before he heard it.

He'd remember that afterwards. That he felt it a second before the sound came through the stone. Hermione was lying on the floor of the drawing room above them, on the deep carpet, under the chandelier, with Bellatrix standing over her, and Bellatrix said one word, quite softly, and Hermione's pain came down through the floor of Malfoy Manor into the cellar and into Harry all at once, and filled him.

He'd felt the Cruciatus Curse before.

He'd felt it on a spider in a classroom in his fourth year, when a false Moody did it to show them, and he'd thought it was the worst thing he'd ever felt from a living creature. He'd felt it on Cedric in a maze, and in his own body in a churchyard. He'd thought he knew what it was.

He'd never felt it on somebody he loved.

It was pure. That was what he couldn't get past. It was pure and endless and had no bottom, and Hermione was in it, all of her, with nothing left over, nothing that was still Hermione and still thinking and still clever, just the pain, going on and on. And through it, very faint, like a voice through a storm, she was holding on to one thing. She wasn't saying anything. Bellatrix was asking her over and over, *where is the Cloak, where is Potter keeping it, who are the others, where is the Cloak*, and Hermione wasn't saying anything, and the one thing she was holding on to, beneath the pain, at the very bottom, was that she wouldn't.

Then she screamed.

It came through the stone. Ron was on his feet. He was shouting. He was throwing himself at the cellar door at the top of the stairs with his tied hands, over and over, shouting Hermione's name, and Luna was saying something, and Ollivander was weeping on his sacks, and above them Bellatrix laughed and said the word again.

Harry stood in the middle of the cellar.

He didn't throw himself at the door. He didn't shout. He stood quite still in the dark with his hands tied behind him and his swollen face and his eyes shut, and he reached up.

Through the stone. Through the floor of the drawing room and the deep carpet and the chandelier, up to the hot, loud, glad thing standing over Hermione with its wand out.

He found Bellatrix.

He found the gladness first. It was enormous. She was glad the way he'd read Dudley in a play park and Rita Skeeter in a broom cupboard and Umbridge in a pink office, glad all the way down, glad in a way that went on for ever with no floor. He went down through the gladness, fast, the way he'd gone down through the grey in twelve people in Courtroom Ten, and at the very bottom of her he found what she was made of.

It was cruelty.

Not anger, and not hatred. Cruelty, plain and old and tended, the cruelty of a person who'd looked at it years ago and liked what she saw and decided to keep it, and had fed it every day since, and loved it more than she'd ever loved anything except one man.

Harry took hold of it.

He'd done this once before. He'd done it at eleven, in a room under the school, in terror, without knowing what he did, to a man who'd been kind to him. He'd taken the thing Quirrell was most ashamed of and given it back to him, larger, and Quirrell had died.

He wasn't in terror now.

He knew exactly what he was doing.

He took Bellatrix Lestrange's cruelty, the whole of it, all the years of it, every scream she'd ever enjoyed and every face she'd ever watched change, and he turned it round and gave it back to her.

Louder.

The laughing stopped.

There was a silence above them. One second. Two. Then Bellatrix screamed. Nothing like Hermione's scream. Higher, and much longer, with something in it Harry had never heard come out of a person before, a kind of astonishment, as though what was happening to her was something she'd done to so many people that she'd forgotten it could happen to her.

Ron had stopped hitting the door.

Harry didn't stop.

He held it. He stood in the dark of the cellar and held Bellatrix's own cruelty inside her and made it louder and louder, and felt her feel it, every scream she'd ever enjoyed coming back at once, and it was easy. It was the easiest thing he'd ever done. It was easier than the twelve in Courtroom Ten and much easier than a face on two thousand people. It was just holding a door open and letting the wind come through.

He liked it.

He didn't notice that he liked it. Not then. He'd notice later. He stood in the cellar with his eyes shut and Bellatrix screaming above him, and there was something in him that wasn't the reading and wasn't the push, something quite warm and steady and pleased, and it was aimed at the screaming, and it wanted more, and he gave it more.

"Potter."

It came from very close. From in front of him. Sharp.

He didn't stop.

"*Potter.*"

Louder. Much louder. The voice of somebody who very rarely raised it.

Harry opened his eyes.

Evelyn was standing in front of him in the dark. Her tied hands were up between them, flat against his chest, pushing. Not hard. Just enough that he could feel them. Her face was a foot from his, and he couldn't read it, and it was white.

He let go.

Above them the screaming stopped. It didn't die away. It stopped all at once, and then there was a sound like somebody falling, and then a long ragged sobbing breath, and then Narcissa's voice saying *Bella, Bella, what is it, what happened*, and Bellatrix's voice, very high, saying *I don't know, I don't know, something, something in me*, and then nothing.

Evelyn took her hands off his chest.

She said nothing else. She stood in front of him in the dark of the cellar and looked at him, and Harry looked back at her, and he didn't know what was in her face, and he found that for the first time in six years he didn't want to.

* * *

There was a crack in the middle of the cellar.

"Harry Potter," said a high squeaky voice out of the dark, very fast. "Harry Potter, sir. Dobby has come. Neville Longbottom's coin is hot in the kitchens and Neville Longbottom is saying to Dobby, *Malfoy Manor, the cellar*, and Dobby is knowing the cellar, sir, Dobby is knowing it very well, Dobby was scrubbing it for eleven years." The house-elf stood in the middle of the floor in a tea cosy and a great many odd socks, his tennis-ball eyes shining in the dark and his long ears trembling. "Dobby is come to rescue Harry Potter."

Harry looked at Evelyn.

She had one shoe off. She was standing on one foot on the cold stone floor of the cellar, and in her tied hands, held up, was a fake Galleon with its rim still faintly glowing. She'd had it in her shoe since the Burrow.

"I sent it whilst you were busy," said Evelyn.

* * *

It went very fast after that.

"Can you take people?" said Harry. "Out? Through the wards?"

"Dobby can go where Dobby likes, sir. Elves is not like wizards. Dobby can take three. Maybe four, if they is small."

"Luna," said Harry. "And Mr Ollivander. Somewhere safe."

"Shell Cottage," said Ron. He was still at the foot of the stairs, with blood on his hands where he'd hit the door. His face was grey. "Tinworth. On the cliff. Bill's. Dobby, Bill's house, by the sea, you can't miss it, it's got shells in the wall."

"Dobby knows it, sir." Dobby snapped his fingers and the ropes fell off all of them at once, Harry's and Ron's and Evelyn's and Luna's. "Dobby is coming back. Dobby is coming straight back for Harry Potter and the others. Wait, sir."

He took Luna by one hand and stooped to take Ollivander by the other, and Luna said, "Thank you, Dobby, that's very kind," as though she were being offered a biscuit, and there was a crack, and they were gone.

Above them, a door opened.

"What was that?" It was Lucius's voice, dull and frightened, at the top of the cellar stairs. "What was that noise? Wormtail? Is somebody down there?"

No one answered. Harry stood at the bottom of the stairs in the dark with his hands free and his face still swollen and reached up, and found Lucius at the top of the stairs, alone, grey and wandless and afraid, and he could have made him see anything. An empty cellar. A rat. His own son lying on the floor.

He didn't have to. There was another crack.

"Dobby is back," whispered Dobby at his elbow. "Miss Lovegood is at the house with the shells, sir. And the old wandmaker."

The cellar door at the top of the stairs swung open.

* * *

They went up the stairs together, Harry and Ron and Evelyn and the house-elf in the tea cosy, through the door, past Lucius Malfoy, who saw them come and put his hands up in front of his face and backed into the hall wall, and into the drawing room.

Hermione was on the carpet.

She lay on her side under the chandelier with her hair across her face and one arm flung out, not moving. Bellatrix was on a sofa by the fire with her sister kneeling beside her. She was holding her own head in both hands and rocking, her face gone a dirty yellow-white, her heavy-lidded eyes open very wide and fixed on nothing. Two of the Snatchers stood by the window, arguing. Draco was by the fireplace with his wand in his hand.

They all turned at once.

"*Expelliarmus!*" shouted Ron.

The thin man's wand flew out of his hand and Ron caught it and went for Hermione, straight across the carpet on his knees. Dobby snapped his fingers, and the great deep carpet rolled itself up from the far end like a wave and took the other Snatcher's legs out from under him, and he went down with a crash into a little table full of china.

Draco raised his wand.

He raised it at Harry. Harry saw it come up. He saw it point at his chest from six feet away across a drawing room, the hawthorn wand he'd seen in Draco's hand for six years, in the common room and the corridors and a bathroom full of red water and on a moonlit tower. He read Draco, and the knot in him was still there, four or five things tangled tight, and he couldn't tell what was on top, and he didn't wait to find out.

He didn't use magic.

He crossed the six feet in two steps, took hold of Draco's wrist with one hand and the wand with the other, and twisted hard, the way Dudley had once twisted his arm behind the garage at Privet Drive when they were nine, and the wand came out of Draco's fingers into his.

Draco made a small sound. Not pain. Something else.

Harry stepped back with Draco's wand in his hand.

It was warm. He noticed that. It was warm from Draco's palm, and it was hawthorn, and it was ten inches, and it didn't feel like his own wand at all, and he didn't care. He pointed it at Draco's chest.

Draco looked at him.

His face was very white. The scars stood out on it, silver. He didn't move. He didn't try to get the wand back. He stood by the marble fireplace in his mother's drawing room with his hands empty at his sides and looked at Harry Potter holding his wand, and Harry read him, and the knot was still there, and he still couldn't tell.

"*Harry!*" Ron had Hermione in his arms. She was limp, her head on his shoulder. "*Harry*, come on, *now*, Dobby, *now*…"

Bellatrix was on her feet.

Harry hadn't seen her get up. She was standing beside the sofa with her hair wild and her face still that dirty yellow-white, swaying, and her eyes were on him. On his swollen face. On the wand in his hand. And Harry saw her understand. He didn't need to read it. He saw it cross her face, the thing he'd done to her in the dark and the person who'd done it, and the knowing rose through her like a fish coming up through weed.

"*You*," said Bellatrix.

Dobby had Ron's arm. Ron had Hermione. Evelyn had Dobby's other hand, and with her free one she reached across and took Harry by the back of his collar, quite hard, like a mother pulling a child out of the road.

"*Now*," said Evelyn.

Bellatrix's arm moved.

Harry saw the silver cross the room. He saw it turning in the firelight, end over end, very fast, a small bright thing coming at them from the sofa. He saw it, and he could have done something. He could have put something in her eyes a second ago, before she threw. He could have put Dobby a yard to the left in her head, the way he'd put Sirius a step to the left beside an arch. He'd done it before. He knew how.

He didn't.

He'd think about that for a long time. He didn't, because he was holding Draco's wand and looking at Draco, and because he had nothing left, and because the knowing was still crossing Bellatrix's face and he was watching it with a small warm pleased feeling he didn't notice he had. And because he was too slow.

The drawing room turned and went out.

* * *

They landed on wet grass in a strong wind.

It was dark. There was the sea. Harry could hear it, very loud, below and in front of him, and smell it, salt and cold, and see a long way down the white lines of it breaking on rocks in the dark. Behind them was a cottage with lit windows and shells set in its walls. A door was opening, light spilling across the grass, and voices.

Ron was on his knees with Hermione. Evelyn was on her feet.

Dobby stood in the grass between them, holding Evelyn's hand, looking up at Harry.

"Harry Potter," said Dobby.

There was a knife in his chest.

It was a small knife, very fine, with a silver handle. It had gone in just below where the tea cosy ended. Dobby looked down at it with his great tennis-ball eyes, as though it were something someone had given him and he wasn't sure whether he was meant to keep it.

Then he looked back up at Harry.

Harry read him.

He'd read him once before, in a small bedroom at Privet Drive when he was twelve, and found terror and devotion and a grey grinding misery. He'd read him in a hospital bed. He'd read him on a staircase at Hogwarts, holding a sock. He read him now, on a clifftop in Cornwall in the dark with a knife in his chest, and the misery was gone. It had been gone for five years. And the terror was gone too. What was left was very small and very clear, aimed at Harry, and it was what it had always been beneath everything, since the first night.

It was devotion. Plain and whole. And beneath it, so quiet Harry nearly missed it, Dobby was pleased. Pleased with himself. Pleased that he'd come.

"Dobby came," said Dobby. He sounded surprised, and very proud. "Dobby came, sir."

He sat down in the wet grass, quite slowly, as though he'd decided to.

Then he wasn't anything.

* * *

They buried him in the morning at the top of the cliff, at the end of Bill's garden, where the grass ran out and the wind came straight off the sea.

Bill wanted to do it with magic. He came out at seven with his wand and said he'd dig it, it would take a minute, and Evelyn said, "No."

She said nothing else. Bill looked at her for a long moment in the grey dawn, the wind blowing his long red hair across his face, and then he went back into the cottage and came out again with a spade from the shed and gave it to her, and went in again.

She dug.

She dug for a long time. The ground at the top of the cliff was hard and stony under a skin of turf, full of the roots of sea-pinks and gorse, and she wasn't strong, and she'd never dug anything in her life. She took the turf off first, in squares, very carefully, and stacked them to one side, in order. Then she dug. She put her foot on the spade and leaned on it and it went in an inch, and she leaned again and it went in another, and she levered up a clod and put it on the other side. Then she did it again.

Harry watched her.

He was sitting on the bench by the cottage wall with his back to the shells. The swelling on his face had gone down in the night. Fleur had put something on it that smelt of seaweed. Hermione was inside, asleep, with Ron sitting on the floor by her bed and not sleeping. Luna had gone out at six and come back with a handful of sea-pinks and put them in a jam jar on the windowsill and gone out again. Ollivander hadn't woken.

Harry sat on the bench and watched Evelyn dig a grave.

She didn't stop. She didn't look up. She didn't speak. She dug until the hole was a foot deep, and then she hit a stone, a big one, and couldn't get the spade under it, and knelt on the edge of the hole and got it out with her hands. It took eleven minutes. He counted. Her hands were bleeding at the nails when she'd done it. She didn't look at them. She stood up and went on digging.

He didn't help.

He sat on the bench in the wind with his hands on his knees and Draco Malfoy's wand in his pocket, and watched her, and didn't get up. He couldn't have said why. He'd try to say why later. He'd sit in a dead cinema in Leeds a month from now and try to remember what he'd been thinking on the bench at Shell Cottage on the morning of the eleventh of January, watching a plain girl with bleeding hands dig a grave for a house-elf on a clifftop without magic, alone. And he wouldn't be able to remember thinking anything at all.

She dug until a quarter to ten.

When the hole was deep enough she put the spade down and went into the cottage, and came out with Dobby in her arms, wrapped in a blanket of Fleur's, and knelt at the side of the grave, and laid him in.

She said nothing over him.

She stood up and filled it in again with the spade, clod by clod, the way she'd dug it. Then she put the turf back. She put each square back where it had come from, in order, very carefully, pressing it down with her bleeding hands so it would take. When she'd finished, you could hardly see where it had been, except that the turf was a little higher and there was a line round each square where the grass had been cut.

Luna came and laid the sea-pinks on it, out of the jam jar.

Evelyn went and found a white stone at the edge of the cliff, about the size of a loaf, and carried it back in both arms, and set it at the head of the grave. Then she took Bill's penknife, which he'd left on the bench beside Harry, and knelt, and scratched at the stone with the point of the knife, slowly, for a long time.

When she stood up, Harry could read it from the bench.

*DOBBY. A FREE ELF.*

She put the penknife back on the bench beside him without looking at him. Her hands had blood on them. Her face was exactly as it always was. She went into the cottage and shut the door.

Harry sat on the bench and looked at the grave.

It was very neat. The turf was pressed down. The sea-pinks stirred a little in the wind. The white stone stood at its head with the letters cut into it, rough and careful, and the sea was very loud below.

He looked at it for a long time.

He looked inside himself for what he felt about it, the way you look for a coin in a pocket, carefully, in every corner.

There was nothing there.

## Chapter 73: Hogsmeade

The Hog's Head hadn't changed, because in this world nobody had ever given it a reason to.

Harry came in out of the sleet at half past six on the first Tuesday in February, wearing the face of a tired middle-aged wizard with a sack over his shoulder, and stood just inside the door and let the room rise round him. It was dark and low and filthy. The windows were so grimy that the light from the high street came through them brown. There was sawdust on the floor and a smell of goats, and four customers at four different tables, all hooded, none of them looking at any of the others. Behind the bar a tall old man with a long grey beard was wiping a glass with a cloth that was making it dirtier.

Harry knew him.

He'd stood in this room at thirteen, in another world, with a girl beside him he couldn't read and a gold watch that had stopped, and a tall old man with a long grey beard had looked at the two of them over this bar and said *you'd better come upstairs, the pair of you, before somebody else notices you*. He'd taken them up and kept them for eight weeks. He'd fed them. He'd shouted at them. He'd taught Harry to milk a goat called Mabel, and he'd looked at the watch in Evelyn's hand and gone quite white and refused to say why, and on the last night, in the room above the bar, he'd said *my brother will use you, boy. He uses everyone he loves.*

This wasn't that man.

This was the same man, in the same bar, wiping the same glass, and he'd never seen Harry in his life.

Harry crossed the sawdust to the bar and set the sack on it.

"Potatoes," he said. "From Leeds. For the passage."

Aberforth Dumbledore looked at the sack. Then he looked at Harry, at the tired middle-aged wizard with the sack, and Harry read him.

Suspicion on top, old and dry and permanent, like the dirt on the windows. Beneath it, much quieter, a weariness that went all the way down, the weariness of a man who'd watched a great many people come into his bar and go out of it to die. And beneath that, at the very bottom, so faint Harry nearly missed it, a kind of stubborn, grudging tenderness, aimed at nothing in particular. At the whole of the dark room, at the hooded people at the four tables and the goats in the yard and the children at the end of the passage behind the back room, who weren't his, and whom he'd decided, without telling anybody, to keep alive.

It was the same. It was exactly the same as the other one.

"Back room," said Aberforth.

"Thank you."

"Don't thank me. Take it through."

Harry picked up the sack. He didn't move.

Aberforth's eyes narrowed. They were very blue. They were his brother's eyes in a different face, a face that had been angry for a hundred years and had stopped noticing.

"What," he said.

"Nothing."

"You're looking at me."

"Sorry."

"You're looking at me," said Aberforth slowly, "like you know me. People don't look at me like that. They look at me like I'm the bloke behind the bar." He put the glass down. "Who are you?"

Harry very nearly said his name.

Not *Harry*. The other one. The name he'd nearly said in a pub in another world at thirteen and bitten back, and nearly said here at fifteen, ordering a butterbeer before the first meeting of a defence group, and bitten back again. He felt it come up now quite easily, as it always had, as though some part of him had been waiting since he was thirteen to say it to this face and be answered.

He didn't say it.

"I met somebody very like you once," he said instead. "A long time ago. He kept goats."

Aberforth looked at him for a long moment.

"Lot of people keep goats," he said.

"Yes."

"Was he any good? The bloke you met?"

Harry thought about a room above a bar, and two children in it who didn't belong in that world, and a man who hadn't had to take them in, and had.

"He was the best man I've ever met," said Harry.

Aberforth made no answer.

He picked up the glass again and went on wiping it with the dirty cloth, and Harry read something go through him, very quick, beneath the suspicion and the weariness. Not belief. Something more like embarrassment, aimed at himself, the embarrassment of an old man who's been told something kind by a stranger and doesn't know where to put it.

"Back room," said Aberforth gruffly, to the glass. "Go on."

* * *

Lockhart was in the back room, unpacking a crate of tinned peaches by candlelight and singing.

He wasn't in disguise. He was meant to be. He'd told Harry so on the radio in January. *Alive and well and in disguise, my dear fellows, somewhere with a very good view.* The disguise turned out to be a pair of spectacles with plain glass in them and a false moustache he hadn't stuck on properly. Beneath it he was entirely Gilderoy Lockhart, in his sugared-apricot cloak with gold at the cuffs and hem, kneeling on the stone floor of Aberforth Dumbledore's back room with a tin of peaches in each hand.

"*Harry!*" he cried. "My dear fellow. You've brought potatoes. Splendid. We're very short of potatoes. The young are eating nothing but peaches, which is delightful for them and very bad for their teeth." He stood up, beaming, and the moustache slipped. "Is that you under there? It is, isn't it? You've done something very clever with your nose."

"You're meant to be in disguise," said Harry.

"I *am* in disguise." Lockhart touched the moustache. "Nobody's recognised me for a week."

"Everybody in Hogsmeade's recognised you."

"Well, yes. But they're very discreet. They're on our side, you see. Rosmerta winks at me." He took the sack of potatoes from Harry and looked into it with great satisfaction. "Marvellous. Come through. Come and see."

There was a door at the far side of the back room, low and narrow, and behind it a passage ran down into the dark. Harry knew where it went. It went under the lane and under the fields and up, a long way up, into a room on the seventh floor of the castle that was whatever you needed it to be. Neville Longbottom was living in that room with thirty-one other students who'd decided they'd rather not go to lessons with the Carrows, and every week since Christmas the village had been feeding them through this door.

Lockhart had organised it.

He told Harry so, for twenty minutes, by candlelight, with a great many flourishes. He had a list of every family in Hogsmeade who'd given anything, in purple ink on a roll of parchment three feet long. He had a rota. He had a system of signals involving the curtains at Madam Puddifoot's. He'd made friends with the Carrows' house-elf, which nobody else had managed, by signing a photograph for her. On two occasions he'd led a Death Eater patrol in a circle round the back of the village for an hour by walking ahead of them in the dark in the character of a confused old man looking for his cat.

"I was magnificent," said Lockhart. "I wish you'd seen it. I had a limp. A very small one. Subtle. Here." He walked three steps across the back room with a very small, subtle limp. "You see? The cat was called Mr Whiskers. I said it with great feeling. *Mr Whiskers*. One of them very nearly helped me look."

Harry laughed.

It came out of him short and surprised, the first time in some weeks, and he noticed it as it went.

Lockhart noticed too. He stopped limping. He looked at Harry by the candlelight, the moustache crooked and the plain glass of his spectacles catching the flame, and Harry read him, and found, beneath the vanity and the warmth and the great bright pleasure in his own magnificence, something quite different, steady and plain and aimed at Harry.

It was worry.

"You're very thin," said Lockhart.

"I'm fine."

"You're not, you know. You're very thin, and you've got a look about you." He tilted his head. "I've seen it before. On other people. In the Himalayas, once. A man I knew. He walked a Path too, you know. Not yours. A different one. He got that look at the end."

"What happened to him?"

Lockhart looked at him a moment longer.

Then he smiled, brilliantly, the old smile, and turned back to the crate of peaches.

"Oh, he was fine," he said. "Perfectly fine. Lived to a great age. Took up beekeeping." He held out a tin. "Have a peach, my dear fellow. Have two. You're far too thin."

Harry didn't read whether that was a lie. He found he didn't want to.

He took the peaches.

"Gilderoy," he said at the door.

"My dear fellow?"

"If they come. For the village. Because of this." He nodded at the passage, the crates, the purple list. "What will you do?"

Lockhart considered it. He took the false moustache off at last, looked at it on his fingertip, and put it in his pocket.

"Something memorable," he said. "Obviously."

"I mean it."

"So do I." Lockhart smiled at him. It was a smaller smile than usual, one Harry had seen perhaps twice. "I've had a very good run, Harry. Better than most. I've been everywhere and met everybody and written it all down, slightly improved. If they come, I shall go and stand somewhere inconvenient and be extremely annoying for as long as I possibly can." He put a tin of peaches in Harry's other hand. "And you'll hear all about it, because I shall make sure somebody tells you."

"That's not a plan."

"It's the only plan I've ever had," said Lockhart. "It's served me beautifully. Mind the step."

* * *

The silver badger came through the wall of the Majestic at thirteen minutes to three on the morning of Thursday the twenty-sixth of February.

Harry was at the screen. He'd been at the screen since eleven. He was making Diagon Alley in the rain, with two hundred people in it, every one different, and he was holding it without effort, the way he held everything now, and thinking about nothing at all.

The badger walked through the left-hand wall by the side boxes and down the aisle to the orchestra pit, as the doe had in October, and stopped and looked up at him.

It spoke in Neville Longbottom's voice.

It wasn't Neville's ordinary voice. Harry had heard that for six years, round and anxious and kind. This was the voice of somebody who'd been shouting for some time and had stopped because there was no longer any point.

"They've come for the village," said the badger. "For feeding us. Forty of them. More. They're burning it. Lockhart's at the bridge. He's holding them so the families can get to the passage. He sent me to send this. He said tell Harry. Please. Harry. *Please*."

Then it was gone.

Harry let Diagon Alley go.

He stood below the screen in the dark for perhaps three seconds. He didn't think. He reached up behind him, through the ceiling, to the projection room, and found Ron asleep and Hermione asleep, the slow warm untidy feelings of sleep, and in the far corner by the projectors, where Evelyn's camp bed was, the place in the building where there was nothing.

He didn't wake them.

He'd think about that later. He'd think about the three seconds below the screen, and the three people asleep upstairs, and how easy it had been not to. He didn't think about it then. He went up the side aisle and through the foyer and out of the fire door into the alley, where the Apparition ward let you out if not in, and turned on the spot.

* * *

He came out on the lane above Hogsmeade at twenty-four minutes past three, between two hedges that had been cut back hard in the autumn, and stood still.

It was beginning to snow.

The first flakes were coming down out of a sky he couldn't see, slowly, in no hurry, in air so still they fell quite straight. One landed on the back of his hand. It didn't melt at once.

Below him, the village was burning.

Not all of it. Most of the fire was out. But halfway along the high street the Three Broomsticks was still alight, a dull orange glow inside its broken windows, smoke rising from the roof in a thick grey column, straight up, not bending at all, because there was no wind. Further down there were other glows, smaller, going out. There was a smell of wet ash.

There was no noise.

He reached.

He reached down the lane and into the village, the whole of it, the way he'd learned to read a building at the Ministry, and he found it.

At the top end, behind the Hog's Head, very far down, underground, there were people. A great many. Frightened and grieving and in pain and alive. Forty, perhaps. More. They were in the passage. They'd got there. They were going up it slowly in the dark, carrying each other.

In the yards behind the shops there were a few more. Hiding. Hurt.

In the high street there were fourteen.

They were pleased.

He found that first, before anything else, standing on the lane in the falling snow. Fourteen people in the high street, and every one of them was pleased. Nothing like the cold pleasure of the churchyard or the lawn. Hotter and louder and far more stupid. It was the pleasure of men who'd done what they'd been told and enjoyed it more than they'd expected, and were now standing about in the wreck of it, drinking somebody else's mead out of the bottle, laughing and kicking things.

And between them and the passage, at the bottom of the high street, on the bridge, there was nothing at all.

The place where a person had been.

He went down the lane.

* * *

He went down past the houses. He didn't count the windows. He'd learn later that eleven were broken on the left and four on the right, because somebody told him. He didn't see them. He didn't see the open door of Gladrags, or the broom on the pavement outside the apothecary, or the black cat on the Honeydukes sill. He went down the lane to the bottom of the high street, to the bridge, in the falling snow.

Lockhart was lying on it.

He was on his back. His wand lay a yard from his right hand, in the gutter of the bridge against the parapet. His right hand lay palm up on the stones beside him, open, the fingers a little curled, as though he were waiting to be handed something. The spectacles with the plain glass were gone. The false moustache was gone. His face was quite calm. His eyes were open, looking up at the snow coming down out of the dark, and a flake landed on one of them, and it didn't blink.

He was wearing the cloak.

Of course he was. Sugared apricot, with gold at the cuffs and the hem. Madam Malkin had made it for him specially. It was a colour nobody would ever have chosen to wear to a war. It was spread round him on the stones of the bridge like a flag, the most absurd colour Harry had ever seen anyone die in, and the snow was beginning to settle on it.

Harry stood on the bridge and looked at the road on the village side.

The scorch marks went across it in a wide half circle. Dozens of them, hundreds, black stars and long black streaks burnt into the cobbles. Every spell that had been thrown down the high street at the bridge for however long it had gone on, an hour, two hours, and every one of them had stopped at the same place. At the near end of the bridge. In a line as straight as the edge of a ruler.

Nothing had got past it.

Not one spell had crossed that line whilst the man in the sugared-apricot cloak stood behind it with his wand up, holding a bridge alone, and forty people went past behind him, up the stream and through the yards, carrying their children, into the passage, into the dark.

Harry looked at the line.

He thought about a crate of tinned peaches.

He thought about a limp, very small, very subtle. *Mr Whiskers*. He thought about a tunnel under the school a long time ago, when he was twelve, collapsing, and a man in a ridiculous cloak holding it up with a spell so a boy could go on, and staying there, holding it, until his back broke.

He thought about *you're very thin*.

He didn't feel anything.

He noticed that. He noticed it standing on the bridge with the snow coming down, quite clearly, as a fact. He'd stood by Cedric in a churchyard and by Dumbledore on a lawn and felt them go, the place where a person had been, and something had happened in him each time, something large, something he hadn't been able to turn down. He hadn't felt Sirius go. He'd been running. He'd felt the laughter stop and kept running and hadn't stopped since.

He didn't feel anything now.

He looked inside himself for it, carefully, as he had on a bench at Shell Cottage, and it wasn't there.

And he thought, quite calmly, standing on the bridge, that that was right.

It was a very simple thought. It came with no feeling of its own. It came the way a sum comes out once you've done all the working. There was a war. In a war people died, and the ones left had to do things. Feeling things was what you did afterwards, if there was an afterwards. It was a luxury. It was for people who had time. It was for people who weren't at war. And he was at war, and had been since an orchard in August, and he'd been wasting a great deal of time.

He stepped round Lockhart's open hand without touching it and went up into the high street.

* * *

They saw him at once.

He didn't hide. He walked up the middle of the high street in his own face, in the snow, with his hands in his pockets, and the fourteen men in black stood about in the road and on the pavements in the light of the burning inn and watched him come.

He read them as he walked.

He read them one at a time, slowly, the way he read the people in Diagon Alley on the screen, to get them right.

The big one nearest the bridge, with the beard, was the most pleased. He had a bottle of Rosmerta's oak-matured mead in one hand and his mask pushed up on his forehead, and he was pleased because he'd been the one to set the Three Broomsticks alight, and he'd enjoyed watching the woman inside try to put it out with her hands. The one beside him, thin, with a long neck, was pleased in a fussier way, pleased that it was done and done properly and that somebody would tell the Dark Lord so. The two who'd been kicking a handcart over by the kerb were pleased the way boys are pleased after a fight. The one in the doorway of the bookshop was pleased and bored, and had been thinking about going in to see if there was anything worth taking.

The youngest stood in the gutter outside Scrivenshaft's. He was about Evelyn's age. He was pleased too, but it was thinner than the others' and newer, and beneath it, a little way down, he was frightened of how pleased he was. It was the first time. He'd killed a man on the stream bank an hour ago, an old man with a lantern, and it had been easy, and he hadn't expected it to be easy, and he couldn't stop thinking about how easy it had been.

Harry knew that feeling.

He'd read it in a cousin in a play park two and a half years ago, from a gate. He'd read it in himself more recently, in the front row of a dead cinema. He put it with the rest.

"Well, look at *this*," said the big one with the beard.

He said it with great delight, lifting his bottle. He was the first to see the scar, and Harry felt the recognition go through him and then through the others one after another, like a match going along a row of candles, and every one of them grew more pleased.

"Potter," said the thin one with the long neck. "That's Potter. That's *Harry Potter*."

"Come to see the bonfire, have you, Potter?"

"Bit late, son. Party's over."

"Your mate on the bridge put up a good show, though. Didn't he? We'll give him that. Funny little man. Wouldn't shut up. Kept *talking*." The big one laughed. "Kept saying *come on, gentlemen, is that the best you've got*, right to the end. In that bloody cloak."

Several of them laughed.

Harry stopped in the middle of the high street, about level with the post office, and stood in the snow and looked at them.

They had their wands out now. Most of them. Not hurrying. There were fourteen of them and one of him, and he was seventeen and very thin and had his hands in his pockets, and they were pleased, and in no hurry at all.

"Don't think the Dark Lord'll mind if we have a bit of fun first," said the big one. "Do you, Rowle?"

"He said alive," said the thin one.

"Alive's a broad church."

Harry read them all at once.

He didn't need to reach. They were very close and very loud. He stood in the snow and let the fourteen of them rise up into him, all fourteen pleasures, all fourteen sets of everything beneath the pleasures, and he went down through each one quickly, the way you go through the drawers of a desk when you're looking for one particular thing.

He was looking for the worst night.

Everybody had one. He'd known that since he was six. Everybody he'd ever read had one night somewhere in them that was worse than all the others, that they didn't think about, that they'd built everything else on top of so they'd never have to look at it again. It was always there. It was always at the bottom. It was always the same shape, in everybody, a door with something behind it that they'd shut and walked away from and would give anything never to open.

He found it in all fourteen.

The big one with the beard had a night when he was nine, in a kitchen, with his father and a belt, and a younger brother under the table, and a choice. The thin one with the long neck had a night in a hospital, by a bed, with his mother in it, and something he'd promised to do for her and hadn't, and the door closing. The one in the bookshop doorway had a cellar. One of the boys by the handcart had a girl, and a lake, and ice. The youngest, in the gutter outside Scrivenshaft's, had an hour ago, and an old man with a lantern on the stream bank, and how easy it had been. It had already sunk to the bottom of him. It had gone straight there, in an hour. He'd carry it there for the rest of his life.

Harry thought about that.

He thought about it for perhaps a second, standing in the snow. He thought it would be a long life, and a long time to carry it.

Then he opened the doors.

* * *

He didn't do it the way he'd done the illusions on the screen. He didn't build anything. There was no need. It was all already there in each of them, perfect, every detail, every word, every smell and sound, built by themselves over years with great care, in the dark at the bottom of their own minds.

He just let them in.

He put each of the fourteen men in the high street inside his own worst night, all of it, and made it real, and made it now.

And he didn't put an end on it.

That was the only thing he built. It was very small. It was the smallest illusion he'd ever made, and it was the one that mattered. A night has an end. Every worst night anyone's ever had has an end, a morning, a moment when it stops and you're on the other side of it and it's behind you. He took the end away. He took it out of all fourteen of them, quietly, the way you take the last page out of a book, so that when they reached where it should have been, they were back at the beginning.

It took less than a second.

The big man with the beard dropped his bottle.

It hit the cobbles and didn't break, and rolled, and the mead ran out of it across the snow in a dark stain. The big man didn't look at it. He was looking at a place in the air about a yard in front of him and a little to the left, at the height of a small boy hiding under a kitchen table, and his face had gone quite still, and then it began, steadily, without any noise at all, to cry.

The thin one with the long neck turned his head very politely to one side, as though somebody had spoken to him.

"No," he said. "No, I've told you. After supper. I said I'd do it after supper."

The one in the bookshop doorway went half round and stopped, as though he'd been about to go in and had remembered something.

One of the boys by the handcart went down on his knees and put his hands over his ears. The other knelt beside the cart and held his hands out in front of him, palms up and open, the way you'd hold them out to somebody under the ice.

The youngest, in the gutter, took hold of his own left wrist, the wrist of his wand hand, very tightly, in his right. And after a moment he began to laugh. Two short breaths and a pause. Two short breaths. Neither happy nor unhappy. The sound of somebody who's understood a joke a long time after it was made.

They were all quite still.

None of them moved his feet. None of them looked at Harry. Their wands hung from their fingers or lay in the snow, and their eyes were open, and each pair was looking at something different, and none of the things they were looking at was in the high street.

Harry stood among them and read them.

He read them living it.

He read the big one under the table, and the thin one in the hospital, and the youngest on the stream bank with the old man and the lantern, all of it at once, coming to the end that wasn't there and going back to the beginning, and coming to it again. It was very loud. It was the loudest thing in the village.

He didn't turn it down.

He looked for something in himself about it.

There was nothing there. He'd expected that. He'd decided it on the bridge.

He held it, and it held itself. That was what he'd think about later, and didn't think about at all now. He didn't have to do anything. He'd built one small thing, the missing end, and they did the rest themselves, all fourteen of them, over and over, with their own minds, and it cost him nothing to keep it going. It was the cheapest illusion he'd ever made.

He looked round the high street at the fourteen men standing in the snow, and decided it would do.

Then he went and sat down.

* * *

The post office had three steps up to its door.

He sat on the second. He didn't choose it. It was the one his feet found. He sat with his elbows on his knees and the fourteen in front of him, scattered up and down the high street between the post office and the bridge, the way people stand about in a room before a party's properly started.

The snow was coming down more thickly now.

It came down quite straight in the still air, out of a sky he couldn't see, and settled on the fourteen men. It settled on their shoulders and the folds of their hoods and the tops of their pushed-up masks. It settled on the big man's hair. It settled in the crook of the youngest one's elbow, where he held his own wrist. It settled on the handcart and the bottle and the dark stain of mead and the open door of Gladrags and the broom outside the apothecary.

It settled on Harry.

He didn't brush it off.

He put his hand in his coat pocket for no reason and found an apple.

He looked at it. It was a green one. He'd bought it at Kirkgate Market on Tuesday from a woman at the end of the fruit row who called everybody *love*, and put it in his pocket, and forgotten it. It was cold right through.

He took his right glove off to eat it.

He laid the glove on the step beside him, palm up, and took a bite of the apple, and it was very cold and very sour, and he chewed it slowly and watched the high street.

He didn't feel the cold.

He would have, once. He'd have felt it in his hand, and noticed it, and put the glove back on. He didn't notice it. He sat on the post office step with the apple in his bare hand and the snow coming down on him and on everything, and watched the fourteen, and was perfectly calm.

It was the calmest he'd been in his life.

He watched them the way some people watch a fire. He wasn't waiting for them to do anything. He watched them because they were there, doing what they did, and he had nowhere in particular to be.

At some point in the night he wanted there to be flowers.

He didn't know why. He didn't think about it. He was looking at the snow round the big man's feet, at the half-filled print of his boot, and thought it would be nice if there were flowers in it, so there were. They came up through the snow round the feet of all fourteen of them, slowly, as he watched. White ones first, too big for snowdrops. Then blue ones. Then others. They pushed up out of the white round the black boots and opened in the dark, in February, in the snow, and there was no reason for them at all, and he didn't need one.

He looked at them for a while.

They were very pretty.

He took another bite of the apple.

* * *

It got light at about seven.

It came up grey and then white behind the hills on the far side of the village, and some time after that the snow stopped, and the smoke from the Three Broomsticks went on rising straight into a white sky, and the fourteen stood in the high street with snow on their shoulders, living it.

People came.

Not up the high street. Nobody came up the high street. They came at the top end, round the back of the Hog's Head and down through the yards behind the shops, along the frozen stream, over the wall behind the bookshop. They were carrying things. They were looking for people. A door kept banging somewhere, and someone kept going back to shut it. A child was asking where its shoes were.

He read them as they came.

They were frightened, and grieving, and very tired. And when they looked down the high street at the fourteen men standing in the snow, and at the boy sitting on the post office step at the far end eating an apple, they were frightened of something else as well.

He read that too. He didn't mind it.

At some point a witch with a box of bandages came out of the alley by the bookshop and stopped dead and looked at him down the length of the street. Hestia Jones. He knew her a little, from the Order. He read her. She was horrified, and sorry, and beneath both was something like the feeling you get looking over the edge of a cliff, when part of you wants to step off. She came no closer.

Nobody came any closer.

He didn't want them to.

He sat on the step and watched the fourteen, and the clock over the post office door, with a crack across its face, went on above his head. He didn't look at it. He heard it. It was a very small, very ordinary tick, quite steady, and apart from the youngest one's laughter it was the only thing in the high street that made any noise.

He finished the apple, except for the core.

He found another in his other pocket, a red one, and started on that.

* * *

At about twenty to ten somebody came down the lane.

He heard them before he read them. He heard feet in the snow coming down from the top of the lane where it ran out between the hedges, slowly, stopping and starting. The feet came down into the high street and went past the open door of Gladrags and the broom on the pavement and the cat on the Honeydukes sill. They went to the bridge.

They stopped at the bridge for a long time.

Then they came up into the high street, slowly, and went in among the fourteen. They stopped by the big one. They stopped by the thin one with the long neck, long enough to listen to him. They went to the youngest, in the gutter outside Scrivenshaft's, and stopped there, very close.

Harry didn't look up.

He reached for whoever it was, idly, the way he reached for everybody, without deciding to.

There was nothing there.

He noticed it the way you notice a step that isn't where you expected it, and then forget it. There was a person walking about among the fourteen men in the high street, quite slowly, stopping, looking, and when he reached for the person there was nothing. No fear. No grief. No horror. Not even the cliff-edge thing he'd read in the witch with the bandages. Nothing at all. A gap in the morning shaped like somebody.

He didn't find it interesting.

He went back to the street.

After a while the feet came on. They went to the alley by the bookshop and stopped, and he heard two voices, low. Then one set of feet went away up the alley. Then the other set stood still in the road for a long time, and went back once to the gutter outside Scrivenshaft's.

Then they came towards him.

They came quite slowly, straight up the middle of the high street through the snow. Forty-one paces. He didn't count them. Somebody did.

They stopped at the foot of the post office steps.

Harry looked up.

There was a girl standing at the bottom of the steps in the snow with her hands in the pockets of a grey cardigan. She had straight brown hair, tied back. She had an ordinary face, the kind of face people didn't remember. She was looking at him.

He looked at her.

He looked at her the way he'd looked at the street and the handcart and the cat on the sill, and he reached for her, as he'd reached for everything all night, and found nothing. Nothing in her at all. Not even silence. Just a girl at the bottom of some steps with snow on her shoulders, in a cardigan, who'd come down from the lane.

There was nothing there that needed doing.

He smiled at her.

It was a perfectly nice smile. It was the one he used on shop assistants and train guards and Madam Pince and Mr Akhtar at the newsagent's. He'd been using it since he was six. It cost him nothing at all.

"I wouldn't stand so close to them, if I were you," he said pleasantly. "They're busy."

He took another bite of the apple.

She didn't move. He didn't mind. He'd gone back to the street.

He thought for a moment, watching the youngest laugh in the gutter, that she must be one of the villagers. Somebody from the passage, come down to look. Somebody's daughter.

He didn't wonder whose.
