## Chapter 74: Far Gone

He knew who she was by about four o'clock that afternoon.

It came back the way feeling comes back into a foot you've been sitting on, a little at a time and then all at once, and when it came he was sitting on the end of his camp bed in the projection room at the Majestic with his boots still on and the snow melted off them into two dark puddles on the floor, and she was sitting on the end of hers, opposite him, hands in her lap, watching him.

He didn't know how he'd got there.

He knew it in the ordinary way afterwards, because Ron told him. She'd stood at the foot of the post office steps in Hogsmeade for nine minutes. Then she'd gone up the steps and taken him by the arm, quite hard, the way she'd taken him by the collar in a drawing room in Wiltshire, and said *we're going now*, and he'd let her, because it was easier than not. She'd walked him up the lane between the hedges to the place where you could Apparate. He'd brought the apple core with him. He'd still had it in his hand when they landed in the alley.

He didn't remember any of it.

He remembered the step. He remembered the snow coming down, and the fourteen, and the flowers. He remembered a plain girl in a grey cardigan at the bottom of the steps whom he hadn't known, and had smiled at. And then he was sitting on a camp bed in Leeds at four in the afternoon, and the girl was sitting opposite him, and he looked at her, and she was Evelyn.

"Selwyn," he said.

She was quiet for a moment.

"Yes," she said.

"I didn't…" He stopped. "This morning. I didn't know you."

"No."

"I'm sorry."

She looked at him. He couldn't read her. He never could. He looked at her face and found nothing in it, as always, and for the first time in six years the nothing didn't feel like rest. It felt like a wall with something behind it he didn't want to see.

"It's all right," said Evelyn.

It was the first lie he'd ever caught her in. He knew it was a lie the way he knew when a step was missing. He didn't say so.

He put his glove back on. He'd been holding it in his left hand since Hogsmeade without knowing, and his right hand was still blue across the knuckles. He put the glove on, lay down on the camp bed with his boots on, turned his face to the wall, and was asleep before she'd moved.

* * *

The fourteen men stood in the high street at Hogsmeade for three days.

Harry learned that from the radio. Kingsley came on the pirate programme on the Saturday night, very late, with the password *Lockhart*, and spoke for four minutes in the deep slow voice, and the four of them sat round Ron's wireless on the floor of the projection room and listened.

The Order had tried to move them, said Kingsley. On the Thursday, and again on the Friday. Nobody could. They couldn't be woken. They couldn't be Stunned out of it or Enervated out of it, or even carried, because the moment anyone laid a hand on one of them he screamed, and went on screaming, and didn't stop until he was let go. Two Healers had come from St Mungo's on the Friday night in secret and gone away again white. There was no counter-charm. There was nothing there to counter. Whatever had been done to them, they were doing it to themselves now.

The snow had gone on falling, on and off, all Thursday and Friday.

On the Saturday morning, said Kingsley, the youngest of them had sat down in the gutter outside Scrivenshaft's, still holding his own wrist. By the afternoon he'd stopped laughing. By the evening the others had begun to sit down, one after another, in the snow.

None of them had got up.

The radio went quiet. Then Lee Jordan's voice came back, quite subdued, and read the names of the eleven villagers who'd died, and the name of Gilderoy Lockhart, Order of Merlin Third Class, who'd held the bridge, and the programme played a song and went off the air.

The projection room was very quiet.

Harry read them. He did it without deciding to, the way he did everything now. Ron was horrified, and the horror was aimed at the wireless, and beneath it, close to the top, he was trying very hard not to look across the floor at Harry. Hermione was horrified too, more quietly. And beneath the horror, a long way down, she was frightened, and the fear was aimed at Harry, and she hadn't let herself know it yet.

Evelyn was silent.

Harry reached for the wireless and turned it off.

"They burned Rosmerta's hands," he said.

Nobody answered him.

"They killed an old man with a lantern. The youngest one did. On the stream bank. It was his first. He liked it."

"Harry," said Hermione, very quietly.

"I'm only saying."

"I know what you're saying." Hermione's voice was quite steady. She had her hands flat on her knees. "I'm asking you not to say it like that."

He looked at her.

"Like what?"

Hermione didn't answer. She looked at him for some time across the projection-room floor, and then she got up and went down the stairs into the dark of the auditorium, and after a minute Ron went after her.

Harry sat on the floor by the wireless.

Evelyn hadn't moved. She was sitting on her camp bed with the stopped watch in her hand, as she sat most evenings now, and she was looking at him, and he couldn't read her.

He didn't try.

He got up and went down to the screen.

* * *

It went on like that for three weeks, and it worked.

That was what he'd remember about those weeks afterwards, when he tried to remember anything. Not what he felt. He didn't feel very much. He remembered that it all worked. Everything he did in those weeks worked better than anything he'd ever done.

They went out four times in the first week alone.

Theo's coin came every night now, sometimes twice, and Harry decoded it in thirty minutes instead of forty because he no longer needed to write the squares down. There was a safe house in Bradford, a terraced house on a back street off Manningham Lane, where three Death Eaters were keeping a Muggle-born family of five in the attic until the Commission wanted them. There was a Ministry warehouse on the river at Wapping, full of confiscated wands in numbered crates. There was a farm in Norfolk, out on the flat black fields beyond Swaffham, where somebody was keeping a werewolf in a barn and selling tickets.

Harry went in first every time, in a different face.

He didn't plan the faces any more. He didn't need to. He walked up to the door in Bradford as a tired postman with a parcel, and the Death Eater who opened it saw a tired postman with a parcel, and Harry walked past him and up the stairs whilst the man was still signing for it. He walked into the warehouse at Wapping as a night watchman with a torch, and the real night watchman, a bored Ministry wizard with a flask of tea, looked up and saw his own face coming towards him across the concrete, and sat with his mouth open whilst Harry took the keys off his belt. He crossed the farmyard in Norfolk at two in the morning as the farmer's own dog.

It worked.

All of it worked. The family of five in Bradford came down out of the attic, and the youngest, a girl of six called Shazia, asked Ron whether he was a policeman, and Ron said yes. The wands at Wapping went out in Hermione's bag, all three hundred and forty of them, and over the following week went back, by owl and coin and Bill Weasley's old boots, to the people they belonged to. The werewolf in Norfolk turned out to be a thin frightened man of forty called Dennis, who'd been bitten in 1971 and had a wife in Fakenham, and he wept in the back of the farmer's own van all the way to the A47.

Theo's next message said only *THEY ARE CALLING YOU THE OTHER ONE.*

Harry didn't know whether *they* meant the Death Eaters or the resistance. He found it didn't matter.

* * *

He forgot to take the face off on the ninth of March.

He came in through the fire door at a quarter past six in the morning after a raid on a house in Altrincham, alone, because he'd gone alone, and went up the stairs to the projection room and sat at the folding table and poured himself a cup from the pot Evelyn had made at six. Ron, climbing out of his sleeping bag on the other side of the table, looked at him and went for his wand.

"Who the *hell*…"

Harry looked up.

Ron had his wand out. It was pointing at Harry's face across the table, and Ron's face was white, and his hand was quite steady, which Harry noticed with something close to approval, because a year ago it wouldn't have been.

"It's me," said Harry.

"Prove it."

"I gave you the Cannons. In the eleventh row. You stood on your seat."

Ron stared at him for a long moment.

Then he slowly lowered the wand.

"Take it off," he said.

"Take what…"

"The *face*, Harry. Take it off. You've got some bloke's face on. Ginger moustache. Glasses. About fifty." Ron's voice wasn't quite steady, though his hand had been. "You're sitting at our table drinking our tea in some bloke's face and you don't even know."

Harry put his hand up to his face.

It felt like his face. It always did. It was only ever in other people's eyes. He reached for the illusion and found it, a thin steady thing he'd been holding on Ron and Hermione and the stairs and the auditorium and the whole building without noticing, since Altrincham, since four in the morning, for two and a quarter hours, the way you go on holding a cup after you've finished drinking.

He let it go.

Ron looked at him for a long time. Then he sat down heavily on the other side of the folding table, put his wand on it, and laid his hands flat beside it.

"Who was he?" said Ron.

"Who?"

"The bloke. The face."

Harry thought about it.

"I don't know," he said. "Somebody in Altrincham. He was on a bus."

Ron let it drop.

Harry read him. Ron was frightened. It wasn't loud. It was very quiet and very steady and aimed straight across the folding table at Harry, and beneath it, quite close to the top, Ron was grieving, and the grief was aimed at Harry too.

Harry didn't know what it was for.

He drank his tea.

* * *

Ron wanted to go home on the twelfth.

He said so at supper. They were eating sausages, because Harry still cooked when he was there, and he was there. The coin had gone warm at six with a message from Ginny, who'd left Hogwarts at Christmas and was at Muriel's. *DAD HURT. NOT BAD. RAID AT MURIEL'S. ALL MOVED. DON'T COME.*

Ron read it twice. Then he put down his fork.

"I'm going," he said.

"Ron," said Hermione.

"I'm going. I'm not asking. I'm telling you. Dad's hurt. They've been raided. They've moved, and I don't know where, and Mum'll be…" He stopped. "I'm going. Tonight. I'll find them. Bill'll know. I'll go to Bill's."

"It says don't come."

"I know what it says. Ginny always says don't come. She said don't come when I broke my leg."

"Ron, if they're being watched…"

"Then I'll be careful." Ron was on his feet, his face red. "I've been careful for seven months. I've been careful in a *cinema*. My dad's hurt and I'm sitting in a cinema in *Leeds* eating *sausages*."

Harry read him.

He was very loud. All of him. Fear, for his father and his mother and Ginny and the twins and all of them, scattered, raided, moved, nowhere. Homesickness, so large and so old now that it had stopped being a feeling and become a place he lived. And anger, hot and simple and Weasley, aimed at the cinema and the sausages and the war and at himself for being here.

And Ron was right. Harry could see that quite clearly. Ron was right that his family needed him and right that he wanted to go.

But they needed him here more. They had a raid planned for the fourteenth. A Commission holding centre in Sheffield. Twenty people. Ron was the only one of them who could fly the brooms in the dark without a light.

Harry didn't ask.

He didn't decide to. He didn't think it through. He reached across the folding table into Ron, the way he'd reached into twelve people on a bench in Courtroom Ten, and found the anger and the fear and the homesickness, all of it, very loud, and he turned it down.

Not off. Down. The way you turn down a wireless.

He took the anger and made it smaller. He took the fear and made it quieter. He went down through Ron to the place where Ron kept the plain stubborn Weasley calm that had stood on a chessboard at eleven and let itself be taken so a friend could go on, and he found it, and made it larger.

It took about two seconds.

Ron stood by the folding table with his face red. Then the red drained out of it. Not all at once. Slowly, the way colour goes out of a sky. He looked down at his plate.

"I…" said Ron.

He sat down.

He looked at his hands on the table, and then at the coin beside his plate, and then at Hermione.

"It says don't come," he said slowly. "Doesn't it."

"Yes," said Hermione.

"And they've moved. So if I went, I wouldn't even know where." He rubbed his face. "And Bill'll write. He always writes. If it was bad, Bill'd write." He looked at his sausages. "And we've got Sheffield. On the fourteenth."

"Yes," said Harry.

"Right." Ron picked up his fork. "Right. I'll wait for Bill."

He ate a sausage.

Hermione was looking at Harry.

She said nothing. She was looking at him across the folding table, quite steadily, her fork in her hand and her food going cold, and Harry read her and found that she'd seen it. She didn't know what she'd seen. She'd seen Ron stand up red and furious and sit down calm in two seconds, and she'd been at a chair in Courtroom Ten with the chains in her hand when twelve people stood up all at once as though somebody had pulled a string.

She said nothing.

Nor did Harry.

* * *

He did it to Hermione on the fourteenth.

He did it on the roof of a disused cutlery works in Sheffield at one in the morning, with the Commission's holding centre across the road in what had once been a Methodist chapel, twenty people in its basement and four Death Eaters at its doors. Hermione was frightened. She was always frightened before a raid now, since the Manor. It was a cold, tight, private fear, aimed at a drawing room with a chandelier in it and a woman's voice saying one word softly, and it made her hands shake.

She needed her hands not to shake. She was doing the wards.

So Harry made her unafraid.

It was easier than Ron. Her fear was quieter, and he went in under it, and took it, and put it somewhere she wouldn't find it until morning, and in its place he put something cool and steady and sure that he found further down in her, a girl of eleven on a train, very certain she knew every spell in the first-year book.

Her hands stopped shaking.

She did the wards in eleven seconds. Twenty people came up out of the basement of a Methodist chapel in Sheffield, and none of the four Death Eaters at its doors ever knew how.

Hermione didn't notice. Not that night.

She noticed on the sixteenth.

She came down to the screen at eleven at night in Ron's jumper with the sleeves over her hands and sat in the front row, where Evelyn sometimes sat, and watched him make a street in Lisbon for twenty minutes before she spoke.

"Harry."

"Mm."

"Can I ask you something?"

"Yes."

"On the roof. In Sheffield." She was looking at the screen, not at him. At the street in Lisbon, with its yellow trams and washing on the balconies. "Before the wards. Were you…" She stopped. "Did you do something? To me?"

Harry held the street.

He held it quite easily. A tram went down the hill. A woman leaned out of a third-floor window and took in a sheet.

"Yes," he said.

Hermione didn't move.

"What?"

"You were frightened. Your hands were shaking. You needed them not to." He made the tram stop at the bottom of the hill and let two people off. "So I took the fear and put it somewhere you wouldn't find it until morning. And I gave you something else to hold instead. From when you were eleven. On the train. You were very sure of yourself on the train."

"I was insufferable on the train."

"You were very sure of yourself."

A long silence. The woman on the third floor folded the sheet over her arm and went in.

"You didn't ask," said Hermione.

"No."

"Why not?"

Harry thought about it. He thought about it honestly, because she'd asked honestly, and because he didn't have anything to hide from her that he could find.

"Because you'd have said no," he said. "And then your hands would have shaken. And the wards would have taken a minute instead of eleven seconds. And one of the four on the door might have looked up." He let the street go all at once, and the screen went grey. "Twenty people came out of that basement, Hermione."

"I know they did."

"Then I don't understand what you're asking."

Hermione turned round in her seat and looked at him.

She looked at him a long while in the dark from the front row, with her hands inside the sleeves of Ron's jumper. Harry read her. She wasn't angry. He'd thought she might be. She was something much quieter than angry, and much sadder, and he didn't have the patience to go down and find out what.

"No," said Hermione at last. "I can see that you don't."

She got up and went back up the aisle.

At the top she stopped by the doors to the foyer, her hand on the brass plate.

"Ron?" she said. "On the twelfth? When he wanted to go?"

Harry didn't answer.

He didn't need to. She stood at the top of the aisle with her hand on the door a moment longer, then went through it, and he heard her climb the stairs quite slowly, one at a time. He went back to the screen and made Lisbon again from the beginning, with the trams.

* * *

He heard them on the night of the seventeenth.

He was at the screen. It was half past two. They thought he was at the screen and couldn't hear them, and in the ordinary way that was true. They were in the foyer at the far end of the building, by the old ticket booth with its brass grille, sitting on the stairs to the circle where Evelyn sometimes sat, talking quietly, and between them and Harry were two sets of double doors and a great deal of dark.

He didn't need to hear them.

He read them, and he could read more now than he used to. Not words. Not quite. But at peaks, when people felt something very strongly, a word would sometimes come up with the feeling, the way a stone comes up in a net. It had been like that since his second year. It was more like that now than it had ever been.

They were frightened.

Both of them. Quite loud. And it was aimed down the length of the building, through the doors and the dark, at the screen, at him.

*…on Thursday. Before Sheffield. I wasn't frightened. Ron, I wasn't frightened at all. I'm always frightened, since… and I wasn't, and I didn't know why, and then I…*

*…the twelfth. When I wanted to go. I was so angry, Hermione, I was going to go, I was going out the door, and then I just… wasn't. Just like that. And I thought it was me…*

*…the people in the courtroom. He told us. He told us what he did to them, he wasn't even…*

*…is he doing it to us?*

*…I don't know. I think so. I think he has been. I don't think he even…*

*…he had some bloke's face on, at breakfast. He didn't know. He didn't know he had it on…*

*…Hogsmeade…*

*…I keep thinking about Hogsmeade…*

*…I'm frightened of him, Ron.*

*…yeah. Me too.*

Harry stood below the screen and read them, through two sets of doors and the whole length of a dead cinema. Two people he'd sat with at a wedding. Two people who'd stood either side of another Harry in another world without looking at each other first. He read that they were frightened of him and right to be, and that they were grieving for something, and that the something was him.

He didn't mind.

He looked for minding, carefully, and it wasn't there. They were frightened, and they were right, and it didn't matter, because he was keeping them alive, and they were still here, and Sheffield had worked.

He went back to the screen.

He made rain. He was very good at rain now.

* * *

Evelyn didn't talk to him, and he didn't talk to Evelyn.

He didn't decide it. He'd have said, if anyone had asked, that nothing had changed. He went out on raids, and she came on some of them and stood beside him at doors and told him when a face was slipping, which it never was now. He cooked sausages, and she ate them. She made tea at six and he drank it. They passed each other on the projection-room stairs a dozen times a day.

He didn't look at her.

He couldn't read her. He never had been able to. For six years that had been what drew him, the one silence in a world full of noise, the place he went to rest. He didn't want to rest. He didn't want silence. He'd stopped looking at anything he couldn't read, the way you stop looking at the sun, and he hadn't noticed he'd stopped.

And when he did look at her, which wasn't often, he didn't like what he saw.

It wasn't anything in her face. There was never anything in her face. It was the way she looked back. She looked at him, across the projection room or the folding table or the dark of the auditorium, the way she'd looked at him at the foot of the post office steps. As though she could see something he couldn't.

She could.

She was the only person in the world his illusions had never touched. She saw him as he was, every time, whatever face he had on, whatever he was holding on whom. She'd seen the polite stranger's face from Altrincham at the folding table, and Harry through it. She'd seen fourteen men in the snow, and no flowers.

He didn't want to know what she saw.

So he didn't look.

* * *

Evelyn had counted.

She sat on the end of her camp bed in the projection room at eleven o'clock on the night of the eighteenth of March, the red notebook open on her knee and the stopped watch in her other hand, and counted again, to be sure.

Nineteen days.

He'd said her name on the twenty-sixth of February, at four in the afternoon, on the camp bed opposite. *Selwyn.* He hadn't said it since. He'd said *we're going in at two* and *Bradford* and *they're on the second floor* and *thank you* for the tea. He hadn't said *Selwyn*, or *Evelyn*, or anything at all that was meant for her and not for whoever else was in the room.

Nineteen days.

She'd tried everything she knew.

She'd made a list. It was on the previous page. She'd written it out on the second of March and added to it every night since, crossing things out as she tried them, one line through each, neatly, so she could still read what it had been.

*Talk to him.* She'd tried, on the first, the fourth, the seventh. He'd answered every question she asked, quite politely, and hadn't been there.

*Leave him alone.* She'd tried. For four days. He hadn't noticed.

*Make him angry.* She'd told him on the ninth, at the folding table, that the illusion of the farmer's dog in Norfolk had had the wrong number of legs for a full second as it crossed the yard, which was true. He'd said *thank you, I'll watch that*, and hadn't been angry at all.

*Go with him.* She'd gone on every raid he'd let her go on. She'd stood at doors.

*Follow him.* On the eleventh she'd begun following him when he went out alone. He hadn't known. She'd stood in a bus shelter in Altrincham in the rain at four in the morning and watched a man with a ginger moustache come out of a house and walk away down the road, and known it was Potter by the way he held his shoulders, and known he didn't know she was there.

*Tell Weasley and Granger.* She hadn't needed to. They knew. She'd heard them on the stairs.

*Write to somebody.* There was nobody to write to. Her grandfather was dead. Dumbledore was dead. Sirius was dead. Professor McGonagall was at Hogwarts with the Carrows and couldn't be reached. She'd sat with the pen over a clean page for a long time on the fourteenth and couldn't think of one single person alive who could do anything.

All crossed out.

She turned the page.

There was one thing left.

She'd known it was there for some time. She'd known it since a staircase at Hogsmeade, since a gap in the morning shaped like somebody, since the moment he'd looked at her from the post office step and smiled the smile he used on Madam Pince. She'd known it, and hadn't written it down, because writing it down would make it something that could be done.

She wrote it down.

It was one line. Only a few words. She wrote it in her small square hand at the top of a clean page, under the date, and looked at it.

She looked at it for some minutes.

It was the most frightening thing she'd ever written. She'd written *Justin Finch-Fletchley* and a time. She'd written *My grandfather is dead*. She'd written once, at twenty-one minutes past two in the morning in the library in her seventh year, *I am frightened for Potter*, and underlined it. This was worse than any of them. She didn't know what would happen if she did it. Nobody did. Nobody had ever done it. She'd been told every morning from the age of five, by a woman she'd loved more than anyone, that she must never, ever, under any circumstances, do it.

She drew a line through it.

It wasn't a neat line. It went through the words and out the other side and across the page, and the nib caught on the paper and tore it a little at the end.

She closed the notebook and put it under her pillow with the watch.

She lay down on the camp bed with her face to the wall, and didn't sleep, and listened for him to come up the stairs.

He came up at ten past four. She heard him lie down. She heard his breathing slow.

She didn't take the notebook out again.

She didn't need to. She could see the line in the dark with her eyes shut. She could see it quite clearly, and the words beneath it, and the small tear at the end where her hand had pressed too hard.

She noted that she hadn't made it illegible.

* * *

Severus Snape read the reports at the headmaster's desk at a quarter to one in the morning by the light of a single candle, as he read everything now.

The office was very quiet. The silver instruments on the spindle-legged tables had stopped whirring at midnight, as they always did, though nobody had ever told him why. The Sorting Hat was asleep on its shelf. Fawkes's perch was empty. On the walls the portraits of the headmasters and headmistresses of Hogwarts slept or pretended to, chins on their chests, and Phineas Nigellus snored, and Dilys Derwent muttered.

Behind the desk, in a plain dark wooden frame, Albus Dumbledore slept with his hands folded and his half-moon spectacles on the end of his nose.

He'd been asleep for eight months.

Snape didn't look at him. He didn't need to. He knew exactly where the frame was. He knew it the way you know where the window is in a room you've lived in a long time, by the draught.

He read the reports.

There were seven of them. They'd come in the usual ways, which weren't ways anybody else in the building knew about. A letter from Yaxley, who now ran the Commission's investigators and wrote like a man filling in a form. A note from Rowle's widow, very short, asking whether the school could tell her anything about how her husband had died, because nobody at the Ministry would. A copy of a report from two Healers at St Mungo's who'd gone to Hogsmeade in secret on a Friday night and written down very carefully, in the plain language of people trying not to scream, what they'd found standing in the snow.

*No external enchantment detected. No curse. No residue. No counter possible. In our opinion each subject is experiencing a single traumatic memory as present reality, repeatedly, without remission. The memory appears to have been located within the subject and released. The mechanism by which it repeats is unknown to us. Any attempt at physical contact results in extreme distress. We were unable to assist. We recommend that nobody else be sent.*

They'd died on the Saturday, of cold. All fourteen. Sitting in the snow.

There was a report from the Ministry about a Death Eater called Selby, who'd been taken in a raid on a house in Bradford on the second of March and found two days later, on the fourth, sitting in a public lavatory at Leeds railway station with his back against the wall. He'd told the Aurors who found him everything. Every name. Every safe house. Every meeting. He'd told them in a calm, clear, helpful voice, for nine hours without stopping, and when they'd finished asking, he'd turned round and begun telling it all again, to the wall.

He was in St Mungo's now. He talked to the wall of his room. He was quite happy. He didn't know anyone else was there.

Snape put the reports down.

He sat at the desk with his hands flat on the papers and looked at the candle.

He thought about a boy of eleven in the Great Hall, under the Sorting Hat, with his mother's eyes.

He thought about a boy of fourteen in his office, in a lesson meant to teach him to close his mind, who hadn't closed it, who'd gone the other way, who'd come into Snape's own head uninvited, as nobody ever had, and read what was there. Read it. Not seen it. *Felt* it. A playground. A girl on a swing. Felt what Snape had felt, from the inside, as though it were his.

Snape had thrown him out of the room and never forgiven him.

He thought about a courtyard last June at the foot of the tower. About standing in it alone, thinking himself unseen, looking up at the parapet and unable to close. About turning round and finding the boy on the low wall by the greenhouse gate, looking at him. Reading him. And about the boy's face afterwards. It had changed. It had trusted him. It had trusted him completely from that moment, without a word, and gone on trusting him, and the doe had gone to the cinema in Leeds four times since October, and every time the boy had said *thank you* to it, quietly, in the dark. Snape knew. The doe told him.

He thought about the Astronomy Tower in April of last year.

It had been a moonless night. Albus had asked him to come up, and he'd come, and Albus had shut the door at the top of the stairs and stood at the parapet in the dark, silent for a while. Then he'd said it.

Snape had refused.

He'd refused for an hour. He'd never once in sixteen years refused Albus Dumbledore anything that mattered, and he'd refused this, on a tower, in the dark, for an hour, over and over, until Albus turned from the parapet and looked at him, and Snape saw in his face that he was afraid. Not of dying. He'd already decided how he'd die. Of something else.

*If he becomes what Tom became*, Albus had said, *you will have to stop him. I could not stop Gellert in time. Do not make my mistake.*

Snape had said yes.

He'd said it because Albus was afraid, and he'd never seen Albus afraid of anything, and because he hadn't believed, then, that it would ever come to anything. A boy of sixteen. A boy who felt sick looking at a memory of Tom Riddle at eleven. A boy who'd cried in Albus's office at fourteen, Albus said, over a Hufflepuff he'd barely known.

Snape looked at the reports.

Fourteen men in the snow, until they died of cold. A man who talked to a wall.

*The memory appears to have been located within the subject and released.*

He thought about the Dark Lord at sixteen, in the headmaster's office in Dippet's time, being charming. He'd heard the stories. Everybody in Slytherin had. He thought about the Dark Lord at sixty-nine on a lawn, taking a wand out of a dead man's hand very gently, the way you'd take a toy from a sleeping child.

He thought about Lily's eyes.

They were in that face. They'd always been in that face. He'd looked at them across a classroom for six years and hated the face they were in and been unable to look away, and they'd looked back at him from the low wall by the greenhouse gate, trusting him, and they were looking now, from a step in the snow in Hogsmeade, at fourteen men freezing to death, and they were perfectly calm.

He looked up at the frame behind the desk.

Albus was asleep, hands folded, spectacles on the end of his nose. He'd been asleep for eight months. Phineas said he hadn't woken once, and Phineas was a liar, but not about that.

"You were right," Snape told the sleeping portrait.

His voice was quite flat.

The portrait didn't wake. Its chest rose and fell very slightly under the painted midnight-blue robes. Snape watched it for a long moment. He didn't know whether it was asleep, or pretending, or whether a portrait could pretend. He'd never asked.

He didn't want to know.

He took a clean sheet of parchment from the drawer, dipped his pen, and held it over the page.

He sat like that for some time.

Then he began to write, in a small cramped hand quite unlike his usual one, a message that a doe would carry.

## Chapter 75: The Shrieking Shack

The doe came for the fifth time on the night of Sunday the twenty-second of March, at ten past one, and it didn't come to warn him of anything.

Harry was below the screen. He'd stopped making anything on it some time before. He was standing in the orchestra pit with his hands in his pockets and the grey canvas in front of him, doing nothing, which he did more and more now between raids, for an hour at a time. He didn't think about anything when he did it. He was simply there.

The doe came through the left-hand wall by the side boxes, as it always did, walked down the side aisle, stopped in front of the screen, and looked at him.

He read it.

He didn't have to. He knew what it was made of. He read it anyway, because he always did, and it was the same as it had been every time. One love, very old, kept in a very small closed place, aimed at a girl with red hair.

It was the same.

He'd think afterwards that he ought to have noticed it was the same. That a man who'd decided to do what this man had decided to do would have had something else in him somewhere, and it would have got into the doe. It hadn't. The doe was made of the love, and the love hadn't changed in twenty years, and it didn't change now.

The doe opened its mouth.

"Tuesday," it said, in the flat colourless voice made not to be recognised. "Midnight. The Shrieking Shack. Come by the village side, through the back, the door to the old kitchen. Come alone. Bring the Cloak."

Harry didn't move.

"He knows where it is," said the doe. "Not the place. The house. He has had it from a prisoner. He will have the cinema by Friday. The Cloak must not be there when he comes. I will take it somewhere he will not look. Come alone. Tell nobody. If you tell anybody, he will have it from them, as he had the cinema."

It stood a moment longer.

Then it walked into the screen and stood there, silver on the grey, and faded from the edges in, the way it always did.

Harry stood in the orchestra pit.

He thought about it. He thought about it clearly and calmly, the way he thought about everything now. A prisoner had talked. That was quite possible. There'd been a great many prisoners. Selby had talked to the Aurors for nine hours. Somebody, somewhere, in some cellar, had talked about a cinema in Leeds. And the Dark Lord had two of the three, and wanted the third more than he'd wanted anything since a door in a dark round room, and the third was folded into a small square in the inside pocket of Harry's coat.

He thought about a courtyard at the foot of a tower last June.

He thought about a man standing alone in it, looking up at a parapet, unable to close.

He thought about a wand held out across a tower roof without a word.

He trusted it.

He told nobody. That was easy. He'd stopped telling anybody anything three weeks ago, and nobody had noticed, except perhaps the one person he didn't look at.

* * *

He went on Tuesday at a quarter past eleven.

He didn't go up to the projection room to say he was going. He went out through the foyer, past the ticket booth with its brass grille, past the stairs to the circle where nobody was sitting, and out of the fire door into the alley. It was raining, the thin cold steady rain of Leeds in March, and it had been raining for four days.

He didn't look up at the small square windows of the projection room as he went.

If he had, he wouldn't have seen anything. The projection room was dark. Ron was asleep. Hermione was asleep. And the camp bed in the far corner by the projectors had a shape on it under a blanket, face to the wall, quite still, which would stay quite still until Ron got up at seven and found it was two pillows and a rolled-up cardigan.

Harry didn't know that.

He turned on the spot in the rain.

* * *

He came out at the end of the lane that ran past the Shrieking Shack, on the far side of Hogsmeade from the high street, where the village gave up and the hill began.

There was no rain here. It was very cold and very clear, with a moon nearly full, and the frost lay white on the long grass of the hill and on the brambles and the broken fence round the Shack's overgrown garden. Below him to the left the village lay dark. He could see the high street from here, a long pale line between black roofs, with the bridge at the bottom and the post office at the top.

There was nobody in the high street now.

He didn't look at it for long.

The Shack stood at the top of its garden, black against the frost. It was as he remembered it. He'd been inside it once, at thirteen, in the dark, at the end of a tunnel, with a man who wasn't yet his godfather and a rat with a toe missing, and a werewolf and a Potions master and a girl he couldn't read. The windows were boarded. The roof sagged. The chimney leaned. It had been the most haunted house in Britain for twenty-five years because a boy had screamed in it once a month, and the boy was a man now, somewhere in the north among the packs, sending messages on a coin signed R.L.

Harry went round to the back.

There was a door to the old kitchen, as the doe had said. It hung off one hinge. It had been forced a long time ago and nobody had ever mended it. He pushed it, and it went in with a long low scrape like the fire door at the Majestic, and he went through into the dark.

He reached ahead of him as he went.

He found the house empty. Rats in the walls, small and frightened and hungry. An owl in the roof. Nothing else. No people. No feeling anywhere in the house, from cellar to attic, except the rats and the owl.

And in the front room upstairs, the one with the four-poster bed, the one he remembered, there was nothing.

Not empty. Nothing. The particular nothing he'd felt every day for seven years in the Great Hall at the staff table, at the front of a dungeon classroom, across a desk in an office lined with jars. A closed mind. Very closed. Closed the way a door is closed when somebody's leaning on it from the other side.

It ought to have warned him.

He'd think that afterwards, many times. He'd read this man closed for seven years and open exactly twice. He'd read him open in a courtyard with grief, and open on a tower with permission, and both times it had been because something had happened to him that was too large to hold the door against. He'd trusted the man because of those two times. And now the man was in a room at the top of the stairs, waiting for him, and the door was shut and leaned on, harder than Harry had ever felt it.

He went up the stairs.

* * *

Severus Snape was standing by the boarded window.

There was a candle on the floor, the only light. It stood in the middle of the dusty boards between the door and the four-poster and threw Snape's shadow up the wall behind him and across the ceiling, very tall and very thin. He was in black, as he always was. His hands were folded in front of him. He didn't have his wand out.

He looked older. Harry hadn't seen him since a courtyard in June, nine months ago, and he looked ten years older, and much thinner, and his face was the colour of the candle.

"Potter," he said.

"Professor."

"You came alone."

"Yes."

"You brought it."

Harry put his hand on the inside pocket of his coat. He didn't take the Cloak out.

"Yes."

Snape looked at him.

He looked at him for a long moment across the candle from the window. Harry reached for him out of habit and found the door, shut, and the weight on the other side of it. Nothing came through. Nothing at all.

"Sit down," said Snape.

"I'll stand."

"As you like." Snape didn't move from the window. "I am going to say some things. It will take about a minute. Then we will do what we came here to do." He paused. "I would be obliged if you did not interrupt. I have been thinking for some days about how to say them, and I would like to say them in the right order."

Harry waited.

"Your mother," said Snape, "was the best person I ever knew."

The candle burned. Somewhere in the walls a rat moved.

"You know that. You've known it since your fourth year, when you came into my head in a lesson that was meant to teach you to keep people out of yours, and took it. You didn't see it. Anybody can see a memory. You felt it. What I felt for her. You were the first person who ever did, and I have never forgiven you for it, and I never will." He said it quite flatly, as though reading out a list. "I mention it so you will understand that I know what you are. I knew before Albus did. I have watched it grow in you for seven years, in my classroom and my house, with her eyes in your face. I have known exactly what you could do since you were eleven."

He took a breath.

"Albus knew too. He was afraid of it. He was afraid of very few things, and he was afraid of you. He told me so. On the tower. In April of last year." Snape's eyes didn't leave Harry's face. "He asked me to do something, if it came to it. I said no. I said no for an hour. I didn't believe it would ever come to it. I thought he was a tired old man who had seen one boy go wrong and was seeing ghosts."

He looked at Harry.

"I have read the reports from Hogsmeade," said Snape. "I have read what the Healers wrote. I have read about Selby, who talks to the wall. I have read that the Dark Lord's people are calling you *the other one*, and I have thought about what they mean by it, and I think they are right."

Harry kept silent.

He didn't feel anything. He noticed that. He stood in the candlelight in the room with the four-poster bed and heard the man who'd held out a wand across a tower roof tell him that the Dark Lord's people were right about him, and he looked for what he felt about it, and there was nothing there.

He thought that was probably what Snape was talking about.

"You were the boy who felt sick," said Snape. "Albus told me. When he showed you Tom at eleven, in the orphanage, you felt sick. He said that was the difference. That was the whole of it. What you felt about the people in the way." He unfolded his hands. "What did you feel, Potter, on the step? At Hogsmeade? Watching them?"

Harry thought about it honestly.

"Nothing," he said.

"No," said Snape. "I thought not."

He drew his wand from his sleeve.

He did it quite slowly. He didn't point it at Harry. He held it loosely at his side and looked at Harry across the candle with his black eyes, and for one second, less, the door in him moved, a crack, and through the crack Harry felt what was on the other side of it, leaning.

It was grief.

Not for Harry. For her. For a girl on a swing. It had been made larger tonight than Harry had ever felt it, larger than in the courtyard, larger than in the doe, and it was aimed at the green eyes in Harry's face, and it was saying goodbye.

Then the door shut again.

"I am going to take it away from you," said Severus Snape. "All of it. The reading. The illusions. Every door you have. I am going to go into your head and close them, one after another, from the inside, the way I have closed my own every day for twenty years, and I am going to lock them, and I am going to break the keys. When I have finished, you will never feel another person again. Not one. Not ever. You will be what everyone else is." He raised the wand. "And then I am going to take the Cloak and burn it, so that he never has it. And then you can go home."

Harry understood.

He understood all of it at once, quite clearly, standing in the candlelight. The doe, the same as always, because the love in it was the same as always and always would be. The message. *He will have the cinema by Friday.* Perhaps true, perhaps not. *Come alone. Tell nobody.* The courtyard. The tower. *If he becomes what Tom became.*

He understood, and he felt nothing about it, and he reached for his wand.

"*Legilimens*," said Snape.

* * *

It wasn't like the lessons.

He'd had lessons in his fifth year, in Snape's office, and they'd been duels, and he'd won one of them and been thrown out of the room for it. In the lessons Snape had come into his head the way a man comes into a house to look for something, quickly, opening drawers, and Harry had learned to go the other way, back down the line into Snape's own house, and open his.

Snape wasn't looking for anything.

He came into Harry's head the way a man comes into a house to shut it up for the winter.

He went straight to the doors.

Harry felt him go. He felt him walk in, very cold and very quick, past everything, past the cupboard under the stairs and the Sorting and the Chamber and the graveyard and the lawn, past every memory Harry had, without stopping to look at a single one, the way you walk past furniture in a house you're closing, to the back of the house, where the doors were.

Harry had never known there were doors.

He knew now. He felt Snape find them. There was one for the reading, the oldest, the one that had always been open, that he'd never once in his life closed or even known could be closed. There was one beside it for the push. There was one, newer and much larger, for the illusions. There were others. Small ones. Ones he didn't know the names of. They were all open. They'd always been open. That was what he was.

Snape put his hand on the first one and began to close it.

* * *

Harry fought.

He fought the way he fought everything now, without feeling, very fast, very hard. He threw a wall in front of the doors, a wall of the Majestic, red plush and gilt and the faces of women with stars in their hair, and Snape walked through it as though it weren't there, because it wasn't, and he knew it.

He threw a crowd. Two hundred people in Diagon Alley in the rain, every one of them different, walking between Snape and the doors. Snape walked through them too. He didn't look at them. A crowd is weak and full of holes, and Snape went through the holes.

He threw Lily.

He didn't decide to. He was losing, and he reached for the strongest thing he had, and the strongest thing he had was in the man in front of him. He took the girl on the swing out of a memory he'd stolen at fourteen and put her between Snape and the doors, at eleven, laughing, her red hair flying.

Snape stopped.

For one second, less, he stopped in the back of Harry's head and looked at her.

Then he went past her.

He went past her the way you go past a photograph of someone you've loved on the wall of a house you're closing, without stopping, because if you stop you'll never finish. Harry felt him go past. He felt what it cost. It cost more than anything Harry had ever felt anyone pay, and Snape paid it, and kept walking, and put his hand back on the door.

The first door began to close.

Harry felt it go. It didn't hurt. That was the worst thing. It was quiet and slow and didn't hurt at all. He felt the world begin to go quiet round him. Not the room. Further out. The owl in the roof went first. Then the rats in the walls. Small things at the edges going out like the lights of a town seen from a train, one after another, into the dark. He reached for the owl, and it wasn't there. He reached for the rats, and they weren't there.

He did the only thing left.

He went the other way.

He went back down the line into Snape's head, the way he had in his fifth year, the way that had won him a lesson and lost him a teacher. He went to find the worst night. Everybody had one. It was at the bottom. It was always behind a door they'd shut and walked away from. He'd open it, and take the end off it, and Snape would stand in this room until he died of cold.

He found it at once.

Not at the bottom, and not behind any door. A lake shore on a bright day, and a word said in anger to a girl with red hair, and her face as she heard it. And it was standing wide open at the very front of Snape's mind, where anybody could see it, where Snape could see it every time he turned round.

He'd never shut it.

He'd looked at it every day for twenty-two years. He'd walked past it every morning on his way to everything else. It had no end because it had never had an end, and Snape had never needed one, because Snape had never once tried to get away from it.

There was nothing to open.

Harry couldn't use it. He stood at the front of Snape's mind with the worst night of Snape's life in front of him, wide open, and there was nothing he could do with it that Snape hadn't already done to himself, every day, on purpose, for twenty-two years.

Snape knew who he was.

That was the thing. Harry understood it standing there. Snape was weaker than he was, much weaker, in every way that could be measured. But Snape knew exactly who he was, and what he'd done, and what it had cost, and he'd looked at all of it every day, and he was standing on all of it. And Harry had built a cinema, and a crowd, and fourteen men in the snow, and a stranger's face at breakfast, and he'd gone into every one of them so far that there was nothing left in the middle to stand on.

He had no centre.

Snape found that before Harry did.

He felt Snape find it, and turn back to the doors, and close the first one all the way.

* * *

Harry was on the floor.

He didn't remember falling. He was on his knees on the dusty boards beside the candle with his hands flat on the floor and his wand somewhere he couldn't see, and the room was very quiet.

The reading was going.

Not gone. Going. He could still feel Snape a little, through the door Snape had left open in himself to come through. He couldn't feel the owl, or the rats, or the village below, or anything beyond the walls of the room. It was like going deaf. It was like the whole world going deaf at once. He'd never in his life been in a room where he couldn't feel the next room.

Snape was standing over him. He could see the hem of the black robes. He could see the wand, held quite steady, pointing down.

The second door was closing.

Harry reached for anything at all.

And something went past.

It went past him in the dark at the back of his head, in the house being shut up for the winter, very quick. Not his. One of Snape's, shaken loose by the fighting, the way a picture comes off a wall when someone slams a door. It was a memory. It went past like a lit window going past a train.

A tower. A moonless night. The door at the top of the stairs shut. An old man at the parapet with his back to the room, white hair, hands on the stone.

*If he becomes what Tom became,* said Albus Dumbledore quietly, without turning round, *you will have to stop him.*

The window went past.

Harry was on his knees on the floor of the Shrieking Shack, and he couldn't feel the owl, and he couldn't feel the rats, and he understood that he was going to be stopped, and that Dumbledore had asked for it, and he found, looking for it, that he didn't feel anything about that either.

His face was going empty.

He could feel it go. Not the face in other people's eyes. His own. From the inside. The way you feel your face go when you're falling asleep at a table, your mouth slack, your eyes no longer looking at anything.

The third door began to close.

* * *

Evelyn had been in the passage under the stairs for eleven minutes.

She'd followed him from the Majestic. She'd followed him for three weeks now, every time he went out alone, and he hadn't known once. She'd been on the camp bed with her face to the wall at a quarter past eleven, as she was every night, listening, and she'd heard him come up from the screen and stop in the foyer and go out of the fire door, and she'd been off the bed and down the stairs with her wand and her coat before the door had finished closing, leaving two pillows and a rolled-up cardigan under the blanket.

She'd held his sleeve in the alley as he turned on the spot.

He hadn't felt it. She'd made very sure he wouldn't. She'd touched only the very edge of the cuff, with two fingers, from behind, in the rain, at the exact moment he turned, the way her brother had taught her to take a sweet out of somebody's pocket when she was eight. She'd come with him, side by side in the dark, and landed at the end of a lane on a hill above Hogsmeade, and let go, and stepped back into the shadow of a hedge, and he'd never once looked round.

She'd watched him go into the Shack.

She'd waited four minutes. Then she'd gone in after him, through the kitchen door off its hinge, and up as far as the turn of the stairs, and stopped there in the dark with her back to the wall and her wand in her hand, and listened.

She'd heard Snape.

She'd heard every word. She'd stood on the stairs in the dark of the Shrieking Shack and heard Severus Snape say *your mother was the best person I ever knew*, and *Albus was afraid of you*, and *what did you feel, Potter, on the step*, and Potter say *nothing*.

She'd heard *I am going to take it away from you. All of it.*

She hadn't moved.

She'd stood with her back to the wall and her wand in her hand and thought, very clearly and very fast, that this was what she'd crossed out. That Snape was going to do what she couldn't bring herself to do, from the other side. That if Snape closed every door in Potter's head, Potter would never again make fourteen men stand in the snow until they died. He'd never again move Weasley's feelings round like furniture. He'd never again sit on a step and look at her and not know who she was.

She'd thought it might be the right thing.

She'd thought it for eleven minutes.

Then she heard Potter fall.

* * *

She went up the last six stairs and stood in the doorway.

The candle was on the floor in the middle of the room. Snape stood over Potter with his wand pointing down. Potter was on his knees on the boards beside the candle with his hands flat on the floor, and his head had come up, and he was looking at nothing.

She looked at his face.

She'd looked at his face for six and a half years. She'd looked at it when he was eleven and lying to her about a troll, and twelve and frightened for her, and thirteen in another world, and fourteen in a locked classroom saying *you're the only person I can't read*. She'd looked at it on a step in the snow, smiling at her as though she were a stranger. She knew every single thing it did.

It wasn't doing any of them.

In front of her eyes it was going empty. Not the way it went when he was holding an illusion, the small careful stillness she'd learned to see through. Not the way it had been on the step, which was a face with nothing behind it that was still, in its way, his. This was something else. This was a face going out like a candle when the wax is all gone. His mouth was slack. His eyes were open and fixed on a place on the floorboards a foot in front of him, and they weren't looking at it. They weren't looking at anything. There was nobody behind them doing the looking.

It wasn't an illusion. She'd have seen through an illusion.

It was real.

She knew one spell that would end it.

She'd never cast it. She'd never wanted to. She'd heard about it from Potter on the floor of a classroom on the fourth floor at two in the morning a year ago, in the dark, whilst she sat beside him for an hour and eleven minutes and he told her everything. A spell from the margin of a book. *For enemies.* A bathroom full of red water, and a boy going quiet. And a man kneeling in the water, singing a counter-curse three times, who'd written it in the margin in the first place.

She didn't think about it.

She'd think afterwards, many times, that she ought to have. That there must have been some other way, some spell, some word, some way of putting herself between them. She'd lie awake and go through them all, every spell she'd ever learned, in order, the way she went through everything. She wouldn't find one fast enough.

She didn't think about any of them then.

She raised her wand.

"*Sectumsempra*," said Evelyn.

* * *

It was very quick.

Snape went over sideways. He went over the way a tree goes over, all at once, without bending, and hit the floor beside the four-poster with a sound that shook the dust off the curtains. His wand flew out of his hand and rolled away across the boards and stopped against the leg of the bed.

He didn't get up.

Something had opened in him, in several places at once. Evelyn saw it and looked away and made herself look back. There was a great deal of it, very dark in the candlelight, spreading quite quickly across the dusty boards round him in no particular shape.

She didn't look at it again.

She looked at Potter.

He was still on his knees. But his head had moved. His eyes had come up off the floorboards. They'd gone to the man on the floor beside the bed, and they were looking at him, and there was somebody behind them doing it.

Snape's eyes were open.

He lay on his back with his head turned on the boards towards Potter. His face was the colour of the candle, and then whiter, and his mouth was moving. Something was coming out of him. Not blood. Something silver. It was coming from the corners of his eyes, and from his ears, and from his mouth, in thin bright threads, like smoke, like water, like neither, lying on the air above the floor and drifting.

Potter crawled to him.

He did it on his hands and knees, across the boards, through the dust, round the candle. He knelt beside Snape. Snape's hand came up off the floor, very slowly, and took hold of the front of Potter's coat, and held it.

"Look," said Snape.

It was barely a voice. Evelyn heard it from the doorway. The voice of a man with almost nothing left to say it with.

"Look at me."

Potter looked at him.

He looked down into Snape's face from a foot away in the candlelight with Snape's hand on his coat, and Snape looked up. He looked up into Potter's eyes, quite steadily, for a long moment. Evelyn couldn't see what he saw there. She knew whose eyes they were. She knew what colour they were. She knew who'd had them first.

Snape's hand went loose on Potter's coat.

It didn't fall. It stayed there on the cloth with the fingers still curled, but there was nothing holding it there any more. His eyes stayed open. They stayed on Potter's face. The silver went on drifting up out of them, very slowly, and hanging in the air.

He didn't look away.

He wouldn't now.

* * *

Evelyn stood in the doorway.

She was still holding her wand. It was still raised. It was pointing at the place where Severus Snape had been standing a minute ago, by the candle, over Potter, and there was nobody standing there now, and she hadn't lowered it.

She looked at her hand.

It was her right hand. It was holding a wand of pear wood, eleven inches, quite rigid, which she'd bought in Diagon Alley at eleven, the week after a gold watch was put into her other hand by a woman she loved. She'd used it every day for eight and a half years. She'd used it to light lamps and mend books and do her Charms homework and take a lock off a ship and throw wands across the floor of a courtroom. She'd used it once to still a cup of water in the air, and the whole of a box full of darkness.

She'd used it just now to kill a man.

She looked at the hand holding it.

It was quite steady.

She noted that. She noted it from a very long way off, from somewhere at the far end of a corridor in her own head she hadn't known was there, where she seemed to be standing, quite calmly, taking notes. *Twenty-four March nineteen ninety-eight. The Shrieking Shack. The upstairs front room. Eleven minutes past midnight. Severus Snape.* She noted that the candle was guttering. She noted that the silver was still coming. She noted that Potter hadn't moved.

She noted that her hand was perfectly steady.

She didn't lower it.
