## Chapter 76: Open

Evelyn began to shake at fourteen minutes past twelve.

She noted the time. She'd always note the time. She noted it from the far end of the corridor in her own head, where she seemed to be standing, and she noted that she was standing in the doorway of the upstairs front room of the Shrieking Shack with her wand still raised, and that her hand, which had been perfectly steady for three minutes, wasn't steady any more.

It began in the hand.

It was a small movement at first, a fine quick trembling at the tip of the wand, so that its point drew tiny circles on the air above the place where Severus Snape had been standing. Then it went up her arm. Then it was in her shoulders, and her knees, and her teeth.

She lowered the wand.

It didn't help. She stood in the doorway with the wand at her side and shook. Her whole body shook in long hard shudders that came up from her feet, and she couldn't stop them, and she didn't know what they were.

She'd never shaken in her life.

She hadn't shaken when she was five years old and her grandmother sat her down in the east wing at Selwyn Hall and taught her to close a door she'd never open again. She hadn't shaken in the Chamber, or in the other world, or in a lay-by on the A49 at four in the afternoon holding an old man's hand, or on a staircase in Nurmengard. She hadn't shaken in Courtroom Ten with her father looking at her. She hadn't shaken in a walled courtyard at the foot of a tower, holding a room still for four minutes whilst a boy died inside it. She'd cried afterwards, for twenty-two minutes. She hadn't shaken.

She was shaking now.

She noted it. She noted that it was very strange, and didn't seem to have anything to do with her, and that she couldn't make it stop by noting it.

She noted that she'd killed a man.

* * *

Harry got up.

He did it slowly, the way you get up when you've been kneeling a long time and your knees have stiffened. Snape's hand slid off the front of his coat as he rose. It didn't fall. It slid, and turned over, and lay on the dusty boards palm up, the fingers a little curled.

Harry stood and looked down at him.

The room was very quiet. It was quieter than any room Harry had ever been in. He noticed that vaguely, the way you notice a clock has stopped without knowing which clock. He couldn't feel the owl in the roof. He couldn't feel the rats in the walls. He couldn't feel anything beyond the walls of the room at all, and inside them there was Snape, who was nothing now, the place where a person had been, and there was the doorway, where there'd always been nothing, and there was Harry.

He didn't reach for anything. He didn't think to.

He looked at Snape's face.

It was turned up to the ceiling. The eyes were open. They were black, and they were looking at where Harry's face had been a moment ago, when he was kneeling, and they hadn't moved when he stood, so they were looking at nothing now. The silver was still coming out of them, more slowly. It hung in the air above the body in long thin threads, the way smoke hangs in a room with no draught.

Snape had been going to close every door in his head.

Snape had been going to make him what everybody else was.

Harry looked down at the man who'd held out a wand across a tower roof without a word, and sent a silver doe to a cinema in Leeds five times, and lured him here with it, and been afraid of him, and been right.

"Good," said Harry.

* * *

He took a phial out of the inside pocket of his coat.

It was the small one he carried for nosebleeds, stoppered, with an inch of dittany in it, which Hermione had given him in October. He took out the stopper and tipped the dittany onto the floor, where it ran into the dust and the dark, and he knelt again beside Snape and held the phial up to the silver threads.

They went in.

They went in slowly, curling, the way milk goes into tea. He didn't know how he knew to do it. He'd seen Dumbledore do it in a round office, with a wand to his own temple, years ago. He held the phial up to the threads as they came out of the dead man's eyes, and they came, and the phial filled, very bright, lighting his fingers from inside.

He put the stopper back in.

He didn't think about what was in it. He thought it might be useful. That was all. A man who'd been in the Dark Lord's inner circle for seventeen years, and in Dumbledore's confidence for the same seventeen years, had just given up every memory he had in a silver stream on the floor, and some of them would be about where things were kept, and who could be trusted, and what the Dark Lord meant to do next. It would be useful.

He put the phial in his inside pocket next to the Cloak.

He didn't look at the doorway.

He didn't decide not to. He simply didn't. There was nothing in the doorway he could read, and there never had been, and for a month now he hadn't looked at things he couldn't read. He hadn't looked at them the way you don't look at the sun. He knelt on the boards beside Snape with the phial of memories in his pocket and the candle guttering beside him, and stood up, and looked at the boarded window, and the four-poster, and the floor, and Snape's wand against the leg of the bed, and not once at the doorway.

He heard it close.

It was the door of the room. It closed quite quietly with a click of the latch. Somebody had stepped inside and shut it behind them, and was standing now with their back against it, inside the room, with him.

He didn't look round.

"Potter," said Evelyn.

* * *

He turned round then.

She was standing with her back against the door, her wand hanging at her side in her right hand, and she was shaking.

He saw that. He saw it the way he saw the candle and the bed and the body on the floor. He couldn't read her, so he looked at her the way he looked at any of those things, and he saw that she was shaking all over in long hard shudders, and that her face was quite white, and that her mouth was shut very tight, as though she were holding something in it.

He didn't know what it meant. For a moment he didn't even wonder.

"Selwyn," he said. "We should go."

She didn't move.

"We should go," Harry said again. "Somebody'll have felt that. The wards on the village. Or him." He looked at Snape. "He'll have told somebody where he was going. Or he won't, and they'll come looking anyway. We've got about ten minutes."

"I have just killed a man," said Evelyn.

Her voice was quite steady. It was the only thing about her that was.

"I have just killed a man for you," she said. "At eleven minutes past twelve. In the Shrieking Shack. With a spell I read about in the margin of a book, that you told me about on the floor of a classroom at two o'clock in the morning a year ago. A spell he wrote. He was our Head of House for six and a half years. He taught me Potions for five. He gave me an Outstanding. He was the only teacher in the castle who ever spelled my name right on a report without being told." She stopped. Her teeth were chattering. She shut her mouth on them hard and opened it again. "I have never killed anything in my life, Potter. I have never killed a spider. I put them out of the window in a glass. And I have just killed a man so that you could go on being whatever it is you are, and I would like you to look at me whilst I tell you, because I don't think you have looked at me for nineteen days."

Harry looked at her.

He looked at her because she'd asked, and it was reasonable, and there was no reason not to. He looked at the white face against the door, and the shaking, and the wand. He couldn't read any of it. He never could. There was nothing there.

"Thank you," said Harry.

He meant it. He said it the way he'd have said it to Ron for passing the salt.

"It was the right call," he said. "He'd have finished in another minute. Maybe less. He'd closed the first one already." He frowned slightly, put his hand to his temple, and took it away. "I can't feel the village. I'll have to see if that comes back. But you did the right thing, Selwyn. You did exactly the right thing, and you did it fast, and nobody else could have. You're the only one he couldn't have stopped. I'd have done the same if it had been the other way round." He looked at the window. "Now we should go."

Evelyn looked at him.

She looked at him for a long moment from the door, shaking. He waited. He didn't mind waiting. He had nowhere in particular to be.

Then she said, in a voice he'd never heard her use, very low, not to him, "*Oh*," and something in her face gave way.

Not much. He saw it. He wouldn't have seen it in anyone else. He saw it in her because he'd looked at her face for six and a half years and knew everything it did, and he'd never seen it do this. It was as though somebody had been holding the face up from behind and had let go.

"All right," said Evelyn.

She put her wand in her pocket.

"All right," she said again, and he didn't know whom she was saying it to.

And she opened.

* * *

He'd been reading people for as long as he could remember.

He'd read his aunt in a kitchen when he was four and his uncle in a car when he was five and Dudley in a play park and a hundred thousand people at a Quidditch World Cup. He'd read Hagrid on a rock in the sea on the night of his eleventh birthday, the first warm loud thing he'd ever felt aimed at himself, the loudest thing in the world, and he'd thought at eleven that nothing would ever be as loud as that again.

He'd read Evelyn Selwyn every day for seven years and found nothing.

Nothing. Silence. The one quiet place in a world full of noise. He'd found it unsettling, then fascinating, and then, over years, the place he went to rest. He'd stood beside it at the World Cup with a hundred thousand people screaming and leaned on it like a wall. He'd rested on it in a marquee and an Atrium and a cellar. He'd known it better than any feeling in anyone, because it was no feeling at all, only the absence of one, perfect, constant, the same every day of every year since a stool in Madam Malkin's, and at some point he'd stopped even noticing it was there. The way you stop noticing the floor.

The floor went.

It went all at once. There was no warning. There was nothing, as there'd always been nothing, and then there wasn't nothing, and it came through the closed door in the back of his head that Snape had shut a quarter of an hour ago as though the door were made of paper, and it was the loudest thing he'd ever felt in his life.

Louder than Hagrid on the rock.

Louder than a hundred thousand people. Louder than the stands at the end of a maze, or a marquee going from joy to terror in one second, or a Great Hall grieving as one thing. Louder than all of them together. It was one person. It was one person standing against a door in an empty house, and it was everything she'd ever felt, all at once, every feeling of nineteen years kept behind a door since she was five, and the door was open, and it all came out.

He couldn't stand up in it.

He found he wasn't standing. He was on the floor. He didn't know how. He was on his hands and knees on the dusty boards of the Shack with his head down and his eyes shut, and it was coming into him, and he couldn't turn it down. He reached for the place inside him where he turned things down, the place he'd used since he was six, and it wasn't there, or it was there and it was nothing against this, a hand held up against the sea.

He fought it.

He didn't decide to. It was the thing in him that had sat on a step in the snow for six hours and felt nothing, and it didn't want this. It fought the way you fight waking. The way you fight when somebody pulls the covers off in a cold room and you curl up and reach for them and pull them back over your head, and they're pulled off again. He fought hard. He put up walls. They went. He put up the Majestic, red plush and gilt and the women with stars in their hair, and it went like wet paper. He put up the snow in Hogsmeade, and the calm, and the step, and the apple, and they went.

It came anyway.

And it wasn't anything he could build an illusion against, because it wasn't looking at him. It had no eyes to fool. It was simply there, all of it, in him, and it wouldn't stop being there.

It was the killing.

That was first. That was on top. It was a minute old and enormous, and he felt it the way she felt it, from inside. A wand raised in a doorway and a word said, and a man going over sideways like a tree, and something opening in him in several places at once, and the dark spreading across the boards. And the knowing. The plain, flat, total knowing, arriving all at once and never going to leave again, that she'd done it, she, Evelyn Selwyn, who put spiders out of windows in a glass.

It was terror.

Beneath the killing, filling every space round it, so large the killing floated on it. She was terrified. She'd been terrified for nineteen days. She'd been terrified for a month. She'd been terrified on a staircase at Hogsmeade, going down towards a step, knowing before she got there what she'd find. And she was terrified now, of this, of what she was doing, of the door standing open behind her for the first time in her life and everything going out of it and anyone in the world able to walk in.

She was doing it anyway.

It was fury.

He'd felt fury before. He'd felt it in Uncle Vernon and in Sirius, and once in Dumbledore, coming through a door that had been blasted in. This was different. It was cold and very clear and it had a list. It was aimed at him. It was aimed at a boy who'd looked at her from a step and smiled at her like a shop assistant, and who'd moved Weasley's feelings round like furniture, and who'd made fourteen men stand in the snow until they died, and who'd sat on a bench at Shell Cottage with Draco Malfoy's wand in his pocket and watched her dig a grave with her hands and not got up. It was nineteen days of it. Every one of the nineteen, counted.

It was grief.

It was for her grandfather in a tower, and the watch on the projection-room table that didn't tick. It was for Dobby under a white stone. It was for Justin on a stripped bed by a window. It was for Sirius, who'd danced with her once and stood on her feet four times and been trying very hard. It was for Lockhart. It was for Snape on the floor, whom she hadn't liked and had killed. And it was for something else, larger than all of them, so large it took him a long time to see its edges.

It was for him.

She was grieving for him.

He understood that on his hands and knees on the floor. She was grieving for him as though he'd died. She'd been grieving for him for a month. She'd been standing at the edge of a grave for a month, the way she'd stood at the edge of Dobby's on the cliff, and he'd been in it, and he hadn't known.

It was him.

He saw himself. He saw himself the way she saw him. Not a reading. A picture, very clear and very exact, laid down in her over a month, piece by piece, every piece noted. A thin young man with hair that needed cutting, sitting on a step in the snow with a blue hand, eating an apple, perfectly calm. A thin young man with a stranger's face at the breakfast table, drinking tea. A thin young man below a screen in a dark cinema making rain, very well, for hours, with nobody watching. A thin young man who didn't look at her.

He didn't recognise him.

He looked at the young man in her, on the step, in the snow, and didn't know who it was. And he understood, with the part of him still able to understand anything, that this was what she'd seen at the foot of the post office steps. A stranger, smiling.

And beneath all of it, at the very bottom, beneath the killing and the terror and the fury and the grief, holding them all up, there was one more thing.

It was the loudest.

He didn't have a word for it. He had a great many words. He'd been finding words for what people felt since before he could spell them. He had words for love, many kinds, more than he could count. He'd felt a mother's love in a mirror and in a churchyard, and Hagrid's on a rock, and Sirius's perfect happiness at the head of a table, and the other Sirius's love for another Harry in a room above a bar. He'd felt Snape's love for a girl on a swing, pressed in a book for twenty years.

This wasn't like any of them.

It was very plain. It was very large. It didn't want anything. It had never asked for anything, not once, in seven years. It was aimed at him, and it had been aimed at him, he understood, for a very long time, behind a door, where he couldn't feel it and she couldn't show it. It had been there on a stool in Madam Malkin's, small, without either of them knowing. It had been there at the edge of a maze, watching. It had been there in a cellar, saying *Potter*, twice. It had been there on a staircase in the dark of this house for eleven minutes whilst she decided, and it had decided.

He mattered to her.

That was all. That was the whole of it. It was the simplest thing he'd ever felt in anyone. He mattered to her more than she had words for, more than anything, more than the rule her grandmother had given her every morning from the age of five, more than the door. He mattered to her so much that she'd opened it.

It was louder than Hagrid on the rock.

It was louder than anything he'd ever felt in his life.

* * *

*She will open the door for you once.*

It came to him from a long way off, very clearly, in an old man's voice, elegant and amused and not amused at all. A cell at the top of a tower. A bed. Snow on the slot of a window. An old man propped on pillows, looking at Harry as he came back alone for a girl's forgotten scarf, and saying without any preamble, as though he'd been waiting all afternoon to say it.

*She will open the door for you once. Do not make her do it twice.*

He'd never told her. He'd said *he said thank you for the rain*, and put it away, and not thought about it again.

He thought about it now.

He was on his hands and knees on the floor of the Shrieking Shack with everything she'd ever felt going through him like the sea through a broken wall, and he understood that it was happening, now, the once. That she'd done it. That she was standing against the door with it open behind her and every part of her that had been closed for nineteen years going out into the room, where anybody could reach it, where he could reach it, and she'd done it knowing exactly what it cost and not knowing whether it would work.

He stopped fighting.

He didn't decide to. He found he'd stopped. The way you find, after holding something heavy for a long time, that your hands have opened.

He let it in.

* * *

He was sitting on the floor.

He didn't remember getting there. He was sitting on the dusty boards of the Shack with his back against the wall under the boarded window and his knees drawn up, and the candle was nearly out, and he was himself.

He knew it the way you know you're awake. Not by any one thing. By everything at once. The cold of the floor coming up through his trousers. The ache in his knees. The smell of dust and old damp and something else beneath it that he didn't let himself name. The weight of the phial in his inside pocket. Snape on the floor four feet away, on his back, with his eyes open.

He looked at Snape.

He felt it then. All of it. It rose in him the way water rises in a well that's been dry, slowly, from the bottom, then faster, then over the top.

Snape. A man who'd held out a wand without a word. Who'd been afraid of him. Who'd been right.

Fourteen men in the snow.

He'd made fourteen men stand in the snow until they died. He'd sat on a step and eaten an apple and watched them. He'd made flowers.

A man in Leeds called Selby, talking to a wall.

Ron standing up red at a folding table, and sitting down calm, and not knowing why.

Hermione on a roof in Sheffield with her hands not shaking.

A plain girl at the foot of some steps, whom he'd smiled at, and not known.

A white stone on a cliff, and a girl with bleeding hands, and a bench, and himself on it, not getting up.

It came up and up. He didn't turn it down. He couldn't have, and he didn't try.

And then, beneath all of it, from the very bottom, slowly, the last thing came. The oldest. The one he hadn't let himself have since an orchard in August.

A kitchen door.

The Burrow, every window lit. A man in a mustard-and-plum coat with his back to the door and his wand up and the light behind him, laughing. Very good. Very fast. The happiest Harry had ever felt anyone. Holding the door so the Weasleys could get through it to the fire, and laughing, and then not laughing, the laughter stopping all at once, whilst Harry turned away across the garden with a child in his arms and ran and didn't stop and didn't look back.

Sirius.

Harry put his face in his hands.

He cried.

He hadn't cried since he was very small. He hadn't cried at the Burrow, or in the back row of a cinema with three people beside him, or at a funeral he hadn't gone to, or on a bridge, or on a step. He hadn't cried for Dumbledore on a lawn or for Cedric in a churchyard. He cried now, on the floor of the Shrieking Shack with his face in his hands and his back against the wall, and it wasn't quiet and it wasn't dignified and it didn't stop. It went on for a very long time. It went on until the candle went out, and after, in the dark, with the moon coming through the cracks in the boards across the window in thin white lines.

She sat down beside him.

He felt her do it. He didn't need to look. She crossed the room in the dark, past the body on the floor, and sat on the boards beside him with her back against the same wall, close, her shoulder against his.

She said nothing.

She didn't touch him except with her shoulder. She didn't put her arm round him or take his hand. She sat beside him in the dark with her shoulder against his, and her mind was still open, and he could feel her.

He could feel her.

She was still frightened. He could feel that. It was very loud, and it hadn't gone anywhere, and it was aimed at him and at the dark and at the door standing open in her. She was still grieving. She was still a little furious, beneath everything, a cold clear list that hadn't been crossed out. She was shaking less. And she was there. All of her was there beside him in the dark, and every part of her he could feel was staying.

He cried until there was nothing left to cry with.

Then he sat with his head back against the wall and his eyes shut, and breathed.

* * *

He didn't say any of it.

He'd never say it, to her or to anyone. He sat on the floor with his back against the wall and her shoulder against his, and understood it the way you understand where you are when you wake in a strange room.

He'd been living in an illusion for a month.

Not one he'd made on anybody else. One he'd made on himself. He'd made a young man who didn't feel things, because feeling things was a luxury, and he'd stepped inside him on a bridge in the snow and pulled the door shut behind him, the way he'd taken the end off fourteen men's worst nights, so that it would go on. And it had gone on. It had been the best illusion he'd ever made. He'd believed it completely. He'd sat inside it, on a step, at a breakfast table, below a screen, and never once known he was in it, and nobody in the world could have seen it from outside except one person, whom it couldn't touch.

Oswin, the apprentice in Slytherin's journal, had walked this Path all the way up. And at the top of it, the journal said, he couldn't find the door back to himself.

Harry knew where the door was now.

He knew where it was the way you know where a door is in a room you've been led out of by the hand. He could find it again. He could go back in if he had to. He could go a long way in. He could go further than he'd gone, and come out.

But he couldn't find it from the inside. Not alone. Nobody could. That was what Oswin hadn't had. You needed somebody on the other side of it. Somebody it couldn't touch. Somebody standing outside the door, in the snow, at the foot of the steps, who knew who you were when you didn't, and wouldn't go away.

He opened his eyes.

The moon was coming through the boards in white lines across the floor. One lay across Snape's open hand. One lay across his own knees. One lay across hers.

* * *

"I can't close it," said Evelyn.

She said it into the dark quite flatly, after a long time. Her shoulder was still against his.

"I've been trying," she said. "Since you stopped. I've been trying for twenty minutes. I've closed it every morning since I was five, Potter. I've never not been able to. I don't even think about it. It's like breathing." She paused. "I can't find the door."

Harry stayed quiet.

He could feel her trying. He could feel it very clearly through her shoulder and the dark. A girl standing in the middle of a room where every wall had been taken down, turning round and round, looking for the place where the door had been, and not finding it.

"It's partly there," she said. "I can get some of it. Some of it's closing. It's like a window that's been painted shut. I can get it down most of the way, and then it sticks." She was quiet a moment. "Anyone could read me. Now. Anyone at all. Not just you. Anybody with a wand and the word."

"I know."

"I've never been read in my life."

"I know."

"My grandmother would be…" She stopped. He felt what was under the stop. He let it be.

They sat in the dark.

He could feel her. He could feel all of her still, not as loud now, but there, like the warmth of a fire in another room. She was tired, very, all the way down. She was still frightened about the window that wouldn't close. Her knees were sore from the floor. She was cold. And she was something else, small and new and very near the top, that he'd never felt in her because he'd never felt anything in her, and he looked at it for a while in the dark before he understood what it was.

"You're hungry," said Harry.

There was a pause.

"I haven't eaten since lunch," said Evelyn. "It isn't an emotion."

"It is from here."

"Stop that."

"I can't. You're very loud."

"I'm aware," said Evelyn, "that I'm very loud." She shifted her shoulder against his. "I've been aware of it for twenty minutes. It's like going out in the street with no clothes on. You could at least have the decency not to *comment*."

He felt it go through her as she said it. Embarrassment, quite sharp. Beneath it, something very nearly a laugh, which she didn't let out.

He felt himself smile in the dark.

Not the polite smile, the one for shop assistants and train guards. His own. He hadn't felt it on his face for a month, and it felt strange there, stiff, like a door that hasn't been opened in a long time.

"Selwyn," said Harry.

"What."

"You've been following me."

"For twenty-two days."

"I didn't know."

"No," said Evelyn. "That was rather the point." She was quiet a moment. "You're very easy to follow, Potter. You never look behind you. You never have. You assume that if anybody's there you'll feel them." He felt her turn her head in the dark towards him. "I've been there for seven years."

He didn't answer that. He couldn't.

He sat on the floor of the Shrieking Shack with his back to the wall and her shoulder against his and the moon in white lines across the boards, and a dead man four feet away, and a window in her that wouldn't close, and he could feel her.

"Light something," said Evelyn after a while. "Please. I'd like to see where I'm putting my feet before I have to walk anywhere."

He found his wand in the dark. He lit it.

She was looking at him. Her face was white and very tired and streaked with dust, quite plain, exactly as it always was. Her hands were in her lap. They'd nearly stopped shaking.

"There's dust on your face," said Harry.

"There's dust on yours. And a great deal of something else." She glanced at his knees, and away. "We'll go to the Hog's Head. The back way. Aberforth won't ask questions. He doesn't like the answers." She paused. "Weasley will have found the pillows by now. Granger will be making lists."

"Yes."

"They'll be frightened."

"I know," said Harry. "I can feel you thinking it."

"Stop *doing* that."

"I'm not doing anything. You're doing it at me."

Evelyn looked at him for a moment in the wandlight with her mouth shut tight. He felt the nearly-laugh again, quite close to the top, and felt her hold it down, and felt her decide not to bother.

"I'd like it noted," she said, "that I have still not had anything to eat."

"It's noted," said Harry.

## Chapter 77: The Prince's Tale

Aberforth Dumbledore opened the back door of the Hog's Head at a quarter to one in the morning in a nightshirt and a pair of boots with no laces, holding a lantern, and looked at the two of them standing in his yard among the goats.

He looked at Harry first. Then at Evelyn. Then at Harry again, for a long time, by the lantern light.

"You've been crying," he said.

"Yes," said Harry.

"Good." Aberforth held the door wider. "About time somebody round here did. Get in. Mind the goat."

* * *

He didn't ask questions.

Evelyn had been right about that. He sat them down at the table in the back room where Lockhart had unpacked tinned peaches seven weeks ago, and put a pot of tea in front of them and a plate of bread and dripping, and Evelyn ate four slices without a word. Harry read her eat them, and she looked at him across the table with her mouth full, and he stopped.

Aberforth stood by the range with his arms folded and watched them.

Harry told him where Snape was.

He didn't tell him how. He said *the Shrieking Shack, upstairs, the front room*, and Aberforth looked at him, and Harry let him look and didn't put anything in the way. After a moment Aberforth unfolded his arms, took his lantern and a coat off the hook by the back door, and went out into the yard. They heard the gate. They heard nothing else for an hour and twenty minutes.

When he came back he hung the coat on its hook and put the lantern on the table and sat down heavily on the bench across from them, and poured himself a cup of the cold tea.

"I've seen to it," he said.

Nobody asked what that meant.

"He used to come in here," said Aberforth after a while, to his tea. "Years ago. Before your time. Sat in the corner by the window on his own. Drank one glass of mead in two hours. Never talked to anybody." He drank. "Came in one night in nineteen eighty and sat in the corridor upstairs, outside my brother's room, whilst my brother was interviewing some woman for a job. Got thrown out on his ear by the barman. That was me." He put the cup down. "Never came back. I used to wonder what he'd heard."

Harry said nothing.

He knew what Snape had heard. He'd heard it himself, in a Hall of Prophecy, in another world, at thirteen.

Aberforth looked at the bulge in Harry's inside pocket. Harry hadn't known it showed. The phial was very bright. It glowed faintly silver through the cloth of his coat, like a torch held under a blanket.

"That his?" said Aberforth.

"Yes."

Aberforth got up. He went out of the back room and up the stairs, and they heard him moving about overhead in a room above the bar, and something heavy being dragged across a floor. Then he came down again slowly, carrying a stone basin in both arms, very old, chipped round the rim, carved with marks worn almost smooth.

He set it on the table between the bread and the teapot.

"Our mother's," he said. "Albus had it first. Then he got himself a better one, and I got this. I've never used it." He looked at the phial in Harry's pocket. "Take it. Bring it back when you've done. Or don't." He sat down again. "I don't want to know what's in it. I've had enough of my brother's business for one lifetime, and I reckon that was my brother's business, one way or another."

* * *

They came back to the Majestic at twenty past six in the morning with a stone basin wrapped in a horse blanket, and Ron was waiting in the alley.

He was standing by the fire door in the rain with his wand out and no coat, his face grey, and he'd clearly been standing there for some time. He saw them come out of the air at the end of the alley, Evelyn first, Harry behind her with the basin, and he didn't lower his wand.

"Who are you," he said.

He said it to Harry.

"It's me," said Harry.

"Prove it."

Harry looked at him. He looked at Ron Weasley standing in the rain in a back alley in Leeds with his wand steady and his face grey, and he read him, and it was all there. Fear. Grief. Anger, a great deal of it, very hot, aimed at Harry. And beneath all three, quite near the top and not hidden at all, relief, so large that Ron was holding it down with both hands.

"On the twelfth of March," said Harry, "you wanted to go and find your dad. You were right. You should have gone. I turned you down like a wireless so you'd stay for Sheffield. I didn't ask you. I'm sorry."

Ron stared at him.

"And on the fourteenth," said Harry, "on the roof. Hermione. I did it to her too. I took her fear and put it somewhere. She knows. She asked me. I told her I didn't understand what she was asking." He shifted the basin in his arms. "I do now. I'm sorry. I won't do it again. To either of you. Not without asking."

The rain came down.

Ron lowered his wand.

He did it very slowly, as though his arm were stiff. He stood there with it at his side, and his face did several things at once, and Harry read every one of them and didn't look away from any.

"You're back," said Ron.

It wasn't a question.

"Yes."

"Properly. Not… You're back."

"Yes."

Ron looked at him a moment longer. Then he looked at Evelyn, standing a little behind Harry with her hands in her cardigan pockets and her hair wet. He frowned.

"What's the matter with you?" he said.

"Nothing's the matter with me, Weasley."

"Something is." Ron looked at her harder. "You look different. You look…" He couldn't find the word. Harry watched him not find it. Ron had never read anybody in his life and never would, and he was standing in an alley in the rain looking at Evelyn Selwyn's plain wet face and seeing something in it that had never been there before, the way you notice a room's been rearranged without being able to say which chair has moved. "I dunno. You look like you've been crying, or something. Except you haven't."

Evelyn looked at him.

Harry felt what went through her. He couldn't help it. It was very loud and very quick, something close to horror, and it was aimed at herself.

"I'm going in," said Evelyn. "It's raining."

She went past Ron and through the fire door, and they heard her go up the stairs to the projection room very fast, two at a time.

Ron looked at Harry.

"What happened?" he said. "Last night. Where've you been? She left *pillows*. Hermione's been up all night making a list of places you might be, it's got forty-one things on it, she was going to start at the top at seven…"

"Snape's dead," said Harry.

Ron's mouth stayed open.

"He was going to take it all away," said Harry. "Everything. The reading. The illusions. He asked me there to do it. Dumbledore asked him to, last year. In case I turned into… In case." He looked at the fire door. "She stopped him."

Ron was quiet for a long time.

"Blimey," he said at last, very softly. Then, after another moment, "With what?"

"His own spell."

Ron looked at the fire door too.

"Blimey," he said again.

* * *

They looked at the memories that afternoon in the projection room, at three o'clock, with the rain on the roof.

Harry went in alone. He'd asked Evelyn whether she wanted to come, and she'd said no, quite quickly, and then *no, thank you*, more slowly, and he'd felt why and hadn't asked again. Ron and Hermione sat on their camp beds and watched him tip the phial into the stone basin. The silver went in slowly, the way it had gone into the phial, curling, and filled the basin almost to the chipped rim, and lay there, moving, very bright.

Harry put his face down into it.

* * *

A playground.

It was summer. It was a small dusty play park at the bottom of a street of brick houses, with a river behind it and a mill chimney beyond the river, and two girls on the swings. One was older, thin, with a long neck, sitting very upright and swinging carefully. The other was smaller and had red hair, and she was swinging as high as the swing would go, and higher, and at the top of the arc she let go.

She flew.

She went up off the swing and through the air and came down slowly, much too slowly, like a leaf, and landed on the grass on her feet, laughing.

Behind a bush at the edge of the play park, a thin boy in clothes much too large for him was watching her.

Harry read him.

It was faint, as feelings were in memories. Like smoke. But it was there, and Harry knew it. He'd read it twice before. He'd read it at fourteen in a lesson in a dungeon, and he'd read it in a silver doe five times in a cinema in Leeds. He read it now, at its beginning, in a boy of nine behind a bush.

It wasn't love yet. Not quite. It was the thing just before love. Wonder, and recognition, and hope, all at once, aimed at the girl on the grass. *She's like me. She's like me. I'm not the only one.*

The memory went.

* * *

A kitchen. Shouting through a ceiling. A boy on a bed with his hands over his ears. What he felt was flat and old and familiar, and it took Harry a moment to place it. He'd felt it in himself, in a cupboard under some stairs, when he was very small.

A riverbank. The boy and the girl, older, eleven, lying in the long grass, talking about Dementors and Azkaban and the school, and the girl asking whether it mattered that her parents weren't magic, and the boy saying *no*, and meaning it, and the feeling in him so large and bright it filled the whole riverbank like sunlight.

A train. The two of them in a compartment, and two other boys, one with untidy black hair and a face Harry had seen in photographs all his life. A sneer. A door slammed.

The Great Hall, very young, very large, full of candles. The girl under the Sorting Hat. *Gryffindor*. The boy watching her walk away to the other table, and the feeling in him draining, quite slowly, like water going out of a basin.

Then the boy under the Hat himself. *Slytherin*. A cheer from the far side of the Hall. A young man with long pale hair and a prefect's badge, clapping him on the shoulder.

The memory went.

* * *

They came faster after that, one after another, like pages turned in a wind.

Corridors. Years. The girl laughing with her friends. The boy with his. The two of them in a courtyard, arguing in low voices. *They're your friends, Sev. They're horrible. Mulciber. Avery. You know what they did to Mary.* The feeling in him was hurt, and pride, and fear of losing her, and fear of losing them, all knotted, and none of it coming loose.

And then a lake.

Harry knew this one. He'd been in it before, in a lesson, at fourteen, by accident, and been thrown out of the room. He was in it now on purpose. A bright day in June. Exams over. A tall boy with untidy black hair and a friend with long dark hair, laughing, and a thin boy hanging upside down in the air by his ankle, his robes fallen over his head and his grey underwear showing and the whole lake shore watching.

The girl, coming across the grass. Angry. Telling them to stop.

And the boy, hanging upside down, humiliated, with every eye on the lake shore on him, saying it to her.

Harry didn't hear the word. He didn't need to. He felt it go out of the boy, and he felt what it was made of. It wasn't hate. It was shame, so large it had nowhere to go but outwards, at the one person it should never have touched. And he felt it land in her, on her face. And then he felt, in the boy, the moment after.

It was the worst thing Harry had felt in anyone in a memory.

It was the moment of somebody who's just broken the only thing they had, and knows it, and knows it will never mend, and has to go on hanging there upside down in front of everybody whilst he knows it.

He'd felt that moment once before. In a lesson. It hadn't been as clear then.

Snape had looked at it every day for twenty-two years.

* * *

The memories went dark after that.

Not dark the way the playground had been bright. Dark the way a corridor is dark when the lamps have been put out. Older boys in a room with the curtains drawn, and masks. A long table. A man at the head of it with a face that was still nearly handsome, and red eyes, and a voice quiet and pleased and very interested. *Severus. Welcome.* What the young man at the table felt was pride, and hunger, and relief at being wanted, and beneath it, very far down, a grey cold place where something had died on a lake shore and never been buried.

The Hog's Head. A dark corridor upstairs, and a door, and a woman's voice behind it, high and strange, saying something about a boy, and the end of July, and a power. The young man pressed against the door, listening. A hand on his collar. A barman with a long grey beard, much younger, dragging him down the stairs. *Out. Out, and don't come back.*

The young man kneeling on a long carpet in front of the man with the red eyes, telling him. Telling him all of it. Half of it. As much as he'd heard.

The red eyes, very interested.

And then a night, a long time after, the same young man on a hillside in the dark, in the rain, with his hands up, shouting into the wind, and an old man appearing out of nowhere in front of him with a long silver beard and a wand. *It's her. The one he's going to. It's her boy he means. I didn't know. I swear I didn't know when I told him. Put them somewhere. Put them all somewhere he can't find.*

The feeling in him was like nothing Harry had ever felt in a memory. It was terror, and it wasn't for himself.

*You are asking a great deal, Severus. What are you offering?*

*Whatever you want. Whatever you want.*

* * *

A house.

A small house at the end of a village street, with a hedge, and a gate hanging off one hinge, and the roof of an upstairs room blown open to the sky. It was night. It was very quiet.

The young man went up the path and through the open door and up the stairs, past a man lying at the bottom of them with untidy black hair and his glasses gone.

He didn't stop for the man. Harry felt him not stop.

He went into the room at the top of the stairs.

There was a cot, with a child in it, crying. There was a woman on the floor beside the cot, on her back, her red hair spread out on the boards and her eyes open.

The young man knelt beside her and took her in his arms.

Harry had read grief. He'd read it in Amos Diggory on a Quidditch pitch, and in Hagrid on a lawn, and in himself on the floor of a house twelve hours ago. He'd read it in Snape in a courtyard at the foot of a tower, and thought it the rawest thing he'd ever felt.

He hadn't felt this.

It had no shape. It had no direction. It wasn't aimed at anything, because the thing it would have been aimed at was gone. It was a man kneeling on the floor of a room with a hole in its roof and the rain coming in, holding a woman who was the place where a person had been, rocking, making a noise Harry could hear through the smoke of the memory and couldn't bear and didn't look away from, because Snape hadn't.

In the cot, the child went on crying.

The young man didn't look at it.

* * *

An office. A round office with portraits and silver instruments and a phoenix on a perch, much younger. The young man sitting in a chair with his face in his hands. Dumbledore behind the desk, no white in his hair yet, only silver.

*You said you would hide her. You said.*

*They chose whom to trust, Severus, and they chose badly. You know something about that.*

*Then let me go. There's nothing left. Let me go.*

*Go where?* Dumbledore leaning forward across the desk. *There is a child in a cot in that house who was crying when you left him. He is alive. He has her face about the eyes, I am told. If there is anything left in you that she would recognise, you will stay, and you will help me keep him alive.*

The young man lifting his head. What he felt was a grief so large it had nowhere left to go, finding suddenly somewhere. A direction. A boy with her eyes.

*You will tell nobody what she was to me. Nobody. Not him. Him least of all.*

*You have my word, Severus.*

Harry felt it set in him. The promise, and the direction, and the grief, all at once, setting like plaster round a love that would never be allowed to change again. He felt it set, and he understood the doe.

* * *

Then the memories he didn't know.

They came in the same office, over and over, through the years, and the man in the chair grew older and the man behind the desk grew whiter, and they talked about him.

*He is kind, Severus. He is a kind child. Minerva saw it at once. He went into the bathroom on Hallowe'en after the Bulstrode girl.*

*He is arrogant. He is his father. He looks at people as though he can see through them.*

*Perhaps he can.* A pause. *I have wondered.*

Another year. *The Heir. Everybody believes it. He sits alone in the library. He is twelve. Can you not…*

*It must run its course, Severus. I am sorry for the boy. I am sorrier than you know. But it must.*

The man in the chair was angry, coldly, across the desk. Harry hadn't known. He hadn't known that anybody had been angry for him that year, in that office, at that desk, and said so.

Another year. Dumbledore at the window with his back to the room.

*He lied to me, Severus. In March. About four days. Perfectly. I looked straight into his face and he lied to me and I believed every word, and I did not know until weeks later, and I am still not certain what he was lying about.* A silence. *I have only ever been lied to like that once before.*

The man in the chair, very still. *By whom?*

Dumbledore didn't answer.

Another year. The same office after midnight, a phoenix asleep on its perch, and Dumbledore at the desk with his hands flat on it and his face grey.

*He came into my mind tonight. After the graveyard. I could have stopped him. I did not. He came in through the door I had left open to look at him, and he brought the whole of that churchyard with him, and pushed it into me. Every second. What he felt. I felt it, Severus. I have never felt another person in my life, and I felt him.*

*Then you know what I mean. About his father's son.*

*No.* Dumbledore looking up. *No. It is not his father I am afraid of.*

Harry read what was in him, through the smoke. He'd read it once before, in the same office, the same night, from the other side of the desk, at fourteen, and noted it and not understood it.

Fear. Old and small and aimed at Harry. The fear of a man looking at something he's seen before and never wants to see again.

Harry understood it now.

* * *

More.

Snape at the desk after a lesson. *He came into my head. Into mine. I have kept the Dark Lord out of my mind for fourteen years and a boy of fifteen walked in. And he did not look. He felt.*

Dumbledore, very quiet. *What did he feel?*

Snape didn't answer. What was in him was shame, and a hatred that was new, and beneath them, Harry felt with a kind of slow astonishment, something else. Something very small. Something almost like respect.

Another year. Snape in the courtyard at the foot of the tower after the funeral, a memory Harry hadn't known he was in. Snape looking up at the parapet, then turning and seeing a boy on the low wall by the greenhouse gate. And Snape's feeling at being seen was fury, and fear, and a strange wrenching thing Harry didn't recognise until he'd gone past it, and then did. Relief. That somebody had seen. That somebody knew.

And then the tower.

* * *

It was the memory Harry had glimpsed in the Shack, going past like a lit window. He was in it now. He stood on the roof of the Astronomy Tower in April of the year before, on a moonless night, with the door at the top of the stairs shut behind him, and watched.

Dumbledore was at the parapet with his back to the room and his hands on the stone. He was very old already, by then. He was wearing a plum dressing gown.

Snape stood by the door.

*No*, said Snape.

*I have not asked you yet.*

*I know what you are going to ask. No.*

They stood there. Harry felt the hour go past him like water, faster than an hour, the way time goes in a memory. He felt Snape refuse over and over in different words from the door. He felt Dumbledore not argue. He felt Dumbledore simply stand at the parapet with his back to the room and wait, the way he'd once waited in an office with a boy of fourteen, and Harry had never been waited for before.

Then Dumbledore turned round.

*Severus. I have watched one boy become Tom Riddle. I watched it, and I told myself that it would not happen, that he was only a child, that I was seeing ghosts. And I did nothing until it was far too late to do anything at all. I watched another become Gellert Grindelwald, and I loved him, and I did nothing then either, and a great many people died of my doing nothing.* He was very quiet. *I am going to die soon. You know how. When I am gone, there will be nobody who can stop Harry if he goes the way they went. Nobody except you.*

*He is not Tom.*

*No. He is not. He is kind, and he is brave, and he feels sick when he looks at cruelty, and that is the whole of the difference, Severus, the whole of it. And if he ever stops feeling sick…* Dumbledore stopped. *If he becomes what Tom became, you will have to stop him. I could not stop Gellert in time. Do not make my mistake.*

*How will I know?*

Dumbledore looked at him for a long moment in the dark.

*You will know,* he said, *because he will stop knowing what people feel. Not the reading. He will always have the reading. He will stop knowing what it means. He will look at a person and see a thing. That is what Tom did. That is all Tom ever did.*

Snape stood by the door.

*And if I am wrong?*

*Then you will have done a terrible thing to a boy who did not deserve it.* Dumbledore didn't look away. *And I will have asked you to. And that will be mine to carry, not yours.*

Snape said yes.

Harry felt him say it. He felt what it cost. He felt that Snape didn't believe, then, standing by the door on a moonless night, that it would ever come to anything.

* * *

And after that, a desk.

The headmaster's desk at a quarter to one in the morning, by the light of a single candle. Seven reports. A Healers' report. *The memory appears to have been located within the subject and released.*

Snape sitting with his hands flat on the papers.

Harry read him.

It was the last of the memories, and the newest, and the clearest, because it was only a week old. And what was in Snape at the desk, with the reports in front of him and a sleeping portrait behind him, wasn't certainty.

It was doubt.

It was enormous. It went all the way down. He didn't know. He'd never known. He'd watched Harry for seven years and hated his father's face and been unable to look away from his mother's eyes, and he'd never once in all that time been sure what the boy was. He'd refused on the tower for an hour because he wasn't sure. He'd sent a doe to a cinema in Leeds four times because he wasn't sure. He'd sat at this desk in the dark with the reports in front of him three nights running and not written anything, because he wasn't sure.

And then he'd read the Healers' report again.

*The memory appears to have been located within the subject and released.*

Harry felt it happen. He felt the doubt in Snape, enormous and old and patient, turn over quite slowly and settle on one thing. Not on certainty. On a step. On a boy sitting on a step in the snow eating an apple, watching fourteen men live the worst night of their lives until they died of cold, with Lily's eyes, perfectly calm.

*He will look at a person and see a thing.*

Snape picked up the pen.

The memory went out.

* * *

Harry came up out of the basin and found himself sitting on the floor of the projection room with his back against the leg of a camp bed, dark outside the small square windows, and Hermione holding a cup of tea out to him.

He took it.

He didn't drink it. He sat on the floor with the cup in his hands and looked at the stone basin on the folding table, with the silver still moving in it, very bright.

He read himself.

He'd never done that. Not like this. He'd always known what he felt the way you know the temperature of a room, without looking. He looked now. He sat on the floor of the projection room in the dark and turned the reading inward, carefully, the way you turn a lamp, and looked at what was there.

He was angry.

It was very large. It was aimed at a round office and an old man behind a desk, at a tower on a moonless night, at a basin full of years in which two men had sat and talked about him, and decided about him, and never once asked him. *Him least of all.* He'd thought, after a lawn and a white tomb and a letter, that there was nothing left that Dumbledore hadn't told him. There'd been this. *If he becomes what Tom became.* Dumbledore had looked at him across a desk on a Friday night in May and said *no* when Harry asked if anything else was being withheld, and it had been a lie, and Harry had read the lock, and let it go.

He was angry at Snape. For the doe. For using the one thing Harry had trusted, the one feeling in the world he'd been sure of, to bring him to an empty house in the dark.

And he understood.

That was there too, just as large, right beside the anger, not beneath it. He understood every word. He'd sat on a step in the snow and eaten an apple. He'd looked at fourteen men and seen fourteen things. He'd looked at Evelyn Selwyn at the foot of the steps and seen a girl, somebody's daughter, nothing that needed doing. He'd stopped knowing what it meant. Dumbledore had said he would, and had been afraid of it, and he had.

Dumbledore had been right to be afraid.

Snape had been right about Hogsmeade.

And they'd been wrong. They'd both been wrong in the same way, at the same desk, for seventeen years. They'd thought it was something you could stop from outside. That if the boy went far enough, somebody would have to go in and close the doors. They'd never thought there might be somebody already outside the door, in the snow, waiting, who'd open her own.

Neither of them had known about her.

He sat with it. The anger and the understanding side by side, both large, neither giving way. He'd felt them both at once before, in an office after an Atrium, at sixteen, and they hadn't settled then either.

He didn't try to make them settle.

He drank the tea. It had gone cold.

"Harry?" said Hermione, very quietly.

"I'm here."

"Was it… Are you all right?"

He thought about how to answer that honestly, because she'd asked honestly.

"No," he said. "But I'm here."

* * *

Evelyn couldn't close it.

She tried every morning. She tried at seven, as she always had, sitting on the end of the camp bed with the stopped watch in her hand, the way her grandmother had taught her in the east wing at Selwyn Hall when she was five. She closed her eyes and found the door and pulled it to. And every morning it came most of the way and then stuck, the way a sash window sticks when it's been painted, an inch or two from the sill, and the cold came in under it, and so did anybody who wanted to.

She noted it every morning in the red notebook. *Thursday 26 March. Most. Not all.* *Friday 27 March. Most. Not all.* *Saturday 28 March. As before.*

She didn't write what it was like.

It was like being looked at. That was the nearest she could come. She'd been looked at very little in her life. People looked at her and their eyes slid off, and she'd always been glad of it. Now she felt looked at all the time, by everybody, even when nobody was looking, the way you feel looked at in a dream where you've come to school without your clothes. She felt it in the projection room and on the stairs and in the foyer and in the alley. She felt it most when Potter was in the room.

He was very careful.

She noted that too. He didn't read her. Or he did, because he couldn't help it, any more than she could help being read, but he didn't let her see that he did. He didn't say *you're hungry* again. He didn't look at her when she came into a room. He looked at the floor, or the screen, or the teapot, and let her come in, and she could tell it cost him something. Once, on the Saturday, when she was standing at the folding table pouring tea and thinking about her grandfather's chair, he got up quite suddenly and went down to the screen and didn't come back for an hour.

She didn't ask him why. She knew why. It was the same reason she didn't ask.

Weasley was worse.

Weasley couldn't read anybody. He never had. He was the least perceptive person she'd ever lived with, and that included her father, who perceived everything and cared about none of it. And Weasley kept looking at her.

"You're doing it again," he said on the Sunday at breakfast.

"Doing what."

"That face."

"This is my face, Weasley. I've had it for nineteen years."

"Yeah, but it's *doing* something." He frowned at her across the folding table over his toast. "It never used to do anything. You always looked like you were waiting for a bus. Now you look like…" He stopped. "I dunno. Like a person."

Granger kicked him under the table.

"What? I'm being nice."

"You're being Ron," said Granger. She looked at Evelyn. She looked very kind. She'd looked very kind since Thursday morning, and Evelyn had noted it and found it almost unbearable. "Ignore him."

"I always do," said Evelyn.

She put her hand on the watch in her cardigan pocket.

She'd kept her hand on it all that week. She noted that she was doing it. She didn't stop. It didn't tick. It hadn't ticked since the seventeenth of December at eleven minutes past seven, and she knew it wouldn't, and she kept her hand on it anyway, all day, the way you keep your hand on a banister in the dark in a house where you used to live.

* * *

The watching charm on the roof woke her at twenty to midnight on Thursday the second of April.

It was one of Varga's. It made no sound. It simply put a picture into her head, very clear, of the street at the front of the Majestic as the roof saw it. Wet tarmac, a streetlamp, the boarded doors of the cinema beneath the elephants on the façade. And six people standing on the pavement in front of the doors in dark cloaks, in the rain.

She was off the camp bed before she'd finished seeing it.

Potter was already awake. He was sitting up on his camp bed by the projectors with his face turned towards the front of the building, and she could see in the dark that he was reading them.

"Six," he said, very low. "On the pavement. They're waiting for something." He was quiet a moment. "Somebody's in the alley."

"Who?"

He didn't answer at once. She felt him reach. She felt it go past her, out through the wall and down, and she felt him find something, and felt what his face did in the dark when he found it.

"Your brother," said Potter.

* * *

She went down alone.

He asked first. She noted that on the stairs. He sat on the edge of the camp bed and asked, quite quietly, so as not to wake the others. *Do you want me to make him see an empty building?* And she stood in the dark with her coat half on and thought about it for four seconds and said *no*.

"He'll know," she said. "He's reading me. I can feel him doing it. He's standing in the alley reading me through the wall, the way you do. He came in through the wards because they let in Selwyn blood, and he's got it, and I didn't think of that when I set them." She did up her coat. "If you show him an empty building, he'll know there's somebody in it who can show him an empty building. And there's only one person in Britain who can."

"Then let me come."

"No. If he sees you, he has to bring you in. He won't have a choice. If he sees me…" She stopped. "I don't know what he'll do if he sees me. I'd like to find out."

Potter looked at her in the dark for a long moment.

"I'll be listening," he said.

"I know you will," said Evelyn. "You can't help it."

* * *

Lucan was standing in the foyer when she came down the stairs from the circle.

He'd come in by the fire door. He hadn't needed to force it. The chain was on the inside, and he'd simply taken it off with a small neat charm she'd seen him use on the wine cellar at Selwyn Hall when she was nine, and come through, and walked up the dark corridor past the projection-room stairs into the foyer, and stood there in the light of his own wand, waiting for her.

He was standing beneath a poster.

It was the last poster anybody had ever put up in the Majestic. It had been there since the summer of 1985, in a glass case on the wall by the ticket booth, behind dirty glass, its colours gone yellow and blue with thirteen years of light. It showed a man in a dinner jacket and a woman with a great deal of hair, and an airship, and the Eiffel Tower, and the words *A View to a Kill*.

Lucan looked up at it as she came down the last stairs.

"I've always rather liked these," he said. "Muggle spy films. Father would have a fit."

"Hello, Lucan."

"Hello, Evelyn."

He turned round.

He looked exactly as he always looked. He was twenty-two. He was tall and well made, his fair hair cut very short, and he wore a dark grey travelling cloak over the plain black robes of the Minister's office, beautifully cut, and he was smiling his father's smile. He'd been practising it since he was twelve. It was very good. It showed all his white teeth and nothing else.

She couldn't read him. She'd never been able to read anybody.

He could read her.

She felt him do it. She felt it the moment he turned and looked at her, the way you feel a draught on the back of your neck. It went into her through the inch of open window she couldn't close, quite gently and very skilfully, and looked about.

"Oh, Evie," said Lucan softly.

He hadn't called her that since she was nine.

"Don't," said Evelyn.

"I'm sorry. I'm sorry. It's just…" He was still looking at her. Into her. She could feel him looking. "I've never seen you. Do you know that? Twenty-two years. I've never once seen what was going on in there. None of us have. Grandmother made very sure of it." He tilted his head. "And now it's all just *there*. Everything. Like a house with the front taken off."

"Yaxley felt it," said Evelyn. "Didn't he."

"From the Ministry. On Wednesday last week. About half past twelve at night." Lucan's voice was very pleasant. "He felt something open. Somewhere in the north. Something that had never been open before. He's very good, Yaxley. He's the best Legilimens in the Commission. He spent a week narrowing it down. And then he came to my office this morning, very pleased with himself, and told me he'd found a mind in Leeds that he'd never felt before, but that it felt a great deal like mine." He smiled. "Family resemblance, he said. He wanted to know if I had any relations in Yorkshire."

"What did you tell him?"

"That I'd look into it." Lucan put his hands in his pockets. "I've got six men outside, Evie. On the pavement. They don't know who's in here. They think it's a Muggle-born family. Yaxley's orders are that whoever's in here comes back with me to London tonight." He looked at her. "Father's orders too, as it happens. He's been very worried about you. Since Courtroom Ten."

"He saw me."

"He saw you." Lucan's smile didn't change. "He hasn't said a word about it. To anybody. Not to me, not to Mother, not to the Minister. He sat in that courtroom and watched his daughter throw wands across the floor, and then he went home and had dinner and talked about the weather." He paused. "He's never not said anything about something so loudly in his life."

Evelyn didn't answer.

"Come home," said Lucan.

He said it quite gently.

"Come home, Evie. Come back with me. Tonight. I'll tell Yaxley it was a mistake. I'll tell him you'd run away, that you'd got mixed up with the wrong sort, that you were frightened and hiding and didn't know what you were doing. He'll believe me. Father will see to it. You'll be safe." He looked at her. "You were always the one who was supposed to be safe, you know. You were the one piece on the board Father never had to move. He told me that once, when I was fifteen. *Evelyn will always be safe, because nobody will ever think about her.*" Lucan's smile slipped just a little at one corner. "He was so pleased with that."

"Go away, Lucan."

"Evie…"

"Go away." Her voice was quite steady. "Go back out of the door you came in by, and take your six men off the pavement, and go back to London, and tell Yaxley there was nobody here. Or don't. Tell him whatever you like. I'm not coming home. I haven't got a home. I left it in March last year, at fourteen minutes past eight in the morning, and I haven't been back, and I'm not going back." She looked at him. "You can read me. You know I mean it."

Lucan looked at her.

He looked at her for a long time in the foyer of a dead cinema, beneath a poster for a film from 1985. She could feel him looking. She could feel him in the inch of open window, moving about carefully, not touching anything, like a man walking through somebody else's house in his socks. She didn't know what he was finding. She couldn't tell. She'd never been able to tell what anybody felt, and she couldn't tell now, and it was the first time in her life she'd minded.

He said nothing.

His face didn't change. It was their father's face, very still, with their father's smile on it. Somewhere behind it, he was deciding.

She waited.

Then Lucan took his hands out of his pockets, turned, and walked across the foyer to the front doors.

They were boarded on the outside and chained on the inside, and he took the chain off with the same neat charm and pushed one door open a foot, and the rain and the streetlight came in across the dusty carpet. He stood in the gap with his back to her.

"Nothing," he said to somebody on the pavement. His voice was quite clear and quite bored. "Rats. Some Muggle's been sleeping in the projection room, I think, but they've gone. Nobody here." A pause. Somebody said something she couldn't hear. "No, I'm quite sure. Yaxley's got his wires crossed. It'll be a Squib or a Muggle with a funny mind. They get them up here. Go home. I'll write the report."

He stood in the doorway a moment longer.

Then he looked back over his shoulder at her.

It was a very short look. It lasted perhaps a second. She couldn't read it. She'd never in her life wished more that she could read anything.

"Goodnight, Evelyn," said Lucan.

He went out and pulled the door to behind him, and she heard six pairs of feet on the wet pavement, then six small cracks, then a seventh.

She stood in the foyer for a long time.

She'd never know which it was. She'd think about it on and off for the rest of her life. Whether her brother had stood in the foyer of the Majestic and read her and found something there he couldn't bring himself to take back to London. Or whether he'd read her and found she wasn't worth the trouble, or that the trouble wasn't worth the risk, or that there was a better use for a sister who owed him something than a sister in a cell. Or whether he'd simply looked at the piece on the board his father never had to move and decided, as their father would have, that it wasn't yet the moment to move it.

She noted, standing there, that the cinema was known now.

Whatever he told Yaxley. Whatever he wrote in the report. Yaxley had felt her open mind across a city and come within one street of it, and Lucan knew exactly where she was.

They'd have to go.

* * *

Harry laid it out at a quarter past one on the folding table in the projection room, with the stone basin pushed to one side and the four of them round it and a candle in a saucer.

He hadn't slept. Nobody had. Ron sat on his camp bed in his coat with his rucksack already packed beside him. Hermione had the beaded bag in her lap and was putting things into it without looking at them. Evelyn sat very upright on the end of her own bed with her hand in her cardigan pocket, and Harry could feel her a little through the inch that wouldn't close. Tired, and cold, and very steady, and beneath the steadiness, at the bottom, a long slow ache with her brother's name on it.

He didn't look at it. He let her have it.

"He's got two," said Harry.

They looked at him.

"Two of three. The wand. He took it off Dumbledore on the lawn. And the stone. It's in the ring he wears, the Gaunt ring, and he knows what it is now. He didn't, for a year and a half. He does now." He looked at Evelyn, and then away. "Somebody told him. In December."

Evelyn said nothing. He felt it go through her, quick and cold, and settle.

"He wants the third," said Harry. "He wants it more than anything. More than the war. A whole soul's afraid of dying, Grindelwald said, and he's whole now, and he's afraid, and the three of them together are the only thing anybody's ever found that might be the way out." He laid his hand flat on the inside pocket of his coat, where a small square of silver cloth was folded. "And I've got it. And he knows I've got it. He's known since Malfoy Manor at least, when Bellatrix asked Hermione where I kept it."

"So he'll come for it," said Ron.

"He'll come for it himself. He always does. He came to the lawn for the wand himself. He went to Nurmengard himself." Harry looked at the candle. "He likes to see people's faces."

"Then we hide it," said Hermione. "We hide it somewhere he'll never…"

"No."

"Harry…"

"We let him come." Harry looked round at them. "That's the plan. We let him come for it. But we choose where."

Nobody spoke.

"His Pinnacle gets stronger with people," said Harry. "I saw it on the lawn. Every mind he holds, he gets bigger. A thousand children at the windows, and he was stronger than Dumbledore. If he comes with his army, in the middle of them, there's nothing anybody alive can do to him. Dumbledore couldn't. I couldn't. I made the best illusion I've ever made on that lawn and he didn't even notice it. A candle against a furnace."

He thought about the lawn. He thought about it quite clearly, and let himself feel it, which he hadn't done in nine months.

"Mine's the other way round," he said. "Mine gets weaker with every person. A crowd's full of holes. Snape walked straight through one. But one mind…" He stopped. "One mind is the strongest thing I can do. One mind, on its own, with nobody else in it, and I could make him see anything. I could make him live anything."

He didn't say *like Hogsmeade*. He didn't need to. He felt all three of them think it.

"So he has to be alone," said Hermione slowly.

"He has to be alone. Away from them. All of them. Just him. And me." Harry looked at the table. "He'll come with an army. He always does. So the army has to be somewhere else, doing something else, and he has to come away from it, on his own, to get the one thing he wants more than the war."

"Where?" said Ron.

"Hogwarts."

They looked at him.

"Neville's there," said Harry. "In the Room. With thirty-one people. More, now. The village is feeding them, what's left of it. Aberforth's there. McGonagall's there, under the Carrows, waiting. Half the castle would fight if somebody told them it was time." He looked at the candle. "It's where he'll think I'd go. It's where he'll want to come. He grew up there. He thinks it's his. And it's big. There's the castle and the grounds and the lake and the Forest, and an army can be in the castle, fighting, and a man can be in the Forest, alone, with nobody for a mile."

"And you'll be in the Forest," said Hermione.

"Yes."

"Doing what you did at Hogsmeade. To him."

"Worse," said Harry. "Bigger. All of it. Everything I've got, on one mind." He looked at her. "And I'll go in so far that I won't be able to find my way out. I know that. I've been there. I was there for a month, and I didn't know I was there." He looked at the floor. "I'll need somebody at the door."

Nobody spoke.

The candle burned in its saucer. Outside, the rain had stopped. Somewhere in the walls a rat moved, and Harry felt it, small and quick and hungry, and was glad, quite simply, that he could.

He didn't look at Evelyn.

He didn't need to. He felt her before she spoke. He felt it rise in her through the inch of window that wouldn't close, quite quietly, very steady, and he knew what she was going to say before she said it, which had never once happened in seven years.

"I'll be at the door," said Evelyn.
