## Chapter 79: Ultimate Deceit

It was nine hundred and twelve paces from the bottom of the castle steps to the first trees of the Forest.

Evelyn counted them. Harry knew she was counting, because she was a pace behind his shoulder and her mind was open an inch, and he could feel the numbers going through her, steady as a clock, beneath everything else. He didn't count. He walked down the long slope of the lawn in the dark with the Cloak over his arm and the wet grass soaking through his trainers and the lights at the bottom growing bigger, and he thought about nothing very much.

He thought about Hagrid's hut, which they passed on the left, its door open and no light inside.

He thought about the pumpkin patch.

He thought about a boy of eleven coming down this lawn for the first time behind a man the size of a wardrobe, in a coat too big for him, reading the man's gladness the whole way, warm and loud and plain, and not knowing yet that it would ever stop.

"Harry," said Neville behind him.

"Yes."

"When you… When it starts. What do we do?"

"Stand round me," said Harry. "I'll fall down. Don't try to wake me. Don't move me. Whatever comes back through the trees, don't let it near me." He thought about it. "It'll look like I'm asleep. I won't be."

"How long?"

"I don't know."

"Right," said Neville. He said it the way he'd said *I counted* at the top of a staircase with his face wet. "Right."

"Brilliant plan," said Ron. "Love it. Really thorough."

"Ron," said Hermione.

"I'm just saying. Stand round him. Don't let anything near him. I could've come up with that."

"You didn't, though," said Millicent.

Ron opened his mouth and shut it again. Harry felt him a pace behind on the left, frightened and grieving and, for one second, very nearly amused, and was more grateful for that second than he'd have known how to say.

At six hundred and forty, somebody came out of the dark on the right.

Millicent had her wand up before Harry turned. Ron's came up a second later. Neville's came up so fast he nearly dropped it.

"Don't," said Draco Malfoy.

He came up the slope towards them quite slowly, his hands a little away from his sides and his mother's wand in one of them, pointing at the grass. His face was white. There was dust on his robes and a cut on the back of one hand, and he'd come, Harry could tell, from the castle, the long way, round the side of the greenhouses, in the dark, alone.

He stopped a yard away.

No one spoke.

Harry read him. He did it without meaning to, as he'd done it for seven years every time Draco came into a room. And the knot was there, exactly as it had been on the third stair and in a drawing room and on a tower, four or five things wound so tightly round each other that Harry couldn't find where any of them began.

He couldn't tell why Draco had come.

He looked for it. He looked carefully, the way you look for a word in a language you only half know, and it wasn't there. There was fear, and his mother, and the tower, and a bathroom full of water, and a drawing room, and none of it was a reason. None of it pointed anywhere.

Draco looked back at him. He knew Harry was reading him. He always had.

"Don't ask," said Draco.

"I wasn't going to."

"Good." Draco looked down the slope at the lights. "Because I couldn't tell you."

He fell in on the left, behind Ron, who looked at him for a long time and then, without a word, moved over to make room.

Harry walked on.

At nine hundred and twelve the grass ended and the trees began.

* * *

Two of them were waiting where the trees began. Yaxley, whom Harry had last seen at a desk in the Ministry, and a heavy-shouldered man with a scarred face whom Harry didn't know. They held their wands up, lit, and they were glad.

Harry read the gladness and didn't mind it. It was useful. Glad people didn't look very hard.

He let them see one boy.

It was the easiest illusion he'd made all night. Two minds, both glad, both looking for exactly what they saw. A thin boy in a dirty coat carrying the Cloak, alone, come to give himself up. He didn't even have to make the others invisible. He only had to make them unimportant, six shapes in the dark that didn't matter, the way you don't notice the furniture in a room you've been told to search for a person. Yaxley looked straight through Evelyn and saw a tree.

"Potter," said Yaxley.

His voice was pleased. He was a Legilimens, the best in the Commission, and he reached for Harry's mind with it quite lazily, the way you put out your hand for a banister you know is there.

Harry let him find a frightened boy.

"I've come," said Harry.

"So I see." Yaxley smiled. "He'll be so pleased. Walk in front of me. Slowly. Keep your hands where I can see them."

Harry walked in front of him.

The others came behind, six unimportant shapes in the dark between the trees.

* * *

They walked perhaps ten minutes into the Forest, along a path that wasn't a path, between oaks and beeches and great old dark firs, downhill, towards the sound of a stream. And Harry felt it before he saw anything.

The Forest was leaning.

It was the oddest thing he'd ever felt. He didn't feel it the way he felt people. He felt it through people. Through Yaxley behind him and the scarred man beside Yaxley, and through every Death Eater in the clearing ahead, three hundred of them, more. They were all leaning the same way. Their wills were leaning, the way grass leans in a wind, all in one direction, towards one point, and it was less a feeling than a pull. It was as though the ground had tilted very slightly everywhere, and everything that could move had begun, without noticing, to slide.

He'd felt it once before. On a lawn, on a summer night, beneath a tower, with a thousand children at the windows.

*Sovereign*, thought Harry.

It wasn't open. Not all the way. It was open the way a door is open when somebody has a hand on it, a crack, a promise. But it was enough that the trees either side of the path had begun, very slowly, to bend in towards the clearing. The branches on the near side of every trunk were longer than those on the far side. The ferns all lay one way. Even the stream, when they crossed it on stepping stones, was running at a slant against its own bank.

Ron, behind him, made a very small sound.

Harry didn't look back. He could feel Ron, and Hermione, and Neville, and Millicent, and Draco. He could feel all of them beginning to lean.

And he could feel Evelyn a pace behind his shoulder, not leaning at all.

* * *

They stopped short of the clearing, in the trees, whilst Yaxley went ahead.

Harry stood still and let him go. He let the scarred man stand beside him with a wand at his ribs. He reached into the scarred man very lightly and showed him a boy standing quite still and frightened, and the man was satisfied and looked away into the clearing.

Evelyn was at his shoulder.

He turned his head an inch and spoke without moving his lips, the way they'd spoken at the back of Potions for six years.

"If you hold Dead Calm round me, nothing can touch me," he said. "But you won't feel anything. You won't be able to call."

"And if I don't, you've only got them."

"Yes."

She didn't answer for a moment. He felt her think about it. He felt it go through her very fast, the whole sum, every number, the six of them and the three hundred and the time it would take and the place he'd be, so far in that nobody could follow. He felt her come to the end of it.

"I'll call," said Evelyn. "They'll hold."

Behind them in the dark, Millicent said very quietly, "Course we will."

* * *

The clearing was large and round and full of people, with a fire in the middle, and Voldemort was standing by the fire.

He wasn't doing anything. He stood with his back to the flames and his hands folded in front of him, the way a man stands at the end of a long table waiting for his guests to finish their soup. He was tall and thin and very pale, in plain black, holding a wand quite loosely, and the wand was long and pale with a small dark mark halfway down it like a burn. There was a ring on his right hand. A heavy gold ring with a black stone, on the second finger.

Two of three, thought Harry.

The Death Eaters stood all round the clearing beneath the leaning trees, three and four deep. Harry didn't count them. He read them all at once, and they were glad, and hungry, and very frightened, and beneath the fear, in every one of them, was the lean. They were all leaning towards the man by the fire, the way iron filings lean towards a magnet, and most of them didn't know it.

Bellatrix was at the front near the fire, so glad she was almost singing. Lucius Malfoy was at the back in the shadow of an oak, grey and wandless and ashamed. Beside him, very straight, with her hands together in front of her and no wand at all, stood Narcissa.

She was afraid. It was all for one person. And the person wasn't in the clearing, and she didn't know where he was.

Harry didn't look at her for long.

He looked at Voldemort.

He reached for him once, carefully, the way you put your hand on a door to see whether it's hot. And it was the mountain again. A closed mind so large and so still and so certain of itself that his reaching went up against it and stopped, and didn't even leave a mark.

He'd known it would be. He'd known since a lawn in summer. You couldn't deceive a closed mind. Snape had been the only person alive who knew that better than Harry did.

He'd have to wait for it to open.

Yaxley came back across the clearing.

"My Lord," he said, and bowed. "He is here. Alone. He has brought it."

Voldemort turned his head.

He looked at the trees, at the place where a boy stood very still with a wand at his ribs and a silver-grey cloak over his arm. His eyes were red. They weren't angry. They were interested, very interested, the way a man is interested in a picture he's bought and hasn't yet hung.

"Harry Potter," said Voldemort. "Come here."

* * *

He didn't go.

He stood where he was beneath the oaks and did what he'd been taught to do on a lawn at the Burrow, in a field, by a man in a sugared-apricot cloak who'd made faces at the hippogriffs.

*Not one perfect lie*, Lockhart had said. *A hundred bad ones. Fast. For minds that aren't thinking.*

There were three hundred minds in the clearing, and not one of them was thinking. They were leaning. They were glad and frightened and leaning, and a mind that's leaning is a mind already going somewhere it hasn't chosen. You didn't have to push it. You only had to show it a direction.

He showed them.

He didn't build anything. He hadn't time to build. He threw it, all at once, like a man flinging a bucket of water across a floor, a hundred bad lies, two hundred, in every direction.

He gave Bellatrix her master's voice in her ear, high and cold and urgent, from the direction of the castle. *The castle. They are breaking out. Go. Now.*

He gave the twenty men nearest the path the sound of Aurors in the trees behind them, a great many Aurors coming fast, and a voice he'd once heard at a desk in the Atrium saying *surround them*.

He gave the men on the far side of the clearing a boy. A thin boy in a dirty coat running away from them into the Forest with a silver-grey cloak streaming behind him, and then another boy running the other way, and another, and another, fifty of them, a hundred, Harry Potter running in every direction at once between the leaning trees, all carrying the Cloak.

They were very bad. They had holes in them. One of the running boys had no feet. One of the voices said *the castle* in a slightly wrong accent. A cleverer man, standing still, would have seen through any of it.

Nobody was standing still.

They went.

They went all at once, the way birds go off a field, in every direction. Bellatrix went first, towards the castle, shrieking for the others to follow. The men by the path turned on Aurors who weren't there and ran into the trees after them, firing. The men on the far side went after the boys. There was shouting and the crack of Apparition and the noise of three hundred people crashing through a forest in the dark, and it spread outwards from the clearing like a ring from a stone dropped in a pond.

Yaxley turned towards the castle with his wand up and his mouth open.

The scarred man let go of Harry's ribs and ran.

And as they went, the lean went with them.

Harry felt it. He felt Sovereign thin. Every mind that left the clearing was a mind no longer leaning, and it was as though, one by one, very fast, somebody were taking the weights off one side of a pair of scales. The trees round the clearing began slowly to straighten. The ferns lifted. The stream went back to its bank.

"*Stop*," said Voldemort.

He didn't shout it. He said it quite quietly, and Harry felt it go out of him like a blow into the dark after them, three hundred wills being told what to do.

But he couldn't move.

He couldn't leave the centre. Harry had known it for two years, since a lawn in summer, since watching him stand in the middle of a thousand children's terror like a man standing in a river. Whilst Sovereign was open, he couldn't move from its heart. And he couldn't command what he couldn't see, and he couldn't see what Harry had shown them. He could only see that they were running.

Lucius Malfoy ran with the rest. Harry let him.

Narcissa didn't run.

She stood under the oak where she'd been, very straight, hands together, and Harry hadn't given her anything, because he hadn't seen any need. She looked round the clearing at the trees and the empty ground and the fire. She looked at the place where Harry stood. And then she turned, quite slowly, and walked away into the Forest, not after anybody, simply away.

He didn't know where she was going.

He hadn't time to find out.

The clearing was empty.

It was empty except for a fire, and a tall thin man beside it with a pale wand in his hand and a ring on his finger, and a boy beneath the oaks holding a cloak. And the dark all round, full of shouting, getting further away.

Behind Harry, in the trees, six people stood very still, and nobody was looking at them at all.

* * *

"Clever," said Voldemort.

He said it quite softly. He was looking at Harry across the empty clearing, and Harry read nothing, and knew from his face that he was very angry, and that the anger wasn't the top of it.

"Lockhart," said Voldemort. "That was Lockhart. My people told me of it. A wedding, and a great many hippogriffs." He tilted his head. "You learned from the fool."

"He wasn't a fool."

"He died on a bridge in a dressing gown."

"It was a cloak," said Harry. "And he held it."

Voldemort looked at him for a long moment. Then he smiled. It was a very small smile, the most courteous thing Harry had ever seen on a face, and it didn't reach anywhere.

"I could kill you from here," he said. "You know that. This wand would do it without my lifting it. It has done finer work than you."

"I know."

"And yet I have not." The red eyes didn't move. "Do you know why?"

"Because you don't know if it's the real one," said Harry.

Voldemort didn't answer.

"You've been asking for it for seven years," said Harry. "You said so. You asked Grindelwald, and he told you about the stone instead, and you killed him anyway." He watched the red eyes. "You've never seen it. Not once. Nobody's ever shown it to you."

"Your father wore it," said Voldemort softly. "He did not wear it on the night I came."

"No. He lent it to Dumbledore."

"And Dumbledore gave it to you." The thin mouth moved. "He gave everything to you, in the end. The cloak. The war. His death. I watched him give you his death on a lawn and call it a lesson."

"He didn't call it anything," said Harry. "He was dead."

He held up his arm with the Cloak over it. In the firelight it was silver and grey and moving like water, and the end of his arm wasn't there.

"I make things people want to see," said Harry. "You know I do. You saw the lawn. You've read the reports from Hogsmeade. You don't know if this is the Cloak, or a coat I've made you see as the Cloak, and the real one's in a drawer in Leeds." He lowered his arm. "If you kill me, and it's not the real one, you'll never find it. Nobody else knows where it is."

It was a lie. It was a good one. It was the best he'd ever told, because it was true in every part except the one that mattered.

Voldemort looked at him.

"Then I shall look," said Voldemort.

And he raised the pale wand, quite slowly, and pointed it at Harry's face, and said very softly the one word Harry had been waiting all night to hear.

"*Legilimens*."

* * *

The mountain opened.

He felt it open. It was the most enormous thing he'd ever felt, a closed mind the size of a range of hills opening a door in its side and reaching out through the door, very fast and very hard, towards him. It came the way it had come through his scar for fifteen years, in dreams and fevers and on a summer night in a room full of glass. It came the way it had come into Grindelwald in a cell at the top of a tower, through a wand a foot from his face. It was looking for the Cloak. It was looking for the drawer in Leeds. It was going to tear through every room in Harry's head to find it, and it didn't care what it broke.

It was open.

For a second, coming through the door, it was a mind with nothing round it. One mind. Alone. With nobody else in it.

Harry went through the door the other way.

He didn't throw anything. He'd thrown everything he had at three hundred people a minute ago, and there was nothing left in his hands, and he didn't need it. He went in along the line of the reaching, the way you walk back along a rope somebody's thrown you, and he went in with the wand he'd carried for seven years, holly and phoenix feather, raised in his hand, and he didn't stop at the door.

He opened it.

He didn't know what to call it. Afterwards, when people asked, he'd say *the Pinnacle*, because that was the word in the books, and because it was easier. But he didn't think of it as a word. He thought of it for the rest of his life as the moment he stopped showing someone a thing and started telling the world what it was.

The clearing went.

It didn't fade. It didn't dissolve, or shimmer, or any of the things illusions did in stories. It simply stopped being true. The fire wasn't there, and the trees weren't there, and the dark wasn't there, and it had never been there, and something else had always been there instead.

What had always been there was this.

* * *

Lord Voldemort stood in a clearing in the Forbidden Forest a little after half past twelve and looked down at the body of Harry Potter.

It lay on its back on the trampled ferns at his feet, eyes open, glasses knocked sideways, mouth a little open, one hand flung out palm up towards the fire. The Cloak was beside it. It had fallen from the boy's arm when the green light took him, and it lay on the ferns in a little silver heap, stirring very slightly in the heat from the fire, like water.

He'd done it with a word. He hadn't even lifted the wand.

He bent and picked it up.

Harry built it.

That was the strange thing. He was there, inside it, as close as his own skin, and he was building it, and he was also lying dead on the ferns at Voldemort's feet with his eyes open, and he was also the ferns, and the fire, and the Cloak, and the cool weight of it in Voldemort's long white hand. He was everything in it. He was the author. There was nowhere in the whole of it that he wasn't.

And he knew what to build, because he knew the man.

He'd known him a long time. He'd known him at sixteen, in a diary, in a bathroom, on long nights in a dormitory with a quill. He'd felt what lay beneath the charm and the patience and the loneliness, the thing that came up every time Harry talked about what he could feel, quick and sharp and bitter, like a dog snapping at a hand. Envy. Tom had always known what people wanted. He'd never once known what they felt. And Harry had felt him want it.

And he'd known him for fifteen years before that without knowing he knew. A fragment, a cold second presence sitting very quietly at the back of Harry's own head since a night in Godric's Hollow, feeling everything Harry felt and wanting all of it. He'd lived with it. He'd grown up with it, the way you grow up with a noise in a house that you stop hearing. And on a night at the Veil it had been torn out of him, and it had gone home, taking fifteen years of Harry with it, and it had come back into this man, and this man had never once looked at what it brought.

Harry had.

He knew what Tom wanted. He didn't have to guess. He'd felt it from the inside.

He gave it to him.

* * *

The Cloak was light. It was lighter than anything Voldemort had ever held. He held it in one hand and the Elder Wand in the other, and the ring was on his finger, and he stood in the clearing by the fire and felt the three of them, all at once, for the first time.

He felt them meet.

It went through him like warmth. Harry made it go through him like warmth, slowly, from the hand that held the Cloak up the arm and into the chest and out to the ends of him, the way warmth goes through a man who's been cold for seventy years without knowing it. He made it feel like the end of something. Like a door shutting behind him on a winter night, with the fire lit on the other side.

He was the Master of Death.

He stood very still and let himself know it.

There was nobody in the clearing to see him. His people were coming back through the trees, he could hear them a long way off, shouting the boy's name. He didn't want them yet. He wanted, for a moment, to stand here alone with it by the fire, with the boy at his feet.

He looked down at the boy.

He felt nothing about him. Harry made sure of that. He let Voldemort look down at Harry Potter dead on the ferns and feel only a mild and pleasant tiredness, the tiredness of a man at the end of a long piece of work, and a faint, faint curiosity, like a man looking at a beetle he's trodden on and wondering idly what it had been doing.

It was easy to build.

It was the easiest thing in the world. Harry had felt it himself, on a step in the snow.

* * *

Somewhere a long way off, somebody was saying his name.

He heard it the way you hear the sea from inside a house with the windows shut. Not in the clearing, and not in the deceit. Somewhere outside both, very faint, a long way up.

*Potter. Potter. Potter.*

And other voices beneath it, further off, like people talking in the next house.

*They're coming back. Ron. Ron, they're coming back…*

*I know. I can see them. Neville, left. Your* left*…*

*How many?*

*Doesn't matter how many. Stand still. Stand still and keep your wand up.* That was Millicent. *Nobody gets past. Right? Nobody.*

He couldn't stop to listen.

* * *

They came back into the clearing, the Death Eaters, and they came on their knees.

Harry built them. He built every one of them out of what Voldemort thought they were, which wasn't people. Three hundred men and women in black coming out of the leaning trees one after another into the firelight, and seeing the boy on the ferns, and seeing the Cloak in their master's hand, and going down. Bellatrix first. She went down on the ferns and put her face to the ground at his feet and wept with gladness, and he didn't look at her. Then the others. Rows of them. A great dark lake of bowed heads round the fire, all the way back into the trees.

He walked through them.

They made way for him. He walked out of the clearing and up through the Forest, which bent to let him pass, every tree leaning out of his way, and out onto the long lawn beneath the stars, the Cloak over his shoulders and the wand in his hand, and they came behind him, all of them, a long dark river of people, up the slope towards the castle.

The castle was waiting.

The great oak doors stood open. The light from the Entrance Hall spilled out across the steps. And on the steps, and on the lawn, and in the courtyard, and at every window on every floor, there were people.

They were kneeling.

All of them. Everyone who'd fought him tonight. Every child in a dressing gown. Every teacher. McGonagall on the top step with her head bowed and her hair coming down. Neville. The Weasley twins, both of them, alive, faces to the ground. Harry put them all there. He put them there because Voldemort wanted them there, and he gave Voldemort what he wanted, all of it, without stinting, and he felt nothing about it at all, because he couldn't afford to.

Voldemort went up the steps between them.

* * *

*Potter*, said the voice a long way up. *Potter.*

It was closer. It had something beneath it now, something that hadn't been there before. He couldn't tell what.

He could feel, very faint, at the very edge of everything, as though through a wall of water, that there were people near his body. He couldn't tell how many. He couldn't tell who. He could only tell that they were there, and afraid, and that some of them were hurt.

One of them was hurt very badly.

He felt it go through her. He felt her go down. He felt her get up again, which shouldn't have been possible, and stand, and go on standing, square and short and stubborn as a gatepost, aimed straight at him.

*Bulstrode. Bulstrode, stay down…*

*'M fine.* It was very thick. *'M fine, Weasley. Get off.*

*You're not fine, you're…*

*I said get off. Watch your side.*

He felt her go down again.

*Draco*, said a voice he didn't know at first. It was Hermione's, and very high. *Draco, behind you…*

And a curse, and a shield, and Draco Malfoy's voice saying something short and savage Harry had never heard him say in seven years, not to Harry, not to anybody.

He couldn't stop.

* * *

Voldemort walked through his castle.

Harry gave him all of it. He gave him the Entrance Hall with its flagstones swept clean and its doors standing open to the night. He gave him the Great Hall with its four long tables, and the enchanted ceiling full of stars, and the candles burning in the air, and every house banner taken down and a single one hung behind the staff table, black, with a serpent on it, and no other colour anywhere. He gave him the staircases, which didn't move under his feet, which stood perfectly still and waited for him to choose.

He gave him the seventh floor.

He gave him a corridor on the third floor, which Voldemort had walked down at sixteen with a prefect's badge on his chest, and a bathroom on the second, and a door behind a statue's feet deep under the school, with two words scratched on it in a boy's hand.

Harry had seen those words. He'd stood before that door at thirteen with Evelyn beside him and read them in the light of a lamp that lit for a heart-reader and had never once lit for Tom. *I WILL.* Over and over, the length of the door, deeper and deeper, the scratches of a boy of sixteen who'd stood there for hours, night after night, with a knife, because a door wouldn't open for him and he couldn't understand why.

Harry didn't give Voldemort that door.

He gave him the door open. He gave him the study lit, the lamp burning cold and white on the black stone desk, the shelves full, as though it had always opened for him. As though it had been waiting.

Voldemort stood in the doorway of Slytherin's study and looked at the light.

Harry felt what rose in him. It rose out of the bottom of a mind as big as a range of hills, a very long way, from a place that had been shut for fifty-five years. It was very small. It was a boy's feeling. The feeling of a boy standing before a door that has finally opened.

It was the only thing Harry had felt from him all night.

He didn't stop.

* * *

*Potter. Potter. Please. Potter.*

*Selwyn, he's bleeding. His nose. Is that…*

*It's all right. It always does that.* Evelyn's voice was quite flat. *Hold the line, Granger. I've got him.*

* * *

The Mirror was in the room behind the study.

There was no room behind the study. Harry put one there. He put a door in its back wall between two shelves, a door that had never been there and had always been there, and Voldemort saw it and went through it, because that was where it went.

The room was small and empty and dim. There was nothing in it except a mirror.

It was very tall, as tall as the ceiling, in a gold frame on two clawed feet, with words carved round the top of the frame in a language that wasn't a language. Harry had found it once in an empty classroom on a Christmas night when he was eleven and stood in front of it until morning.

He'd seen his mother in it. His mother and his father and a great many people behind them with his face about the eyes and his hair, all of them looking at him and loving him, and he'd stood there and felt it from the glass, the first time he'd ever felt anything from anyone that was aimed at him and asked for nothing back.

He'd never told anyone what he saw.

He gave Voldemort the Mirror.

Voldemort knew what it was. He'd read of it. He knew what it showed, the deepest wish of the heart of whoever stood before it, nothing more and nothing less. And he knew what he'd see, because he knew what he wanted, he'd always known, he'd known since an orphanage and a wardrobe on fire. He wanted to live. He wanted to be the man who didn't die.

He'd come, at the end of his long walk through his castle, with the three Hallows on him and his enemies on their knees, to look at himself immortal.

He went and stood before the glass.

Harry felt him go. He felt him cross the small dim room in three long strides and stop, and lift his head, the way a man lifts his head to look at a portrait of himself he's commissioned and hasn't yet seen.

And the Mirror didn't show him.

It showed a boy.

A thin boy of seventeen with untidy black hair that needed cutting and a pair of round glasses mended at the bridge, in a coat that needed washing, alive. Standing in the glass where Voldemort should have been. Looking out at him.

The boy smiled.

It was a polite smile. Harry knew it very well. It was the smile he gave shop assistants and train guards and Madam Pince, and a newsagent in Leeds who asked him every morning whether he was at the college. It was the smile he gave strangers when he couldn't be bothered to feel anything about them. Pleasant and empty and perfectly courteous, and aimed at nobody at all.

It was the deepest wish of Tom Riddle's heart.

Harry had known that for seven years. He'd felt it in a diary at twelve, the envy rising every time he spoke. He'd felt it in the fragment for fifteen years before that, without knowing what he felt. Tom didn't want to live for ever. Not really. Not at the bottom. He wanted to be the boy who could feel what other people felt. He wanted to be Harry.

And he didn't know it.

He'd never once looked.

Harry felt him look now. He felt it go through Voldemort all at once, very fast, from the top of that enormous mind to the bottom, the thing he'd never once in seventy years let himself feel. He felt the incomprehension first. Then the rage. Then, beneath the rage, rising out of the dark like something out of deep water, the small hot bitter thing that had snapped at Harry's hand in a diary when he was twelve.

Voldemort raised the Elder Wand at the boy in the glass.

He didn't think about it. He wasn't thinking. He was a man who'd walked all the way through his own castle to look at himself and found somebody else standing there, smiling at him as though he didn't matter, and he did what he'd always done, since an orphanage, since a bathroom, since a graveyard and a house in Godric's Hollow, to anything that stood where he wanted to stand.

"*Avada…*"

* * *

Harry had built the glass out of his face.

He'd built it the way you build a trap for something you know very well, out of the one thing it will never think to look at. The glass of the Mirror wasn't glass. There'd never been any glass. There was the boy in the frame, smiling, and behind the boy, all the way through, there was nothing at all but the inside of a long pale face in a clearing in the Forest, three feet from the end of its own wand.

He'd learned it at eleven. In an underground room, in terror, on a man he'd loved, who'd turned his wand on the face at the back of his own head because Harry had shown him, without meaning to, what he hated most.

He hadn't meant to, then.

He meant to now.

"*…Kedavra*."

And in the last instant, in the last splinter of the last second, as the word left him, Voldemort felt it.

Harry felt him feel it. Something wrong. Something under the glass. A draught from a door that should have been shut. A man as old and as careful as that doesn't live seventy years without learning the feel of a trap, and he felt it, very faint and very late, and he didn't know what it was, and he did the only thing there was time to do.

He wrenched the wand aside.

Not at the glass. Away from it. Away from whatever lay behind it. Out of the deceit altogether, towards the one real thing he could feel in the whole of that false world, which was the boy's body lying on the ferns in the clearing, with six people standing round it in the firelight.

The curse went at Harry.

Harry felt it come.

He felt it leave the pale wand in a clearing in the Forest, the real one, and go towards his own real body, very fast and very green.

And he felt the wand refuse.

It wasn't a feeling he'd ever had. Wands didn't feel. Objects had nothing. But for a hair of a second, in the clearing, through the last thin edge of the deceit, he felt something in the pale wand turn over, the way a cat turns over in your arms when it's decided it doesn't want to be held. It knew him. He didn't know how. He'd never touched it. It knew him the way a dog knows the man who feeds it, by something beneath the skin, and it wouldn't do this. Not to him.

The curse turned back.

It turned back in the air between the wand and Harry's body, the way water turns back from a wall, and it went the only way left for it to go.

It had always been coming back to him. Harry would think that afterwards, many times, on many nights. Through the glass or through the wand. Either way.

Lord Voldemort fell.

He fell in the clearing by the fire at sixteen minutes to one in the morning on the second of May, quite quietly, on his back on the trampled ferns, his eyes open, his long white hands empty, the ring still on his finger. The pale wand rolled away from him across the ground and stopped against a root.

And inside the deceit, in a small dim room behind a study beneath a school, the Mirror cracked across.

* * *

It came down all at once.

He hadn't built it to come down. He'd built it to hold for as long as it needed to, and it had needed to for exactly as long as there was somebody in it to deceive. There wasn't. There was nobody left in it but Harry.

The Mirror went first. The crack ran across it and then down, and the boy in the glass went with it, smiling, in pieces. Then the walls of the little room. Then the study, the shelves and the black stone desk and the lamp, all going, not breaking, simply ceasing, the way a word stops meaning anything when you say it too many times. Then the corridors, the staircases, the Great Hall with its single black banner. The people kneeling on the lawn. The long dark river of them. The Forest, bending out of the way.

He was standing in the Entrance Hall.

He didn't know how he'd got there. It was the Entrance Hall, and it wasn't, and it was coming apart round him, the flagstones going one by one from the edges inwards like ice going off a pond in spring. There was no light anywhere. There was no sound. There was no one.

He went to the doors.

They weren't there. There was a wall where the doors had been, a plain stone wall, and he put his hands on it, and it went under his hands like sand.

He turned. He went to the staircase. The staircase was going. He went to the passage to the dungeons, and the passage was a long way off and getting further, and when he ran towards it, it receded exactly as fast as he ran.

*Oswin*, thought Harry. *Could not find the door back to himself.*

He'd been here before. He'd lived here for a month, on a bridge, on a step, in the snow, without knowing it was a place. He'd known then, for a whole month, that there was nothing outside. That he was the only thing that was real.

He stood in the middle of the Entrance Hall as it went, and reached.

There was nothing.

He reached for the clearing, for his body, for the six people round it, for anyone. He reached the way he'd reached all his life, the way he breathed, and it went out from him into the dark and found nothing at all, in any direction, for ever. Not silence. Silence was a person. This was nothing. This was the place he'd built, with its builder still inside it and no one else, coming down round him.

He couldn't remember which way was out.

He couldn't remember whether there was an out.

He stood on the last of the flagstones in the dark, and the last of them began to go.

And then, from very close, from no direction at all, from somewhere just behind his shoulder, where she'd always been, somebody said his name.

Not *Potter*.

"Harry," said Evelyn.

She'd never said it before. In seven years. Not once. Not in Madam Malkin's, or a classroom on the fourth floor, or a chamber beneath the school, or another world, or a courtroom, or a shack with the candle going out. She'd said *Potter* ten thousand times. She'd said it dry and flat and patient and furious and frightened, and in the snow, and under a chandelier, and he'd known exactly where she was every time she said it.

She said *Harry*, quite quietly, as though it were the most ordinary thing in the world. As though she'd been saying it in her head for years and had simply decided it was time.

He turned towards it.

There was a door.

It had always been there. It was a plain wooden door, quite small, with an old brass handle, in a wall that wasn't there, just behind his shoulder. He'd walked past it a hundred times. He hadn't been able to see it, because it wasn't his, and everything in that place was his.

He put his hand on the handle.

He opened it.

* * *

He opened his eyes.

He was lying on his back on the ferns. There was a fire, quite close, burning low. There were trees all round, standing straight, the way trees stand. The sky above them wasn't quite black any more. It was the very dark grey that comes about an hour before the light.

Somebody was holding his hand.

He turned his head. It was Evelyn. She was on her knees on the ferns beside him with his right hand in both of hers, holding it so tightly the bones hurt, and her face was white and wet and perfectly still, and she was looking at him.

He looked back at her.

Neither of them spoke.

He turned his head the other way.

Millicent lay beside him on the ferns, quite close, on her side, facing him, her wand still in her hand and her eyes open. There was blood on her face and on the front of her robes and on the ferns beneath her. She wasn't moving.

Beyond her he could see Ron on his knees, and Hermione beside him with her hand on his back, and Neville standing with his wand still up, turning slowly in a circle, looking into the trees. And Draco, a little apart, sitting on the ground with his back to an oak and his mother's wand across his knees, looking at Millicent.

There was no sound in the clearing at all.

Harry lay on the ferns and reached for them.

He reached for Ron, two yards away on his knees. For Hermione beside him. For Neville. For Draco by the oak. For Millicent. For Evelyn, holding his hand.

He reached again.

## Chapter 80: The Great Hall

Neville carried Millicent.

Nobody asked him to. Nobody said anything. Harry was sitting up on the ferns with Evelyn's hands still round his, and Neville put his wand away in his pocket and went down on one knee beside Millicent and got his arms under her, under her knees and her shoulders, the way you'd lift somebody who'd fallen asleep in a chair, and stood up.

She was very heavy. She'd always been heavy. She'd been the biggest girl in their year since they were eleven, and Pansy Parkinson had called her a wardrobe for six years, and Millicent had once picked Pansy up by the back of her robes and put her on top of an actual wardrobe in the second-year dormitory and left her there until supper.

Neville stood up with her. He staggered once. Then he didn't stagger again.

"Right," said Neville.

He began to walk.

* * *

Harry walked beside him.

He didn't remember getting up. He was standing, and Evelyn had let go of his hand at some point, and he was walking beside Neville through the trees, uphill, in the grey before the dawn, Millicent's boots swinging a little at every step. He could see her face. It was turned in against Neville's shoulder. Somebody had closed her eyes.

He looked at Neville.

Neville's face was very white and set and wet, his jaw tight with the weight. Harry looked at him and waited to know what he was feeling.

He didn't know.

He looked at him a little longer. He did it the way he'd done it all his life, without thinking, the way you put your hand on a rail going down a stair. And there was nothing there. Not silence. Not a door. Just Neville's face, white and wet, and Harry looking at it from the outside.

He looked away.

Ron was on his other side, a pace behind. Harry looked at him. Ron had dust in his hair and blood dried down one side of his neck and a long tear in the sleeve of his jumper, and his face was doing something, and Harry couldn't tell what.

He looked away from Ron too.

Behind Ron, Hermione. Behind Hermione, at a little distance, alone, his hands at his sides and his mother's wand in one of them, Draco.

And on Harry's other side, half a pace behind his shoulder, Evelyn.

He didn't look at her. He knew what he'd find. He'd found it for seven years. It didn't matter now.

They came to the clearing's edge, and the stream, running straight in its bank, and the stepping stones.

There was a man sitting on the far bank.

He was in black robes, with a silver mask hanging from his hand by its strap, sitting on the wet grass with his knees drawn up and his wand on the ground beside him, looking at the stream. He was perhaps forty. He had a round face and thinning hair and a small neat moustache. He looked up when they came out of the trees, at Neville, at the girl in Neville's arms, at Harry. He didn't reach for his wand.

His face was wet.

He looked, Harry thought, like a man who's woken up in a strange bedroom and doesn't know how he got there. His mouth was a little open. His eyes went from Neville's face to Millicent's and back, and he didn't seem to understand either of them.

"I don't…" he said. He stopped. "I was in my kitchen."

Nobody answered him.

"I was in my *kitchen*," the man said again, more loudly, as though they'd disagreed. "In Sevenoaks. I was making toast. On Tuesday. I was making toast and somebody came to the door, and…"

He looked down at the mask in his hand.

He let go of it. It fell on the grass. He looked at it lying there as though it belonged to somebody else.

Neville walked past him over the stepping stones without stopping.

Harry stopped.

He stood on the near bank and looked at the man, and the man looked back, and Harry waited, out of seven years' habit, to know whether he was lying. To know what lay beneath the bewilderment. Whether there was shame under it, or relief, or the old hot gladness of a man who'd come up a hill to burn a castle.

He didn't know.

He looked at the man's face. It was a wet round face with a neat moustache. It told him nothing it didn't tell everybody.

"Kingsley will be along," said Harry. "Stay there."

"Yes," said the man. "Yes. All right." He looked at the stream. "I'm so sorry. I don't… I'm so sorry."

Harry crossed the stones.

* * *

There were more of them on the lawn.

He saw them as they came out of the trees in the grey light. They were all over the long slope between the Forest and the castle, in ones and twos, the way people are scattered over a field after a fair. Some were standing. Most were sitting. Some had their masks off and some had them on, pushed up on their foreheads like spectacles. Some had their hands on their heads, the way you put your hands on your head when told to by somebody with a wand, though there was nobody near them with a wand. One woman was walking very slowly in a circle near the pumpkin patch, round and round, her arms wrapped round herself. One man lay on his back looking at the sky.

Kingsley's people were moving among them. There were Aurors in the grounds now, a great many, in the plain dark robes of the Ministry. Some had arrived in the night from London, and some, Harry saw, were still wearing the black robes they'd fought in, their masks gone.

"What happened?" said Harry.

He said it to Ron. He had to. He didn't know whether Ron knew.

Ron looked at him.

"You don't know?"

"No."

"I thought you'd…" Ron stopped. He looked at Harry's face, and something crossed his own, and Harry couldn't tell what it was. "When he died. When he went down. It all just… stopped. Like that." He snapped his fingers. It made no sound. His fingers were too dirty. "They were coming at us. All round. Thirty of them, forty, through the trees. Bulstrode was…" He didn't finish. "And then he went down, and they all just stopped. In the middle of a curse. One of them was halfway through a word. They all just stood there and looked at each other, like they'd all woken up in the same room, and then about half of them sat down on the ground, and the rest legged it."

"Kingsley says it's the same in London," said Hermione. "He sent a Patronus at about two. The Ministry. Everyone who was under the Imperius. Everyone who'd been *held*, he said. They all came out of it at once. A quarter to one. There are people in the Atrium in their nightclothes who don't know what year it is."

"Held," said Harry.

"That's what he said."

He thought about the lean. The Forest leaning, the trees, the ferns, the stream at a slant against its bank. Three hundred minds leaning one way like grass in a wind, most of them not knowing it. A thousand children at the windows on a lawn last summer, going down on their knees.

He hadn't done it. He knew that quite clearly. He hadn't freed anybody. He'd been inside a falling castle, looking for a door. The man by the stream had stopped making toast because the man who'd made him stop had died, and it would have happened whoever killed him, and however.

He looked at the woman walking in circles by the pumpkin patch.

He waited to know what she was feeling.

He walked on.

* * *

The Great Hall was full.

There were people in it from every house and every year, and from the village and from London, and the four long tables had been pushed back against the walls, and the enchanted ceiling was the grey of a morning that hadn't quite decided to happen. The noise was very great. Harry stood just inside the doors with Neville beside him and Millicent in Neville's arms and let it come at him, the way he'd let the noise of every room in his life come at him, and turned to turn it down.

There was nothing to turn down.

There was the noise. There were voices. Hundreds of them. Somebody crying near the staff table, and somebody laughing near the windows, a high cracked laugh that went on too long, and a great many people talking at once. He could hear it. He could hear all of it.

He didn't know what any of it was.

He stood just inside the doors and looked out across the Hall at three hundred people, and they were faces. They were only faces. They were moving and talking and crying and laughing and holding on to each other, and he looked at them one after another, the way you look along a shelf for a book, and every one of them was closed. Every one of them was the way Evelyn had been for seven years. Not even a door. Just a face, from the outside.

He reached again. He reached for the girl crying near the staff table, who was eleven or twelve and holding the hand of a boy her own age, and he found her face, and her hand, and the boy's hand, and that was all.

He reached for the boy.

He reached for the man by the window with the cracked laugh. For Professor Flitwick, standing on a bench, counting heads. For Madam Pomfrey, moving along the row under the windows.

"Harry," said Neville quietly. "Where shall I put her?"

He looked at Neville.

"Next to Hagrid," said Harry. "She liked Hagrid."

* * *

The row ran the whole length of the wall beneath the windows on the left-hand side.

There were more than there had been at midnight. Harry walked along it with Neville. He didn't want to, and he did. He walked behind Neville down the length of the Great Hall and looked at every one, because somebody ought to, and because Evelyn was behind him, and she was looking at every one as well. He knew that without looking at her. She'd be counting.

Fred was near the doors, with his mother beside him.

Mrs Weasley was sitting on the floor with her back to the wall and Fred's head in her lap. She was stroking his hair. She was doing it very slowly, from the forehead back, over and over, the way you stroke the hair of a child with a temperature, and she wasn't crying. She'd stopped crying. Arthur was beside her with his arm round her and a bandage round his head, and George sat on Fred's other side with his knees drawn up and his face on his knees.

Harry stopped.

Mrs Weasley looked up at him. She looked at him for a long moment, her face swollen and blotched and quite still, and he didn't know what was in it. He didn't know whether it was grief or blame or love or nothing. He'd known what was in Molly Weasley's face at every meal in the Burrow kitchen, and at a wedding, and on a dance floor with Sirius treading on her feet. He didn't know it now.

"Harry, love," she said.

She held out her hand.

He took it. He didn't know what else to do. He stood there holding Molly Weasley's hand over her dead son's head in the Great Hall, and she held his very hard, and he didn't know why.

Then she let go and went back to stroking Fred's hair.

Harry walked on.

Lupin was in the middle of the row. Somebody had crossed his hands on his chest and put his wand in them, and his face had been washed, and it was still turned a little to one side, because nobody had been able to straighten it. The scar through his eyebrow was very white. There was a coin on the flagstones beside his hand. Harry knew it, because he'd seen Lupin touching it all evening in the Room. It was one of Hermione's coins. Somebody had taken it out of Lupin's pocket and put it there, and there were two letters scratched small on the rim with the point of a knife. *R.L.*

He looked at the coin for some time.

He'd read the determination in Lupin at the top of the steps. The new raw thing over the old grief. He hadn't asked what it was for. Nobody, now, would ever be able to tell him.

He walked on.

Hagrid was at the end of the row.

He was still on the door they'd carried him in on. Nobody had been able to move him off it. It had taken six of them to bring him in, Bill and Charlie and Kingsley and two Aurors and the man who'd come up from the Hog's Head with Aberforth, and they'd laid the door down on the flagstones at the end of the row and covered him with three tablecloths from the staff table, and the tablecloths didn't reach his boots.

Fang lay beside him with his head on Hagrid's boot.

He didn't get up when Neville came. He moved his eyes, and his tail thumped once on the flagstones, and then he put his head back down.

Neville knelt, very carefully, and laid Millicent down beside the door.

He did it slowly. He straightened her legs and put her arms by her sides and moved her hair off her face, and then he took off his own cloak and laid it over her, up to her chin, and looked at her for a while, and pulled it up over her face.

Then he stayed kneeling.

Harry stood over them. The three of them. Hagrid on his door under the tablecloths, and Fang, and Millicent under Neville's cloak, her boots sticking out at the end because Neville's cloak wasn't long enough either.

*Mum says if I die she'll kill me.*

He reached for Neville. He didn't decide to. He reached for him the way you put your tongue into the gap where a tooth has been, again and again, to see if it's still gone. It was still gone. Neville was kneeling a foot away on the flagstones with his head bowed, and Harry could see the back of his neck and the dirt on his collar and his hands on his knees, and that was all there was.

He tried again.

He told nobody he was doing it. He stood at the end of the row and did it over and over, the way you keep pressing on a bruise.

"Potter," said Evelyn.

She was beside him. He hadn't heard her come. He hadn't felt her. He'd never felt her in seven years, and he'd always known where she was, and he hadn't known she was there until she spoke.

He looked at her.

"Yes," he said.

She looked at him for a moment, the way she looked at a page of figures where something didn't add up.

"Nothing," said Evelyn. "Come and sit down."

* * *

There was one at the very end of the row, near the doors, that nobody had covered.

It was a young man in plain black robes with fair hair full of dust. He lay on his back where they'd put him at midnight, his eyes closed and his hands at his sides, one of them palm up.

People walked past him. They walked past him on their way in and out of the doors, and some looked down and saw the robes, which were the robes of the Minister's office, and their faces did something, and they walked on a little faster. One of the Aurors had stopped beside him at about five o'clock with a list and a quill, looked at him, looked at his list, written something, and gone on. Nobody had sat with him. Nobody had put anything over his face.

"Who is he?" a woman Harry didn't know asked the man beside her, by the door.

"Selwyn. The son. Corvin Selwyn's boy."

"*Selwyn*." The woman's face changed. "What's he doing in here? With ours?"

"Somebody brought him in."

"Well, somebody can take him out again."

Evelyn was sitting at the end of the Ravenclaw bench three yards away with a cup of tea Hermione had given her. She didn't look round.

Harry looked at the back of her head.

He didn't know what she was feeling. He'd never known. It was exactly as it had always been, and completely different, and he couldn't have said how.

He got up and went to the staff table and took the last tablecloth off it, the one with the gravy stain at one end, and came back and laid it over Lucan Selwyn, up to the chin, and then over his face.

The woman by the door watched him do it. Her face did something. He didn't know what.

He went and sat down beside Evelyn at the end of the Ravenclaw bench.

She said nothing. She drank her tea.

* * *

Draco and Narcissa left at twenty past five.

Harry saw them go. He was sitting on the bench with his back to the table and his elbows on his knees, the way he'd sat on a step in the snow, and he was watching the doors, because he couldn't think of anything else to watch.

Narcissa came in at ten past. She came in alone, from the Entrance Hall, in the same dark dress she'd worn in the clearing, with leaves caught in the hem and her hair down. She looked at nobody. She stood just inside the doors and looked along the Hall from one end to the other, very slowly, at all the faces, the way a woman looks along a railway platform.

Then she found him.

Draco was sitting on the floor against the wall at the far end, alone, with his mother's wand across his knees, where he'd been since they came in.

She went down the Hall to him. She didn't hurry. People got out of her way without knowing who she was, and some knew who she was and got out of her way faster. She stopped in front of him. She said nothing. She put out her hand.

Draco looked up at her.

He gave her the wand.

She took it and put it away somewhere in her dress, then put her hand down again, and Draco took it, and she pulled him up off the floor as though he weighed nothing, and they walked back up the Hall together towards the doors, side by side, not touching, without a word to anyone.

Harry watched them come.

They passed within a yard of him. Narcissa didn't look at him. She looked straight ahead at the doors, her face quite still, her hands together, leaves in the hem of her dress.

Draco looked.

He looked back once from the doorway, over his shoulder. It was a very short look. It lasted perhaps a second. He looked at Harry on the Ravenclaw bench, and his face was white and tired and quite still, and there was something in it.

Harry didn't know what it was.

He'd known what was in Draco Malfoy's face since a Sorting feast when they were eleven. He'd known it every day for seven years. It had been the whole of what there was between them. *Harry always knows when Draco is afraid*, and *Draco knows he knows*. He'd read it on a train and in a common room and across a Quidditch pitch, in a bathroom full of water and on a tower and in a drawing room, and on a lawn in the dark four hours ago, and in a clearing, where it had been a knot he couldn't untie.

He looked at it now, in the doorway of the Great Hall, and it was a face.

Then Draco turned and went out with his mother, and Harry didn't see him again for a very long time.

He was still holding Draco's wand. It was in his inside pocket, hawthorn, ten inches. He hadn't given it back. He hadn't thought to.

He thought about getting up and going after them.

He didn't.

* * *

"Has anybody seen Theo?" said Harry.

He asked everybody. He asked Kingsley, who was standing by the staff table with a list. He asked Professor McGonagall, who had a bandage on her arm and was talking to a Healer from St Mungo's. He asked Ginny, and Seamus Finnigan, and the three young Slytherins who'd come up from the common room with their wands out and their faces white and were sitting together now at the Slytherin table, very close, like birds on a wire. He asked an Auror called Proudfoot who'd been on the stairs to the dungeons at midnight.

Nobody had seen him.

"Nott," said Kingsley. "The son. Not the father."

"The son."

Kingsley looked down his list.

"We've got the father," he said. "He's on the lawn. He's alive. He's been sitting by the greenhouses since one o'clock asking for the boy." He looked up. "I haven't got the son. He's not in here, and he's not out there, and he's not in the dungeons, and he's not with the Aurors." He paused. "Amycus Carrow's still tied to a bed in your dormitory. Somebody's put a blanket over him. I don't know who."

"He fought," said Harry. "For an hour. On the stairs. Then he went to look for his father."

"Well," said Kingsley, "his father's still looking for him."

Harry went out onto the lawn and found Mr Nott.

He was sitting on a low wall by the greenhouses in black robes with no mask, an old man, older than Harry had expected, with a long grey face and a very good watch on his wrist. He had his hands between his knees. When Harry stopped in front of him, he looked up.

"You're Potter," said Mr Nott.

"Yes."

"My son was your friend."

"He is my friend," said Harry.

Mr Nott looked at him for a long time. Harry looked back. And he didn't know whether the old man was grieving, or afraid, or ashamed, or angry, or all of them, or none. He didn't know whether he'd found his son on the stairs last night and done something, or never found him at all. He didn't know what lay beneath the long grey face.

He'd have known yesterday. He'd have known from across the lawn.

"He was a spy," said Mr Nott. "They told me. On the hill. Carrow told everybody. My son was a spy for you for eighteen months, and I sat across a table from him at Christmas and did not know." He looked down at his hands. "I would like to know where he is."

"So would I," said Harry.

He went back up the lawn.

He didn't find Theo. Nobody did. Nobody had seen him leave.

* * *

Evelyn worked it out at a quarter to six, in the courtyard with the broken fountain, whilst she was looking at the water.

She'd gone out there to be on her own. She noted that she'd gone out there to be on her own, which wasn't something she did, as a rule, because she'd been on her own most of her life and had never needed to go anywhere to manage it. But the Great Hall was very loud and very full, and she'd been sitting on a bench for forty minutes with a cup of tea she hadn't drunk, beside Potter, who didn't know what she was feeling, and who kept looking at people's faces as though he'd lost something in them.

So she went out to the courtyard.

The fountain was broken. Somebody had blown the top off it in the night, and the water was still welling quite gently out of the broken pipe in the middle of the basin and going over the edge and across the flagstones in a long thin sheet towards the drain. There was a place by the fountain where the flagstones were very clean. Somebody had washed them. She didn't look at it for long.

She sat on the edge of the basin.

And she found, sitting there, that her mind was shut.

She didn't know when it had happened. She noted that. She hadn't noticed it close. She'd gone into the Forest at midnight with it open an inch, as it had been for five weeks, a sash window painted into its frame with the cold coming in under it. She'd knelt on the ferns for four hours holding his hand and saying his name, and it had been open then, she was almost certain, because she remembered being afraid something would come in through it whilst she was busy, and nothing had. And now it was shut. All the way down to the sill. She reached for it, the way her grandmother had taught her at seven in the morning in the east wing at Selwyn Hall, and it was shut, and she hadn't shut it.

It must have come down in the night. Some time between midnight and now. Some time whilst she was saying *Potter* on the ferns with her eyes shut. Some time when she wasn't looking.

It made no difference.

She noted that too. It made no difference now. He couldn't have read her if it had been wide open.

She sat on the edge of the fountain with her hands in her lap and watched the water running across the flagstones, and thought about the clearing.

She thought about the curse.

She'd seen it. Nobody else had. Weasley and Granger and Longbottom and Malfoy had been facing outwards into the trees, holding the line, and she'd been on her knees beside Potter's body facing in, with her eyes open for once, because something had made her open them. She'd seen the man by the fire raise the pale wand slowly, his face gone strange, as though he were looking at something a long way off that he didn't like. She'd seen him wrench it round all at once towards Potter. Towards her. She'd seen the green light leave the end of it.

She hadn't moved. There hadn't been time.

And she'd seen the light stop. In the air. About two feet from Potter's chest. It had stopped the way a horse stops at a fence, and hung for a fraction of a second, very bright, and then gone back the way it had come.

She'd been thinking about it ever since. In the Forest, and on the walk, and on the bench. She'd been turning it over the way you turn over a figure that won't reconcile, looking for the place where somebody had carried a one.

Curses didn't stop in the air. They didn't change their minds. A wand did what it was told by the person holding it, and a Killing Curse stopped for nobody, and the man who'd cast it had been the most powerful wizard alive.

Unless the wand wouldn't.

She sat up.

She knew a great deal about wands. She'd read Gregorovitch's *Wandlore and the Theory of Allegiance* in the Restricted Section in her fourth year because it had been misshelved in Ancient Runes, and she'd read it all the way through because it was there, and she'd thought most of it nonsense. Wands chose their wizards. Wands could be won. A wand taken from its owner by force might change its allegiance to the one who took it. Some wands more than others. Some wands, the old book said, very old ones with a history of being taken, would follow nothing else.

The Elder Wand had a history of being taken. It was the whole of its history.

She thought about the tower.

She hadn't been on the tower. She'd been in the east courtyard, holding Dead Calm, whilst a boy died in it. But Potter had been on the tower under the Cloak, and he'd told her everything the next day, in order, with nothing left out, because that was what they did. He'd told her Malfoy had come up the stairs and said *Expelliarmus* and the Headmaster's wand had gone over the parapet end over end. He'd told her Snape had fetched it back up from the grass and held it out without a word. And he'd told her that the Headmaster, in the last minute, on the lawn, had glanced down at it for half a second as though it had answered him late.

She thought about a drawing room.

She'd been there. She'd been standing at the end of a line with her hands tied, and she'd watched Potter cross six feet of very deep carpet and take hold of Malfoy's wrist and twist it, quite hard, the way you'd wring a wet cloth, and take the hawthorn wand out of his hand by force. Malfoy hadn't resisted. He'd made a small sound. And Potter had kept the wand. It was in his pocket now. She'd seen the end of it when he sat on the bench.

She sat on the edge of the broken fountain and laid it out in order, as though checking a column of figures in a register.

The Headmaster had won the wand from her grandfather in a field outside Wrocław in 1945.

Malfoy had taken it from the Headmaster on the tower, without ever touching it.

Potter had taken it from Malfoy in the drawing room, without ever knowing it was there.

And the man by the fire had taken it out of a dead man's hand on a lawn, which wasn't winning it at all. It was picking it up.

She checked it twice.

Then she got up and went to find him.

* * *

He was standing in the Entrance Hall at the foot of the staircase, looking at a curtain.

There was something under the curtain. She knew what it was. She'd heard it fall. She hadn't looked at it then, and she didn't look at it now.

"Potter," said Evelyn.

He turned round.

"I've found an error," she said. "I'd like to report it."

He looked at her. He looked at her the way he'd looked at everybody all morning, very carefully, as though trying to read small print in bad light. Then he seemed to give up, and simply looked.

"Go on," he said.

She told him.

She told him exactly as she'd laid it out on the edge of the fountain. Wrocław. The tower. The drawing room. The lawn, which wasn't winning but picking up. The curse that had stopped two feet from his chest and hung there and gone back. She left nothing out and added nothing. She gave him the dates where she had them. She said *in my opinion* once, about the book, because it had been misshelved and she'd never been able to check its sources.

He listened to all of it in silence.

When she'd finished, he slowly put his hand into his inside pocket and took out a wand.

It wasn't the hawthorn. It was long and pale, with a pattern down it like knots in wood, and halfway down a small dark mark like a burn.

"Longbottom picked it up," said Potter. "Off the ground, by a root. He gave it to me on the walk back. I didn't think about it." He looked at it in his hand. "I put it in my pocket."

"That would be about right," said Evelyn.

He looked at it for a long time. She watched him look at it. She noted that it was a perfectly ordinary-looking piece of wood now, in the grey light, in his dirty hand, in the Entrance Hall, with the dust in the air and the curtain on the floor.

"It knew me," he said. "In there. At the end. I felt it. I didn't know what it was." He turned it over. "It turned over. Like a cat, when you pick it up and it doesn't want to be held."

"Yes. Well." Evelyn looked at the wand. "It's yours. It's been yours since the tenth of January. You've been carrying the master of it about in your coat for four months and you didn't know." She paused. "That's two of the three, if you're counting."

"I'm not."

"I am," said Evelyn.

He looked at her.

He put the wand back in his pocket beside the hawthorn and the Cloak, quite carefully, the way you put away something you haven't decided what to do with.

* * *

The Selwyn business came up at six.

It came up the way things came up that morning, in pieces, from people who'd been told by somebody who'd been told. A Patronus from London to Kingsley, which Kingsley read out in the Entrance Hall to the Aurors without seeing her. The Muggle-born Registration Commission's offices on Level Ten had been found empty at three in the morning. The Chairman's desk had been cleared. There was ash in his grate. Corvin Selwyn hadn't been at the Ministry when it woke, and he wasn't at the Ministry now, and he wasn't at his house in London, and the Aurors who'd gone to look for him had found the door open and the cat fed and nobody at home.

"Gone abroad," said Kingsley. "We think. There's an international Portkey record from Croydon at ten past one. Name's wrong. Description fits."

"And the wife?"

"At the family place. In Shropshire. Selwyn Hall." Kingsley's mouth went thin. "Sent an owl at five asking for news of her son. Her elf's still sitting on our doorstep in London waiting for an answer."

Nobody spoke for a moment.

"Well," said one of the Aurors, a heavy man with a list. "What do we do with them?"

"With who?"

"The Selwyns." He looked at his list. "The brother's dead. The son's dead. The father's fled. The mother's in Shropshire with a bottle, from what I hear. And there's a daughter somewhere. Nobody seems to know where." He frowned. "Do we arrest the name? Do we put a watch on the house? Nobody's ever been able to say for certain whose side half that family were on, and now there's hardly any of them left to ask."

Evelyn was standing four yards from him at the foot of the staircase, beside the curtain. His eyes went over her the way everyone's always had, all her life, and slid off, and went back to his list.

"The daughter's here," said Potter.

The Auror looked up.

"She's standing next to me," said Potter. "She killed Severus Snape. She was at Nurmengard. She threw the Commission's wands across Courtroom Ten in front of her own father. She held the courtyard on the night Dumbledore died. She's been fighting your war for seven years whilst you were filling in that list." He paused. "She's the only Selwyn you'll ever need to know about."

The Auror looked at her. He looked properly this time. She could see him trying to fix her face. She could see it not quite working.

"Oh," he said. "Right. Sorry, miss."

"It's quite all right," said Evelyn. "People don't."

* * *

They went down to the lake at twenty past six, the two of them, without telling anybody.

It was the first time they'd been alone since a projection room in Leeds. They walked down the slope of the lawn on the castle side, away from the Forest, past the white tomb, which was a little scorched along one side. The grass was very wet. There were birds. A great many birds, all at once, in every tree, as though they'd been told.

The sun came up whilst they were walking.

It came up over the mountains on the far side of the lake, very fast, the way it does in May, and the whole of the water went from grey to silver to a pale clear gold in about the time it took them to reach the shore. The mist lifted off the surface in long thin threads. The giant squid put one arm up out of the shallows, quite lazily, then thought better of it and took it down again.

It was a beautiful morning.

Harry noted that. He didn't know what to do with it.

They stood on the shingle at the edge of the water. He had his hands in his pockets. His right hand was closed round three things. A folded square of silver cloth, a hawthorn wand, and a long pale wand with a mark like a burn. He let go of all of them.

Evelyn stood beside him with her hands in her cardigan pockets.

He looked at her.

He didn't try to read her. He didn't need to try. He knew what he'd find, and it was exactly what he'd found for seven years, every day, in every room, since a robe shop in Diagon Alley. Nothing. The plain quiet face people forgot. The silence.

It made no difference now.

He looked out across the lake. On the far shore there were people, very small, moving along the water's edge from the direction of the village. He could see them. He didn't know who they were, or what they felt, or whether they were glad or sorry or frightened or anything at all. They were people walking along a shore.

Everyone was like her now.

He didn't say it. He stood on the shingle with the sun on his face and said nothing for a long time. Nor did she. And it was, he found after a while, not the worst silence he'd ever stood in. He'd stood in it for seven years beside her and called it rest.

He couldn't have said, then, what it was now.

"What time is it?" said Harry.

He didn't know why he asked. He had a watch. It was on his wrist. He hadn't looked at it since before the Forest. He didn't look at it now.

Evelyn took her hand out of her pocket.

She had the gold watch in it. She'd had it in her hand, he realised, the whole way down the lawn. The small gold watch with the worn ivy leaves on the lid, which her grandmother had given her when she was eleven and which she'd wound every morning of her life until a morning in December, at eleven minutes past seven, when it had stopped and never started again.

She opened the lid. She did it without thinking, with her thumb, the way she'd done it ten thousand times, thirty times a day, for seven years. She looked down at the face.

It said eleven minutes past seven. It had said eleven minutes past seven for a hundred and thirty-six days.

She looked at it for a moment.

Then she closed the lid.

"I don't know," said Evelyn.

He turned and looked at her.

He'd known her seven years. He'd heard her give the date of every goblin rebellion in the history of the world, and the number of stairs in the Astronomy Tower, and the exact time of every train she'd ever caught, and how many feet a man had trodden on at a wedding. He'd heard her correct teachers, and Ministers, and a dead man in a cell, and once, across a courtroom, a Dark Lord's lieutenant on a point of procedure.

He'd never once heard her not know something.

She didn't look at him. She stood on the shingle with the closed watch in her hand and the sun on the water, looking out across the lake at the far shore, with her plain quiet face that told him nothing, that had always told him nothing.

"I don't know," she said again, quite steadily, as though noting it down.
