## Chapter 81: Funerals

They buried Millicent Bulstrode on the ninth of May, in the churchyard of St Botolph's in a village four miles outside Louth, in the rain.

Her mother had moved there from Swindon two years before, for the dog. Harry learned this at the gate, from her mother, who was standing under a large black umbrella with the dog on a lead beside her, and who told him before he had said anything at all.

"You're Potter," she said.

"Yes."

"Thought so. She said you'd be thin." She looked him up and down. "You're thinner than she said."

She was very big. She was as tall as Harry and twice as wide, in a black coat that strained at the buttons and a black hat with a small sad feather in it, and she had Millicent's square jaw and Millicent's small sharp eyes and Millicent's way of standing with her feet apart, as though somebody might try to move her. The dog was a lurcher, mostly, large and grey, with its ears going in two directions. It looked at Harry with great interest and sat on his foot.

"Brian," said Mrs Bulstrode. "Off."

Brian did not get off.

"He likes you," said Mrs Bulstrode. "Doesn't like anybody. Ate a chair in Swindon. That's why we came here. More room, and the chairs are further apart." She looked at Harry again. "She liked you as well."

Harry looked at her face.

He did not know what was in it. He looked for a long time, under the umbrella, in the rain, with a dog on his foot, and it was a large plain wet face under a hat with a sad feather, and he did not know whether she hated him. He thought she might. He thought he would, in her place. Her daughter had gone to the Forest because of him, and stood in front of his body for four hours in the dark, and been hit, and got up, and been hit, and not got up.

He would have known, three weeks ago. He would have known from the lane.

"Mrs Bulstrode," said Harry. "I'm very sorry. I don't… I'm not very good at telling, any more. What people are feeling. I used to be. I'm not now." He stopped. It was the first time he had said it to anybody. "So I'm going to have to ask you. Are you angry with me?"

Mrs Bulstrode looked at him.

"Yes," she said.

He nodded.

"I'm angry with everybody," said Mrs Bulstrode. "I'm angry with the vicar. I'm angry with the rain. I'm angry with Brian, and he's never done a thing wrong in his life except the chair." She looked down at the dog. "And I'm angry with you. Because she'd still be here if it wasn't for you." She looked back up. "And she wouldn't have been anything like as happy. Not for a minute of it. Not since she was eleven."

Harry did not say anything.

"She wrote to me every week," said Mrs Bulstrode. "Seven years. Every Sunday. Do you know what she said about you? First letter. First week. She said *there's a boy in my house called Potter who came in the girls' bathroom when there was a troll and stood in front of me like an idiot. I think he might be all right.*" Her mouth went very straight. "Last letter, she said the same. Word for word. Except she took out *might*."

The rain came down on the umbrella.

"She thought you were an idiot," said Mrs Bulstrode. "She thought you were the cleverest idiot she'd ever met, and you never ate properly, and you'd die if somebody didn't keep an eye on you, and she was the one to do it, because nobody else would think of it." She looked at him. "That's what she thought. In case you can't tell any more."

"Thank you," said Harry.

"Don't mention it," said Mrs Bulstrode.

She turned and went up the path to the church, with the dog, and after a moment Harry followed her.

* * *

They buried Hagrid on the edge of the Forest on the twelfth, and it took three hours, because the centaurs came.

Evelyn noted the time they arrived. It was a quarter past ten. The grave had been dug by Hagrid's brother, alone, with his hands, the evening before, at the place on the edge of the trees where Hagrid had once kept a pumpkin patch and a dragon's egg and a three-headed dog, and it was eleven feet long and seven feet deep and very neat at the corners. Nobody had asked him to make it neat. He had looked at it afterwards for a long time and then gone back into the trees.

He came out again at ten, carrying Fang.

He did not carry him because Fang could not walk. Fang could walk. He had walked from the castle to the grave behind the coffin, very slowly, with his nose almost on the ground. But when the giant came out of the trees he went to Fang and picked him up in one hand, the way you would pick up a cat, and stood at the head of the grave with the dog held against his chest, and Fang let him.

The centaurs came at a quarter past.

There were forty-one of them. Evelyn counted. They came out of the trees all together and stood in a long line along the edge of the Forest behind the grave, with their bows on their backs, not speaking. One of them, a grey-haired one with a beard, stepped forward and said something in a language Evelyn did not know, and then said it again in English, quite formally, for the humans, as though he were reading a treaty.

"He was a friend of the Forest," said the centaur. "He was foolish. He was kind to things that did not deserve it. He did not understand the stars." He paused. "We will remember him."

Then he stepped back.

McGonagall spoke. Professor Sprout spoke, and cried, and could not finish, and Professor Flitwick finished it for her. Ron and Hermione stood with the Weasleys. Neville stood with his hands folded in front of him, very straight, at the head of eleven children from Hufflepuff and Ravenclaw who had asked to come and had been allowed to, and who had made a wreath out of the flowers from the greenhouses, very badly, and put it on the coffin. The Ravenclaw girl had shoes on now.

Evelyn stood beside Potter.

She was watching him. She noted that she was doing it. She had watched him for seven years, the way you watch a pan on a stove, and she had never once needed to, because he had always known exactly where she was and what she was not saying, and that had been enough. Now she watched him and he did not know she was there.

He was looking at the giant.

He looked at him for a long time. She knew why. She could see him doing it, the thing he did now, all the time, without seeming to know he did it. He looked at a person and waited. Then he looked a little harder, the way you look at a page in bad light. Then he looked away.

He had always been able to feel Hagrid from anywhere.

She had heard him say it, once, at fifteen, half asleep on a train: *I could find Hagrid in the dark from the other end of the country. He's the loudest thing there is.*

The giant stood at the head of the grave with Fang held against his chest and his great face wet, and Potter looked at him and waited, and did not find anything, and looked away.

At one o'clock they lowered the coffin.

It took nine people and a charm. The giant did not help. He stood and watched them do it, and when it was down, he knelt, very slowly, the way a building comes down when you take out the bottom floor, and put Fang on the ground, and put one enormous hand flat on the earth beside the grave.

He said something. One word. Evelyn did not hear what it was.

Then he got up and went back into the trees, and the centaurs went with him, and Fang did not.

Fang stayed at the grave. He lay down at the head of it with his nose on his paws, and when McGonagall tried to lead him back to the castle, he would not come. When Neville tried, he would not come. When Potter knelt beside him and put a hand on his head, he lifted his eyes, and his tail moved once in the grass, and he put his head back down.

"He'll come when he's hungry," said Weasley.

He did not come when he was hungry. Neville took food out to him every evening for nine days. On the tenth day he came, very slowly, up the lawn to the castle, and lay down in the doorway of the empty hut, and stayed there.

* * *

Gilderoy Lockhart's funeral, on the fifteenth of May, was attended by three thousand, two hundred and eighty people, eleven photographers, a brass band and a hippogriff.

Harry did not know who had brought the hippogriff.

It was at Highgate Cemetery, in the old West part, among the ivy and the stone angels and the great black Victorian tombs leaning into each other under the trees. It was a hot bright morning. There were banners. There were a great many banners. They had been made by the Gilderoy Lockhart Appreciation Society, which had two hundred and forty branches in nine countries, and they were mostly lilac, and they said things like *GILDEROY: A LIFE OF MAGIC* and *HE FACED THE BANSHEE* and *FOREVER CHARMING*, in gold letters, and one, held up very proudly by two elderly witches from Bognor Regis, said *WE STILL HAVE ALL YOUR BOOKS*.

Lockhart had planned it.

All of it. He had left instructions with his solicitor in 1993, in a long letter written from a bed in St Mungo's with his back in a cast, a month after a tunnel under a school had come down on him. The solicitor, a small dry man named Mr Fothergill, read some of them out at the start, in a voice that suggested he had been reading them to himself for five years and had given up being surprised. The music was to be loud. The flowers were to be peonies, which were the only flower with any sense of occasion. The coffin was to be lilac, with gold handles. Nobody was to wear black, because black made everyone look ill, and he would not have his mourners looking ill in the photographs.

Nobody wore black.

Harry wore a dark green jacket of Sirius's that was too big in the shoulders. Evelyn wore her grey cardigan. Ron wore maroon, because his mother had made him, and Hermione wore blue. In front of them a wizard of about ninety, in robes the colour of a ripe apricot, wept loudly and steadily into a lilac handkerchief through the whole thing and would not be comforted.

And at the end, Mr Fothergill unfolded the last sheet of the letter and read the eulogy Lockhart had written for himself.

Harry had expected it to be funny.

It was, in places. There was a paragraph about the yeti that made the whole of Highgate Cemetery laugh at once, three thousand people under the trees, and a line about his own hair that made the elderly witches from Bognor Regis sob. But most of it was not funny. Most of it was very simple. It was a man of forty, lying in a hospital bed with his back broken, writing down what he would like people to know if he did not get up again.

*I have always been told I am vain,* Mr Fothergill read. *This is true. I am very vain. I have spent my life wanting to be looked at, and I have been, a great deal, and it has never once been enough, and I do not expect it ever will be.*

*But I should like it to be known that everything in my books happened.*

*Not the way I wrote it. I wrote it better. I always made myself a little taller, and the banshee a little louder, and my hair a great deal better than it was in the Bandon rain. But I was there. I did it. Every time. I stood in front of things that were very frightening, and I was frightened, and I stood there anyway, because there were people behind me, and because somebody had to, and because I have never in my life been able to resist an audience.*

*If I have died doing something foolish, in front of something frightening, with people behind me, then I should like you all to know that I would not have had it any other way, and that I expect I looked marvellous.*

*Please do not be sad for very long. It does not suit anyone.*

*With my very warmest wishes, and, of course, my signature,*

*Gilderoy Lockhart, Order of Merlin, Third Class.*

Mr Fothergill folded the letter.

There was a silence under the trees. Three thousand people. Nobody moved. And then, from somewhere near the back, one of the elderly witches from Bognor Regis began, quite shakily, to clap, and then the person next to her did, and then all of them, the whole of Highgate Cemetery, three thousand two hundred and eighty people under the ivy and the stone angels, clapping, on and on, for nearly four minutes, until the brass band gave up waiting and began to play.

Harry stood in the middle of it.

He could hear it. He could hear all of it. He did not know what any of them were feeling.

He found that he was clapping too.

* * *

Severus Snape was buried on the nineteenth, in the municipal cemetery at the end of a long street of red-brick terraces in a mill town in the north, with a disused chimney over it and the river going past at the bottom of the hill.

There were six of them.

Evelyn counted them twice, because she could not believe the number. Potter. Herself. Professor McGonagall, in black, very straight. Professor Slughorn, who had come by Floo to a pub on the corner and walked up the hill in a velvet waistcoat, and was out of breath, and kept dabbing at his forehead with a handkerchief. The man from the council, who had dug the grave and was standing at a respectful distance by his barrow, smoking. And an old woman.

Nobody knew who she was.

She was very old. She was in a brown coat with a fur collar that had mostly worn away, and she was standing on the far side of the grave from the rest of them, by herself, with a string bag in one hand with two oranges in it. She did not speak to anybody. She did not look at anybody. She stood at the grave with her string bag and looked down at the coffin, which was plain, and black, and had no name on it, because Aberforth had not known what to put.

Professor McGonagall said a few words.

They were very short. She said that Severus Snape had been a pupil of hers, and a colleague, and that she had not understood him, and that she had been wrong about a great many things, and that she did not know yet which of them. She said she would think about it. Then she stopped.

Slughorn said something about Potions.

It was quite long, and it was about a boy of eleven who had come into his dungeon and made a Draught of Peace on his first attempt that was better than his own, and it was the kindest thing anybody said that day, and Evelyn could see that Slughorn did not know it was kind. He thought it was an anecdote.

Then nobody said anything.

The man from the council put out his cigarette and came forward with his spade.

Evelyn stood at the edge of the grave and looked down.

She thought about a candle on a floor.

She thought about a voice saying *Look at me*, to somebody else.

She thought about the six and a half years she had sat in his dungeon, at the back, on the left, by the store cupboard. The thirty-nine reports he had written on her in his small cramped hand, every one with her name spelled correctly, without being told. The Outstanding he had given her in her fifth year, which she had not expected and which she had kept, folded in four, in the back of her copy of *The Nine Tailors*.

She thought about the word she had said, in a doorway, with her hand perfectly steady.

She did not say anything.

The old woman with the string bag looked up, once, across the grave. She looked at Evelyn. It was a very short look. Then she looked down again, and after a moment she bent, quite stiffly, and put one of the oranges on the edge of the grave, on the clay, and turned round, and went away down the hill between the stones towards the terraces and the river, and did not look back.

Nobody went after her.

The man from the council began to fill the grave in.

* * *

They walked down the hill afterwards, she and Potter, the two of them, along the long street of terraces towards the station. There was washing out. Somebody had a radio on in a back yard, playing something by the Verve.

She was quiet as far as the corner.

Then she said, "I've been through every spell I know."

He looked at her.

"Since March," said Evelyn. "Every one. I made a list. In the notebook. Every spell I could have used in that doorway instead of that one. Disarming. Stunning. Full Body-Bind. Impediment. Every jinx and hex and charm I've ever read, and some I've only read about. Two hundred and eleven." She was looking straight ahead, at the end of the street. "I timed them. In my head. How long each one takes to say, and how long it takes to land, and how long it would have taken him to finish closing the door." She paused. "None of them would have been fast enough. Not one. I checked them all twice."

They walked on.

"I wanted you to know I checked," said Evelyn.

Potter was silent.

He did not try. She noted that. He walked beside her down the long street of red-brick terraces, with the washing out and the radio going, and he did not tell her it had not been her fault, or that she had saved his life, or that Snape would have destroyed him, or any of the things that were true. He did not say anything at all.

She was more grateful for it than she would have known how to say.

* * *

The trials began on the first of June, in Courtroom Ten, and went on all summer.

Harry went to most of them. He sat on the second bench from the front, on the left, where he could see the chair in the middle of the floor with its chains, and he listened. He testified, when he was asked to. He did not testify when he was not. He sat in the dark courtroom day after day, under the high stone benches full of witches and wizards in plum-coloured robes, and he watched the faces of the people in the chair, and he did not know what any of them felt.

That was the strangest part.

He had sat in this room before. He had stood in the doorway of it, last summer, and read every person on the benches at once, and known which of them were frightened and which of them were pleased and which of them were thinking about their lunch. Now he sat and watched Lucius Malfoy in the chair, grey and very thin and perfectly composed, answering every question in a low courteous voice, and he could not tell whether Lucius was ashamed, or afraid, or neither, or only very tired.

Lucius was given eleven years.

He did not look at anybody when they read it out. He stood up when he was told to and went out between the two Aurors with his head up, and the door shut behind him.

Narcissa was tried on the eighth. She sat in the chair in a grey dress with her hands folded and answered everything, very quietly, in as few words as possible, and when they asked her where she had been on the night of the first of May, she said, "In the Forest. Looking for my son."

"And did you find him?"

"Not until the morning."

They called Draco.

He came in from the side door in plain dark robes, very white, and sat down in the witness chair, which was not the chair with the chains but was close enough to it that Harry saw him look at the chains once and then not again. He answered four questions. He said he had been in the Forest. He said he had been one of the people standing round Harry Potter's body. He said he had held his position until the fighting stopped. He said he did not know why he had gone.

"You don't know?" said the witch asking the questions.

"No," said Draco.

He did not look at Harry. Harry was on the second bench from the front, on the left, eleven feet away, and Draco did not look at him once, not when he came in, not while he answered, not when he went out.

Narcissa was given a fine and three years' probation and the loss of her wand for one year, which was the wand Draco had carried into the Forest. The Wizengamot did not say, in so many words, that it was because of where her son had been on the night of the first of May. It did not need to.

Corvin Selwyn was tried on the twenty-second, in his absence.

His chair was empty. They read out the charges to it, all twenty-nine of them, one after another, in a clerk's flat voice: the Commission, the registers, the hearings in Courtroom Ten, the cells under it. Evelyn sat beside Harry on the second bench and listened to all twenty-nine without moving. When they read out the sentence, which was life, in Azkaban, if he should ever be found, she wrote it down in the red notebook, with the date and the time, and closed the notebook.

Then, at the end of that day, a clerk read out a list.

It was a list of names. Death Eaters who had been identified, by the Mark or by witnesses, and who had not been taken, or found, or accounted for among the dead. The clerk read them out one after another, in the same flat voice, and after each one paused, and looked up at the benches, in case anybody had anything to say.

"Theodore Nott," read the clerk.

He paused. He looked up.

Harry stood up.

"He was ours," he said. "He was a spy. For eighteen months. He fed us everything. He fought for the castle on the night of the first of May for an hour and then he went to look for his father." He stopped. "I asked him to take the Mark. It was my idea."

There was a murmur on the benches.

"Is the gentleman present?" said the clerk.

"No."

"Then the name will remain on the list," said the clerk, "until such time as the gentleman is present to answer for it." He made a note. "Next. Augustus Rookwood."

Harry sat down.

Nobody had seen Theo. Nobody had heard from him. His coin, which Harry still had the pair of, had not been warm once since twenty to nine on the first of May.

* * *

It was in June, too, that Harry gave an interview to the *Daily Prophet*.

He had not meant to. He had not given an interview in his life. But the reporter was waiting for him on the steps of the Ministry visitors' entrance one evening, a pleasant young man in a good suit called Edwin Thrupp, who said he was not interested in the battle, he was sick of the battle, everybody was sick of the battle, he only wanted to know about the people. The ones who had been there. The ones nobody had heard of.

Harry looked at him.

He looked the way he looked at everyone now. And he saw a young man with a nice open face who seemed to mean it.

He would have known, before. He would have known in a second, on the steps, from across the street. He would have read him and found whatever was under the nice open face, the small cold pleased thing that Harry had found in a dozen reporters in seven years, and he would have smiled his shop smile and walked past.

He talked to Edwin Thrupp for forty minutes.

He told him about Millicent. He told him about Neville at the door on the bridge, counting. About Lockhart's supply line and the Carrows' house-elf. About a girl nobody had ever noticed who had stood in Courtroom Ten and thrown the Commission's confiscated wands across the floor in front of her own father. He told him that the same girl had killed Severus Snape in the Shrieking Shack, to save his life.

He did not think about it. He was telling him about the people nobody had heard of. She was the person nobody had ever heard of. It was the whole of what she was.

It was on the front page the next morning.

*SELWYN GIRL KILLED SNAPE: Potter Reveals Chairman's Daughter's Secret War.* There was a photograph. Nobody knew where it had come from. It was Evelyn at fifteen, at a Quidditch match, in the stands, looking at something off to one side, and it was blurred, but it was her.

Harry read it in the kitchen at Grimmauld Place, standing up, twice.

He went to find her. She was at the table with a cup of tea and a copy of the *Prophet* folded in four, and she looked up when he came in, and he did not know what was in her face. He had never known. That was not new. What was new was that he did not know what was in anybody's, and he had just told a man on a step everything she had spent her life not being.

"I'm sorry," said Harry. "I didn't… I couldn't tell he was…"

"No," said Evelyn. "I know."

"Are you angry?"

She looked at him for a long time.

"Yes," she said. "Quite."

He nodded.

"A woman in Diagon Alley looked at me this morning," said Evelyn. "In Flourish and Blotts. She looked at me and she knew who I was. She looked at me for nearly a minute." She moved her cup an inch to the left. "Nobody has ever done that in my life."

He did not say anything.

"It'll pass," said Evelyn. "People forget my face. It's the one thing I've always been able to rely on." She looked at the paper. "It'll take about a month, I expect. Perhaps six weeks."

It took five.

* * *

He got Ron wrong in the third week of June.

It was at the Burrow, on a Sunday. Ron had been very quiet all through lunch, and short with him, twice, about nothing, and when Harry asked him whether he wanted to go out and throw a Quaffle about in the orchard after, Ron had said *no* in a voice that made Mrs Weasley look up. And Harry had sat at the table with his plate in front of him and looked at Ron's face across the table and known, quite clearly, the way he had always known things, that Ron was angry with him.

For Fred. For the wall on the seventh floor. For bringing the war to the castle on purpose, because it was the plan.

He had known it for an hour. He sat with it all through pudding.

Then he went and found Ron in the orchard, by the hedge, sitting on the ground with his back to a tree.

"Are you angry with me?" said Harry.

Ron looked up at him.

His face went through several things. Harry could not tell what any of them were. Then it settled on something that looked very much like astonishment.

"*What?*"

"You've been… At lunch. You were…" Harry stopped. "I thought you were angry with me. About Fred. About the castle. I'd understand if you were. It was my plan. I brought him there."

Ron stared at him.

"Mate," he said. "No. Blimey. *No*." He rubbed his face with both hands. "I'm not angry with you. I'm… It's just Fred. That's all. It's just Fred, all the time. I keep thinking of things to tell him. Stupid things. I was eating my lunch and I thought, I'll tell Fred about Percy's new hat, he'll love that, and then I remembered." He looked at Harry. "That's all it was. I wasn't even thinking about you. Sorry."

Harry sat down beside him on the grass.

"I couldn't tell," he said.

"No. I know." Ron looked at him sideways. "You never used to have to ask, did you."

"No."

"Must be weird."

"It is," said Harry. "It's very weird."

Ron thought about it.

"Well," he said, "you can ask me. Any time. I'll tell you." He picked a blade of grass and looked at it. "I'm not very good at it. Saying. But I'll tell you."

He did. He was not very good at it. It took him a long time, sitting under the tree in the orchard with a blade of grass, and he got some of it in the wrong order, and some of it he could only say by saying something else. But he told him.

Harry had to ask everybody now. He asked Hermione what she meant when she went quiet. He asked Mrs Weasley whether he had upset her when she cried at the stove. He asked Neville, and Luna, and McGonagall, and the girl at the till in the Tesco on the Euston Road. He asked so often that he heard himself doing it in his sleep. It was exhausting. It was like walking everywhere in a country where he had always been able to take a taxi.

And people told him.

That was the part he had not expected. He asked, and they stopped, and they thought, and then they told him, in words, things he had always just known, and it was not the same. It was slower and stranger and full of mistakes, and they said things they had not known they felt until he asked. And sometimes, when they had finished, they looked at him differently, as though they had been asked something nobody had ever asked them before.

He did not have a word for that either.

* * *

The Office of Magical Registers was on Level Six of the Ministry of Magic, at the far end of a corridor behind the Floo Network Authority, past a broom cupboard and a door marked *GOBSTONES (DISCONTINUED)*, and it was the smallest office Evelyn had ever seen.

It was eleven feet by nine. She measured it on the first morning. It had one window, which was enchanted to show a view of a car park in Swindon, for reasons nobody could remember. It had two desks, one large and one small, and shelves on every wall to the ceiling, and on the shelves there were registers. Births, deaths, marriages, name changes and wand registrations for every witch and wizard in Britain since 1692, bound in green cloth and numbered in white ink, eleven thousand, four hundred and six volumes, and it smelt of glue.

The large desk belonged to Mr Pike.

Mr Pike was eighty-one. He had been the Senior Clerk of the Office of Magical Registers since 1951, and the only clerk since 1974, when his assistant had retired to Whitby, and he had not been replaced. He was very small and very bald and very neat, and he wore a grey cardigan very like her own, and he had a pair of half-moon spectacles on a chain round his neck, and he looked at her over the top of them on the first morning, the sixth of July, when she came in with her letter of appointment.

"Selwyn," he said, reading it.

"Yes."

"Junior Clerk."

"Yes."

"Good." He handed her the letter back. "That's your desk. Kettle's on the shelf behind the 1840s. Milk's in the drawer under the Gaunts, it keeps cold there, I've never known why. You'll start on Births, 1850 to 1860. Nobody's corrected those in a hundred years and they're a disgrace." He put his spectacles back on and looked down at his own register. "Tea at eleven. Lunch at one. I go home at five. If anybody comes in asking for anything, tell them to fill in a form."

That was all he said.

He did not ask about her family. Evelyn waited for it all that morning, at her small desk, with Births 1850 open in front of her and a pot of red ink. She waited for it at eleven, when he made the tea. She waited for it at one. She had been waiting for it for five weeks, everywhere she went, from everybody, since a front page with a photograph on it. She waited for it all week.

He did not ask.

On the Friday, at four o'clock, she said, "Mr Pike."

"Mm."

"You haven't asked me about my family."

He looked up over his spectacles.

"Should I have?"

"Everybody else does."

Mr Pike considered this.

"I've been in this office since 1951," he said. "I've had every family in Britain through my hands. Born, married, died, changed their names, changed them back. I've had the Blacks and the Malfoys and the Lestranges and the Gaunts, and I've had a family in Hull called Pratt who changed their name to Montmorency in 1911 and back to Pratt in 1912." He looked at her. "Families are what's in the registers, Miss Selwyn. They're not what's at the desk."

He went back to his own register.

Evelyn looked at Births 1850.

Then she picked up her pen and corrected the date of birth of one Ignatius Prewett, which had been entered as the thirtieth of February.

She had chosen it because it was the least important job in the building. She had gone through the list of vacancies on the noticeboard on Level Two in the first week of June, all forty-seven of them, and chosen the one that nobody would ever look at, in the room that nobody would ever come to, under a man who did not care who she was.

She noted, on the Friday evening, at five past five, after Mr Pike had gone home and she was washing the cups, that she had not thought about any of that for nearly four hours.

* * *

Harry turned eighteen on the thirty-first of July, 1998, in the kitchen at Grimmauld Place, with five people.

He had asked for five. He had not wanted the Burrow, or a party, or anybody from the Ministry, or any of the three hundred letters a day that had been coming since May and that Kreacher brought down in a laundry basket every morning and left on the stairs, sighing. He had wanted the kitchen, and the people who would come into it without being asked.

Ron came at six, with Hermione. Neville came at a quarter past, with a plant in a pot that he said was a birthday cactus and that did not appear to be any kind of cactus at all. Luna came at half past, with a necklace of corks for Harry and one for Kreacher, who put his on, and wore it for the rest of the evening, and said nothing whatever about it.

Evelyn came down from her room at seven, as she had last year, with a parcel wrapped in brown paper.

It was a book. It was a second-hand copy of *The Hound of the Baskervilles*, from a shop on Charing Cross Road, with somebody else's name in the front in pencil and a tea stain on page forty.

"It's about a man everybody thinks is under a curse," she said. "It turns out to be somebody with a dog and a tin of phosphorus." She handed it to him. "Happy birthday, Potter."

"Thank you."

"Don't read the end first."

"I never do."

"You did with the last one. I could tell from the spine." She sat down. "Hermione's making a cake."

He looked at Hermione.

Hermione was at the stove, in an apron, with flour on her face and a card propped up against the sugar jar in front of her, and she looked at him, and he did not know what was in her face, and then she said it, which was the thing people did now.

"I found it," she said. "In the drawer. The one by the sink, with the string and the candle ends. It was at the back." She held up the card. It was an old index card, soft at the corners, covered in Sirius's big untidy handwriting in blue ink, with brown splashes on it. "It's his. It's the one he made last year. I thought…" She stopped. "I thought somebody should make it."

Nobody said anything for a moment.

"Right," said Ron. "Brilliant. It was disgusting."

"I know."

"It was the worst cake I've ever eaten in my life."

"I *know*, Ron. I'm following it exactly."

She followed it exactly. It took an hour and forty minutes, and at one point the kitchen filled with smoke and Kreacher came in with his cork necklace on and opened the window without being asked, muttering, and at another point Neville's cactus that was not a cactus put out a long green tendril and tried to take the egg whisk. And at a quarter to nine Hermione took it out of the oven and stood back from it, and they all looked at it.

It was lopsided. It leaned to one side like a house on a hill. It was black round the edges and it had sunk in the middle into a sort of crater, and when Hermione iced it the icing went a strange pale grey, and she wrote on it, very carefully, with a piping bag, exactly as the card said, *HAPY BIRTHDY HARRY*, with the spelling exactly as Sirius had spelled it on the card, because she had decided, she said, that it was part of the recipe.

They put eighteen candles in it. The candles leaned into the crater.

It was just as terrible as it had been last year. It was, if anything, slightly worse, because Hermione had been more exact. Ron ate two pieces and said so after each one. Luna said it tasted like a very old church, and seemed pleased. Neville said nothing at all, very kindly, and fed some of his to the cactus. Evelyn ate one slice from the least black edge, and rated it, when Ron asked her to, at three out of ten, with the three entirely for effort.

Harry ate all of his.

He did not know why. He sat at the head of the long kitchen table in the house that was his now, at eighteen, with five people round him whose faces he could not read, and a terrible lopsided cake, and he ate all of it, and when Hermione asked him whether he was all right, he thought about it honestly, and said, "Yes. I think so. I'll tell you if I'm not."

Afterwards, washing up, Evelyn picked up the recipe card from beside the sugar jar to put it back in the drawer.

She stopped.

She turned it over and looked at the back of it for a moment, and then she put it down on the table in front of him, face down, without a word, and went back to the sink.

There was something written on the back. It was in the same big untidy blue handwriting, but smaller, and the ink was a little different, as though it had been added later, on another day.

*For when he's eighteen,* it said. *In case I'm not about. Make it anyway. It's supposed to be awful. S.*

## Chapter 82: The Hour of Every World

The stone came from a quarry above Loch Rannoch, and it came in blocks about the size of a suitcase, and Harry carried them from the cart to the bridge one at a time, with his hands.

He could have used a wand. Everybody told him so. Aberforth told him so on the first morning, in March, standing on the bank of the stream at the bottom of the high street with his arms folded and his beard blowing about, watching Harry stagger down the slope with the first block held against his chest. *There's a charm for that, you know. They teach it to first-years.* And Harry had put the block down on the grass beside the old bridge, very carefully, and straightened up, and said that he knew.

Aberforth had looked at him for a while.

Then he had gone back to the Hog's Head and come out again ten minutes later with a second pair of leather gloves, and put them on, and picked up the other end of the next block.

That had been seven months ago. It was October now. The old bridge was gone, the little humped one with the cracked parapet and the loaf-sized piece missing, that a charm had held together since the war because nobody in the village could bear to touch it. The new one was nearly finished. It was wider, and lower, and it was built of grey stone from Rannoch, and it had two arches instead of one, and it had been built almost entirely by a nineteen-year-old wizard and a man well over a hundred, by hand, with a great deal of advice from everybody who walked past.

Harry liked the stone.

He had not expected to. He had taken the job because Aberforth had mentioned, in January, quite casually over a pint, that the village was going to rebuild the bridge properly in the spring and could not find anybody who wanted to do it, and Harry had said *I'll do it*, before he had thought about it, because it was something to do with his hands that did not involve anybody's face.

He liked it more than he could explain. He liked the weight of it. He liked the way each block was different, and had to be turned and tried and turned again before it would sit. He liked that you could put your whole hand flat on a piece of stone and know exactly what it was, all the way through, because it was stone, and there was nothing else in it.

It did not feel anything.

He did not feel anything, towards it. There was nothing to read and nothing to miss. He did not stand in front of it and wait. He did not look at it the way he looked at everybody, still, all this time later, in the half second before he remembered.

It was the most restful thing he had ever done.

"That one's wrong," said Aberforth.

"It's not wrong."

"It's upside down."

Harry looked at it. It was the last block but four of the downstream parapet, and he had been trying it for six minutes.

"It hasn't got an upside down," he said. "It's a block."

"Everything's got an upside down," said Aberforth. "Turn it over."

Harry turned it over. It sat.

Aberforth did not say anything. He did not need to. He stood on the bank with his hands in the pockets of his old coat and looked at the parapet, and Harry looked at his face, from habit, and did not know what was in it, and asked.

"What are you feeling?"

"Cold," said Aberforth. "Hungry. Fed up with you asking."

"Is that all?"

Aberforth considered.

"Pleased about the block," he said, after a while, grudgingly. "You can have that one for free."

* * *

On the eighteenth of October, at twenty past eleven, Evelyn found the nine hundred and fourth error in Births, 1857.

She noted it in the margin in red ink, in her small square hand. A child born in Godalming in the April of that year had been entered under her mother's maiden name, and the father's name had been spelled three different ways on three successive lines by a clerk who had evidently been either very tired or very drunk. She corrected all three. She initialled the correction. She moved on.

"How many?" said Mr Pike, from the large desk, without looking up.

"In 1857? Nine hundred and four."

"And the decade?"

"Eleven thousand, two hundred and sixty."

Mr Pike made a small satisfied noise, the kind of noise a man makes when the kettle boils at exactly the moment he expected.

"Disgrace," he said.

"Yes."

"Keep going."

She kept going.

She had been in the Office of Magical Registers for fifteen months. She had a new cardigan, grey, from Marks and Spencer, and she had a room of her own, above a bookbinder's in Rugby Street, two streets from the Ministry's visitors' entrance, with a gas fire and a window over the yard and a shelf for her books that she had put up herself, crookedly, and not straightened. She had moved there in the September of last year, from Grimmauld Place, because she had decided that a person ought to have a door of her own to shut.

She shut it every evening. She found she liked it.

She found she liked most things now, a little. It was a strange thing to notice. She noticed it anyway, the way she noticed the errors in Births, 1857. The milk in the drawer under the Gaunts, which was always cold. The car park in Swindon in the enchanted window, which had had the same blue Ford Cortina parked in the third bay from the left for fifteen months, and which she had come to think of as an acquaintance. Mr Pike, who said perhaps forty words a day, and nineteen of them were *disgrace*, and who had brought her in a slice of his sister's seed cake on her twentieth birthday, in March, wrapped in greaseproof paper, without a word, and put it on her desk, and gone back to his register.

She had not told him it was her birthday. She did not know how he knew.

Then she remembered that he had her date of birth in a green cloth volume on the shelf behind his head, and had probably checked it.

She had nearly laughed.

She had her hand on the watch, in her cardigan pocket. She noted that. She kept her hand on it a good deal still. It did not tick. It had not ticked for twenty-two months. She took it out every morning at seven and opened the lid and looked at the face, out of a habit that was nine years old, and it said eleven minutes past seven, every morning, as though it were waiting for something to happen at twelve minutes past.

At half past eleven, she put down her pen.

"Mr Pike."

"Mm."

"I'm going to take an hour this afternoon. If that's all right. I've got an appointment."

Mr Pike looked up over his spectacles.

"Where?"

"Level Nine."

He looked at her for a moment longer. Then he looked down at his register.

"Fill in a form," he said.

* * *

The Unspeakable was called Ashdown, and he owed Hermione a favour, and he did not say what for.

He met her at the lift on Level Nine at two o'clock, a tall stooping man of about fifty with ink on his fingers and a long sad face like a horse's, and took her along the black corridor to the plain black door without saying a word. Evelyn did not mind. She had been along that corridor before. She had been along it twice, in two different worlds, and she had not liked it either time, and she noted, as they walked, that she did not like it now, but that it was a different sort of not liking. It was the not liking of a person in a corridor. Not of a person in a war.

He took her through the round room with the doors and into the Time Room.

It was as she remembered. The light. The ticking, from everywhere at once, clocks on every surface, standing and hanging and stacked on shelves, all going, all slightly out with each other, so that the room was full of a soft continuous patter like rain on a roof. And the great bell jar at the end, taller than a man, full of a bright glittering current of air that went round and round, and inside it, for ever, a small bird hatched out of an egg and flew up and grew old and fell and went back into its egg and was hatched again.

She did not look at the bell jar for long.

"Sit down," said Ashdown.

She sat down at a long table under a window that looked out on nothing. He sat down opposite her and held out his hand.

She took the watch out of her pocket.

She did not give it to him at once. She held it for a moment in her palm, the small gold watch with the ivy leaves worn smooth on the lid, which her grandmother had given her in the east wing at Selwyn Hall when she was eleven, with two instructions. Wind it every morning. Never wind it backwards. She had done one of those every morning for seven years and the other once, and she had paid for that once in ways she was still counting.

She put it in his hand.

He looked at it for an hour.

She timed it. It was an hour and four minutes. He did not speak once. He opened it, and looked at the face, and at the two hands that said eleven minutes past seven, and at the third hand, the very fine one, so fine that most people never noticed it was there, which had never moved in all the years she had owned it. He closed it. He held it to his ear. He opened the back with a tool from his pocket like a very small silver key and looked inside for a long time with a glass screwed into one eye. He did a number of things with his wand that she had never seen anybody do and that she memorised, because she memorised everything, and that she would later look up and fail to find in any book.

Then he closed it, and put it down on the table between them, and took the glass out of his eye.

"It isn't broken," said Ashdown.

Evelyn looked at him.

"I'm sorry," she said. "I'm not sure I understand. It stopped. Twenty-two months ago. It hasn't moved since. The crown turns and nothing catches."

"Yes. I know. I've just spent an hour on it." He looked at the watch. "Nothing in it is broken. Not a spring, not a wheel, not a jewel. The mechanism is perfect. Better than perfect. I've never seen work like it, and I've been in this room for twenty-six years." He turned it a little on the table with one long finger. "And there's a great deal in it that isn't a mechanism. I'd guess you know that."

"Yes."

"I don't know what most of it is. I'll be honest with you. I don't think anybody alive does." He looked at her. "But I know what it isn't. It isn't broken. It isn't dead. It isn't stopped the way a watch stops when it runs down." He paused. "It's waiting."

The clocks ticked all round them, like rain.

"For what?" said Evelyn.

Ashdown looked at the watch for a long moment.

"I couldn't say," he said.

* * *

She took it back to the Office of Magical Registers and sat down at her small desk and put it beside Births, 1857, face up, with the lid open, and looked at it.

Mr Pike looked at it too, over his spectacles.

"Broken?" he said.

"No," said Evelyn. "Apparently not."

He considered this.

"Well," said Mr Pike, "that's something." And he went back to his register, and she went back to hers, and she found the nine hundred and fifth error in Births, 1857, at twenty to four, and corrected it.

* * *

Ron and Hermione had a flat in Islington, on the top floor of a tall thin house on Cloudesley Road, with a kitchen the size of a wardrobe and a window that looked out over a great many chimneys, and on Wednesday evenings Harry went there for supper and was not allowed to help.

"Sit," said Hermione. "Sit *down*. Last time you helped we were finding onion in the cutlery drawer for a week."

He sat.

Ron was at the stove, stirring something in a large pan with a wooden spoon, very seriously, with a tea towel over his shoulder. He had been learning to cook since the spring. He had learned from his mother, in the Burrow kitchen, on Sundays, and Mrs Weasley had cried every time, and Ron had pretended not to notice, and gone on learning. He was not very good. He was getting better.

"What is it?" said Harry.

"Stew."

"What kind?"

Ron looked into the pan.

"Brown," he said.

Harry looked at his face. From habit. He did not know what was in it, and he asked.

"What are you feeling?"

Ron did not even turn round. He had been asked that question perhaps four hundred times since the summer of the funerals, and he had stopped being surprised by it some time around Christmas.

"Worried about the stew," he said. "Bit tired. Chudley lost on Saturday, so there's that, there's always that." He stirred. "And pleased you're here. You can have that one. Don't get used to it."

"Thank you."

"Hermione's got something to tell you," said Ron. "She's been dying to all day. She's been walking up and down."

"I have not been walking up and down."

"You have. You wore a groove in the hall."

Hermione sat down opposite Harry at the little table under the window. She looked at him. He did not know what was in her face either, and he was about to ask, and she held up a hand.

"Don't," she said. "I'll tell you. I'm not sure what I'm feeling. Nervous, partly. On somebody else's behalf." She folded her hands. "Evelyn went to see Mr Ashdown. On Monday. In the Time Room. About the watch."

Harry looked at her.

"She didn't tell me," he said.

"No. I didn't think she had. She asked me not to say anything until she'd been." Hermione paused. "She told me afterwards. She came round on Monday night. She sat where you're sitting and drank a cup of tea and told me exactly what he said, word for word, and then she went home."

"What did he say?"

"That it isn't broken," said Hermione. "That nothing in it is broken at all. He said it's waiting."

"Waiting for what?"

"He didn't know." Hermione looked at her hands. "Neither did she. She said so. She said *I don't know* in exactly the voice she used at the lake. Do you remember? On the morning after."

Harry remembered.

He sat at the little table in the kitchen the size of a wardrobe, with the window full of chimneys and Ron stirring the brown stew, and thought about a lake at sunrise, and a small gold watch with ivy leaves on its lid, and a girl who had always known the time, saying *I don't know* twice, quite steadily, as though she were noting it down.

"Why didn't she tell me?" he said.

He did not mean to say it out loud. It came out.

Hermione looked at him for a long moment.

"I think," she said carefully, "that you should probably ask her that."

"I ask her things every week."

"You ask her how Births 1857 is going," said Ron, from the stove. "You ask her if she's read the new Ruth Rendell. You ask her if she wants another pot of tea. I've been there, mate. I came once, in February. You asked her if she wanted another pot of tea three times."

"She did want another pot of tea."

"That's not what I'm saying."

"What are you saying?"

Ron turned round from the stove. He had the wooden spoon in one hand and the tea towel over his shoulder, and his face was doing something Harry could not read, and Harry looked at it and waited, and Ron sighed.

"I'm saying," said Ron, "that you ask everybody in London how they're feeling. You ask Mum. You ask Neville. You asked the bloke who sold me my broom how he was feeling and he told you about his divorce for twenty minutes. You ask the woman in the Tesco. You've asked me four hundred times. And you've never once asked her." He pointed the spoon at Harry. "Not once. Not in a year and a half. Have you."

Harry did not say anything.

"Ask her, mate," said Ron.

"Ask her what?"

"You know what."

"I don't," said Harry. "That's the trouble. I don't know anything any more. I don't know what anybody's feeling. I don't know what *she's* feeling, and I never did, and now I don't know what you're feeling either, or Hermione, or the stew." He stopped. "I'm completely in the dark."

Ron looked at him.

"Yeah," he said, quite gently. "Welcome to the rest of us." He turned back to the stove. "It's all right in here. You get used to it. You just have to ask." He stirred the pan. "This is ready, I think. Or it's on fire. Hard to tell with brown."

* * *

They met on Thursdays.

They had met on Thursdays since the September of last year, at six o'clock, at a café on Lamb's Conduit Street called Ferrari's that had been there since 1952 and had never in that time changed its tablecloths, its menu, or, as far as Harry could tell, its waitress. Her name was Pina. She was about sixty, and Italian by way of Clerkenwell, and she called Harry *love* and Evelyn *Miss*, and she brought Evelyn a pot of tea for one and a toasted cheese sandwich cut into four triangles without being asked, every Thursday, because Evelyn had ordered a pot of tea for one and a toasted cheese sandwich cut into four triangles every Thursday for a year.

They sat at the same table. The one at the back, by the radiator, under a framed photograph of a racehorse called Ribot that nobody had dusted since the Coronation.

Harry could not remember whose idea it had been.

He thought it might have been hers. She had moved out of Grimmauld Place in the September, to a room over a bookbinder's in Rugby Street, and the house had been very quiet afterwards, and on the first Thursday he had found himself on Lamb's Conduit Street at ten to six for no reason he could have given, and she had been sitting at the table at the back by the radiator, reading *Tragedy at Law*, with a pot of tea in front of her and a second cup.

She had not said anything. She had poured him some.

They had been doing it ever since.

He came in at four minutes past six on Thursday the twenty-first of October, from Hogsmeade, with stone dust still in the creases of his knuckles, and Pina said *you're late, love*, and he said *I know, sorry*, and went to the back.

Evelyn was there.

She was reading. She did not look up. She had a pot of tea and a second cup and a toasted cheese sandwich cut into four, one triangle gone, and she was reading Josephine Tey, *The Franchise Affair*, which she had read eleven times, and she turned a page, and said, "Four minutes."

"There was a goat on the line at Hogsmeade."

"There isn't a line at Hogsmeade."

"There was a goat on the path to the Apparition point."

"That's more like it." She turned another page. "Sit down. The tea's stewed."

He sat down.

She poured him a cup of stewed tea. He drank it.

And he looked at her.

He did it the way he had looked at her for eight years. He had looked at her across a robe shop and a library table and a classroom on the fourth floor and a chamber under a school and a room above a bar in another world and a courtroom and a shack and a clearing in the Forest, and he had never once known what she felt. Not once. Not for a second. She had been the only person in the world he could not read, and he had looked at her and found nothing, every time, for eight years, and called it silence, and then called it rest.

He looked at her now and found nothing.

He looked round the café. At Pina behind the counter, wiping down the coffee machine with a cloth. At an old man in the window with the *Evening Standard*. At two young women at the next table, students, by their scarves, leaning in towards each other and laughing about something. At a man in a suit by the door, eating soup very fast, looking at his watch.

He found nothing in any of them.

That was not new now. He had stopped expecting it to change. He did not reach for people as often as he had, at the beginning, in the summer of the funerals. He still did it, sometimes, the way you still put your foot out for a step that has been taken away. But mostly he did not. He looked at people's faces, and listened to what they said, and asked, and they told him. Or they did not. And he had learned to live with the not.

He looked back at Evelyn.

She was reading.

And it came to him, sitting at the table at the back by the radiator in Ferrari's on Lamb's Conduit Street, with stone dust in his knuckles and a cup of stewed tea, that for the first time in his life she was not the exception.

She was not the one silence in a loud room. There was no loud room. There was no one he could read and one he could not. There was only this, everywhere, for everyone, the ordinary dark that everybody else had always lived in, where you looked at a face and did not know, and had to ask.

He had always been on the other side of it from her.

He was not, now. They were on the same side. They were in the same dark.

He had not thought of it like that before.

He thought of it now for some time. He thought about it while she finished her chapter and turned to the next one, and while Pina came and took the sandwich plate and said *all right, Miss?*, and Evelyn said *yes, thank you, Pina*, and while the two students at the next table got up and left, still laughing, with their scarves trailing.

Then he put his cup down.

"Selwyn," said Harry.

"Mm."

"Can I ask you something?"

"You usually do."

"What do you feel?"

She looked up.

"About what?" said Evelyn.

"About me."

* * *

She did not answer at once.

She put her book down. She did it quite carefully. She put a paper napkin in it to keep her place, and closed it, and laid it on the tablecloth beside her cup, square to the edge of the table. Then she looked at him across the table for a long moment, with her plain quiet face that had never once in eight years told him anything.

"You've never asked me that," she said.

"I know."

"You've asked everybody else. For a year and a half. You asked Mr Pike, in July, when you came to meet me, whether he was feeling all right, and he nearly had to sit down." She looked at him. "You've never asked me."

"No."

"Why not?"

He thought about it honestly, because she had asked honestly.

"Because I never could tell, with you," said Harry. "Not once. Not ever. So I never knew what I'd lost." He turned his cup on its saucer. "Everybody else, I knew what was gone. I could feel the place where it had been. With you there wasn't a place. It was just the same as it had always been." He looked at her. "And I think I was frightened of asking. Because I'd have to hear it. I couldn't just know."

Evelyn looked at him.

"That," she said, "is the most sensible thing you've said in eight years."

"Thank you."

"It isn't a compliment. The competition isn't very strong." She folded her hands on the tablecloth. "All right. You've asked. I'll tell you."

He waited.

"On an ordinary Thursday," said Evelyn, in exactly the voice in which she had once told Professor Binns that he had a date wrong by eleven years, "I should say I am about thirty per cent irritated with you. That varies. It goes up when you're late, and when you don't eat, and when you ask Pina how she's feeling and then actually listen to the answer for nine minutes while my tea goes cold. It went up to about sixty per cent in June of last year, over the *Prophet*. It's come down since." She considered. "I'd put it at twenty-eight tonight. You were four minutes late, but you had a goat."

"Twenty-eight."

"Roughly. I haven't got instruments." She did not smile. "Then there's fondness. That's harder to measure. It's been going up steadily since about 1992, with a dip in the spring of 1998 when you didn't know who I was on a step and I didn't much like you. It's recovered. I'd say it's at about… a great deal. I'd rather not give a figure. The figure is embarrassing."

Harry did not say anything.

"And then there's the rest," said Evelyn.

She stopped.

He watched her stop. He watched her face, which was perfectly still, and her hands, which were folded on the tablecloth, and which were holding each other, he noticed, rather hard.

"The rest is the part I haven't got a word for," she said. "Or I hadn't. I've been keeping notes on it since I was twelve. There are fourteen notebooks at Grimmauld Place and nine in my room in Rugby Street, and it's in all of them, on and off, and I never once called it anything. I just wrote down when it happened. *Potter came into the library. Potter laughed at something. Potter was in the hospital wing and I stayed until Pomfrey threw me out at four.* I wrote it down the way you'd write down the weather." She looked at her hands. "I didn't know what it was. I was trained not to know what things were. That was the whole point of me."

She was quiet for a moment.

"I opened my mind once," said Evelyn. "In a house in the dark. For you. You were there. You felt all of it. You know what was at the bottom."

"Yes," said Harry.

"You never said."

"No. It was yours. You hadn't said it. I'd only felt it."

"Well," said Evelyn. "I'm saying it now."

She looked up at him. And she said it, without percentages, without notebooks, quite plainly, the way she said everything, as though she were reporting a fact that had been in the register all along and had only now been checked.

"I love you, Potter," said Evelyn. "I have done for a very long time. I don't know exactly how long. I'm usually very good at that sort of thing, and I don't know." She did not look away. "That's what I feel. About you. Since you asked."

The radiator ticked.

At the counter, Pina dropped a spoon, and said something in Italian, and picked it up.

Harry sat at the table at the back of Ferrari's under the photograph of Ribot and looked at her.

He could not feel it.

He had felt it once. In the Shrieking Shack, through a door that had been shut, louder than Hagrid on a rock in the sea. He had felt it come through him like water through a broken wall, and he had known it the way he had known everything, from the inside, without a word. He could not feel it now. He could not feel anything from her. He had her word for it, and her face, and her hands holding each other on the tablecloth, and that was all.

He found that it was enough.

He found that it was a great deal more than enough. He had not known that. He had spent his whole life knowing what people felt before they said it, or instead of their saying it, or when they were saying something else entirely. He had never once in his life been *told*. Not like this. Not by somebody looking straight at him across a table, who did not know whether he would believe her, and said it anyway.

He did not know what to do with his face.

He did not try to do anything with it.

"Can I tell you mine?" he said.

"You'd better," said Evelyn. "I've just said all that out loud in Ferrari's. Pina's listening."

"I'm not," said Pina, from the counter.

Harry looked down at the tablecloth.

He had never done this. That was the thing. He had read a thousand people, ten thousand, a whole Great Hall at once, and he had never once had to say what he felt, because he had never once in his life been with anybody who did not already know, or who could not have found out by looking at him the way he looked at them. He did not know how to do it. He did not know where to start.

So he started where she had.

"I don't know how long either," said Harry. "That's the first thing. I've been trying to work it out. I've been trying to work it out for about a year. I think it might have been Madam Malkin's. I think it might have been a girl on the next stool telling me how many prisoners were in Azkaban without looking up from her book, and me not being able to tell what she felt, and not being able to stop thinking about it." He turned his cup. "But that's not right. That was just… I wanted to know. I wanted to know what you felt because I couldn't. That's not the same."

"No," said Evelyn.

"I don't know when it became the other thing. I couldn't feel it happen. I couldn't feel *you*, so I couldn't feel it change. I can feel things in me. I always could. But I was always so busy looking at everybody else that I never looked." He stopped. "I looked once. After the Pensieve. I sat on the floor in Leeds and read myself, the way I read other people. And it was there, under the anger and the rest of it. Holding it all up. I didn't look at it for long. I didn't know what it was."

He looked at her.

"It was you," said Harry. "It was the same as what was at the bottom of you. In the Shack. I didn't know it was the same thing until tonight. I didn't have anything to compare it with." He stopped again. "I love you. I think I always have. I don't know how long. I don't know when. I'm not very good at saying it. I've never said anything like this to anybody in my life, because I've never had to, and I'm saying it to the one person I can't…" He stopped. "I'm saying it to you. Because it's the only way I've got now. And I think it might be the only way that ever counted."

Evelyn looked at him for a long time.

Her face did something.

He did not know what it was. He would never know what it was, now, not from the inside. He looked at it, and it was her face, plain and quiet, the face people forgot. And it did something he had never seen it do, not in eight years, not once.

He did not know what it meant.

"Are you all right?" said Harry.

"No," said Evelyn. "I'll tell you in a minute."

She picked up her cup. It was empty. She looked into it, and put it down again.

"Finish your tea, Potter," she said.

* * *

It was raining when they came out.

It had been raining all day, on and off, the thin grey London rain that does not so much fall as hang about, and it was dark, and the streetlamps were on, and Lamb's Conduit Street was shining. They stood in the doorway of Ferrari's under the little striped awning, with the bell still going behind them on its spring, and looked out at it.

Neither of them had an umbrella.

"I'm going to get wet," said Evelyn.

"Yes."

"It's two streets."

"I know."

She did up the top button of her coat. She did it with some care. Then she did not go anywhere. She stood in the doorway of Ferrari's under the awning with the rain dripping off the edge of it in a line, and looked out at the street, and he stood beside her, and neither of them moved.

"Selwyn," said Harry.

"Yes."

"Can I ask you something else?"

She turned her head and looked at him.

"Yes," she said. "Before you ask. The answer's yes. I'd like it noted that I said so first."

He kissed her.

It was very brief. It was the doorway of a café on Lamb's Conduit Street, in the rain, with the bell going on its spring behind them and Pina very carefully not looking through the glass, and the awning dripping, and a man going past with a newspaper over his head who did not look at them at all. He did not know what she felt. He did not know, while it was happening, and he did not know afterwards, and he found that he did not need to, because she had told him, and because her hand had come up and taken hold of the front of his coat, quite firmly, by the lapel, the way you take hold of something you have decided not to let go of.

He stepped back.

She did not let go of the coat.

She looked at him. Her face was doing the thing again, the thing he had never seen it do, and he still did not know what it was, and he thought that he might spend a very long time finding out.

Then she let go of his lapel, and smoothed it down, flat, with two fingers, the way you would straighten a page.

"Eight years and eighty-two days," said Evelyn. "Since Madam Malkin's. I worked it out on the way here, in case it came up." She did the top button of her coat up again, though it was already done. "I'd like it noted, Potter. That's a very long time to wait for somebody to ask a question."
